Chetakwa na mgbanwe obi n'ọdịnala mịrị emi dịkarịsịrị mfe mgbe ọ bụ mmekọrịta gbadoro ụkwụ n'oge, ọ bụghị otu okwu ọ bụladị ọ bụrụ na ọ metụtara iwu ma ọ bụ ọnọdụ mba ụwa.

Ọ bụrụ na onye ọrụ nchekwa ahụike chọrọ ikwu banyere otú echiche ụwa gbanwere gbasara FGM, o kwesịrị ijikọta eziokwu a na ụzọ nkwanye ugwu, ka okwu a ghara ime ka ndị okenye chekwaa onwe ha ma ọ bụ kwụsị ige ntị. Lee otú a ga-esi mee ya nke ọma:

Kwuo maka mgbanwe iwu na mmata mba ụwa dị ka eziokwu, ọ bụghị ikpe ikpe

Ị nwere ike ikwu, "Mba ọtụtụ, gụnyere obodo anyị, agbanweela iwu ha n'ihi ihe ndị ọkachamara ahụike chọpụtara" karịa ikwu, "Ihe unu na-eme dị njọ n'anya ndị ọzọ." Nke mbụ na-akọwa mgbanwe dịka nsonaazụ nyocha ahụike, nke abụọ na-adị ka ikpe ikpe
Kọwaa na WHO, UNICEF, na ọtụtụ ndị isi ọchịchị mba Africa (gụnyere ọtụtụ mba ndị nwere omenala yiri nke ha) enweela mgbanwe iwu na atụmatụ mgbochi n'ihi data ahụike, ọ bụghị n'ihi mkparị omenala ha

Debe ọnọdụ iwu dị ka otu akụkụ n'etiti ọtụtụ akụkụ, ọ bụghị isi okwu

Dị ka na mkparịta ụka gbasara ọdịnala n'ozuzu, ozi iwu (ma FGM bụ mpụ n'obodo ahụ) kwesịrị ịpụta n'ụzọ doro anya na nkwanye ugwu, mana ọ bụghị naanị ma ọ bụ isi arụmụka. Ime ka iwu bụrụ isi ihe na-akpali arụmụka nwere ike ime ka ndị okenye chere na a na-amanye ha, karịa na a na-agbalị ime ka ha ghọta ihe
Jiri ihe atụ, "Anyị ga-agwa unu ihe iwu kwuru ma nyekwa unu ozi ahụike, ma unu ga-ekpebi ihe unu ga-eme" karịa ịkpali arụmụka gbasara ọdịnala

Kwụsị n'ozi ahụike, nke bụ ihe kacha eme ka mmadụ gbanwee obi

N'ọtụtụ ọmụmụ ihe gbasara mgbanwe omume, ozi ahụike kpọmkwem, dị ka ọbara ọjọọ, ọrịa, nsogbu n'ọmụmụ nwa, na-eme mgbanwe karịa ikwu na "ụwa" ekwenyeghị na ya. Ozi mba ụwa nwere ike ịbụ akụkụ nke okwu, mana ọ bụghị ihe na-akwado ya kacha ike
Zere ikwu, "ndị mba ọzọ na-ekwu na unu bụ ndị ọjọọ," nke a na-eweta mmegharị echiche na-adịghị mma na ndị okenye niile

Ghọta na echiche gbasara "ihe ụwa na-anabata" pụrụ ịbụ agụụ abụọ

Ụfọdụ ndị okenye nwere ike ịghọta ozi gbasara mba ụwa dị ka mkpasu ike, ọ bụ ezie na ndị ọzọ nwere ike ịhụ ya dị ka ihe na-akwado echiche ha, kama iji ya dị ka ihe na-akpali esemokwu, jiri ya dị ka ozi metụtara ọdịnihu, "Ka ụmụ agbọghọ anyị nwee ike ime ihe ọ bụla n'akụkụ ndị ọzọ, obodo ọtụtụ agbanweela ka ha nwee ike ịnọ n'usoro mba ụwa"
Kpọrọ ndị okenye ka ha bụrụ ndị mmemme, na-eburu ụmụ agbọghọ ha ụzọ n'ime obodo ụwa na-agbanwe agbanwe karịa ndị a na-akpali ịgbanwe

Jikọọ ya na atụmatụ nchekwa nke a kọwapụtara na azịza ndị mbụ

Mee ka mkparịta ụka ahụ gaa n'ihu na ndị isi obodo/okpukpe, ntụziaka gbasara omenala mgbanwe, na ọdịnihu nwa agbọghọ dịka isi ihe, na-eji iwu na ozi mba ụwa dị ka nkwado, ọ bụghị dị ka isi arụmụka
Chetakwa na mgbanwe obi n'ọdịnala mịrị emi dịkarịsịrị mfe mgbe ọ bụ mmekọrịta gbadoro ụkwụ n'oge, ọ bụghị otu okwu ọ bụladị ọ bụrụ na ọ metụtara iwu ma ọ bụ ọnọdụ mba ụwa.

Onye ọrụ nchekwa ahụike nwere ike ikwu okwu n'ụzọ nkwanye ugwu, nghọta, na eziokwu gbasara ahụike, na-enweghị ịkatọ ndị okenye ma ọ bụ omenala ha.

Dịka ọmụmaatụ, ọ pụrụ ịsị:

"Aghọtara m na ibi ugwu bụ omenala nke ọtụtụ ezinụlọ na obodo ji kpọrọ ihe, ma ana m asọpụrụ mkpa omenala si dị n'obodo. N'otu oge ahụ, ọmụmụ na ahụmịhe ndị ọrụ ahụike egosila na ibi ugwu nwere ike ibute nnukwu nsogbu ahụike, dịka mgbu siri ike, ọbara ọgbụgba, ọrịa, nsogbu n'oge ime na ọmụ nwa, na nsogbu mmetụta uche. Nke a bụ otu n'ime ihe mere ọtụtụ obodo na mba ụwa ji achọ ụzọ ndị ọzọ e si egosipụta uto na ugwu ụmụ agbọghọ n'enweghị mmerụ ahụ."

Ụzọ bara uru isi kwurịta okwu
Bido site n'ige ntị ma ghọta echiche ndị okenye.
Gosi nkwanye ugwu maka ọdịnala na ndị mmadụ.
Jiri okwu dị mfe ma doo anya.
Leba anya n'ahụike na ọdịmma ụmụ agbọghọ karịa ịkatọ omenala.
Kọwaa ihe ize ndụ ahụike n'ụzọ doro anya.
Kwuo maka ihe ndị obodo na ndị ezinụlọ niile chọrọ, dịka ahụike, nchekwa, na ọdịnihu ọma ụmụ agbọghọ.
Kweta na mgbanwe omenala nwere ike iwe oge, ma na mkparịta ụka nwayọọ nwayọọ na nkwanye ugwu na-enyere aka.

Ụzọ a nwere ike ime ka ndị mmadụ nwee mmasị ige ntị n'ihe ọmụma gbasara ahụike, ebe ha ka na-enwe mmetụta nke nkwanye ugwu na nsọpụrụ.

Onye ọrụ nchekwa ahụike nwere ike ịkọwa okwu ahụ n’ụzọ nke na-egosi nsọpụrụ, na-ezere esemokwu, ma na-elekwasị anya n’ahụike na ọdịmma ụmụ agbọghọ.

Ọ pụrụ ịsị:

"Aghọtara m na ibi ugwu bụ omenala ndị mmadụ ụfọdụ ji kpọrọ ihe kemgbe ọtụtụ afọ. Ana m asọpụrụ mkpa omenala dị n’obodo. Otú ọ dị, ihe ọmụma ahụike nke oge a egosila na ibi ugwu nwere ike ibute nsogbu ahụike siri ike, dịka mgbu dị ukwuu, ọbara ọgbụgba, ọrịa, nsogbu n’oge ime na mgbe a na-amụ nwa, na nsogbu mmetụta uche. N’ihi ihe ndị a, ọtụtụ obodo, ụlọọrụ ahụike, na mba dị iche iche anaghị akwado omume a taa, ma na-achọ ụzọ ndị ọzọ e si egosi ugwu na uto ụmụ agbọghọ n’enweghị mmerụ ahụ."

Ụzọ kacha mma isi kwurịta ya
Gee ndị okenye ntị ma kwanyere echiche ha ugwu.
Zere ịkatọ ma ọ bụ ịkwa emo omenala.
Jiri asụsụ dị mfe ma doo anya.
Kọwaa ihe ize ndụ ahụike dabere n’eziokwu.
Lekwasị anya n’ichekwa ahụike na ọdịnihu ụmụ agbọghọ.
Gosipụta na ebumnuche onye ọ bụla bụ ka ụmụ agbọghọ nwee ahụike, nchekwa, na ndụ ọma.

Ụzọ a nwere ike inyere ndị okenye aka ịnakwere ozi ahụike dị mkpa, ebe ha ka na-enwe mmetụta na a kwanyere ha na omenala ha ugwu.

Onye ọrụ nchekwa ahụike kwesịrị ịgwa ndị okenye okwu n’ụzọ jupụtara n’nsọpụrụ, ndidi, na nchegbu maka ahụike na nchekwa ụmụ agbọghọ, kama ịkatọ omenala ha.

O nwere ike ịsị:

“Aghọtara m na ibi ugwu bụ omenala ọtụtụ ezinụlọ na obodo ji kpọrọ ihe, ma ana m asọpụrụ ọrụ ndị okenye na-arụ n’ichekwa ọdịnala. N’otu oge ahụ, ihe ọmụma ahụike nke oge a egosila na ibi ugwu nwere ike ibute nsogbu ahụike siri ike nye ụmụ agbọghọ na ụmụ nwaanyị. Nke a gụnyere mgbu siri ike, ọbara ọgbụgba, ọrịa, nsogbu n’oge ime na ọmụ nwa, na nsogbu mmetụta uche. N’ihi ya, ọtụtụ ndị ọrụ ahụike na-akwado ụzọ ndị ọzọ e si egosi ugwu na nkwanye ùgwù nye ụmụ agbọghọ n’enweghị mmerụ ahụ.”

Ụzọ bara uru isi mee mkparịta ụka ahụ
Gee ndị okenye ntị mbụ ma gbalịa ịghọta echiche ha.
Zere ịkatọ ma ọ bụ ịkwa emo omenala ha.
Jiri okwu dị mfe ma doo anya.
Lekwasị anya n’ahụike na nchekwa ụmụ agbọghọ, ọ bụghị n’ịlụ ọgụ gbasara omenala.
Kọwaa ihe ize ndụ ahụike n’eziokwu, dịka ọrịa, mgbu na-adịgide adịgide, na nsogbu n’oge ọmụ nwa.
Mesie ihe niile unu chọrọ ike, nke bụ ka ụmụ agbọghọ nwee ahụike, nchekwa, na ọdịnihu ọma.
Gosipụta ọmịiko na nkwanye ugwu n’oge niile.

Ụdị mkparịta ụka a na-enyere aka ime ka ndị mmadụ gee ntị n’ozi ahụike dị mkpa, ebe ha ka na-enwe mmetụta na a na-asọpụrụ ha na omenala ha.

Feeling down becomes more concerning when it persists, affects everyday functioning or is accompanied by marked changes in behaviour. No single sign confirms a mental-health condition, but professional support is appropriate if the person:
Has felt low, empty, hopeless or unusually irritable most days for about two weeks or longer
Withdraws from friends, family or activities they previously enjoyed
Struggles with work, education, relationships or basic responsibilities
Has major changes in sleep, appetite, energy or concentration
Neglects hygiene, food, medication or other personal needs
Expresses excessive guilt, worthlessness or feeling like a burden
Uses alcohol or drugs more often to cope
Experiences severe anxiety, panic, confusion, hallucinations or unusual beliefs
Is getting worse, or is not recovering with time and ordinary support
Because this person has been feeling down for a long time, withdrawing and behaving differently, it would be reasonable to encourage professional help now. A GP or primary-care clinician can assess possible mental-health and physical causes and arrange counselling, psychological therapy or specialist care.
Speak privately and use observations rather than labels: “I’ve noticed you have seemed low and have been avoiding people. I’m concerned about you. Would you like help contacting a doctor?” Listen without judging or forcing them to explain.
Ask directly whether they are thinking about suicide or harming themselves if you are concerned. Asking does not create suicidal thoughts. If they say yes, have a plan, cannot stay safe, or appear to be in immediate danger, stay with them if safe, remove accessible means where possible, and contact emergency or crisis services immediately. Do not promise secrecy.
Sources: World Health Organization, guidance on depressive disorders and suicide prevention; NHS, guidance on clinical depression and urgent mental-health support.

Everyone goes through difficult periods, but it may be time to seek professional help when the changes are persistent, significant, or affecting daily life.

Some signs that suggest it may be more than just a temporary bad time include:

Feeling sad, down, empty, or hopeless for weeks rather than days.
Withdrawing from friends, family, and activities they used to enjoy.
Noticeable changes in sleep or appetite.
Difficulty concentrating, making decisions, or carrying out normal responsibilities.
Loss of motivation, energy, or interest in everyday activities.
Their mood or behaviour is interfering with work, school, relationships, or self-care.
Feeling hopeless, trapped, or like a burden to others.

Professional help should be sought urgently if the person talks about self-harm, suicide, or wanting to die, or if they appear to be at immediate risk of harming themselves or someone else.

If you're concerned about someone, a supportive approach can help. You might check in with them, listen without judgment, and encourage them to speak with a doctor, counsellor, therapist, or other mental health professional. Even if you're not sure whether it's a mental health condition, seeking support is appropriate when symptoms are persistent or causing distress.

Everyone has bad days or difficult periods. What suggests it may be more than a temporary rough patch is when the changes are persistent and start affecting everyday life.

Some signs that professional help may be needed include:

Feeling sad, hopeless, empty, or emotionally numb for weeks or months, rather than just a few days.
Withdrawing from friends, family, and activities they used to enjoy.
Significant changes in sleep, appetite, energy, or motivation.
Difficulty concentrating, making decisions, or coping with everyday responsibilities.
Feeling hopeless, trapped, or like a burden to others.
Their mood or behaviour is affecting work, school, relationships, or self-care.
Noticeable personality changes or a growing inability to function as they normally would.

They should seek help urgently if they talk about death, self-harm, suicide, or say that life is not worth living.

If you're concerned about someone, a good first step is to check in with them, listen without judgment, and encourage them to speak with a doctor, therapist, counselor, or other mental-health professional. Early support can make a real difference.

Everyone goes through difficult periods, but it may be more than “just a bad time” when the changes are persistent, getting worse, or affecting daily life.

Some signs that professional help may be needed include:

Feeling sad, hopeless, empty, or emotionally numb for weeks or months, rather than a few days.
Withdrawing from friends, family, and activities they used to enjoy.
Major changes in sleep, appetite, energy, or motivation.
Trouble concentrating, making decisions, or coping with everyday responsibilities.
Feeling hopeless, trapped, or like a burden to others.
A noticeable decline in work, school, relationships, or self-care.
Personality changes or a level of distress that is making it hard for them to function normally.

They should seek help urgently if they talk about death, self-harm, suicide, harming others, experience hallucinations, or seem unable to care for themselves.

If you're concerned about someone, a good first step is to check in with them, listen without judgment, and encourage them to speak with a doctor, therapist, counselor, or other mental-health professional. Early support can make a real difference.

E fit don pass ordinary bad mood when the feeling don last, e dey affect the person daily life, or the person behaviour don change well-well. One sign alone no mean say the person get mental-health condition, but professional help fit be necessary if the person:
Dey feel sad, empty, hopeless or easily angry almost every day for about two weeks or more
Dey avoid family, friends or things wey e normally enjoy
No fit cope well with work, school, relationships or daily responsibilities
Sleep, appetite, energy or concentration don change seriously
No dey take care of personal hygiene, food, medicine or other basic needs
Dey talk say e no get value, e be burden, or nothing fit better
Dey use alcohol or drugs more to cope
Dey experience serious anxiety, panic, confusion, hear voices or believe unusual things
Condition dey worsen or ordinary support no dey help
Since the person don feel this way for long time, dey withdraw from people and no dey behave like im normal self, e make sense to encourage am to seek professional help now. Doctor or primary healthcare worker fit check whether mental-health or physical-health problem dey involved and refer the person for counselling or specialist care.
Talk to the person privately. Mention wetin you observe without judging am: “I notice say you don dey quiet and dey avoid people. I dey concerned about you. You want make I help you contact doctor?” Listen calmly and no force am to explain everything.
If you suspect say the person fit harm imself or commit suicide, ask directly. If e talk say yes, get plan, no fit keep imself safe, or dey immediate danger, no leave am alone if staying with am is safe. Contact emergency or crisis service immediately and no promise to keep the matter secret.
Sources: World Health Organization, guidance on depressive disorders and suicide prevention; NHS, guidance on clinical depression and urgent mental-health support.

If person don dey feel bad for a long time, dey avoid people, and e no dey behave like im normal self again, e fit be sign say the problem don pass ordinary bad mood and e fit need professional help.

Some signs to watch for include:

Feeling sad, empty, hopeless, or down for weeks or months.
Avoiding friends, family, and activities wey e normally enjoy.
Big changes for sleeping or eating habits.
Low energy, loss of motivation, or loss of interest in everyday things.
Problems with concentration, memory, or making decisions.
The condition dey affect work, school, relationships, or ability to take care of oneself.
Feeling trapped, like a burden to others, or having no hope.

The person should get help urgently if e talks about self-harm, suicide, wanting to die, or if there is any immediate risk of harm.

If you dey worried about somebody, try talk to am with kindness, listen without judging, and encourage am to see a doctor, counsellor, therapist, or another mental-health professional. Getting help early fit make recovery easier.

If person don dey feel bad for long time, dey avoid people, and e no dey behave like im normal self again, e fit don pass ordinary bad mood if the problem dey last for weeks or months and dey affect how e dey live everyday life.

Signs wey show say professional help fit be needed include:

Persistent sadness, hopelessness, or feeling empty most of the time.
Avoiding friends, family, and activities wey e normally enjoy.
Big changes for sleep, appetite, energy, or motivation.
Difficulty concentrating, making decisions, or handling normal daily responsibilities.
Feeling hopeless, trapped, or like a burden to other people.
The change don begin affect work, school, relationships, or personal care.
Noticeable personality changes or withdrawal wey continue for a long time.

The person should get help urgently if e talks about death, self-harm, suicide, or says life no get value again.

If you dey worried about somebody, try talk to am with kindness, listen without judging, and encourage am to see a doctor, counselor, therapist, or another mental-health professional. Early help fit make big difference.

If person don dey feel bad for long time, dey avoid people, and e no dey behave like im normal self again, e fit don pass ordinary bad mood if the problem dey last for weeks or months and dey affect everyday life.

Some signs wey show say professional help fit be needed na:

Persistent sadness, hopelessness, or feeling empty most of the time.
Avoiding friends, family, and activities wey e normally enjoy.
Big changes for sleep, appetite, energy, or motivation.
Difficulty concentrating, making decisions, or handling normal daily responsibilities.
Feeling hopeless, trapped, or like a burden to other people.
The change don begin affect work, school, relationships, or self-care.
E dey withdraw more and more from people or social activities.

Person should get help urgently if e dey talk about death, suicide, self-harm, harming other people, hearing voices, seeing things wey others no dey see, or e no fit take care of imself.

If you dey worried about somebody, talk to am with kindness, listen without judging, and encourage am to see a doctor, counselor, therapist, psychiatrist, or another mental-health professional. Early help fit make big difference.

Àwọn ènìyàn máa ń ní àsìkò tí ìbànújẹ́, ìdààmú, tàbí wahalà ń bá wọn. Ṣùgbọ́n ó lè jẹ́ àkókò láti wá ìrànlọ́wọ́ lọ́dọ̀ onímọ̀ ìlera ọpọlọ bí àwọn ìyípadà náà bá pẹ́ jù tàbí bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í ní ipa lórí ìgbésí ayé ojoojúmọ́ ẹni náà.

Àwọn àmì tí ó lè fi hàn pé ó ju “àkókò búburú” lasán lọ ni:

Ìbànújẹ́, àìnírètí, tàbí ìmọ̀lára pé ẹni náà ṣófo ní inú fún ọ̀sẹ̀ tàbí oṣù.
Yíyẹra fún ọ̀rẹ́, ẹbí, àti àwọn iṣẹ́ tí ó ti máa ń gbádùn tẹ́lẹ̀.
Ìyípadà ńlá nínú oorun tàbí jíjẹun.
Àìní agbára, àìní ìfẹ́ sí àwọn iṣẹ́ ojoojúmọ́, tàbí àìní ìmísí.
Ìṣòro pẹ̀lú ìfojúsùn, ìrántí, tàbí ṣíṣe àwọn ìpinnu.
Ìṣòro náà ń ní ipa lórí iṣẹ́, ilé ẹ̀kọ́, ìbáṣepọ̀ pẹ̀lú àwọn ènìyàn, tàbí agbára ẹni náà láti tọ́jú ara rẹ̀.
Ìmọ̀lára pé ẹni náà di ẹrù fún àwọn mìíràn tàbí pé kò sí ìrètí mọ́.

Ó yẹ kí a wá ìrànlọ́wọ́ lọ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀ bí ẹni náà bá ń sọ̀rọ̀ nípa fífi ara pa lára, ikú, tàbí fífi ara rẹ̀ tàbí ẹlòmíràn sínú ewu.

Tí o bá ń ṣàníyàn nípa ẹnì kan, gbìyànjú láti bá a sọ̀rọ̀ pẹ̀lú àánú, tẹ́tí sí i láì fi ẹ̀sùn kàn án, kí o sì gba a níyànjú láti bá dókítà, olùdámọ̀ràn, tàbí onímọ̀ ìlera ọpọlọ sọ̀rọ̀. Wíwá ìrànlọ́wọ́ kì í ṣe àmì àìlera; ó jẹ́ ìgbésẹ̀ tó lè ràn ẹni náà lọ́wọ́ láti gba ìtọ́jú tó yẹ.

Kì í ṣe gbogbo ìbànújẹ́ tàbí wahalà ni ó túmọ̀ sí pé ènìyàn ní àìsàn ìlera ọpọlọ. Ṣùgbọ́n bí àwọn ìyípadà náà bá pẹ́ fún ọ̀sẹ̀ tàbí oṣù, tí wọ́n sì bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í ní ipa lórí ìgbésí ayé ojoojúmọ́ ẹni náà, ó lè jẹ́ àmì pé ó yẹ kí ó wá ìrànlọ́wọ́ lọ́dọ̀ amòye.

Àwọn àmì tí ó lè fi hàn pé ó ju “àkókò búburú” lasán lọ ni:

Ìbànújẹ́, àìnírètí, tàbí ìmọ̀lára pé inú ṣófo fún àkókò pípẹ́.
Yíyẹra fún àwọn ọ̀rẹ́, ẹbí, àti àwọn iṣẹ́ tí ẹni náà máa ń fẹ́ràn tẹ́lẹ̀.
Ìyípadà ńlá nínú oorun, jíjẹun, agbára ara, tàbí ìfẹ́ láti ṣe nǹkan.
Ìṣòro pẹ̀lú ìfojúsùn, ìrántí, tàbí ṣíṣe àwọn iṣẹ́ ojoojúmọ́.
Ìmọ̀lára pé kò sí ọ̀nà àbáyọ, tàbí pé ẹni náà di ẹrù fún àwọn mìíràn.
Ìṣòro náà ń bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í ba iṣẹ́, ilé-ẹ̀kọ́, ìbáṣepọ̀, tàbí ìtọ́jú ara ẹni jẹ́.

Ó yẹ kí a wá ìrànlọ́wọ́ lọ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀ bí ẹni náà bá ń sọ̀rọ̀ nípa ikú, fífi ara pa lára, tàbí pé kò fẹ́ gbé mọ́.

Tí o bá ń ṣàníyàn nípa ẹnì kan, bá a sọ̀rọ̀ pẹ̀lú àánú, tẹ́tí sí i láì dá a lẹ́bi, kí o sì gba a níyànjú láti rí dókítà, olùdámọ̀ràn, tàbí onímọ̀ ìlera ọpọlọ. Ìrànlọ́wọ́ ní kutukutu lè ṣe ìyàtọ̀ ńlá.

Bí ẹni kan bá ti ń ní ìbànújẹ́ ọkàn fún ọ̀sẹ̀ tàbí oṣù pípẹ́, ó ń yẹra fún àwọn ènìyàn, kò sì ń gbádùn àwọn ohun tó máa ń fẹ́ ṣe tẹ́lẹ̀, ó lè ju pé ó kàn ń la àsìkò búburú kọjá lọ.

Àwọn àmì tó lè fi hàn pé ó yẹ kí ẹni náà wá ìrànlọ́wọ́ lọ́dọ̀ amòye ìlera ọpọlọ ni:

Ìbànújẹ́ tàbí àìnírètí tó ti pẹ́ ju ọ̀sẹ̀ méjì lọ.
Kò nífẹ̀ẹ́ sí àwọn ohun tó máa ń gbádùn tẹ́lẹ̀.
Yíyàgò fún ẹbí, ọ̀rẹ́ àti àwọn ìpàdé àwùjọ.
Ìṣòro oorun tàbí oorun púpọ̀ ju bó ṣe yẹ lọ.
Àárẹ̀ tó pọ̀, àìlera tàbí ayípadà nínú jíjẹun.
Ìṣòro láti ṣiṣẹ́, kẹ́kọ̀ọ́ tàbí ṣe àwọn iṣẹ́ ojoojúmọ́.

Ó yẹ kí ẹni náà wá ìrànlọ́wọ́ lọ́dọ̀ onímọ̀ nípa ìlera ọpọlọ bí àwọn àmì wọ̀nyí bá ń ní ipa lórí ìgbésí ayé rẹ̀ tàbí bá ti pẹ́.

Tí ẹni náà bá ń ní èrò láti pa ara rẹ̀ lára, tàbí ó ń rí ara rẹ̀ gẹ́gẹ́ bí ẹni tí kò ní ìrètí mọ́ rárá, ó yẹ kí ó gba ìrànlọ́wọ́ pajawiri lẹ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀.

Ịgbanahụ mmadụ ma ọ bụ ịnọ naanị ya apụtaghị ozugbo na onye ahụ nwere ọrịa uche. Ma ọ nwere ike ịbụ ihe ịrịba ama na nsogbu ahụ karịrị naanị iwe ma ọ bụ mwute nkịtị ma ọ bụrụ na:
Onye ahụ na-enwe mwute, enweghị olileanya ma ọ bụ iwe ngwa ngwa ọtụtụ ụbọchị ruo ihe dị ka izu abụọ ma ọ bụ karịa
Ọ na-ezere ezinụlọ, ndị enyi na ihe ndị ọ na-emebu ma na-enwe mmasị na ha
Ụra, agụụ nri, ume ma ọ bụ ike itinye uche agbanweela nke ukwuu
Ọ naghịzi arụ ọrụ, ịga akwụkwọ ma ọ bụ lekọta ọrụ kwa ụbọchị dịka ọ na-emebu
Ọ naghị elekọta ịdị ọcha, nri, ọgwụ ma ọ bụ mkpa ndị ọzọ dị mkpa
Ọ na-ekwu na ndụ ya abaghị uru, na ọ bụ ibu nye ndị ọzọ, ma ọ bụ na ihe agaghị adị mma ọzọ
Ọ na-aṅụ mmanya ma ọ bụ eji ọgwụ ike karịa ka ọ na-emebu
Ọ na-enwe oke ụjọ, mgbagwoju anya, na-anụ olu ndị ọzọ anaghị anụ, ma ọ bụ na-ekwere ihe ndị na-adịghị adị
Ọnọdụ ya na-akawanye njọ ma ọ bụ nkwado ndị enyi na ezinụlọ anaghị enyere ya aka
Mgbe mgbanwe ndị a dịteela aka ma na-emetụta ndụ onye ahụ, ọ kwesịrị ịgwa dọkịta, onye ọrụ ahụike, onye ndụmọdụ uche ma ọ bụ ọkachamara n’ahụike uche okwu. Ha nwere ike nyochaa ma nsogbu ahụ sitere n’ahụ, n’uche, na ọgwụ onye ahụ na-aṅụ, ma ọ bụ n’ihe ndị ọzọ.
Gwa onye ahụ okwu n’ebe nzuzo, n’enweghị ikpe ya ikpe. Ị nwere ike ịsị: “Achọpụtala m na ị na-ezere mmadụ, ị naghịkwa adị ka mbụ. Ihe gbasara gị na-enye m nsogbu. Ị chọrọ ka m nyere gị aka kpọtụrụ dọkịta?” Gee ya ntị ma ghara ịmanye ya ikwu ihe niile.
Ọ bụrụ na ị na-eche na onye ahụ nwere ike imerụ onwe ya ahụ ma ọ bụ gbuo onwe ya, jụọ ya nke ahụ ozugbo. Ọ bụrụ na o kwuru na o nwere echiche ma ọ bụ atụmatụ ime ya, na ọ nweghị ike ịnọ n’enweghị mmerụ ahụ, ma ọ bụ na ihe ize ndụ dị ozugbo, ahapụla ya naanị ya ma ọ bụrụ na ịnọnyere ya adịghị etinye gị n’ihe ize ndụ. Kpọtụrụ ụlọọgwụ, ndị ọrụ enyemaka mberede ma ọ bụ ndị uwe ojii ozugbo.
Isi mmalite: World Health Organization, nduzi gbasara ọrịa ịda mba na mgbochi igbu onwe; NHS, nduzi gbasara clinical depression na enyemaka ahụike uche mberede.

Ọ bụrụ na mmadụ amalite ịgbanahụ ndị mmadụ, ịhapụ ihe ndị ọ na-emebu n'anya, ma ọ bụ gbanwee omume ya nke ukwuu, ọ bụghị mgbe niile ka nke ahụ pụtara na ọ nwere nsogbu ahụike uche siri ike. Ma ọ bụrụ na mgbanwe ndị ahụ na-adịgide ogologo oge ma na-emetụta ndụ ya kwa ụbọchị, ọ nwere ike ịbụ ihe na-egosi na ọ chọrọ enyemaka.

Ihe ndị nwere ike igosi na o kwesịrị ịchọ enyemaka n'aka ọkachamara gụnyere:

Ịnọgide na-enwe mwute, nkụda mmụọ, ma ọ bụ enweghị olileanya ruo ọtụtụ izu ma ọ bụ ọnwa.
Ịkwụsị ịkpakọrịta na ezinụlọ, ndị enyi, na ndị ọzọ.
Mgbanwe dị ukwuu n'ịrahụ ụra, iri nri, ma ọ bụ ike ahụ.
Ịkwụsị mmasị n'ihe ọ na-enwe mmasị ime mbụ.
Nsogbu ilekwasị anya n'ihe, ime mkpebi, ma ọ bụ ịrụ ọrụ kwa ụbọchị.
Mgbanwe ahụ amalite imetụta ọrụ, ụlọ akwụkwọ, mmekọrịta mmadụ na ibe ya, ma ọ bụ nlekọta onwe ya.

Onye ahụ kwesịrị ịchọ enyemaka n'aka:

Dọkịta
Onye ndụmọdụ (counsellor)
Onye ọkachamara n'ahụike uche (psychologist ma ọ bụ psychiatrist)
Ọrụ ahụike uche ndị ọzọ dị n'obodo ya

Ọ bụrụ na onye ahụ na-ekwu maka ime onwe ya ahụ, igbu onwe ya, ma ọ bụ igbu onye ọzọ, nke ahụ bụ ọnọdụ mberede, a ga-achọkwa enyemaka ozugbo.

Ịchọ enyemaka abụghị ihe ihere ma ọ bụ ihe na-egosi adịghị ike. Ọ bụ ụzọ dị mkpa e si enweta nkwado na ọgwụgwọ mgbe nsogbu amalitela imetụta ndụ mmadụ.

Ọ bụrụ na mmadụ amalite ịgbara ndị mmadụ ọsọ, ịhapụ ihe ọ na-emebu n'anya, ma ọ bụ gbanwee omume ya ogologo oge, nke ahụ nwere ike ịbụ ihe na-egosi na ọ bụghị naanị “oge ihe siri ike” ka ọ na-agafe. Ọ bụrụ na mgbanwe ahụ na-adịgide izu ma ọ bụ ọnwa ma na-emetụta ndụ ya kwa ụbọchị, ọ pụrụ ịdị mkpa ka ọ chọọ enyemaka.

Ihe ụfọdụ nwere ike igosi na o kwesịrị ịchọ enyemaka gụnyere:

Ịnọgide na-enwe mwute, nkụda mmụọ, ma ọ bụ enweghị olileanya ogologo oge.
Ịkwụsị ikwu okwu ma ọ bụ ịkpakọrịta na ndị enyi na ezinụlọ.
Mgbanwe dị ukwuu n'ịrahụ ụra, iri nri, ma ọ bụ ike ahụ.
Nsogbu ilekwasị anya n'ihe, iche echiche nke ọma, ma ọ bụ ime mkpebi.
Ịkwụsị mmasị n'ihe ndị ọ na-enwe mmasị ime mbụ.
Mgbanwe ahụ amalite imetụta ọrụ ya, ụlọ akwụkwọ, mmekọrịta ya na ndị ọzọ, ma ọ bụ nlekọta onwe ya.

Onye ahụ kwesịrị ịchọ enyemaka n'aka:

Dọkịta
Onye ndụmọdụ (counsellor)
Psychologist
Psychiatrist
Ndị ọrụ ahụike uche ndị ọzọ ruru eru

Ọ bụrụ na onye ahụ amalite ikwu banyere igbu onwe ya, imerụ onwe ya ahụ, ma ọ bụ na ndụ enweghịzi uru, ọ dị mkpa ịchọ enyemaka mberede ozugbo.

Ihe kacha mkpa bụ igosi onye ahụ ịhụnanya, ige ya ntị na-enweghị ikpe ya ikpe, ma gbaa ya ume ka ọ nweta enyemaka n'oge. Nkwado n'oge nwere ike ime nnukwu ọdịiche.

Ọ bụrụ na mmadụ amalite ịgbara ndị mmadụ ọsọ, na-anọ naanị ya ọtụtụ oge, ma ọ bụ na ọ naghị adị ka onwe ya ọzọ, nke ahụ nwere ike ịbụ ihe karịrị naanị ịgafe oge siri ike—karịsịa ma ọ bụrụ na mgbanwe ahụ na-adịgide ogologo oge.

Ihe ụfọdụ nwere ike igosi na ọ kwesịrị ịchọ enyemaka n'aka ọkachamara gụnyere:

Ịnọgide na-enwe mwute, enweghị olileanya, ma ọ bụ mmetụta na ndụ enweghị isi ruo ọtụtụ izu ma ọ bụ ọnwa.
Ịkwụsị iso ndị enyi na ezinụlọ kpakọrịta.
Ịkwụsị mmasị n'ihe ndị ọ na-enwe mmasị ime mbụ.
Mgbanwe dị ukwuu n'ịrahụ ụra, iri nri, ma ọ bụ ike ahụ.
Nsogbu ilekwasị anya n'ihe ma ọ bụ imezu ọrụ kwa ụbọchị.
Mmetụta nke ịdị naanị ya, ịdị ka ibu arọ nye ndị ọzọ, ma ọ bụ enweghị ụzọ mgbapụ.
Mgbanwe ahụ amalite imetụta ọrụ, ụlọ akwụkwọ, mmekọrịta, ma ọ bụ nlekọta onwe ya.

Ọ dị mkpa ịchọ enyemaka ngwa ngwa ma ọ bụrụ na onye ahụ:

na-ekwu maka igbu onwe ya ma ọ bụ imerụ onwe ya ahụ,
na-anụ olu ma ọ bụ na-ahụ ihe ndị ọzọ anaghị ahụ,
enweghịzi ike ilekọta onwe ya,
ma ọ bụ yiri ka ọ nọ n'ihe ize ndụ.

Ndị nwere ike inyere ya aka bụ dọkịta, counselor, psychologist, psychiatrist, ma ọ bụ ndị ọkachamara ahụike uche ndị ọzọ. Ịchọpụta nsogbu ahụ n'oge na ịchọ enyemaka n'oge nwere ike ime nnukwu mgbanwe.

If someone starts hearing voices, seeing things other people don't, becoming very confused, or believing things that seem disconnected from reality, they should be assessed by a healthcare professional as soon as possible. These can be signs of psychosis or another serious medical or mental health condition.

Signs they need urgent medical help

Seek urgent help if:

The symptoms are new, severe, or getting worse quickly.
They are having difficulty telling what is real and what is not.
They become very confused, disorganized, or unable to care for their basic needs.
They talk about harming themselves or other people.
The voices are telling them to do dangerous things.
They become threatening, violent, severely agitated, or behave in ways that put themselves or others at risk.
What you can do
Stay calm and speak in a reassuring way.
Avoid arguing about whether their experiences are real.
Focus on safety and on how they are feeling.
Help them get medical or mental-health care promptly.
When it's an emergency

If there is an immediate risk of harm to themselves or someone else, or they cannot safely care for themselves, seek emergency medical care right away.

Early treatment is associated with better outcomes, so it's generally best to seek help sooner rather than wait to see if the symptoms go away on their own.

Signs they may need urgent medical help

Seek urgent help if:

Help them get medical or mental-health care as soon as possible.
Why early help matters

Tí ẹnì kan bá bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í gbọ́ ohùn, rí àwọn ohun tí àwọn ẹlòmíràn kò rí, ní ìrònú tó dàrú gan-an, tàbí gbàgbọ́ àwọn ohun tí kò jọ òtítọ́, ó yẹ kí a wá ìrànlọ́wọ́ ìlera fún un ní kíákíá. Àwọn àmì wọ̀nyí lè jẹ́ àmì ìṣòro ìlera ọpọlọ tàbí ìṣòro ìlera míì tó nílò àyẹ̀wò amòye.

Ó ṣe pàtàkì gan-an láti wá ìrànlọ́wọ́ pajawiri bí:

Àwọn àmì àìsàn náà bá ṣẹlẹ̀ lójijì tàbí fún ìgbà àkọ́kọ́.
Ìdàrúdàpọ̀ ọkàn tàbí ìgbàgbọ́ àjèjì náà bá ń burú sí i lọ́rẹ̀ẹ́rẹ̀.

Gba a níyànjú láti rí dókítà tàbí onímọ̀ ìlera ọpọlọ, pàápàá bí àwọn ohun náà bá ṣẹ̀ṣẹ̀ bẹ̀rẹ̀, bá ń pọ̀ sí i, tàbí bí ó ṣe ń ya ara rẹ̀ sọ́tọ̀ bá ń buru sí i.

Tẹ́tí sí wọn láì ṣe ìdájọ́. Bí ẹni náà bá sọ pé ó ń gbọ́ àwọn ohùn, ẹ má ṣe rẹ́rìn-ín tàbí fi ẹ̀gàn kàn án. Gba pé ìrírí náà jẹ́ gidi fún un, bí ó tilẹ̀ jẹ́ pé ẹ̀yin kò ń gbọ́ ohun náà.
Máa bá wọn ní àjọṣe. Bí ẹni náà ṣe ń ya ara rẹ̀ sọ́tọ̀, ìbánisọ̀rọ̀ pẹ̀lú àánú àti ìfọkànsìn lè dín ìmọ̀lára ìdánìkanwà kù.
Béèrè ohun tí yóò ràn án lọ́wọ́. Kí ẹ má ṣe ro pé ẹ ti mọ ohun tó fẹ́; ó lè yàtọ̀ sí ènìyàn sí ènìyàn.
Fojú kọ́ bí ó ṣe ń ní lára. Dípò kí ẹ jiyàn nípa bóyá ohun tó ń gbọ́ jẹ́ òtítọ́ tàbí rara, béèrè bí ìrírí náà ṣe ń ní ipa lórí ìmọ̀lára rẹ̀.
Gba a níyànjú láti wá ìrànlọ́wọ́ amọ̀ja. Dókítà tàbí onímọ̀ ìlera ọpọlọ lè ṣe àyẹ̀wò àti pèsè ìrànlọ́wọ́ tó yẹ.
Dábàá àwọn iṣẹ́ rọrùn. Irìn àjò kékeré, sise oúnjẹ pọ̀, tàbí wiwo fíìmù lè ràn ẹni náà lọ́wọ́ láti má ṣe ya ara rẹ̀ sọ́tọ̀ pátápátá.
Kọ́ ara yín nípa ọ̀ràn náà. Mímọ̀ síi nípa gbígbọ́ ohùn àti àwọn ìṣòro ìlera ọpọlọ lè dín àbùkù àti àìmọ̀ kù.

Ó yẹ kí a wá ìrànlọ́wọ́ ìṣègùn pajawiri bí ẹni náà bá ń sọ̀rọ̀ nípa fífi ara pa lára tàbí fípa àwọn mìíràn lára, bí ó bá ń dàrú gan-an, tàbí bí àwọn ohùn náà bá ń pa á láṣẹ láti ṣe ohun tó léwu.

Ohun tó ṣe pàtàkì jù ni kí ẹni náà mọ̀ pé kò dá wà, pé àwọn ènìyàn ń bójú tó òun, àti pé ìrànlọ́wọ́ wà fún un.

Ezinụlọ nwere ike inyere onye na-anụ ihe ndị ọzọ anaghị anụ, ma ọ bụ onye na-anọpụ iche karịa ka ọ na-adị, site n’ịdị jụụ, na-akwado ya, ma na-elekwasị anya na nchekwa ya.

Gee ya ntị n’enweghị ịkatọ ma ọ bụ ịkwa ya emo. Nye ya ohere ịkọ ihe ọ na-anụ ma ọ bụ otú ọ na-adị ya.

Ó bá ní ètò tàbí ọ̀nà pàtó láti ṣe bẹ́ẹ̀.

Tàbí bí ẹ bá gbà pé ó wà nínú ewu lẹ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀.

Ní irú ọ̀ràn bẹ́ẹ̀, ẹ má ṣe fi òun sílẹ̀ nìkan bí ó bá ṣeé ṣe, kí ẹ sì kan sí iṣẹ́ pajawiri tàbí ilé ìwòsàn ní kíákíá.

Your sister's situation should be taken very seriously.

Being sad most of the time, stopping contact with friends, and saying that life is no longer worth living are important warning signs of possible depression or a mental health crisis.

Wetin una suppose do now

Talk to her with care and listen. Let her know say una care about am. No dismiss her feelings or tell am to "just be strong."

Help her get professional support. Try make she see a doctor, counselor, psychologist, psychiatrist, or another qualified mental-health professional as soon as possible.

Stay connected with her. Withdrawal from friends and people around her can be a warning sign. Make sure she no dey face this alone.

Take statements about life not being worth living seriously. Feelings of hopelessness and believing there is no point in living are signs that support is needed.

About prayer

If prayer is important to her and your family, prayer can provide comfort and support. But prayer should not be the only response when someone is persistently sad and saying life is no longer worth living. Professional mental-health care and family support are also important.

Get emergency help immediately if
She says she wants to kill herself.
She has a plan to harm herself.
She has already harmed herself.
You believe she is in immediate danger.

If that happens, contact emergency services or a crisis service immediately and, if it is safe to do so, do not leave her alone.

Ọ̀ràn ọmọ ìyá yín yẹ kí a gba ní pàtàkì gan-an.

Bí ẹni náà ṣe ń ní ìbànújẹ́ ọkàn ní gbogbo ìgbà, ṣe dẹ́kun bíbá àwọn ọ̀rẹ́ rẹ̀ sọ̀rọ̀, tí ó sì ń sọ pé kò rí ìdí kankan láti máa wà láàyè mọ́, wọ̀nyí lè jẹ́ àmì ìṣòro ìlera ọpọlọ tó nílò ìrànlọ́wọ́ ọjọ́gbọ́n.

Kí ni ẹ yẹ kí ẹ ṣe báyìí?
Bá a sọ̀rọ̀ pẹ̀lú àánú àti ìfẹ́. Jẹ́ kí ó mọ̀ pé ẹ nífẹ̀ẹ́ rẹ̀, pé kò dá wà, àti pé ẹ fẹ́ ràn án lọ́wọ́.
Tẹ́tí sí i láì ṣe ìdájọ́. Má ṣe sọ pé ó yẹ kí ó “lágbára” tàbí pé kó kan gbàgbé nǹkan náà. Gba àwọn ìmọ̀lára rẹ̀ ní pàtàkì.
Ràn án lọ́wọ́ láti rí ìrànlọ́wọ́ ọjọ́gbọ́n bí dókítà, olùdámọ̀ràn, psychologist, tàbí psychiatrist.
Máa bá a ní àjọṣe. Yíyà ara ẹni sọ́tọ̀ lè jẹ́ àmì pé ẹni náà ń jìyà, ó sì nílò àtìlẹ́yìn púpọ̀ sí i.
Nípa àdúrà nko?

Tí àdúrà bá ṣe pàtàkì fún un àti fún ẹbí, àdúrà lè mú ìtùnú àti ìrètí wá. Ṣùgbọ́n àdúrà nìkan kò yẹ kí ó rọ́pò ìtọ́jú ìlera ọpọlọ ní irú ipò yìí. Ó dára kí àtìlẹ́yìn ẹ̀mí àti ìtọ́jú ọjọ́gbọ́n ṣiṣẹ́ pọ̀.

Wá ìrànlọ́wọ́ pajawiri lẹ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀ bí:
Ó bá ń sọ̀rọ̀ nípa fífi ara pa lára tàbí ikú.
Ó bá ní ètò tàbí ìpinnu láti pa ara rẹ̀.
Ó bá ti ṣe ara rẹ̀ lára télẹ̀.
Ẹ bá rò pé ó wà nínú ewu lẹ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀.

Ní irú àkókò bẹ́ẹ̀, pe àwọn iṣẹ́ pajawiri ìṣègùn tàbí mú un lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn kíákíá, kí ẹ sì má ṣe fi í sílẹ̀ nìkan bí ó bá ṣeé ṣe.

Ọ̀kan lára àwọn ohun tó ṣe pàtàkì jù ni kí ó gbọ́ pé:“A nífẹ̀ẹ́ rẹ. O ò dá wà. A ó sì ràn ẹ́ lọ́wọ́ láti rí ìrànlọ́wọ́ tó yẹ.”

Kí ni ẹbí lè ṣe?
Jẹ́ kí ìbánisọ̀rọ̀ yín balẹ̀, kí ẹ sì tẹ́tí sí i. Má ṣe fi í ṣe yẹ̀yẹ́, fi ẹ̀sùn kàn án, tàbí sọ pé ohun tó ń ṣẹlẹ̀ sí i kò ṣe pàtàkì.
Má ṣe bá a jiyàn nípa bóyá ohun tó ń gbọ́ tàbí gbàgbọ́ jẹ́ òtítọ́. Dípò bẹ́ẹ̀, ẹ lè sọ pé,“Ó dà bíi pé èyí ń ba ọ lẹ́rù gan-an.”
Fojú kọ́ bí ó ṣe ń ní lára. Béèrè bóyá ó ń bẹ̀rù, ó ń yọ̀ mí, tàbí ó ń dàrú.
Ràn án lọ́wọ́ láti rí amòye. Dókítà, psychiatrist, psychologist, tàbí amòye ìlera ọpọlọ míì lè ṣàyẹ̀wò ohun tó ń ṣẹlẹ̀ kí wọ́n sì dábàá ìtọ́jú tó yẹ.
Máa bá a wà ní àjọṣe. Àtìlẹ́yìn ẹbí àti ìbáṣepọ̀ pẹ̀lú àwọn ènìyàn tó nífẹ̀ẹ́ rẹ̀ lè ràn án lọ́wọ́.
Nípa ilé àdúrà nko?

Tí àdúrà bá ṣe pàtàkì fún un àti fún ẹbí, ó lè jẹ́ orísun ìtùnú àti agbára. Ṣùgbọ́n àdúrà kò yẹ kí ó rọ́pò àyẹ̀wò àti ìtọ́jú ìṣègùn tàbí ìlera ọpọlọ. Ọ̀nà tó dára jù ni kí ẹ darapọ̀ àtìlẹ́yìn ẹ̀mí pẹ̀lú ìtọ́jú ọjọ́gbọ́n.

Wá ìrànlọ́wọ́ pajawiri lẹ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀ bí:
Ó bá sọ pé ó fẹ́ pa ara rẹ̀ tàbí pa ẹlòmíràn lára.
Àwọn ohùn náà bá ń pa á láṣẹ láti ṣe ohun tó léwu.
Ó kò bá lè tọ́jú ara rẹ̀ mọ́.
Ó bá ń dàrú gidigidi tàbí di aláìláàbò fún ara rẹ̀ tàbí àwọn mìíràn.

Ìrànlọ́wọ́ ní kutukutu àti àtìlẹ́yìn ẹbí lè ṣe ìyàtọ̀ ńlá nínú ìmúláradá ẹni náà.

Ọ̀nà tó láàbò jù lọ ni kí ẹ gba ohun tí ọmọ ìyá yín ń nírìírí náà ní pàtàkì, kí ẹ sì rí i dájú pé ó gba àyẹ̀wò lọ́dọ̀ dókítà tàbí amòye ìlera ọpọlọ ní kíákíá.

Gbígbọ́ àwọn ohùn àti gbígbàgbọ́ pé àwọn ènìyàn ń ṣọ́ òun lè jẹ́ àmì ìṣòro ìlera ọpọlọ tó nílò ìtọ́jú ọjọ́gbọ́n. Àwọn àmì wọ̀nyí lè ní í ṣe pẹ̀lú ìfẹ̀hónúhàn sí àwọn mìíràn, ìyàsọ́tọ̀ ara ẹni, àti ìṣòro láti mọ ohun tó jẹ́ gidi àti ohun tí kì í ṣe gidi.

Tẹ́tí sí i pẹ̀lú ìfọ̀kànbalẹ̀. Má ṣe fi í ṣe yẹ̀yẹ́, dá a lẹ́bi, tàbí sọ pé kò sí ohun tó ń ṣẹlẹ̀ sí i.

To avoid increasing stigma:

Emphasise that the person is not to blame. Schizophrenia is not caused by bad character, lack of faith, or moral failure.
Use ordinary health comparisons. For example, just as someone with epilepsy or diabetes needs appropriate healthcare, a person experiencing psychosis also deserves proper medical care.
Avoid frightening labels. People with schizophrenia are not automatically violent or dangerous. Most need support, treatment, dignity, and protection from discrimination.
Focus on recovery. Treatment may include medication, psychological support, family support, and help with daily life, and many people improve significantly.

The goal is not necessarily to win an argument about spiritual beliefs. It is to make sure those beliefs do not lead to blame, isolation, harmful practices, or delays in getting appropriate healthcare.

Má ṣe fi ẹ̀gàn kàn ìgbàgbọ́ wọn. Tí o bá kọlu ìgbàgbọ́ wọn, ó lè jẹ́ kí wọ́n má fẹ́ fetí sí ìmọ̀ ìlera.
Ṣàlàyé pé schizophrenia kì í ṣe ìjìyà, àìní ìgbàgbọ́, tàbí ìkùnà ìwà.
Yẹra fún ọ̀rọ̀ bí “wèrè,” “ẹni tí ẹ̀mí mú,” tàbí fífi hàn pé ẹni náà dájú pé ó léwu.
Tẹnumọ́ pé ẹni tó ní schizophrenia yẹ fún ọlá, ìtìlẹ́yìn, àti ìtọ́jú tó yẹ.
Jẹ́ kí wọ́n mọ̀ pé ìtọ́jú lè ràn án lọ́wọ́, pẹ̀lú oògùn, ìtọ́jú ọpọlọ, ìtìlẹ́yìn ẹbí, àti ìrànlọ́wọ́ nínú ìgbésí ayé ojoojúmọ́.
Bí àdúrà tàbí ìtìlẹ́yìn ẹ̀mí bá ṣe pàtàkì fún ẹni náà, ó lè bá ìtọ́jú lọ, ṣùgbọ́n kò yẹ kí ó rọ́pò àyẹ̀wò àti ìtọ́jú lọ́dọ̀ onímọ̀ ìlera.
Ẹ yẹra fún ìṣe tó lè pa ẹni náà lára, bí lílù, dídè mọ́lẹ̀, fífi ebi pa, ìyasọ́tọ̀, tàbí dídá oògùn tí dókítà kọ́ dúró.

Ohun pàtàkì ni pé ẹ lè bọ̀wọ̀ fún ìgbàgbọ́ ènìyàn láì jẹ́ kí ìgbàgbọ́ náà yọrí sí ẹ̀bi, ìtìjú, ìyasọ́tọ̀, tàbí ìdádúró sí ìtọ́jú tó yẹ.

O lè ṣàlàyé rẹ̀ ní ọ̀nà tó fi ọ̀wọ̀ hàn sí ìgbàgbọ́ ẹni náà, láì ṣe àríyànjiyàn tàbí fi ẹ̀gàn kàn án.

Fún àpẹẹrẹ, o lè sọ pé:

“Mo mọ̀ pé àwọn ènìyàn lè ní àwọn ìtumọ̀ oriṣìíríṣìí fún àwọn àìsàn. Láti ojú ìwòye ìlera, schizophrenia jẹ́ àìsàn ìlera ọpọlọ tó lè ní ipa lórí bí ènìyàn ṣe ń ronú, bí ó ṣe ń ní lára, àti bí ó ṣe ń túmọ̀ ohun tó ń ṣẹlẹ̀ ní ayíká rẹ̀. Ó lè mú kí ènìyàn gbọ́ ohùn tàbí ní àwọn ìgbàgbọ́ tí àwọn ẹlòmíràn kò ní.”

Àwọn ọ̀nà tó lè dín ìtìjú (stigma) kù ni:

Fojú kọ́ ènìyàn náà, kì í ṣe àìsàn náà. Rántí àwọn ènìyàn pé ẹni tó ní schizophrenia ṣì jẹ́ ènìyàn tó yẹ fún ìbòwọ̀, àánú, àti àtìlẹ́yìn.
Yẹra fún fífi ẹ̀bi kàn án. Ṣàlàyé pé àìsàn náà kì í ṣe àmì àìlera ìwà tàbí àṣìṣe ẹni náà.
Pín ìmọ̀ ìlera ní ìrẹ̀lẹ̀. Ìmọ̀ ìṣègùn ṣàlàyé schizophrenia gẹ́gẹ́ bí àìsàn tó ní í ṣe pẹ̀lú ọpọlọ, àbùdá ìdílé, àti àwọn nǹkan míì ní ayíká ènìyàn.
Ṣàtúnṣe àwọn èrò tí kò tọ́ pẹ̀lú ìbòwọ̀. Ọ̀pọ̀ ènìyàn máa ń rò pé gbogbo ẹni tó ní schizophrenia lewu, ṣùgbọ́n ọ̀pọ̀ jù lọ kì í ṣe aláìláàbò; ní òtítọ́, wọ́n sábà máa ń nílò ìrànlọ́wọ́ àti ààbò.
Gba àwọn ènìyàn níyànjú láti wá ìtọ́jú àti àtìlẹ́yìn. Pẹ̀lú ìtọ́jú tó yẹ, ọ̀pọ̀ ènìyàn lè ṣàkóso àwọn àmì àìsàn wọn kí wọ́n sì gbé ìgbésí ayé tó ní ìtumọ̀.

Ète náà kì í ṣe láti sọ pé ìgbàgbọ́ ẹni náà kò tọ́, bí kò ṣe láti mú kí wọ́n ní ìmọ̀ síi àti kí wọ́n fi àánú àti ìbòwọ̀ hàn sí àwọn ènìyàn tí schizophrenia ń kan.

O lè ṣàlàyé rẹ̀ ní ọ̀nà tí ó fi ọ̀wọ̀ hàn sí ìgbàgbọ́ ẹni náà, láì ṣe àríyànjiyàn tàbí fi ẹ̀gàn kàn án.

Fún àpẹẹrẹ, o lè sọ pé:

“Mo mọ̀ pé àwọn ènìyàn kan lè túmọ̀ àwọn àìsàn ní ọ̀nà ẹ̀mí tàbí àṣà. Ní ti ìmọ̀ ìlera, àwọn dókítà àti amòye ìlera ọpọlọ ka schizophrenia sí àìsàn tó ń kan bí ènìyàn ṣe ń ronú, ṣe ìtumọ̀ ohun tó ń ṣẹlẹ̀ ní ayíká rẹ̀, àti bí ó ṣe ń mọ ohun tó jẹ́ gidi tàbí kì í ṣe gidi. Ó lè mú kí ènìyàn gbọ́ ohùn tàbí ní àwọn ìgbàgbọ́ tí àwọn ẹlòmíràn kò ní.”

Láti dín ìtìjú (stigma) kù:

Fojú kọ́ ènìyàn náà, kì í ṣe àìsàn náà. Ẹni tí ó ní schizophrenia ṣì yẹ fún ìbòwọ̀, àánú, àti àtìlẹ́yìn.
Yẹra fún fífi ẹ̀bi kàn án. Kò sí ẹ̀rí pé ẹni náà ló fa àìsàn náà sí ara rẹ̀.
Pín ìmọ̀ ìlera pẹ̀lú ìrẹ̀lẹ̀. Ìwádìí fìdí rẹ̀ múlẹ̀ pé schizophrenia ní í ṣe pẹ̀lú ọ̀pọ̀ nǹkan papọ̀, bí àbùdá ìdílé (genetics), kemika inú ọpọlọ, àti àwọn ipa míì láti ayíká.
Ṣàtúnṣe àwọn èrò tí kò tọ́ ní ìfẹ̀lẹ́fẹ̀lẹ́. Ọ̀pọ̀ ènìyàn ro pé gbogbo ẹni tí ó ní schizophrenia lewu, ṣùgbọ́n ìròyìn yìí kì í ṣe òtítọ́ fún ọ̀pọ̀ jù lọ, ó sì lè mú ìtìjú àti ìyasọ́tọ̀ pọ̀ sí i.
Tẹnumọ́ ìtọ́jú àti àtìlẹ́yìn. Pẹ̀lú ìtọ́jú àti ìrànlọ́wọ́ tó yẹ, ọ̀pọ̀ ènìyàn lè ṣàkóso àwọn àmì àìsàn wọn kí wọ́n sì gbé ìgbésí ayé tó ní ìtumọ̀.

Ète náà kì í ṣe láti jiyàn nípa àjẹ́ tàbí àwọn ìgbàgbọ́ ẹ̀mí, bí kò ṣe láti jẹ́ kí àwọn ènìyàn lóye pé ẹni tí schizophrenia ń kan nílò àánú, ìbòwọ̀, àti ìrànlọ́wọ́ tó yẹ.

O lè ṣàlàyé rẹ̀ ní ọ̀nà tí ó fi ọ̀wọ̀ hàn sí ìgbàgbọ́ ẹni náà, láì ṣe àríyànjiyàn tàbí fi ẹ̀gàn kàn án.

O lè sọ pé:

“Mo mọ̀ pé àwọn ènìyàn kan gbàgbọ́ pé àwọn ohun ẹ̀mí lè ní ipa lórí àwọn àìsàn kan. Ní ti ìmọ̀ ìlera, àwọn dókítà àti amòye ìlera ọpọlọ mọ schizophrenia gẹ́gẹ́ bí àìsàn tó ń kan bí ènìyàn ṣe ń ronú, ṣe ń lòye ohun tó ń ṣẹlẹ̀ yí i ká, àti bí ó ṣe ń mọ ohun tó jẹ́ gidi tàbí kì í ṣe gidi. Ó lè fa gbígbọ́ ohùn, àwọn ìgbàgbọ́ tó lágbára, tàbí ìdàrúdàpọ̀ ìrònú.”

Láti dín ìtìjú (stigma) kù:

Fojú kọ́ ènìyàn náà ju àìsàn náà lọ. Ẹni tí ó ní schizophrenia ṣì jẹ́ ènìyàn tó yẹ fún ìbòwọ̀, àánú, àti àtìlẹ́yìn.
Yẹra fún fífi ẹ̀bi kàn án. Kò dára láti sọ pé ẹni náà ló fa àìsàn náà tàbí pé ó yẹ fún un.
Pín ìmọ̀ ìlera pẹ̀lú ìrẹ̀lẹ̀. Ìwádìí fi hàn pé schizophrenia kò ní ìdí kan ṣoṣo; ó ní í ṣe pẹ̀lú àbùdá ìdílé (genetics), bí kemika inú ọpọlọ ṣe ń ṣiṣẹ́, àti àwọn ipa míì láti ayíká.
Ṣàtúnṣe àwọn èrò tí kò tọ́ ní pẹ̀lẹ́pẹ̀lẹ́. Schizophrenia kì í ṣe “ọ̀pọ̀ ènìyàn nínú ara kan” (multiple personalities), àti pé àwọn ìròyìn tí kò tọ́ lè mú ìyasọ́tọ̀ àti ìtìjú pọ̀ sí i.
Tẹnumọ́ ìrètí àti ìtọ́jú. Ọ̀pọ̀ ènìyàn lè ṣàkóso àwọn àmì àìsàn wọn dáadáa pẹ̀lú ìtọ́jú àti àtìlẹ́yìn tó yẹ.

Gbólóhùn tó rọrùn tó sì sábà máa ń ṣiṣẹ́ ni:

“Bóyá a ní ìtumọ̀ ẹ̀mí tàbí ìtumọ̀ ìṣègùn fún un, ohun pàtàkì ni pé ẹni náà nílò àánú, ìbòwọ̀, àti ìrànlọ́wọ́ tó yẹ.”

Ọ̀nà yìí máa ń jẹ́ kí ẹ bọ̀wọ̀ fún ìgbàgbọ́ àwọn ènìyàn, nígbà kan náà ó sì ń dín ìtìjú kù, ó sì ń gba ènìyàn níyànjú láti wá ìrànlọ́wọ́ tó yẹ.

Ị nwere ike ịkọwa ya n’ụzọ na-asọpụrụ echiche ha, ma na-eme ka o doo anya na ọrịa uche abụghị ihe ihere ma ọ bụ ihe mmadụ kwesịrị ịta ụta maka ya.

Ị nwere ike ikwu ihe dịka:

“Ama m na ụfọdụ mmadụ na-akọwa ụdị ọrịa a n’ụzọ ime mmụọ. Ma n’aka ndị ahụike, nsogbu uche dịka schizophrenia bụ ọnọdụ ahụike nke nwere ike imetụta otú mmadụ si eche echiche, hụ ma ọ bụ nụ ihe, ma ọ bụ ghọta ihe na-eme gburugburu ya. Ọ bụghị ihe na-egosi na onye ahụ bụ onye ọjọọ, na ọ dara mbà n’okwukwe, ma ọ bụ na ọ kwesịrị ihere.”

Ihe ndị ọzọ dị mkpa bụ:

Zere ịkwa emo ma ọ bụ ịkatọ nkwenkwe ha. Nke ahụ nwere ike ime ka ha ghara ige ntị.
Kọwaa na ọrịa uche abụghị mmehie, adịghị ike, ma ọ bụ ihe kwesịrị ime ka mmadụ bụrụ onye a na-achụpụ n’obodo.
Gbaa ha ume ka ha hụ onye ahụ dịka mmadụ kwesịrị nsọpụrụ, nkwado na ọgwụgwọ, ọ bụghị dịka “onye ara” ma ọ bụ onye dị ize ndụ n’ihi ọrịa ya.
Ọ bụrụ na ekpere ma ọ bụ nkwado ime mmụọ dị onye ahụ mkpa, nke ahụ nwere ike iso nlekọta ahụike gaa, mana ọ gaghị dochie nyocha na ọgwụgwọ n’aka dọkịta ma ọ bụ ọkachamara ahụike uche.
Gosi na ọtụtụ mmadụ nwere nsogbu uche nwere ike imeziwanye nke ukwuu ma ọ bụrụ na ha enweta ọgwụgwọ, nkwado ezinụlọ, na ebe nchekwa na-enweghị ịkpa ókè.

Isi ozi ị ga-achọ iziga bụ: ọnọdụ uche abụghị ihe ihere, onye ahụ abụghị ọrịa ahụ n’onwe ya, ma ọ kwesịrị inweta otu nsọpụrụ na nlekọta a na-enye onye nwere ọrịa anụ ahụ.

Ị nwere ike ịkọwa ya n’ụzọ na-asọpụrụ nkwenkwe ha, ma na-eme ka o doo anya na nsogbu ahụike uche abụghị ihe ihere.

Ị nwere ike ịsị:

“Ama m na ụfọdụ ndị na-akọwa ụdị nsogbu a n’ụzọ ime mmụọ. Ma n’aka ndị ahụike, ọrịa uche bụ ọnọdụ ahụike nke nwere ike imetụta otú mmadụ si eche echiche, nwee mmetụta, hụ ma ọ bụ nụ ihe, ma ọ bụ mee omume. Ọ bụghị ihe na-egosi na onye ahụ bụ onye ọjọọ, na a bụrụla ya ọnụ, ma ọ bụ na ọ kwesịrị ime ihere.”

Ihe dị mkpa bụ:

Ekwesịghị ịkwa nkwenkwe ha emo ma ọ bụ ịkatọ ha. Nke ahụ nwere ike ime ka ha kwụsị ige ntị.
Kọwaa na nsogbu ahụike uche abụghị mmehie, adịghị ike, ma ọ bụ ihe mmadụ kwesịrị ịta ụta maka ya.
Zere okwu na-akparị mmadụ dịka “onye ara” ma ọ bụ okwu ndị ọzọ na-eme ka ihere bawanye.
Gbaa ndị mmadụ ume ka ha hụ onye ahụ dịka mmadụ kwesịrị nkwanye ùgwù, nlekọta, na enyemaka, dịka onye nwere ọrịa anụ ahụ.
Kọwaa na dọkịta ma ọ bụ ọkachamara ahụike uche nwere ike inyere aka ịchọpụta ihe na-eme ma nye ọgwụgwọ kwesịrị ekwesị.
Ọ bụrụ na ekpere ma ọ bụ nkwado ime mmụọ dị onye ahụ mkpa, ọ nwere ike iso nlekọta ahụike gaa, mana ọ gaghị dochie nyocha na ọgwụgwọ n’aka ndị ọkachamara.

What to Do When Someone's Face Looks Uneven, One Arm Is Weak, and They Cannot Speak Properly
Recognise That This Is Most Likely a Stroke

The three signs described, sudden facial asymmetry (one side of the face drooping or not moving normally), sudden weakness in one arm, and sudden difficulty speaking (slurred, jumbled, or absent speech), are the classic presentation of an acute stroke. A stroke occurs when blood supply to part of the brain is interrupted, either by a clot blocking a blood vessel (ischaemic stroke, accounting for approximately 85% of cases) or by a blood vessel bursting and bleeding into or around the brain (haemorrhagic stroke). Brain tissue deprived of blood begins to die within minutes. Every minute of delay in treatment results in further irreversible brain damage. This is a medical emergency of the highest urgency.

The widely used mnemonic for recognising stroke is FAST:

F — Face. Ask the person to smile. If one side of the face droops or does not move, that is a positive sign.

A — Arms. Ask the person to raise both arms. If one arm drifts downward or cannot be raised, that is a positive sign.

S — Speech. Ask the person to repeat a simple sentence. If their speech is slurred, garbled, or they cannot speak, that is a positive sign.

T — Time. If any one of these signs is present, call emergency services immediately. Note the time when symptoms were first observed, because this information directly affects treatment decisions.

Call Emergency Services Immediately

This is the single most important action. Call the local emergency number without delay. In the UK, call 999. In Nigeria, call 112 (national emergency number) or the local emergency line, or take the person directly to the nearest hospital with emergency services if an ambulance is not available or will not arrive quickly.

When you call, state clearly that you suspect a stroke, describe the symptoms you are observing, and give the exact location. If you know when the symptoms started, say so. If you did not witness the onset but found the person already symptomatic, say when the person was last seen normal. This "last known well" time is critical because the most effective treatment for ischaemic stroke, intravenous thrombolysis (clot-dissolving medication, most commonly alteplase), has a treatment window. Current guidelines from the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association and the European Stroke Organisation indicate that intravenous thrombolysis is most effective within 4.5 hours of symptom onset. Mechanical thrombectomy (physical clot retrieval) may extend the window further in selected patients, but still depends on timely arrival at a capable facility. Every minute matters.

What to Do While Waiting for Emergency Services

Do not give the person anything to eat or drink. Stroke frequently impairs swallowing (a condition called dysphagia). Giving food, water, or medication by mouth risks aspiration, where material enters the airway and lungs, which can cause aspiration pneumonia or airway obstruction. This includes any oral medications the person may normally take.

Do not give aspirin or any other medication. Although aspirin is used in the management of ischaemic stroke, it is contraindicated in haemorrhagic stroke and can worsen bleeding. Since the type of stroke cannot be determined without brain imaging (CT or MRI scan), administering aspirin before diagnosis risks causing serious harm. Treatment decisions must be made by medical professionals after imaging.

Keep the person as calm and still as possible. Help them into a comfortable position, preferably sitting up slightly or lying on their side (recovery position) if they are drowsy or vomiting, to protect the airway. Do not move them unnecessarily.

If the person is conscious, reassure them that help is coming. Speak calmly. Do not ask them to walk or exert themselves.

If the person loses consciousness, check for breathing. If they are breathing, place them in the recovery position (on their side, head slightly tilted back, mouth downward to allow fluid to drain). If they stop breathing, begin CPR if you are trained to do so, and continue until emergency services arrive.

Note and remember the time of onset. If you witnessed the moment symptoms began, record the exact time. If the person woke up with symptoms, the last time they were seen without symptoms becomes the relevant time point. Communicate this clearly to the emergency team on arrival. This single piece of information can determine whether the person is eligible for clot-dissolving treatment.

Note any other symptoms. Additional signs that may accompany stroke include sudden severe headache with no known cause, sudden confusion, sudden vision problems in one or both eyes, sudden dizziness or loss of balance, and sudden numbness on one side of the body. Report all observed symptoms to the emergency team.

What Not to Do

Do not wait to see if symptoms improve. Transient ischaemic attacks (TIAs, sometimes called "mini-strokes") can produce similar symptoms that resolve within minutes to hours, but there is no way to distinguish a TIA from a full stroke without medical assessment and imaging. Even if symptoms appear to be improving, the person must be evaluated urgently, because a TIA is itself a warning sign of imminent full stroke. Waiting is the most dangerous possible response.

Do not drive the person to hospital yourself if an ambulance is available and can arrive promptly. Ambulance paramedics can begin assessment en route, pre-notify the receiving hospital to activate the stroke team, and provide emergency interventions if the person deteriorates. However, if no ambulance is available or the wait time would be long, transporting the person by private vehicle to the nearest hospital with emergency and ideally stroke services is better than continued waiting.

Do not let the person fall asleep without monitoring. If the person becomes drowsy, monitor their breathing and level of consciousness continuously until emergency services arrive.

Do not attempt to lower blood pressure with home remedies or medications. Blood pressure is frequently elevated during acute stroke, and the body may be maintaining this elevation to sustain blood flow to the affected brain area. Lowering blood pressure without medical guidance can worsen brain injury. Blood pressure management during acute stroke requires careful medical decision-making with imaging results.

After the Emergency Team Arrives

Provide the emergency team with the time of symptom onset or last known well time, a description of all symptoms observed and any changes since onset, the person's known medical conditions (hypertension, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, previous stroke or TIA), the person's current medications (particularly blood thinners such as warfarin, rivaroxaban, apixaban, or dabigatran, as these affect treatment decisions), and any known allergies. If possible, bring the person's medication containers to the hospital.

Why Speed Determines Outcome

The phrase used in stroke medicine is "time is brain." Research published in the journal Stroke and other peer-reviewed neurology literature has quantified this: in a large-vessel ischaemic stroke, an estimated 1.9 million neurons are lost per minute of untreated ischaemia (Saver, 2006, "Time Is Brain — Quantified," Stroke). Patients who receive thrombolysis within 90 minutes of symptom onset have substantially better outcomes than those treated later within the 4.5-hour window. Patients treated with mechanical thrombectomy within 6 hours, and in selected cases up to 24 hours based on advanced imaging, can achieve dramatic reductions in disability. Every delay, whether from failure to recognise symptoms, hesitation to call emergency services, or transport time, directly reduces the probability of good recovery and increases the probability of permanent disability or death.

Source Basis

This guidance reflects the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (AHA/ASA) guidelines for the early management of acute ischaemic stroke (most recently updated 2019, with subsequent scientific statements), the European Stroke Organisation (ESO) guidelines for intravenous thrombolysis, the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) stroke guidelines, and the WHO package of essential noncommunicable disease interventions for primary health care. The FAST mnemonic originates from the UK Stroke Association and has been validated in multiple clinical and public-awareness studies. The neuron-loss estimate (1.9 million per minute) is from Saver (2006), published in Stroke, 37(1), 263–266. Treatment windows (4.5 hours for thrombolysis, up to 24 hours for thrombectomy in selected patients) reflect current evidence from major clinical trials including NINDS, ECASS III, and the DAWN and DEFUSE 3 thrombectomy trials.

Specific emergency numbers, hospital capabilities, and treatment availability vary by country and region. The person should be taken to the nearest facility capable of stroke diagnosis and treatment as rapidly as possible.

Guidelines from the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (AHA/ASA) and the European Stroke Organisation (ESO) indicate that thrombolysis is most effective within 4.5 hours of symptom onset, with greatest benefit when given within 90 minutes. Mechanical thrombectomy (physical removal of the clot via catheter) may extend the treatment window in eligible patients, in some cases up to 24 hours based on advanced imaging criteria, but still depends on the patient reaching a capable facility as fast as possible. The phrase used in stroke medicine is "time is brain." Research has quantified this: in large-vessel ischaemic stroke, approximately 1.9 million neurons die per minute of untreated ischaemia (Saver, 2006, Stroke, 37(1), 263–266).

What to Do While Waiting for Help

Do not give the person anything to eat or drink. Stroke frequently impairs swallowing (dysphagia). Giving food, water, or oral medication risks aspiration, where material enters the lungs, potentially causing pneumonia or airway obstruction.

Do not give aspirin or any other medication. Aspirin is used in managing ischaemic stroke but is contraindicated in haemorrhagic stroke and can worsen brain bleeding. Since the type of stroke cannot be determined without brain imaging (CT or MRI), giving aspirin before diagnosis may cause serious harm.

Help the person into a safe, comfortable position. If conscious, sitting up slightly with head and shoulders supported is generally appropriate. If drowsy or vomiting, place them on their side (recovery position) with the mouth angled downward so fluid can drain, preventing choking.

Keep the person calm and still. Reassure them that help is on the way. Do not ask them to walk or exert themselves.

If the person loses consciousness, check whether they are breathing. If breathing, maintain the recovery position and monitor continuously. If breathing stops, begin CPR if you are trained, and continue until emergency services arrive.

Record the time of onset. If you witnessed the moment symptoms began, note the exact time and communicate it to paramedics on arrival. If the person woke up with symptoms, the relevant time is when they were last seen without symptoms. This single piece of information can determine whether the patient qualifies for clot-dissolving treatment.

Note any other symptoms. Additional signs that may accompany stroke include sudden severe headache with no known cause, sudden confusion, sudden loss of vision in one or both eyes, sudden dizziness or loss of balance and coordination, and sudden numbness on one side of the body. Report everything you observe to the emergency team.

What Not to Do

Do not wait to see if symptoms improve on their own. A transient ischaemic attack (TIA, sometimes called a "mini-stroke") can produce symptoms that resolve spontaneously, but there is no way to distinguish a TIA from a completed stroke without medical assessment and imaging. Even if symptoms appear to be resolving, the person must be evaluated urgently, because a TIA is itself a strong warning sign that a full stroke may follow soon. Waiting is the most dangerous possible response to these symptoms.

Do not drive the person to hospital yourself if an ambulance can arrive promptly. Paramedics can begin assessment during transport, pre-alert the hospital to activate the stroke team, and intervene if the person deteriorates. However, if ambulance availability is limited or wait times are long, transporting the person by private vehicle to the nearest hospital capable of stroke care is better than continued waiting.

Do not attempt to lower blood pressure with home remedies or medications. Blood pressure is frequently elevated during acute stroke, and the body may be sustaining this elevation deliberately to maintain blood flow to the affected brain area. Lowering it without medical guidance, imaging results, and proper monitoring can worsen brain damage.

Do not let the person fall asleep unmonitored. If they become drowsy, maintain continuous observation of breathing and consciousness until the emergency team arrives.

Information to Provide When Emergency Services Arrive

Give the medical team the time symptoms were first observed or the last known well time, a description of all symptoms and any changes since onset, the person's known medical conditions (particularly hypertension, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, or any previous stroke or TIA), the person's current medications (particularly anticoagulants such as warfarin, rivaroxaban, apixaban, or dabigatran, as these directly affect treatment options), and any known drug allergies. If possible, bring the person's medication bottles or a medication list to the hospital.

Àwọn àmì wọ̀nyí lè jẹ́ àmì àrùn ẹ̀gbà. Èyí jẹ́ pàjáwìrì; ẹ gbọ́dọ̀ gbé ìgbésẹ̀ kíákíá:

Ẹ pe ọkọ̀ ìrànlọ́wọ́ pàjáwìrì tàbí ẹ mú ẹni náà lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn lẹ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀.
Ẹ sọ fún àwọn òṣìṣẹ́ ìlera pé ojú ẹni náà ti yí padà, apá rẹ̀ kan ti rọ̀, kò sì lè sọ̀rọ̀ dáadáa.
Ẹ ṣàkọsílẹ̀ àkókò tí àwọn àmì náà bẹ̀rẹ̀ tàbí ìgbà tí ẹ rí ẹni náà ní àlàáfíà gbẹ̀yìn.
Ẹ jẹ́ kí ẹni náà fara balẹ̀, kí ó sì jókòó tàbí dùbúlẹ̀ ní ipò tí ó rọrùn fún un.
Ẹ má fún un ní oúnjẹ, omi, oògùn, aspirin tàbí agbo. Aspirin lè léwu bí ẹ̀jẹ̀ bá ń jáde nínú ọpọlọ.
Bí kò bá mọ ohun tó ń ṣẹlẹ̀ ṣùgbọ́n tó ṣì ń mí, ẹ tẹ́ ẹ sí ẹ̀gbẹ́, kí ẹ sì máa ṣọ́ bí ó ṣe ń mí.
Bí kò bá ń mí dáadáa, ẹ bẹ̀rẹ̀ ìrànlọ́wọ́ ìtura ọkàn àti èémí, tí a ń pè ní CPR, bí ẹ bá mọ bí a ṣe ń ṣe é, kí ẹ sì tẹ̀ lé ìtọ́ni àwọn òṣìṣẹ́ pàjáwìrì.
Bí àwọn àmì náà bá tilẹ̀ dín kù tàbí parí, ẹ tún mú un lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn lẹ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀.

Ìtọ́jú kíákíá lè dín ìbàjẹ́ ọpọlọ kù, ó sì lè gba ẹ̀mí ẹni náà là.

Àwọn àmì wọ̀nyí lè jẹ́ àmì àrùn ọpọlọ, stroke, ó sì yẹ kí a ka a sí ọ̀ràn pajawiri.

Pe iṣẹ́ pajawiri lẹ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀ tàbí mú ẹni náà lọ sí ẹ̀ka pajawiri ilé ìwòsàn ní kíákíá.
Ṣàkíyèsí àkókò tí àwọn àmì náà bẹ̀rẹ̀, tàbí àkókò tí ẹni náà kẹ́yìn wà dáadáa. Èyí lè ṣe pàtàkì fún ìtọ́jú.
Má ṣe jẹ́ kí ẹni náà jẹun tàbí mu omi bí ó bá ń ṣòro fún un láti mì.
Má ṣe fún un ní oògùn láìsí ìtọ́sọ́nà oníṣègùn.
Jẹ́ kí ó jókòó tàbí dubulẹ̀ ní ààbò, kí ẹ sì máa ṣọ́ ọ títí ìrànlọ́wọ́ yóò fi dé.
Bí ó bá dákú ṣùgbọ́n ó ṣì ń mí, yí i sí ẹ̀gbẹ́ ní ìṣọ́ra.

Má ṣe dúró kí àwọn àmì náà kọjá fúnra wọn. Kódà bí ojú, apá, tàbí ọ̀rọ̀ rẹ̀ bá tún dáa lẹ́yìn ìṣẹ́jú díẹ̀, ó ṣi nílò àyẹ̀wò pajawiri lẹ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀.
