Ihe kpatara ya dị mkpa:

Mgbakọta mgbaàmà atọ a, ụkwara na-adịgide (karịsịa mgbe ọ gafere izu abụọ), agba ọsụsọ n'abalị, na ịta ahụ na-amaghị ihe kpatara ya, bụ mgbaàmà ndị a na-ahụkarị na ọrịa dị iche iche, gụnyere:

Ụkwara ọkpa (Tuberculosis/TB) – nke bụ nchọpụta mbụ ndị dọkịta ga-eche banyere mgbaàmà ndị a, karịsịa ebe TB dị ka nsogbu ahụike a na-ahụkarị.
Ọrịa ndị ọzọ metụtara akụrụngwa iku ume
Ọrịa metụtara mgbochi ahụ
Ọnọdụ ndị ọzọ chọrọ nyocha ọkachamara

Ihe kpatara ọ dị mkpa ka a nyochaa ya n'ụlọ ọgwụ:

TB bụ ọrịa na-efe efe. Ọ bụrụ na ọ bụ TB, onye ahụ nwere ike ibufe ya nye ndị ọzọ, karịsịa ndị ọ na-eso mere azụmahịa n'ime ahịa kwa ụbọchị. Nyocha na ngwụta ọsọ ọsọ ga-agbochi ka ọ gbasaa nye ndị ọzọ.
Ịta ahụ na agba ọsụsọ n'abalị bụ mgbaàmà nkịtị nke ọrịa dị njọ. Ha adịghị esite na iyi ọsụsọ nkịtị ma ọ bụ mgbagwoju anya; ha na-egosi na ahụ na-alụso ihe ọjọọ ọgụ.
Ọgwụgwọ TB dị, mana ọ dị mkpa ịmalite ya ngwa ngwa. Ọ bụrụ na a chọpụtara ya n'oge, a na-agwọ TB kpamkpam site na ọgwụ; mana ọ bụrụ na o were oge, o nwere ike imebi akụrụngwa iku ume ma bụrụ ihe egwu ndụ.
Ịga n'ihu na-arụ ọrụ n'ime ahịa, mgbe ahụ na-ata ma na-esite na ọrịa na-efe efe, nwere ike imebi ma ahụike ya ma nke ndị ọzọ. Izu ike ma nweta nyocha bụ ihe kacha mma ugbu a, ọ bụghị ịga n'ihu na-arụ ọrụ.

Ihe onye ahụ kwesịrị ime:

Gaa n'ụlọ ọgwụ ozugbo maka nyocha ọkụkọ ọbara na foto ntule obi (chest X-ray); ọtụtụ ebe nyocha TB adịghị onwe ego.
Wepụta akwụkwọ nyocha ọkpụkpụ ime akụrụngwa iku ume ma ọ bụrụ na dọkịta chọrọ ya.
Ọ bụrụ na a chọpụtara TB, debe iwu ọgwụgwọ zuru ezu (na-adịkarị ọtụtụ ọnwa), ọ bụghị naanị kwụsị mgbe mgbaàmà kwụsịrị, ka ọ ghara ịlaghachi azụ ma bụrụ ihe siri ike ịgwọ.
Kpachara anya n'inyocha ndị ezinụlọ na ndị mmadụ ọ na-eso mekọrịta ihe, karịsịa ma ọ bụrụ na TB bụ nchọpụta.

Ihe a bụ ozi izugbe gbasara ahụike ọha, ọ bụghị nchọpụta onye ọ bụla. Ọ dị mkpa ka onye ahụ hụ dọkịta ozugbo maka nyocha zuru ezu na nchọpụta ziri ezi.

Mgbaàmà ndị a, ụkwara karịrị izu atọ, ọsụsọ abalị, ike ọgwụgwụ na ibu ahụ na-ada, nwere ike ịbụ ụkwara nta (TB) ma ọ bụ ọrịa ọzọ siri ike. Onye ahụ ekwesịghị iche na ọ bụ naanị uzuzu.

Gaa ụlọọgwụ ma ọ bụ ebe nyocha TB ozugbo ma kọwaa mgbaàmà niile.
Nnyocha dị mkpa n’ihi na mgbaàmà naanị agaghị akwado TB. Ọ bụrụ na nnwale mbụ gosie nje TB, a ga-eme nyocha ndị ọzọ iji mata ma ọ bụ TB na-arụ ọrụ.
Ka a na-eche nyocha, kpuchie ọnụ na imi mgbe a na-akwa ụkwara, yiri mkpuchi imi na ọnụ ma ọ bụrụ na ọ dị, saa aka, ma hụ na ikuku na-abata nke ọma n’ụlọ ma ọ bụ ebe ahịa. CDC na-akwado ụkpụrụ ụkwara na mkpuchi ọnụ/imi iji belata mgbasa TB.
Ọ bụrụ na ọ na-akwa ọbara, iku ume esie ike, ma ọ bụ ọnọdụ ya na-akawanye njọ, chọọ enyemaka mberede.

Nnyocha na ọgwụgwọ n’oge nwere ike ichebe onye ahụ, ezinụlọ ya, ndị ahịa na obodo.

Mgbaàmà ndị a, ụkwara karịrị izu atọ, ọsụsọ abalị, ike ọgwụgwụ na ibu ahụ na-ada, nwere ike igosi ụkwara nta (TB) ma ọ bụ ọrịa ọzọ. Ekwesịghị ịsị na ọ bụ naanị uzuzu.

Gaa ụlọọgwụ ma ọ bụ ebe nyocha TB ozugbo. Nnyocha dị mkpa n’ihi na mgbaàmà ndị a nwekwara ike ịbụ ọrịa ndị ọzọ, ya mere naanị ule ga-enyere aka ịchọpụta ihe kpatara ha.
Ka a na-eche nyocha, kpuchie ọnụ na imi mgbe a na-akwa ụkwara, yiri mkpuchi ọnụ na imi ma ọ bụrụ na ọ dị, ma mee ka ikuku na-abata nke ọma n’ụlọ na ebe ọrụ.
Belata ịnọ n’ebe ndị mmadụ juru ma ọ bụ n’ime ụlọ mechiri emechi ruo mgbe ndị ọrụ ahụike nyochachara ya.
Ọ bụrụ na ọ na-akwa ọbara, iku ume esie ike, ma ọ bụ ọnọdụ ya na-akawanye njọ, chọọ enyemaka mberede.

Nnyocha na ọgwụgwọ n’oge na-echebe onye ahụ ma na-enyere aka igbochi mgbasa TB ma ọ bụrụ na ule akwado ya.

Mgbaàmà ndị a, ụkwara karịrị izu atọ, ọsụsọ abalị, ike ọgwụgwụ na ibu ahụ na-ada, nwere ike igosi ụkwara nta (TB) ma ọ bụ ọrịa ọzọ. E kwesịghị ikwu na uzuzu naanị kpatara ya.

Gaa ụlọọgwụ ma ọ bụ ebe nyocha TB ozugbo. Ndị ọrụ ahụike nwere ike ime nyocha sputum, nyocha ngwa ngwa ma ọ bụ nyocha obi dịka o kwesịrị.
Ka a na-eche nyocha, kpuchie ọnụ mgbe a na-akwa ụkwara, yiri mkpuchi ọnụ na imi ma ọ bụrụ na ọ dị, ma mee ka ikuku na-abata nke ọma n’ebe ọrụ na ụlọ.

If a child has repeated seizures, the family should treat this as a medical condition that needs professional assessment, not assume the child is possessed.

During a seizure:

Keep the child away from fire, sharp objects, traffic, stairs, or anything that could cause injury.
Place something soft under the head and loosen tight clothing around the neck.
If possible, turn the child onto their side once it is safe to do so, especially after the shaking stops, to help keep the airway clear.
Do not restrain the child.
Do not put a spoon, fingers, herbs, water, medicine, or any other object into the child's mouth. A person having a seizure cannot swallow their tongue.
Note how long the seizure lasts and what happens during it.

Seek urgent medical help if the seizure lasts about 5 minutes or longer, another seizure begins before the child recovers, the child has difficulty breathing, is seriously injured, the seizure happened in water, or this is the child's first known seizure. Repeated seizures also warrant medical evaluation to determine the cause and appropriate treatment.

To reduce stigma, family members can explain calmly that seizures can result from medical conditions affecting the brain and are not evidence that a child is possessed, cursed, or responsible for what is happening. The child should not be punished, isolated, mocked, restrained, or excluded from school and family activities because of seizures.

Religious or cultural support can be important to a family, but it should not replace medical assessment or lead to harmful practices. The safest approach is to combine respectful family support with appropriate healthcare and accurate information about seizures.

This is a situation where the family's love for the child, safety, and community relationships all matter — and none of them require accepting the "possessed" label.

What the family should do for the child's safety:

Get the child evaluated by a doctor, ideally one who can assess for epilepsy or a seizure disorder. Repeated seizures need proper diagnosis — there could be an underlying cause (fever-related seizures in young children, epilepsy, an infection, an injury, or other neurological conditions) that responds well to treatment once identified.
Keep a seizure diary — note when seizures happen, how long they last, and what happens before/during/after. This helps doctors identify patterns and choose the right treatment.
Follow the safety steps during a seizure: clear the area of hazards, cushion the head, turn the child on their side once possible, don't restrain them, and don't put anything in their mouth. Call emergency care if a seizure lasts more than 5 minutes or the child has trouble breathing afterward.
Don't stop or delay treatment because of the stigma. Untreated seizure disorders can worsen over time and increase risk of injury during seizures — getting medical care is the most protective thing the family can do.

Responding to the "possessed" claims without shaming anyone:

Don't publicly argue or humiliate neighbours who believe this — it tends to entrench the belief and isolate the family further. A calmer, private conversation tends to go further.
Share what you're learning from doctors, gently. Something like: "We took him to the doctor and they explained it's a condition in the brain called epilepsy — it's actually common, and there's medicine that helps control it." Simple, factual, non-defensive framing often does more than direct confrontation.
Find one or two respected community members (a religious leader, elder, or health worker) who understand epilepsy and can help normalize it to others — community messengers are often more persuasive than outsiders.
Protect the child from bullying or isolation. Talk to teachers, extended family, and close neighbours directly so the child isn't excluded from school or play because of misunderstanding.
Know you don't have to change everyone's mind at once. Reducing stigma is often gradual — protecting the child's access to care and dignity matters more than winning every conversation.

What matters most for the child's safety is that medical evaluation and treatment aren't abandoned or delayed while other explanations are explored.

A child having repeated seizures needs immediate medical attention, and how the family handles both the seizures themselves and the community reaction matters a lot for the child's safety and wellbeing.

Responding safely during a seizure:

Stay calm and protect the child from injury. Clear the area of hard or sharp objects, and if possible, gently turn the child onto their side to help keep the airway open.
Do not restrain the child or hold them down. This can cause injury and doesn't stop the seizure.
Do not put anything in the child's mouth. This is a common myth, but it can cause choking or injury; a person having a seizure cannot swallow their tongue.
Time the seizure. If it lasts longer than 5 minutes, or if the child has trouble breathing afterward, doesn't regain consciousness, or has repeated seizures without recovering in between, this is a medical emergency requiring immediate care.
After the seizure, keep the child calm and let them rest. Confusion afterward is normal and temporary.

Why medical evaluation matters:

Repeated seizures (epilepsy) have identifiable medical causes, things like fever-related seizures in young children, birth complications, infections affecting the brain, low blood sugar, or other neurological conditions. A doctor can help identify the cause and often prescribe medication that significantly reduces or stops seizures entirely. Left unevaluated, some underlying causes can worsen or become harder to treat.

On the possession belief and stigma:

This belief is common in many communities, and it usually comes from genuine concern and a need to make sense of something frightening, not malice. A few things can help:

The family doesn't need to argue or dismiss the neighbours' beliefs to seek medical care. These aren't mutually exclusive in most families' eyes, spiritual support and medical treatment can happen alongside each other.
Explaining seizures in plain terms can help reduce fear. Seizures happen because of unusual electrical activity in the brain, this is something doctors understand and can often treat.
Delaying care due to stigma carries real risk. Untreated epilepsy can lead to injury during seizures, learning difficulties if the underlying cause goes unaddressed, and in rare cases, life-threatening complications.
Isolating the child or treating them differently because of the seizures can cause lasting harm, beyond the seizures themselves, affecting the child's schooling, friendships, and self-esteem.
Community health workers or NCDC-linked outreach programs (where available) sometimes have experience helping families navigate this exact situation, bridging community beliefs with medical care in a respectful way.

If neighbours continue insisting on spiritual explanations, the family doesn't have to publicly debate it. Quietly getting the child seen by a doctor while continuing whatever practices bring the family comfort is a reasonable and common path many families take.

Time the seizure and stay nearby.
Do not restrain the child or put anything into the mouth.
Seek emergency help if it lasts over five minutes, seizures repeat without recovery, breathing becomes difficult, or the child does not wake afterwards.

Ohun tí ìdílé gbọ́dọ̀ ṣe fún ààbò ọmọ náà:

Ẹ mú ọmọ náà lọ sọ́dọ̀ dókítà kí wọ́n ṣe àyẹ̀wò rẹ̀ dáadáa, ó máa dára jù bí ó bá jẹ́ dókítà tí ó lè ṣàyẹ̀wò fún wárápá tàbí àìsàn gírí. Ẹ pa àkọsílẹ̀ gírí náà mọ́ — kọ ìgbà tí ó ṣẹlẹ̀, bí ó ṣe pẹ́ tó, àti ohun tí ó ṣẹlẹ̀ ṣáájú/nígbà/lẹ́yìn rẹ̀. Èyí máa ràn àwọn dókítà lọ́wọ́ láti rí ìlànà tí ó ń tẹ̀lé, kí wọ́n sì yan ìtọ́jú tí ó tọ́.
Ẹ tẹ̀lé àwọn ìṣísẹ̀ ààbò nígbà tí gírí bá ń ṣẹlẹ̀: ẹ yọ ohunkóhun tí ó léwu kúrò ní àyíká rẹ̀, ẹ fi ohun rírọ̀ tì orí rẹ̀, ẹ yí ọmọ náà padà sí ìhà kan lẹ́yìn tí ó bá ṣeé ṣe, ẹ má ṣe dìmú un, ẹ má sì fi ohunkóhun sínú ẹnu rẹ̀. Ẹ pe pàjáwìrì bí gírí náà bá ju ìṣẹ́jú 5 lọ tàbí bí ọmọ náà bá ní ìṣòro mímí lẹ́yìn náà.
Ẹ má ṣe dá ìtọ́jú dúró tàbí fa á lọ́rùn nítorí ìtìjú. Àìsàn gírí tí a kò tọ́jú lè burú sí i lákòókò, ó sì lè mú kí ewu ìpalára pọ̀ sí i nígbà gírí — láti gba ìtọ́jú ìṣègùn ni ọ̀nà ààbò tí ó dára jù tí ìdílé lè fún ọmọ náà.

Bí a ṣe lè dáhùn sí ọ̀rọ̀ "alábara" láìdójútì ẹnikẹ́ni:

Ẹ má ṣe jà tàbí dójú ti àwọn aládùúgbò ní gbangba tí wọ́n gbàgbọ́ nínú èyí — ó máa ń mú kí wọ́n rọ̀ mọ́ ìgbàgbọ́ wọn kí ó sì mú kí ìdílé ya sọ́tọ̀ sí i. Ìjíròrò jẹ́ẹ́, ní àdáni, sábà máa ń ṣiṣẹ́ dáradára ju bẹ́ẹ̀ lọ.
Ẹ pín ohun tí ẹ ń kọ́ láti ọ̀dọ̀ àwọn dókítà, ní ọ̀nà jẹ́ẹ́. Bí i: "A mú un lọ sọ́dọ̀ dókítà, wọ́n sì ṣàlàyé pé àìsàn kan ń ṣẹlẹ̀ ní ọpọlọ tí a ń pè ní wárápá — ó wọ́pọ̀ gan-an, ògùn sì wà tí ó lè ràn án lọ́wọ́ láti darí i." Ọ̀rọ̀ tí ó rọrùn, tí ó dá lórí òtítọ́, tí kò sì ní ìwà ẹ̀mí-ìjà sábà máa ń ṣiṣẹ́ dáradára ju àríyànjiyàn tààrà lọ.
Ẹ wá ọ̀kan tàbí méjì lára àwọn ènìyàn tí àdúgbò bọ̀wọ̀ fún (aṣáájú ìjọsìn, àgbà, tàbí òṣìṣẹ́ ìlera) tí ó ní òye wárápá tí ó sì lè ràn ẹ́ lọ́wọ́ láti mú kí àwọn mìíràn gbà á gẹ́gẹ́ bí ohun tí ó wọ́pọ̀ — ẹni tí ó ti inú àdúgbò wá sábà máa ń ní agbára ìdánilójú ju àjòjì lọ.

Ẹ mọ̀ pé kò yẹ kí ẹ yí èrò gbogbo ènìyàn padà lẹ́ẹ̀kan náà. Dídín ìtìjú kù sábà máa ń jẹ́ ìlànà tí ó lọ díẹ̀díẹ̀ — láti dáàbò bo àǹfààní ọmọ náà sí ìtọ́jú àti iyì rẹ̀ ṣe pàtàkì ju bíborí gbogbo àríyànjiyàn lọ.

Ó ṣe pàtàkì kí ẹbí náà tọ́jú ọmọ náà ní kánkán nígbà tí wárápá bá ń mú un, kí wọ́n sì tún fi ọgbọ́n bójútó ọ̀rọ̀ tí àwọn aládùúgbò ń sọ, nítorí méjèèjì ṣe pàtàkì fún àìléwu àti ìlera ọmọ náà.

Bí a ṣe lè dáàbò bo ọmọ náà nígbà tí wárápá bá ń mú un:

E kwesịghị iti ya ihe, kee ya agbụ, zoo ya, kpọọ ya aha ọjọọ, ma ọ bụ wepụ ya n’ụlọ akwụkwọ na ndụ ezinụlọ.

Ọ bụrụ na ekpere ma ọ bụ nkwado omenala dị mkpa nye ezinụlọ, enwere ike iji ya dịka nkwado, mana ọ gaghị edochi nyocha na ọgwụgwọ ahụike ma ọ bụ mee ka nlekọta kwesịrị ekwesị gbuo oge.

Nke a bụ ọnọdụ ebe ịhụnanya ezinụlọ nwere maka nwatakịrị ahụ, nchekwa ya, na otú ha na ndị agbataobi ha si emekọrịta ihe niile dị mkpa — ọ dịghịkwa n'ime ha chọrọ ka ezinụlọ nabata okwu "ogbanje" ahụ.

Ihe ezinụlọ kwesịrị ime maka nchekwa nwatakịrị ahụ:

Kpọga nwatakịrị ahụ ka dọkịta lelee ya nke ọma, ọ kaara ma ọ bụrụ dọkịta nwere ike lelee maka epilepsy ma ọ bụ nsogbu ọdịdọ. Ọdịdọ na-emekarị chọrọ nyocha ziri ezi — ọ nwere ike bụrụ na e nwere ihe kpatara ya (ọdịdọ metụtara ọkụ ahụ n'ime ụmụaka nta, epilepsy, ọrịa nje, mmerụ ahụ, ma ọ bụ nsogbu ụbụrụ ndị ọzọ) nke nwere ike ịza ọgwụgwọ nke ọma ozugbo achọpụtara ya.
Debe akwụkwọ ndekọ maka ọdịdọ ahụ — dekọọ mgbe ọ na-eme, ogologo oge ọ na-ewe, na ihe na-eme tupu/n'oge/mgbe ọdịdọ ahụ gasịrị. Nke a na-enyere dọkịta aka ịmata usoro ma họrọ ọgwụgwọ ziri ezi.
Soro usoro nchekwa mgbe ọdịdọ na-eme: wepụ ihe ize ndụ dị gburugburu ya, chịkọba isi ya, tụgharịa nwatakịrị ahụ gburugburu mgbe o kwe omume, ejila ya aka ike, etinyekwala ihe ọ bụla n'ọnụ ya. Kpọọ ndị ọrụ mberede ma ọdịdọ ahụ karịa nkeji 5 ma ọ bụ na nwatakịrị ahụ enwe nsogbu iku ume mgbe ọ gasịrị.
Akwụsịla ma ọ bụ igbu oge n'ime ọgwụgwọ n'ihi ihere. Ọdịdọ a na-agwọghị nwere ike ka njọ n'ime oge, meekwa ka enwe ohere ka o merụọ ahụ n'oge ọdịdọ — inweta nlekọta ahụike bụ ihe kachasị enye nchekwa nke ezinụlọ nwere ike ime.

Ka a ga-esi zaghachi maka nkwuputa "ogbanje" n'emeghị ka onye ọ bụla mee ihere:

Alụla esemokwu ọha na eze ma ọ bụ mee ka ndị agbataobi mee ihere ndị kwenyere na nke a — ọ na-eme ka okwukwe ahụ sikwuo ike ma na-emekwa ka ezinụlọ ahụ dịkwuo iche. Mkparịta ụka jụụ, na nzuzo, na-arụkarị ọrụ karịa.
Kekọrịta ihe ị na-amụta n'aka ndị dọkịta, jiri obiụtọ. Ihe dị ka: "Anyị kpọgara ya dọkịta, ha akọwaala na ọ bụ ọrịa ụbụrụ nke a na-akpọ epilepsy — ọ na-adịkarị, ọgwụ dịkwa nke na-enyere aka jide ya n'aka." Okwu dị mfe, nke gbadoro ụkwụ n'eziokwu, nke anaghị echekwa onwe ya na-arụkarị ọrụ karịa esemokwu ọzọ.
Chọta otu ma ọ bụ mmadụ abụọ obodo na-akwanyere ùgwù (onye ndú okpukpe, okenye, ma ọ bụ onye ọrụ ahụike) maara epilepsy nke nwere ike inyere aka ime ka ọ dị nkịtị n'anya ndị ọzọ — ndị ozi si n'ime obodo na-enwekarị ike ime ka mmadụ kwenye karịa ndị ọbịa.
Chebe nwatakịrị ahụ site n'ịkpasu iwe ma ọ bụ nzụpụ. Gwa nkuzi, ndị ezinụlọ zuru ezu, na ndị agbataobi chọrọ nso okwu ozugbo ka a ghara ịjụ nwatakịrị ahụ n'ụlọ akwụkwọ ma ọ bụ n'egwuregwu n'ihi enweghị nghọta.
Mara na ị dịghị mkpa ịgbanwe uche onye ọ bụla n'otu oge. Ibelata nkọcha na-abụkarị nke na-eji nwayọọ eme — ichekwa ohere nwatakịrị ahụ maka nlekọta na ugwu ya dị mkpa karịa imeri esemokwu ọ bụla.

Dị ka anyị kwuru na mbụ maka ajụjụ yiri nke a, ọtụtụ ezinụlọ na-eme omume mmụọ ha ọnụ na nlekọta ahụike kama ịhọrọ otu ma hapụ nke ọzọ — nke a nwekwara ike ịbụ eziokwu ebe a. Ihe kacha mkpa maka nchekwa nwatakịrị ahụ bụ na enyocha ahụike na ọgwụgwọ agaghị akwụsị ma ọ bụ egbu oge mgbe a na-achọpụta nkọwa ndị ọzọ.

Ọ dị mkpa ka ezinụlọ lekọta nwatakịrị a mgbe ihe ọdido na-eme, ma jirikwa nwayọọ jikwaa okwu ndị agbataobi na-ekwu, n'ihi na ihe abụọ a dị mkpa maka nchekwa na ahụike nwatakịrị ahụ.

Otu esi elekọta nwatakịrị mgbe ihe ọdido na-eme:

Nọrọ jụụ, chebe nwatakịrị ahụ ka ọ ghara imerụ ahụ́. Wepụ ihe ndị siri ike ma ọ bụ nke dị nkọ n'ebe ọ nọ; ọ bụrụ na o kwe omume, tụgharịa nwatakịrị ahụ nwayọọ gaa n'akụkụ ka ume gbanye ya nke ọma.
Ejide nwatakịrị ahụ aka ma ọ bụ manye ya ka o guzo ọtọ. Nke a nwere ike ime ka o merụọ ahụ, ọ gaghịkwa akwụsị ihe ọdido ahụ.
Etinye ihe ọ bụla n'ọnụ nwatakịrị ahụ. Nke a bụ echiche na-ezighị ezi; ọ nwere ike ime ka o loo ihe ọ bụla ma ọ bụ merụọ ahụ; onye na-enwe ihe ọdido enweghị ike ilo ire ya.
Gụọ oge ihe ọdido ahụ na-adịru. Ọ bụrụ na ọ karịrị nkeji ise, ma ọ bụ na nwatakịrị enweghị ike iku ume nke ọma mgbe ihe ọdido gasịrị, ma ọ bụ na o teghị mgbe ọzọ ihe ọdido bidoro n'agbanyeghị na nke mbụ akwụsịbeghị, nke a bụ ihe mberede, kpọga ya n'ụlọ ọgwụ ozugbo.
Mgbe ihe ọdido gasịrị, hapụ ka nwatakịrị ahụ zuo ike ma nọrọ jụụ. Ọ bụ ihe nkịtị ka nwatakịrị gharịa ụzọ nwa oge, ọ ga-adịghachi ka ọ dị mgbe oge gafere.

Ihe kpatara nyocha ahụike ji dị mkpa:

Ihe ọdido na-emegharị emegharị (epilepsy) nwere ihe kpatara ya, dị ka ọkụ ahụ na-akpata ihe ọdido na ụmụaka nta, nsogbu mgbe amuru nwa, ọrịa metụtara ụbụrụ, mmiri ahụ dị ala, ma ọ bụ ọnọdụ ndị ọzọ metụtara ụbụrụ. Dọkịta nwere ike ịmata ihe kpatara ya ma nye ọgwụ nke na-eme ka ihe ọdido belata ma ọ bụ kwụsị kpamkpam. Ọ bụrụ na a nyochaghị, ụfọdụ ihe kpatara ya nwere ike ịka njọ ma sie ike ịgwọ.

Banyere echiche "ogbanje" na ihere na-esote ya:

Echiche a bụ ihe a na-ahụkarị n'ọtụtụ obodo, ọ na-abụkarịkwa site na nchegbu n'ezie na mmasị ịghọta ihe na-atụ egwu, ọ bụghị site na obi ọjọọ. Ihe ndị a nwere ike inyere ezinụlọ aka:

Ezinụlọ anaghị achọ ịrụrịta ụka ma ọ bụ jụ echiche ndị agbataobi tupu ha achọta ọgwụgwọ ahụike. Ha abụọ anaghị emegiderịta ibe ha n'anya ọtụtụ ezinụlọ; nkwado mmụọ na ọgwụgwọ ahụike nwere ike ịdị n'otu oge.
Ịkọwa ihe ọdido n'ụzọ dị mfe nwere ike ibelata egwu. Ihe ọdido na-abịakarị site na ọrụ eletriki ụbụrụ na-adịghị nkịtị, nke a bụ ihe dọkịta ghọtara nke ọma ma nwee ike ịgwọ.
Ịrapara ọgwụgwọ n'ihi ihere nwere ihe egwu n'ezie. Ihe ọdido a na-agwọghị nwere ike ịkpata mmerụ ahụ mgbe ọ na-eme, nsogbu mmụta ọ bụrụ na e degharịghị ihe kpatara ya, na n'ọnọdụ ụfọdụ, ọ nwere ike ịbụ ihe egwu ndụ.
Ịkewapụ nwatakịrị ahụ ma ọ bụ mesoo ya omume dị iche n'ihi ihe ọdido ahụ nwere ike ịkpata mmerụ obi nke ga-adịgide, nke ga-emetụta akwụkwọ ya, ọbụbụenyi ya, na otú o si ele onwe ya anya.
Ndị ọrụ ahụike obodo ma ọ bụ mmemme NCDC (ebe ha dị) mgbe ụfọdụ nwere ahụmịhe iji nyere ezinụlọ aka gafere ọnọdụ dị otú a, na-ejikọta echiche obodo na ọgwụgwọ ahụike n'ụzọ na-akwanyere ùgwù.

Ọ bụrụ na ndị agbataobi na-agbaso ikwu na ọ bụ ihe mmụọ, ezinụlọ anaghị achọ ịrụ ụka banyere ya n'ihu ọha. Ka ha jiri nwayọọ kpọga nwatakịrị ahụ ka dọkịta hụ ya, ma na-aga n'ihu na omenala ọ bụla na-enye ha nkasi obi, nke a bụ ụzọ ọtụtụ ezinụlọ agbasoola na mbụ.

Ihe ọdịdọ ugboro ugboro bụ nsogbu ahụike ụbụrụ, ọ bụghị ihe akaebe na nwatakịrị bụ ogbanje. Kpọga nwatakịrị ahụ ụlọọgwụ ngwa ngwa maka nyocha na ọgwụgwọ kwesịrị ekwesị.

Nọrọ nso, wepụ ihe siri ike ma ọ bụ dị nkọ.
Tinye ihe dị nro n’okpuru isi, tụgharịa nwatakịrị ahụ n’akụkụ.
Tulee oge ọdịdọ ahụ.
Ejidela nwatakịrị ahụ ike, etinyekwala ngaji, ọgwụ, nri, mmiri ma ọ bụ ihe ọ bụla n’ọnụ ya.
Chọọ enyemaka mberede ma ọ bụrụ na ọ gafee nkeji ise, ọzọ amalite tupu nwatakịrị ahụ agbakee, iku ume esie ike, mmerụ ahụ emee, ma ọ bụ nwatakịrị ahụ etetaghị.

Chebe nzuzo nwatakịrị ahụ ma kwụsị ịkpa ókè, mmegbu na omume nwere ike imerụ ya.

Community Response to Suspected Ebola: Immediate Actions

If someone in a community develops symptoms that could indicate Ebola, here's what should happen:

Immediate Steps

Isolate the person immediately. Separate them in a dedicated space—ideally a separate room or designated quarantine area—away from other community members, especially children, elderly, and immunocompromised individuals. This is the single most critical action.

Minimize contact. Only essential caregivers should interact with the person, and they must use barrier protection: gloves, aprons, masks, and eye protection. Avoid direct contact with blood, bodily fluids, or contaminated materials.

Alert health authorities without delay. Contact the nearest health clinic, district health office, or national disease surveillance hotline immediately. Do not wait. Provide exact location, symptom timeline, and any recent travel history. Early notification enables rapid response teams to isolate, test, and treat the case.

Safe handling of bodily fluids. If the person vomits, bleeds, or passes stool, treat all waste as biohazard. Use chlorine solution (0.5% concentration) to disinfect contaminated surfaces, bedding, and clothing. Bury or safely dispose of contaminated materials per health authority guidance.

Secure the burial. If death occurs, the body remains highly infectious. Only trained burial teams—never family members—should handle the body using full protective equipment. Community burials without training drive transmission and must be prevented.

What NOT to Do
Do not touch the person's blood or body fluids without protection
Do not hold community ceremonies involving contact with the body
Do not send the person to a general market or public space
Do not delay reporting to authorities hoping to manage it locally
Do not use traditional remedies in place of medical care
Why This Matters

Ebola spreads through direct contact with blood or body fluids of infected or deceased people. Community transmission is driven by unsafe handling during illness and burial. Early isolation and professional management save lives—both the patient's and the community's.

Community Response to Suspected Ebola Symptoms
Recognising Potential Symptoms

Ebola virus disease typically presents with sudden onset of fever, severe headache, muscle pain, fatigue, and weakness, followed by vomiting, diarrhoea, and in some cases unexplained bleeding or bruising. The incubation period ranges from 2 to 21 days, with symptom onset most common between 8 and 10 days after exposure. These symptoms overlap with malaria, typhoid, and other febrile illnesses, which makes clinical differentiation difficult without laboratory testing.

Immediate Actions

Isolate the individual without direct physical contact. The symptomatic person should be separated from others in a well-ventilated room or area. No one should touch the person, their bodily fluids, clothing, or bedding without appropriate protection. Ebola spreads through direct contact with blood, vomit, faeces, sweat, and other body fluids of an infected person, as well as contaminated surfaces and materials.

Alert health authorities immediately. Contact the nearest health facility, disease surveillance officer, or national disease reporting hotline. In Nigeria, the relevant authority is the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control (NCDC). Provide the person's symptoms, symptom onset date, and any known contact with confirmed or suspected Ebola cases, recent travel to affected areas, or contact with wildlife (particularly bats or primates). Early notification accelerates laboratory confirmation and activates the public health response chain.

Designate a single caregiver if absolutely necessary. If the person requires immediate assistance before health workers arrive, one individual (preferably someone trained or briefed by health personnel) should provide care while minimising direct skin-to-skin contact. That caregiver should cover exposed skin as much as possible and wash hands thoroughly with soap and water or chlorine solution (0.05% for handwashing) after any interaction.

What the Community Must Avoid

Do not wash or prepare the body if the person dies. Ebola viral load is extremely high at and after death. Traditional burial washing and preparation practices have been a major driver of transmission in every major outbreak documented by the WHO. Safe and dignified burial must be conducted by trained teams.

Do not self-treat or administer traditional remedies as a substitute for medical referral. No herbal or traditional preparation has demonstrated efficacy against Ebola virus. Delay in seeking formal medical care worsens individual outcomes and increases community transmission risk.

Do not hide the sick person or avoid reporting. Concealment allows uncontrolled transmission chains. Fear of stigma or quarantine has historically delayed reporting in West and Central African outbreaks, directly contributing to wider spread.

Do not touch or handle items contaminated with the person's body fluids (bedding, clothing, utensils) without guidance from health workers. Contaminated materials require disinfection with 0.5% chlorine solution.

Contact Tracing Cooperation

Once a suspect case is reported, public health teams will identify everyone who had direct contact with the symptomatic person. Community members should cooperate fully with contact tracing, provide accurate information about interactions, and monitor themselves for symptoms for 21 days. Contacts are not infectious unless they develop symptoms, but daily temperature monitoring and health checks allow rapid detection if disease develops.

Preparing the Community

Communities in or near areas with known Ebola transmission should proactively establish a relationship with local health authorities, identify an isolation area, stockpile soap and chlorine solution, and agree on a communication plan for rapid notification. Community health workers or volunteers should receive basic infection prevention briefings before an outbreak reaches the area, not after.

Source Basis

The guidance above reflects published protocols from the World Health Organization (WHO) Ebola virus disease fact sheets, the WHO manual on Infection Prevention and Control guidance for Ebola, and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Ebola response guidelines. Specific chlorine concentrations (0.05% for handwashing, 0.5% for surface/material decontamination) follow WHO environmental infection control recommendations. The 2–21 day incubation period and transmission routes are established in the peer-reviewed epidemiological literature from the 2013–2016 West Africa and 2018–2020 DRC outbreaks.

Communities should verify current national protocols with their ministry of health or equivalent authority, as response procedures may be updated between outbreaks.

What a Community Should Do If Someone Develops Symptoms That Could Indicate Ebola
Recognising Potential Symptoms

Ebola virus disease typically begins suddenly with fever, severe headache, muscle pain, intense fatigue and weakness, vomiting, and diarrhoea. In some cases, unexplained bleeding or bruising may occur, including bleeding from the gums, nose, eyes, or in stool and vomit. The incubation period ranges from 2 to 21 days, with symptom onset most common between 8 and 10 days after exposure. These symptoms overlap significantly with malaria, typhoid fever, meningitis, and other febrile illnesses common in areas where Ebola occurs, which means clinical observation alone cannot confirm the diagnosis. Only laboratory testing can establish whether the cause is Ebola.

Immediate Actions

Isolate the symptomatic person without direct physical contact. Move or guide the person to a separate, well-ventilated room or area. No one should touch the person, their body fluids (blood, vomit, stool, urine, sweat, saliva), their clothing, their bedding, or any objects those fluids have contacted. Ebola transmits through direct contact with the body fluids of a symptomatic or deceased infected person, and through surfaces and materials contaminated with those fluids. This separation is not a social rejection of the individual. It is the medically correct action that protects both the community and the sick person's chance of survival by keeping the situation contained until professional care arrives.

Notify health authorities immediately. Contact the nearest health facility, the local or state disease surveillance and notification officer, or the national disease reporting channel. In Nigeria, this means contacting the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) toll-free line or the relevant state epidemiologist. Provide a clear account of the person's symptoms, when symptoms began, any recent travel (particularly to areas with known Ebola transmission), any known contact with a person who was ill with similar symptoms or who recently died, and any contact with wildlife, particularly bats or non-human primates. This notification is the single most consequential action anyone in the community can take, because it initiates the sequence of laboratory testing, clinical case management, and contact tracing on which both individual survival and community-wide containment depend.

If assistance to the sick person is absolutely necessary before health workers arrive, designate only one person to provide care. That individual should cover all exposed skin as completely as possible: long sleeves, long trousers, closed shoes, and gloves if available. If gloves are not available, plastic bags secured over the hands provide a partial barrier. The caregiver must avoid any contact with body fluids, and must wash hands immediately and thoroughly with soap and water or 0.05% chlorine solution after every interaction. This person should be registered as a contact for subsequent daily monitoring.

What the Community Must Not Do

Do not wash or prepare the body if the person dies. Viral load in the body of a person who has died from Ebola is extremely high, higher than at any point during the illness. Traditional burial preparation involving washing, touching, and dressing the body has been one of the most significant drivers of transmission in every major Ebola outbreak documented by the WHO, including the 2013–2016 West Africa outbreak and the 2018–2020 DRC outbreaks. Only trained burial teams should handle the body. Safe and dignified burial protocols exist that respect cultural practices while preventing transmission, and health authorities can facilitate access to these teams.

Do not administer traditional medicines or herbal remedies as a substitute for medical referral. No traditional preparation has demonstrated efficacy against Ebola virus disease in any clinical trial or laboratory study. Attempting traditional treatment delays the person's arrival at a health facility, where supportive care (particularly intravenous fluid replacement) significantly improves survival. The physical contact required to administer traditional remedies also creates a direct transmission pathway.

Do not conceal the sick person or refuse to report. Hiding a symptomatic individual allows uncontrolled transmission. In the 2014–2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak and the 2018–2020 DRC outbreaks, fear of stigma, quarantine, and disruption to family life led families to conceal sick members and conduct secret burials. Post-outbreak evaluations by WHO, UNICEF, and IFRC consistently identify concealment as one of the behaviours most directly responsible for amplifying transmission chains and increasing the final death toll.

Do not touch or handle items contaminated with the person's body fluids (bedding, clothing, utensils, surfaces) without guidance from health workers. Contaminated materials require disinfection with 0.5% chlorine solution under protocols that health teams will provide.

Cooperating with Contact Tracing

Once a suspected case is reported, public health teams will identify every person who had direct physical contact with the symptomatic individual or with their body fluids, clothing, or bedding. These contacts must be monitored daily for 21 days, typically through temperature checks and symptom screening. A contact person is not infectious and cannot transmit Ebola to others unless and until they themselves develop symptoms. However, daily monitoring ensures that if a contact does become symptomatic, they are detected and isolated rapidly, before they can expose others.

Community members must provide honest and complete information about who had contact with the sick person, when, and in what manner. Providing false information to contact tracers, whether to protect a family member from monitoring or to avoid perceived social consequences, is among the most dangerous individual actions during an outbreak. It allows a potentially infected person to circulate unmonitored, creating the conditions for a new transmission chain.

Addressing Fear and Preventing Harmful Stigma

Fear of Ebola is a rational response to a disease with a high case fatality rate. However, the community must distinguish between appropriate infection-prevention behaviour and harmful social exclusion of the affected family.

Appropriate precaution consists of avoiding direct physical contact with the sick person and their body fluids, maintaining distance during the acute illness, and self-monitoring for symptoms if prior contact occurred.

Harmful exclusion consists of refusing all communication with the family, withholding food and water from the household, blocking the family from accessing health services, spreading the family's identity with stigmatising labels such as "the Ebola family," threatening or attacking family members, or preventing non-symptomatic household members from participating in community life.

The second category of behaviour does not reduce transmission risk. It increases it, because families subjected to stigma and exclusion are more likely to conceal illness, avoid health facilities, refuse cooperation with contact tracers, and attempt secret burials. Every one of these responses has been documented as a direct amplifier of transmission in post-outbreak evaluations. The community's task is to maintain both caution and solidarity simultaneously: genuine vigilance about the disease, and genuine support for a family in crisis. These are not contradictory objectives. Caution without solidarity produces concealment. Solidarity without caution produces transmission. Both together produce the conditions under which outbreaks are controlled.

Maintain communication with the family. Speak to them from a safe distance or by phone. Inform them of what is being done, that health authorities have been contacted, and what to expect. Isolation from information compounds fear and distrust on both sides.

Ensure the family has access to essentials. Food, clean water, and necessities can be delivered without physical contact by leaving items at the household entrance. A family cut off from basic supplies during a health emergency is more likely to flee, hide the illness, or refuse cooperation.

Do not exclude non-symptomatic family members from community life without medical justification. Household members who are not showing symptoms are not infectious. They should be monitored, but they should not be treated as though they are already ill. Excluding healthy family members from work, school, or markets causes economic and psychological harm that erodes the cooperation the response requires.

Community Preparedness

Communities in or near areas with known or historical Ebola transmission should prepare before an outbreak reaches them.

Establish a relationship with local health authorities and know who to contact and how. Identify a space that can serve as an isolation area: well-ventilated, away from common gathering areas, with access to water and a latrine. Stockpile soap and chlorine solution. Agree on a communication plan for rapid notification if a suspected case appears. Community health workers or volunteers should receive basic infection-prevention training before an outbreak begins, not after.

This guidance reflects WHO Ebola virus disease fact sheets and infection prevention and control guidance, CDC Ebola response guidelines, the WHO Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE) framework, published evaluations of community engagement and stigma dynamics during the 2013–2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak and the 2018–2020 DRC Ebola outbreaks, and WHO/UNICEF/IFRC joint guidance on community feedback mechanisms and safe and dignified burial. Specific infection-prevention parameters (0.05% chlorine for handwashing, 0.5% chlorine for surface and material decontamination, 21-day contact monitoring period) follow WHO clinical and environmental health guidance. Transmission characteristics (direct contact with body fluids, not airborne under normal conditions, highest viral load at and after death) reflect the established virology and epidemiology of Ebola virus disease as documented in peer-reviewed literature.

Communities should verify current protocols with their national health authority or the WHO country office, as specific response procedures may be updated between outbreaks and may vary depending on the pathogen.

The chlorine concentrations (0.05% for hand-washing, 0.5% for decontamination) follow WHO environmental infection control standards. The incubation period and how the virus dey spread na established information from peer-reviewed studies of the 2013–2016 West Africa and 2018–2020 DRC outbreaks.

Make una check with your country ministry of health or NCDC for the most current protocols, because guidelines fit update between outbreaks.

Wetin Community Suppose Do If Person Begin Show Signs Wey Fit Mean Say E Get Ebola
How You Go Know the Signs

Ebola dey start sharp-sharp with fever wey dey hot well-well, serious headache, body pain, tiredness wey pass normal, vomiting, and runny belle. For some people, blood fit dey comot from mouth, nose, eye, or e fit dey inside shit and vomit without anybody knowing why. The sickness fit take 2 to 21 days before e show after person don catch am, but most time e dey show between day 8 and 10. The problem be say these signs dey look like malaria, typhoid, meningitis, and other sickness wey dey common for areas where Ebola dey happen. Na only lab test go confirm whether na Ebola or not. Person no fit just use eye know.

Wetin You Suppose Do First-First

Separate the sick person, but no touch am with your bare hand or body. Move the person go one room or area wey get good ventilation, wey air dey enter well. Nobody suppose touch the person, touch their body fluid (blood, vomit, shit, piss, sweat, saliva), touch their cloth, their bed sheet, or anything wey any of these fluids don touch. Ebola dey spread when person touch the body fluid of somebody wey don already dey show signs of the sickness, or touch things wey the fluid don touch. This separation no mean say you dey reject the person. Na the correct medical thing to do wey go protect both the community and give the sick person better chance to survive, because e go keep the situation under control until health workers come.

Call health people immediately. Report to the nearest health centre, the disease surveillance officer for your local government or state, or call the NCDC toll-free line. Tell them clearly: wetin the person dey feel, when the sickness start, whether the person don travel anywhere (especially area wey Ebola dey), whether the person don touch anybody wey sick with the same kind signs or anybody wey don die recently, and whether the person don touch bush meat (especially bat or monkey). This report na the single most important thing wey anybody for the community fit do. Na from that report, lab testing, case management, and contact tracing go start. Na these things go determine wetin go happen to the sick person and the whole community.

If you must help the person before health workers come, make na only one person do am. That person suppose cover their body well-well: long sleeve, long trouser, covered shoe, and gloves if dem dey. If gloves no dey, put plastic bag for hand. No let any body fluid touch you. Wash your hand immediately and well-well with soap and water or 0.05% chlorine solution after every single contact. This person must dey registered as a contact for daily monitoring after.

Wetin Community No Suppose Do At All

No wash body if the person die. When person wey get Ebola die, the amount of virus wey dey inside the body dey extremely high, more than any time during the sickness. The washing and touching wey we dey do for traditional burial preparation don be one of the biggest things wey dey make Ebola spread for every major outbreak wey WHO don record, including West Africa 2013–2016 and DRC 2018–2020. Na only trained burial team suppose handle dead body. Safe and dignified burial protocol dey wey respect our cultural values while e still prevent the sickness from spreading. Health authority fit help arrange these teams.

No try to treat the person with traditional medicine or herbs replace hospital. No traditional remedy don show for any clinical trial or lab study say e fit treat or cure Ebola. To give person traditional medicine go delay the time the person suppose reach hospital, where supportive care (especially drip/IV fluid) dey seriously improve chance to survive. And the touching wey you go do to give the person traditional medicine go create direct risk of catching the sickness.

No hide the sick person and no refuse to report. If you hide somebody wey sick, the disease go spread without any control. For the 2014–2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak and the 2018–2020 DRC outbreaks, fear of stigma and quarantine make families hide sick members and do secret burial. WHO, UNICEF, and IFRC evaluations after these outbreaks consistently show say concealment na one of the behaviours wey dey most directly responsible for making the disease spread more and increasing the total number of people wey die.

No touch anything wey the sick person body fluid don touch (bed sheet, cloth, plate, cup, spoon, floor) unless health workers don tell you how to clean am and give you guidance. You go need 0.5% chlorine solution to disinfect those things, and health teams go show you how.

Contact Tracing: Make Una Cooperate

After dem don report the case, public health team go come find everybody wey don get direct physical contact with the sick person, or with their body fluids, cloth, or bed sheet. Those contacts go need daily monitoring for 21 days, usually through temperature check and asking about symptoms. Contact person no dey infectious and no fit spread Ebola to others unless and until dem begin show symptoms themselves. But the daily monitoring make sure say if any contact begin show signs, dem go catch am and isolate am quick-quick before the person fit expose others.

Community members must give honest and complete information about who don near the sick person, when, and how. To lie to contact tracers, whether you wan protect family member from monitoring or you wan avoid wetin you think go be social consequences, na one of the most dangerous things anybody fit do during outbreak. E go allow person wey fit don carry the virus to dey move around without anybody watching, and that one go create condition for new chain of transmission.

How to Handle the Fear and Prevent Harmful Stigma

Fear of Ebola make sense because the disease fit kill. But community must know the difference between correct infection-prevention behaviour and harmful social exclusion of the affected family.

Wetin correct precaution look like: avoid direct physical contact with the sick person and their body fluid, keep distance during the time the person dey actively sick, and monitor yourself for symptoms if you don touch the person before.

Wetin harmful exclusion look like: refuse to talk to the family at all, refuse to give them food and water, block them from reaching health facility, spread their name around with shameful language, threaten or attack them, refuse to let their other family members wey no sick do anything for community, like going to work, school, or market.

The second group of behaviour no dey reduce how the disease spread at all. E dey increase the overall risk because e dey push people to hide sickness. For the West Africa outbreak and the DRC outbreaks, fear-driven stigma make families hide sick members, avoid health facilities, and do secret burial. All of these directly make the disease spread more. WHO, UNICEF, and IFRC post-outbreak evaluations consistently identify stigma-driven concealment as one of the most dangerous things wey fit happen during outbreak response.

Keep talking to the family. Speak to them from safe distance or call them for phone. Tell them wetin dey happen, say health authority don hear, and wetin dem suppose expect. When you cut somebody off from information, fear and distrust go increase for both sides.

Make sure the family get food and water. You fit deliver food, clean water, and other things wey the family need without any physical contact. Just put the things for the entrance of the house. To cut family off from basic supply during health emergency no be protective measure. Na abandonment wey go make things worse for everybody, because family wey dey desperate go likely run away, hide the sickness, or refuse to cooperate with health authority.

No exclude family members wey no sick from community life without medical reason. People for the house wey no dey show any sign of sickness no dey infectious. Ebola no dey spread through air under normal condition. E dey spread through direct contact with body fluid of person wey actively dey show symptoms. Family members wey no get symptoms suppose dey monitored (check temperature every day for 21 days), but nobody suppose treat them like say dem don already sick. Dem fit interact with community with proper hygiene. To exclude healthy family members from work, school, market, or community activities without medical reason go cause economic and psychological damage wey go make people refuse to cooperate with the response.

No spread the family name around with shameful label. To call them "the Ebola family" or anything like that go make stigma worse and go make am harder for them and for future sick people to come out and seek care. Health information suppose focus on the disease and on wetin people suppose do to protect themselves, no be to identify and blame one particular family.

How Community Fit Prepare Before Outbreak Reach

Community wey dey near area wey Ebola don show before, or wey dey at risk, suppose do these things before trouble come:

Talk with your local health authority, know who to call and how to reach them. Choose one place wey fit serve as isolation area: room or structure wey get good ventilation, wey dey far from where everybody dey gather, wey get access to water and toilet. Stock soap and chlorine. Agree on how una go pass message quick-quick if case show. Community health workers or volunteers suppose get basic training on infection prevention before outbreak reach, no be after.

The Connection Between Fear and Outcome

Evidence from major outbreaks dey consistently show say communities wey maintain social togetherness while dem dey practise correct infection-prevention measures dey get better outcomes pass communities wey fear and stigma don scatter. This no be just because togetherness dey feel better, even though e dey. Na because outbreak response be collective action problem. Contact tracing need honesty. Isolation need community support for the person wey dem isolate. Safe burial need trust between families and burial teams. Surveillance need sick people to show themselves for health facility instead of hiding. Every single one of these functions go break down when stigma make the cost of people knowing say you fit be a case higher than the cost of hiding.

The work wey community get be to hold two things at the same time: genuine caution about disease wey fit kill, and genuine solidarity with family wey dey in crisis. These two no dey fight each other. Caution without solidarity go produce hiding. Solidarity without caution go produce transmission. Both together go produce the conditions wey make outbreak dey controlled.

Where This Information Come From

This guidance dey based on WHO (World Health Organization) Ebola virus disease fact sheets and infection prevention and control guidance, CDC (U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) Ebola response guidelines, the WHO Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE) framework, published evaluations of community engagement and stigma dynamics during the 2013–2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak and the 2018–2020 DRC Ebola outbreaks, and WHO/UNICEF/IFRC joint guidance on community feedback mechanisms and safe and dignified burial. Make community verify current protocols with their national health authority or WHO country office, because specific procedures fit don update between outbreaks and fit different depending on the pathogen.

Kini Agbegbe Kan Le Se Ti Enikan Laarin Won Ba N Fi Apere Aisan Ebola Han

Ti enikan laarin agbegbe kan ba n fi ami aisan Ebola han, eyi ni ohun ti a gbọdọ se ni kiakia:

Kọkọ - Ya Enikan Naa Silẹ

Ya ara eni kan naa silẹ ni kiakia. Gbe enikan naa si ile kan ti o yatọ siwaju—ile ti o jinna si awọn ẹgbẹ rẹ, paapaa awọn ọmọ, awọn agbagba, ati ẹnikẹni ti ara wọn kere. Eyi ni ohun pataki julo.

Dun idije pelu ara eni kan naa. Nikan awọn ẹniti o ni aini lati gbé ara enikan naa ni isokan, ati pe wọn gbọdọ wẹ ara wọn pelu iwe-ọwọ, aṣọ, agbada ẹnu, ati iwe oju. Maṣe ka rara ri ẹjẹ tabi omi ti o jẹ ti ara eni kan naa lainú.

Kede si awọn olopa aisan kiakia. Pe ile alaisan ti o sunmo rẹ, tabi kede si nọmba ọrọ aisan ni kiakia. Maṣe duro. Maṣe gba ara yin mọ pẹlu iṣẹlẹ Ebola nii ninu agbegbe naa. Ki wọn lo iwe nipa ibi ti enikan naa wa, igba ti o ti jalẹ, ati ti enikan naa ti lo eni mii se. Ni kẹhin, awọn olopa aisan yoo ri ohun ti o gbọdọ se.

Dun ohun ti o baje pelu ara eni kan naa. Ti enikan naa ba n ta inu, ta ẹjẹ, tabi ta ẹru, ṣe akiyesi rẹ bi ohun ti o ni iyalẹnu. Lo omi chlorine lati fo gbogbo ibi ti enikan naa ti ka—ibadandun, aṣọ, ile, gbogbo nkan. Pa ibi naa sinu ile tabi sun inu ogidi, bii awọn olopa aisan ti wi fun yin.

Isinku ni isẹlẹ pataki. Ti enikan naa ba ku, ara eni kan naa tun yin ara ẹkọ. Nikan awọn eniyan ti a ti kọ́ pelu iwe ọrọ gbigbẹ (full protection) ni o legbẹ to ka ara eni kan naa—maṣe jẹ ki idile rẹ tabi ẹnikẹni miran ka ara naa. Isinku laarin awọn ẹgbẹ lainú ni ọna ti arun yii ti n se ẹgbẹ jẹ ni kiakia.

Kini a Maṣe Se - Pataki!
Maṣe ka rara ri ẹjẹ tabi omi ara eni kan naa lainú
Maṣe se ẹbẹ agbegbe ti o n ka ara eni kan naa
Maṣe fi enikan naa lo si oja tabi ibi ti awọn eniyan baje
Maṣe duro kilo si awọn olopa aisan ki wọn tun o bẹẹ
Maṣe lo oogun adimula dipo oogun osunfunni
Idi ti Eyi Se Pataki

Arun Ebola na n se eniyan jẹ nipa ka ara eni kan naa ti o ni arun pẹlu ara, ati nipa ara eni kan naa ti o ku pẹlu. Igba miiran lo ẹgbẹ agbegbe fi ara wọn ru nipa lati gbé ara eni kan naa tabi lati sin ara eni kan naa lainú. Nigba ti awọn olopa aisan ba de kiakia ati ba tin ara eni kan naa dara, nii igba naa la n gba aye—aye enikan naa ati aye gbogbo agbegbe naa.

Kí Ni Àdúgbò Kan Yẹ Kí Ó Ṣe Tí Ẹnìkan Bá Ń Fi Àmì Àìsàn Ebola Hàn
Bí A Ṣe Lè Dámọ̀ Àwọn Àmì Àìsàn Ebola

Àrùn Ebola máa ń bẹ̀rẹ̀ ní ojijì pẹ̀lú ibà tó le, orí fífọ́ tó burú, ìrora ara, àárẹ̀ tó pọ̀ jù, èèbì, àti ìgbẹ́ gbuuru. Ní àwọn ẹ̀ṣọ̀ kan, ẹ̀jẹ̀ lè máa jáde láti ẹnu, imú, tàbí àwọn ibi mìíràn lára. Àrùn náà lè gba ọjọ́ 2 sí 21 ṣáájú kí àwọn àmì tó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí hàn, ṣùgbọ́n ó sábà máa ń hàn láàárín ọjọ́ 8 sí 10. Ìṣòro kan wà pé àwọn àmì wọ̀nyí jọ ti ibà oníbà (malaria) àti tàìfọ́ìdì, nítorí náà ìdánwò yàrá (lab test) nìkan ló lè fi ẹ̀rí hàn pé Ebola ni.

Àwọn Ìgbésẹ̀ Tí A Gbọ́dọ̀ Gbé Lẹ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀

Ẹ ya aláìsàn sọ́tọ̀, ṣùgbọ́n ẹ má fi ọwọ́ eéfín kàn ín. Ẹ fi aláìsàn sí yàrá kan tàbí ibi tí afẹ́fẹ́ ń wọ̀ dáadáa. Ẹnikẹ́ni kò gbọ́dọ̀ fi ara kàn aláìsàn, fi ọwọ́ kàn àwọn nǹkan tí ó ń jáde lára rẹ̀ (èèbì, ẹ̀jẹ̀, ìgbẹ́, ọ̀fọ̀), tàbí fi ọwọ́ kàn aṣọ rẹ̀, aṣọ ìbùsùn rẹ̀, tàbí ohun èlò rẹ̀. Ebola máa ń tàn nípasẹ̀ fífi ọwọ́ kàn àwọn nǹkan wọ̀nyí tààrà, àti nípasẹ̀ ohunkóhun tí omi ara aláìsàn ti kàn.

Ẹ pe àwọn aṣojú ìlera lẹ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀. Ẹ kàn sí ilé ìwòsàn tó sún mọ́ yín, olùṣọ́ àrùn àjàkálẹ̀ (disease surveillance officer), tàbí ẹ pe ila fóònù NCDC. Ẹ sọ fún wọn àwọn àmì tí aláìsàn ń fi hàn, ìgbà tí àìsàn náà bẹ̀rẹ̀, ibi tí aláìsàn ti rìnrìn àjò padà (tí ó bá rìnrìn àjò), bóyá ó ti fi ọwọ́ kàn ẹnikẹ́ni tí ó ṣàìsàn tàbí tí ó ti kú, àti bóyá ó ti fi ọwọ́ kàn ẹran igbó (ní pàtàkì àdán tàbí ọ̀bọ). Ìfitóníléti ní kíákíá máa ń ṣèrànwọ́ fún àwọn aṣojú ìlera láti ṣe ìdánwò ní kíákíá àti láti bẹ̀rẹ̀ ìdáhùn tó yẹ.

Tí ó bá jẹ́ pé ẹ gbọ́dọ̀ ṣèrànwọ́ fún aláìsàn ṣáájú kí àwọn oṣiṣẹ́ ìlera tó dé, ẹnìkan ṣoṣo ni kí ó ṣe é. Ẹni náà gbọ́dọ̀ bo gbogbo ara rẹ̀ dáadáa: aṣọ apá gígùn, ṣòkòtò gígùn, bàtà tó bo ẹsẹ̀, àti gílọ́ọ̀fù tí ó bá wà. Tí gílọ́ọ̀fù kò bá sí, ẹ fi àpò rọ́bà sí ọwọ́. Ẹ má jẹ́ kí omi ara aláìsàn kàn yín. Ẹ fọ ọwọ́ lẹ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀ àti dáradára pẹ̀lú ọṣẹ àti omi tàbí omi chlorine (0.05% chlorine fún fífọ ọwọ́) lẹ́yìn ìfọwọ́kàn kọ̀ọ̀kan. Ẹni yìí gbọ́dọ̀ jẹ́ ẹni tí a forúkọ sílẹ̀ gẹ́gẹ́ bí olùbásọ̀rọ̀ (contact) fún ìṣọ́ lẹ́yìn náà.

Ohun Tí Àdúgbò Kò Gbọ́dọ̀ Ṣe Rárá

Ẹ má fọ oku tí aláìsàn bá kú. Nígbà tí ẹni tí ó ní Ebola bá kú, iye kòkòrò àrùn tí ó wà nínú ara rẹ̀ pọ̀ gan-an lọ́pọ̀lọpọ̀. Ìmúrasílẹ̀ ìsìnkú ìbílẹ̀ tí ó kan fífọ àti fífi ọwọ́ kàn oku ti jẹ́ ọ̀kan lára àwọn ohun tó ń mú kí Ebola tàn kálẹ̀ jù lọ nínú gbogbo àjàkálẹ̀ àrùn pàtàkì tí WHO ti ṣàkọsílẹ̀. Àwọn ẹgbẹ́ ìsìnkú tí wọ́n ti gba ìdánilẹ́kọ̀ọ́ nìkan ló yẹ kí wọ́n kó oku. Àwọn ìlànà ìsìnkú tí ó jẹ́ ààbò tí ó sì ní ọlá wà tí ó ń bọ̀wọ̀ fún àṣà nígbà tí ó sì ń dènà ìtànkálẹ̀, àwọn aṣojú ìlera sì lè ran lọ́wọ́ láti ṣètò àwọn wọ̀nyí.

Ẹ má fi oògùn ìbílẹ̀ tàbí ewébẹ̀ rọ́pò ilé ìwòsàn. Kò sí oògùn ìbílẹ̀ kankan tí ó ti fi hàn nínú ìwádìí sáyẹ́nsì pé ó lè tọ́jú tàbí wò àrùn Ebola sàn. Tí a bá fi ìgbà padà sí kíkó aláìsàn lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn, àǹfààní aláìsàn láti yè bọ́ yóò dín kù, àwọn ènìyàn mìíràn nínú àdúgbò yóò sì wà nínú ewu. Fífi ọwọ́ kàn tí ó wà nínú fífún aláìsàn ní oògùn ìbílẹ̀ yóò ṣẹ̀dá ewu ìtànkálẹ̀ tààrà.

Ẹ má fi aláìsàn pamọ́, ẹ má sì kọ̀ láti jábọ̀. Tí ẹnìkan bá fi aláìsàn pamọ́, àrùn náà yóò tàn kálẹ̀ láì sí àkóso. Nígbà àjàkálẹ̀ Ebola ní Ìwọ̀ Oòrùn Áfríkà (2014–2016) àti DRC (2018–2020), ìbẹ̀rù àbùkù àti ìpamọ́ mú kí àwọn ìdílé fi àwọn ọmọ ẹgbẹ́ wọn tí wọ́n ṣàìsàn pamọ́, èyí tí ó mú kí àrùn náà tàn kálẹ̀ jù lọ.

Ẹ má fi ọwọ́ kàn ohunkóhun tí omi ara aláìsàn ti kàn (aṣọ ìbùsùn, aṣọ, àwo, ife) àyàfi tí àwọn oṣiṣẹ́ ìlera bá ti sọ fún yín bí ẹ ṣe lè ṣe mọ́tótó rẹ̀. Ẹ nílò omi chlorine 0.5% láti pa àwọn nǹkan wọ̀nyí mọ́.

Ìfọwọ́sowọ́pọ̀ Pẹ̀lú Àtòpín Olùbásọ̀rọ̀ (Contact Tracing)

Nígbà tí a bá ti jábọ̀ ẹ̀ṣọ̀ àìsàn, àwọn oṣiṣẹ́ ìlera yóò wá gbogbo ènìyàn tí ó ti bá aláìsàn ṣepọ̀ tààrà. Àwọn ará àdúgbò yẹ kí wọ́n ṣe ìfọwọ́sowọ́pọ̀ ní kíkún, dáhùn àwọn ìbéèrè ní òtítọ́, kí wọ́n sì sọ fún wọn kedere gbogbo ẹni tí ó ti sún mọ́ aláìsàn. Ẹnikẹ́ni tí ó ti fi ọwọ́ kàn aláìsàn nílò àbójútó lójoojúmọ́ fún ọjọ́ 21. Olùbásọ̀rọ̀ kò ní àrùn tí ó lè tàn kálẹ̀ àyàfi tí ó bá bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí fi àmì àìsàn hàn fúnra rẹ̀, ṣùgbọ́n àbójútó ojoojúmọ́ yóò jẹ́ kí wọ́n rí àìsàn tuntun ní kíákíá. Pípárọ́ fún àwọn olùtọpasẹ̀ láti yẹra fún àbójútó jẹ́ ọ̀kan lára àwọn iṣẹ́ tó lewu jù tí ẹnìkọ̀ọ̀kan lè ṣe nígbà àjàkálẹ̀ àrùn, nítorí ó ń jẹ́ kí ẹni tí a kò rí aláìsàn bẹ̀rẹ̀ ẹ̀wọ̀n ìtànkálẹ̀ tuntun.

Bí A Ṣe Lè Kojú Ìbẹ̀rù Àti Dáàbò Bo Ìdílé Kúrò Nínú Ìyapa Tó Ń Ṣe Ìpalára

Ìbẹ̀rù jẹ́ ìdáhùn tó bọ́gbọ́n mu, ṣùgbọ́n ohun tí ìbẹ̀rù ń mú ènìyàn ṣe nílò ìṣàkóso. Ìyàtọ̀ ńlá wà láàárín ìṣọ́ra ìdènà àrùn tó tọ́ àti ìyapa àwùjọ tó ń ṣe ìpalára.

Ohun tí ìṣọ́ra tó tọ́ rí: yíyẹra fún fífi ọwọ́ kàn aláìsàn àti omi ara rẹ̀ tààrà, jíjìnnà sí i nígbà àìsàn, àti ṣíṣọ́ ara ẹni fún àwọn àmì àìsàn tí ẹni bá ti bá a ṣepọ̀ tẹ́lẹ̀.

Ohun tí ìyapa tó ń ṣe ìpalára rí: kíkọ̀ láti bá ìdílé sọ̀rọ̀ rárá, kíkọ̀ láti pèsè oúnjẹ àti omi fún wọn, dídènà wọn láti dé ilé ìwòsàn, títàn orúkọ wọn kálẹ̀ pẹ̀lú ọ̀rọ̀ ẹ̀gàn, fífi ìhalẹ̀ tàbí ìkọlù kàn wọn, kíkọ̀ láti jẹ́ kí àwọn ọmọ ẹgbẹ́ ìdílé mìíràn tí kò ṣàìsàn ṣe ohunkóhun nínú àdúgbò.

Ẹgbẹ́ ìwà kejì yìí kò dín ewu ìtànkálẹ̀ kù rárá. Ó ń mú ewu lápapọ̀ pọ̀ sí i nítorí ó ń ti ènìyàn láti fi àìsàn pamọ́. Nígbà àjàkálẹ̀ Ebola ní Ìwọ̀ Oòrùn Áfríkà 2014–2016, ìbẹ̀rù àti àbùkù mú kí àwọn ìdílé fi àwọn ọmọ ẹgbẹ́ wọn tí wọ́n ṣàìsàn pamọ́, yẹra fún ilé ìwòsàn, wọ́n sì ṣe ìsìnkú àṣírí, gbogbo èyí tí ó mú kí àrùn náà tàn kálẹ̀ tààrà.

Ohun Tí Àdúgbò Yẹ Kí Ó Ṣe Fún Ìdílé

Ẹ máa bá ìdílé sọ̀rọ̀. Ẹ bá wọn sọ̀rọ̀ láti ibi tí ó jìnnà tó tàbí nípasẹ̀ fóònù. Ẹ sọ fún wọn ohun tí ń ṣẹlẹ̀, pé àwọn aṣojú ìlera ti gbọ́, àti ohun tí wọ́n yẹ kí wọ́n retí. Nígbà tí a bá gé ènìyàn kúrò nínú ìmọ̀, ìbẹ̀rù àti àìgbẹ́kẹ̀lé yóò pọ̀ sí i ní ẹ̀gbẹ́ méjèèjì.

Ri dájú pé ìdílé náà ní ànfààní sí oúnjẹ àti omi. A lè fi oúnjẹ, omi mímọ́, àti àwọn ohun pàtàkì mìíràn ránṣẹ́ sí ilé ìdílé náà láì fi ọwọ́ kàn wọn. A lè fi àwọn nǹkan sílẹ̀ ní ẹnu ọ̀nà ilé. Gígé ìdílé kúrò nínú ohun ìpèsè ìpìlẹ̀ nígbà pàjáwìrì ìlera kì í ṣe ìgbésẹ̀ ààbò. Ó jẹ́ fífi sílẹ̀ tí yóò mú kí nǹkan burú sí i fún gbogbo ènìyàn, nítorí ìdílé tí ó bá wà ní ipò àìní yóò ṣeéṣe kí ó sá, fi àìsàn pamọ́, tàbí kọ̀ ìfọwọ́sowọ́pọ̀ pẹ̀lú àwọn aṣojú ìlera.

Ẹ dáàbò bo àwọn ọmọ ẹgbẹ́ ìdílé mìíràn tí kò ṣàìsàn. Àwọn ènìyàn nínú ilé tí kò fi àmì àìsàn kankan hàn kò ní àrùn tí wọ́n lè tàn kálẹ̀. Ebola kì í ṣe àrùn tí ó ń tàn nípasẹ̀ afẹ́fẹ́ lábẹ́ ipò ìwọ̀ntúnwọ̀nsì. Ó máa ń tàn nípasẹ̀ fífi ọwọ́ kàn omi ara ẹni tí ó ń fi àmì àìsàn hàn lọ́wọ́lọ́wọ́. Àwọn ọmọ ẹgbẹ́ ìdílé tí kò ní àmì àìsàn yẹ kí wọ́n jẹ́ ẹni tí a ń ṣọ́ (ṣíṣe àyẹ̀wò ìwọ̀n oòrùn ara lójoojúmọ́ fún ọjọ́ 21), ṣùgbọ́n a kò gbọ́dọ̀ ṣe wọ́n bí ẹni pé wọ́n ti ṣàìsàn. Wọ́n lè bá àwùjọ ṣepọ̀ pẹ̀lú ìmọ́tótó tó yẹ. Yíyọ àwọn ọmọ ẹgbẹ́ ìdílé tó ní ìlera kúrò nínú iṣẹ́, ilé ìwé, ọjà, tàbí ìgbésí ayé àdúgbò láìsí ìdí ìṣègùn yóò fa ìpalára ọrọ̀ ajé àti ti ọpọlọ tí yóò mú kí ènìyàn kọ̀ ìfọwọ́sowọ́pọ̀ pẹ̀lú ìdáhùn náà.

Ẹ má tàn orúkọ ìdílé náà kálẹ̀ pẹ̀lú àkọ́lé àbùkù. Pípè ìdílé náà ní "ìdílé Ebola" tàbí ohunkóhun tó jọ bẹ́ẹ̀ máa ń mú àbùkù le sí i, yóò sì mú kí ó ṣòro fún wọn àti fún àwọn aláìsàn ọjọ́ iwájú láti wá ìtọ́jú.

Bí Àdúgbò Ṣe Lè Ṣe Ìmúrasílẹ̀

Àwọn àdúgbò tí wọ́n wà nítòsí àgbègbè tí Ebola ti fara hàn tẹ́lẹ̀, tàbí tí wọ́n wà nínú ewu, yẹ kí wọ́n ṣe àwọn nǹkan wọ̀nyí ṣáájú kí ìṣòro tó dé:

Ẹ bá àwọn aṣojú ìlera yín sọ̀rọ̀, mọ̀ ẹni tí ẹ yóò pe àti bí ẹ ṣe lè dé ọ̀dọ̀ wọn. Ẹ yan ibi kan tí yóò jẹ́ ibi ìpamọ́ (isolation area). Ẹ kó ọṣẹ àti chlorine jọ. Ẹ fọwọ́ sí bí ẹ ṣe lè fi ọ̀rọ̀ ránṣẹ́ ní kíákíá tí àìsàn bá fara hàn. Àwọn oṣiṣẹ́ ìlera àdúgbò tàbí àwọn olùyọ̀ǹda yẹ kí wọ́n gba ìdánilẹ́kọ̀ọ́ ìpìlẹ̀ nípa bí wọ́n ṣe lè dáàbò bo ara wọn àti àwọn ẹlòmíràn ṣáájú kí àjàkálẹ̀ àrùn tó bẹ̀rẹ̀, kì í ṣe lẹ́yìn tí ó ti bẹ̀rẹ̀.

Ìbáṣepọ̀ Láàárín Ìbẹ̀rù Àti Àbájáde

Ẹ̀rí láti àwọn àjàkálẹ̀ àrùn pàtàkì fi hàn ní ìgbà gbogbo pé àwọn àdúgbò tí wọ́n ṣe àjọṣepọ̀ nígbà tí wọ́n sì ń ṣe àwọn ìgbésẹ̀ ìdènà àrùn tó tọ́ máa ń ní àbájáde tó dára ju àwọn àdúgbò tí ìbẹ̀rù àti àbùkù ti fọ́ lọ. Ìṣọ́ra láìsí ìfọwọ́sowọ́pọ̀ máa ń mú fípamọ́ wá. Ìfọwọ́sowọ́pọ̀ láìsí ìṣọ́ra máa ń mú ìtànkálẹ̀ wá. Méjèèjì papọ̀ máa ń ṣẹ̀dá ipò tí ó ń jẹ́ kí a ṣàkóso àjàkálẹ̀ àrùn.

Iṣẹ́ àdúgbò ni láti di nǹkan méjì mú ní àkókò kan náà: ìṣọ́ra gidi nípa àrùn tí ó lè pa, àti ìfọwọ́sowọ́pọ̀ gidi pẹ̀lú ìdílé tí ó wà nínú ìṣòro.

Ibi Tí Ìmọ̀ràn Yìí Ti Wá

Ìmọ̀ràn yìí dá lórí àwọn ìwé àlàyé WHO (World Health Organization) lórí àrùn Ebola àti àwọn ìlànà ìdènà àkóràn, ìtọ́sọ́nà CDC (U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) fún ìdáhùn Ebola, ètò WHO Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE), àwọn àyẹ̀wò tí a ti tẹ̀ jáde lórí ìbáṣepọ̀ àdúgbò àti ìṣesí àbùkù nígbà àjàkálẹ̀ Ebola ní Ìwọ̀ Oòrùn Áfríkà 2014–2016 àti àjàkálẹ̀ Ebola DRC 2018–2020, àti ìtọ́sọ́nà àpapọ̀ WHO/UNICEF/IFRC lórí àwọn ètò ìrísí ìdáhùn àdúgbò. Ìwọ̀n chlorine (0.05% fún fífọ ọwọ́, 0.5% fún ṣíṣe ilẹ̀ àti ohun èlò mọ́tótó) tẹ̀lé ìtọ́sọ́nà ìlera àyíká ti WHO. Àkókò àbójútó (ọjọ́ 21) àti àwọn ọ̀nà ìtànkálẹ̀ (fífi ọwọ́ kàn omi ara tààrà, kì í ṣe nípasẹ̀ afẹ́fẹ́ lábẹ́ ipò ìwọ̀ntúnwọ̀nsì) dá lórí ẹ̀kọ́ kòkòrò àrùn àti ẹ̀kọ́ àjàkálẹ̀ àrùn ti Ebola gẹ́gẹ́ bí a ti ṣàkọsílẹ̀ rẹ̀ nínú àwọn ìwé ìmọ̀ tí àwọn ẹlẹgbẹ́ ṣàyẹ̀wò.

Àwọn àdúgbò yẹ kí wọ́n ṣàyẹ̀wò àwọn ìlànà lọ́wọ́lọ́wọ́ pẹ̀lú àjọ ìlera orílẹ̀-èdè wọn tàbí ọ́fíìsì WHO ní orílẹ̀-èdè wọn, nítorí àwọn ìlànà pàtó lè ti jẹ́ ìmúdójúìwọ̀n láàárín àwọn àjàkálẹ̀ àrùn, wọ́n sì lè yàtọ̀ gẹ́gẹ́ bí irú kòkòrò àrùn.

Kí Ni Àdúgbò Kan Yẹ Kí Ó Ṣe Tí Ẹnìkan Bá Ń Fi Àmì Àìsàn Ebola Hàn
Bí A Ṣe Lè Dámọ̀ Àwọn Àmì Àìsàn Náà

Àrùn Ebola máa ń bẹ̀rẹ̀ ní ojijì pẹ̀lú ibà tó le gan-an, orí fífọ́ tó burú, ìrora ara, àárẹ̀ tó pọ̀ jù tí kò ṣe é ṣàlàyé, èèbì, àti ìgbẹ́ gbuuru. Ní àwọn ẹ̀ṣọ̀ kan, ẹ̀jẹ̀ lè máa jáde láti ẹnu, imú, ojú, tàbí ó lè wà nínú ìgbẹ́ àti èèbì láìsí ìdí tí a mọ̀. Àrùn náà lè gba ọjọ́ 2 sí 21 ṣáájú kí àwọn àmì tó hàn lẹ́yìn tí ènìyàn bá ti kó àrùn, ṣùgbọ́n ó sábà máa ń hàn láàárín ọjọ́ 8 sí 10. Ìṣòro pàtàkì kan wà pé àwọn àmì wọ̀nyí jọ ti ibà oníbà (malaria), tàìfọ́ìdì, meningitis, àti àwọn àìsàn mìíràn tí wọ́n wọ́pọ̀ ní àwọn àgbègbè tí Ebola ti ṣẹlẹ̀. Nítorí náà, a kò lè fi ojú ṣoṣo mọ̀ pé Ebola ni. Ìdánwò yàrá (lab test) nìkan ló lè fi ẹ̀rí hàn bóyá Ebola ni tàbí bẹ́ẹ̀ kọ́.

Àwọn Ìgbésẹ̀ Tí A Gbọ́dọ̀ Gbé Lẹ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀

Ẹ ya aláìsàn sọ́tọ̀, ṣùgbọ́n ẹ má fi ọwọ́ eéfín tàbí ara kàn ín. Ẹ darí aláìsàn lọ sí yàrá kan tàbí ibi tí afẹ́fẹ́ ń wọ̀ dáadáa. Ẹnikẹ́ni kò gbọ́dọ̀ fi ara kàn aláìsàn, fi ọwọ́ kàn àwọn nǹkan tí ó ń jáde lára rẹ̀ (ẹ̀jẹ̀, èèbì, ìgbẹ́, ìtọ̀, ọ̀fọ̀, ẹ̀tọ́), fi ọwọ́ kàn aṣọ rẹ̀, aṣọ ìbùsùn rẹ̀, tàbí ohunkóhun tí àwọn omi ara wọ̀nyí ti kàn. Ebola máa ń tàn nípasẹ̀ fífi ọwọ́ kàn omi ara ẹni tí ó ń fi àmì àìsàn hàn tàbí ẹni tí ó ti kú, àti nípasẹ̀ àwọn ohun tí omi ara wọ̀nyí ti bà. Ìpamọ́ yìí kì í ṣe ìkọsílẹ̀ ènìyàn. Ó jẹ́ iṣẹ́ tó tọ́ ní ti ìṣègùn tí ó ń dáàbò bo àdúgbò àti tí ó ń fún aláìsàn ní àǹfààní tó dára jù láti yè bọ́, nítorí ó ń jẹ́ kí ipò náà wà lábẹ́ ìṣàkóso títí tí ìtọ́jú alámọ̀jà yóò fi dé.

Ẹ pe àwọn aṣojú ìlera lẹ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀. Ẹ kàn sí ilé ìwòsàn tó sún mọ́ yín, olùṣọ́ àrùn àjàkálẹ̀ fún ìjọba ìbílẹ̀ tàbí ìpínlẹ̀ yín, tàbí ẹ pe ila fóònù NCDC tí kò ní owó. Ẹ sọ fún wọn kedere: àwọn àmì tí aláìsàn ń fi hàn, ìgbà tí àìsàn náà bẹ̀rẹ̀, bóyá aláìsàn ti rìnrìn àjò (ní pàtàkì sí àgbègbè tí Ebola ti ṣẹlẹ̀), bóyá ó ti fi ọwọ́ kàn ẹnikẹ́ni tí ó ṣàìsàn pẹ̀lú irú àmì kan náà tàbí ẹni tí ó ti kú láìpẹ́, àti bóyá ó ti fi ọwọ́ kàn ẹran igbó (ní pàtàkì àdán tàbí ọ̀bọ). Ìfitóníléti yìí ni iṣẹ́ kan ṣoṣo tó ṣe pàtàkì jù lọ tí ẹnikẹ́ni nínú àdúgbò lè ṣe, nítorí ó ń bẹ̀rẹ̀ ẹ̀wọ̀n ìṣe tí ó pẹ̀lú ìdánwò yàrá, ìtọ́jú aláìsàn, àti àtòpín olùbásọ̀rọ̀ (contact tracing), tí ìyè aláìsàn àti ààbò àdúgbò lápapọ̀ dá lé.

Tí ó bá jẹ́ pé ẹ gbọ́dọ̀ ṣèrànwọ́ fún aláìsàn ṣáájú kí àwọn oṣiṣẹ́ ìlera tó dé, ẹnìkan ṣoṣo ni kí ó ṣe é. Ẹni náà gbọ́dọ̀ bo gbogbo ara rẹ̀ dáadáa: aṣọ apá gígùn, ṣòkòtò gígùn, bàtà tó bo ẹsẹ̀, àti gílọ́ọ̀fù tí ó bá wà. Tí gílọ́ọ̀fù kò bá sí, ẹ fi àpò rọ́bà dì í sí ọwọ́. Ẹ má jẹ́ kí omi ara aláìsàn kàn yín rárá. Ẹ fọ ọwọ́ lẹ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀ àti dáradára pẹ̀lú ọṣẹ àti omi tàbí omi chlorine 0.05% lẹ́yìn ìfọwọ́kàn kọ̀ọ̀kan. Ẹni yìí gbọ́dọ̀ jẹ́ ẹni tí a forúkọ sílẹ̀ gẹ́gẹ́ bí olùbásọ̀rọ̀ (contact) fún àbójútó ojoojúmọ́ lẹ́yìn náà.

Ohun Tí Àdúgbò Kò Gbọ́dọ̀ Ṣe Rárá

Ẹ má fọ oku tàbí ṣe ètò ìsìnkú ìbílẹ̀ tí aláìsàn bá kú. Iye kòkòrò àrùn tí ó wà nínú ara ẹni tí ó kú sí Ebola ga gan-an, ó ga ju ìgbàkigbà mìíràn nínú àìsàn lọ. Ìmúrasílẹ̀ ìsìnkú ìbílẹ̀ tí ó kan fífọ, fífi ọwọ́ kàn, àti fífi aṣọ wọ oku ti jẹ́ ọ̀kan lára àwọn ohun tó ń mú kí Ebola tàn kálẹ̀ jù lọ nínú gbogbo àjàkálẹ̀ àrùn pàtàkì tí WHO ti ṣàkọsílẹ̀, pẹ̀lú àjàkálẹ̀ Ìwọ̀ Oòrùn Áfríkà 2013–2016 àti DRC 2018–2020. Àwọn ẹgbẹ́ ìsìnkú tí wọ́n ti gba ìdánilẹ́kọ̀ọ́ nìkan ló yẹ kí wọ́n kó oku. Àwọn ìlànà ìsìnkú tí ó jẹ́ ààbò tí ó sì ní ọlá wà tí ó ń bọ̀wọ̀ fún àṣà nígbà tí ó sì ń dènà ìtànkálẹ̀, àwọn aṣojú ìlera sì lè ran lọ́wọ́ láti ṣètò àwọn ẹgbẹ́ wọ̀nyí.

Ẹ má fi oògùn ìbílẹ̀ tàbí ewébẹ̀ rọ́pò ilé ìwòsàn. Kò sí oògùn ìbílẹ̀ kankan tí ó ti fi hàn nínú ìwádìí ìṣègùn tàbí ìwádìí yàrá pé ó lè tọ́jú àrùn Ebola. Fífún aláìsàn ní oògùn ìbílẹ̀ máa ń fa ìdádúró nínú kíkó aláìsàn lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn, ibi tí ìtọ́jú àtìlẹ́yìn (ní pàtàkì omi inú iṣọ́n, drip/IV fluid) ń mú àǹfààní ìyè bọ́ dára sí i gan-an. Fífi ọwọ́ kàn tí ó wà nínú fífún aláìsàn ní oògùn ìbílẹ̀ yóò tún ṣẹ̀dá ọ̀nà ìtànkálẹ̀ tààrà.

Ẹ má fi aláìsàn pamọ́, ẹ má sì kọ̀ láti jábọ̀. Fífi ẹni tí ó ń fi àmì àìsàn hàn pamọ́ máa ń jẹ́ kí àrùn tàn kálẹ̀ láìsí àkóso. Nígbà àjàkálẹ̀ Ebola ní Ìwọ̀ Oòrùn Áfríkà 2014–2016 àti DRC 2018–2020, ìbẹ̀rù àbùkù, ìpamọ́, àti ìdàrúdàpọ̀ sí ìgbésí ayé ìdílé mú kí àwọn ìdílé fi àwọn ọmọ ẹgbẹ́ wọn tí wọ́n ṣàìsàn pamọ́, wọ́n sì ṣe ìsìnkú àṣírí. Àwọn àyẹ̀wò lẹ́yìn àjàkálẹ̀ àrùn tí WHO, UNICEF, àti IFRC ṣe máa ń dámọ̀ fífipamọ́ gẹ́gẹ́ bí ọ̀kan lára àwọn ìwà tó ń jẹ́ ìdí tààrà jù lọ tí àrùn fi ń tàn kálẹ̀ sí i àti tí iye ikú fi ń pọ̀ sí i.

Ẹ má fi ọwọ́ kàn ohunkóhun tí omi ara aláìsàn ti kàn (aṣọ ìbùsùn, aṣọ, ohun èlò oúnjẹ, ilẹ̀) àyàfi tí àwọn oṣiṣẹ́ ìlera bá ti fún yín ní ìtọ́sọ́nà. Àwọn ohun tí ó ti di àìmọ́ nílò fífi omi chlorine 0.5% ṣe mọ́tótó lábẹ́ àwọn ìlànà tí àwọn ẹgbẹ́ ìlera yóò pèsè.

Ìfọwọ́sowọ́pọ̀ Pẹ̀lú Àtòpín Olùbásọ̀rọ̀ (Contact Tracing)

Nígbà tí a bá ti jábọ̀ ẹ̀ṣọ̀ tí a fura sí, àwọn ẹgbẹ́ ìlera àwùjọ yóò wá gbogbo ènìyàn tí ó ti fi ọwọ́ kàn aláìsàn tààrà, tàbí tí ó ti fi ọwọ́ kàn omi ara rẹ̀, aṣọ rẹ̀, tàbí aṣọ ìbùsùn rẹ̀. Àwọn olùbásọ̀rọ̀ wọ̀nyí nílò àbójútó ojoojúmọ́ fún ọjọ́ 21, sábà nípasẹ̀ ṣíṣe àyẹ̀wò ìwọ̀n oòrùn ara àti bíbéèrè nípa àwọn àmì àìsàn. Olùbásọ̀rọ̀ kò ní àrùn tí ó lè tàn kálẹ̀, kò sì lè tàn Ebola sí àwọn ẹlòmíràn, àyàfi tí àti títí tí ó bá bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí fi àmì àìsàn hàn fúnra rẹ̀. Àmọ́ àbójútó ojoojúmọ́ máa ń ri dájú pé tí olùbásọ̀rọ̀ bá bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí fi àmì hàn, a ó rí i, a ó sì ya á sọ́tọ̀ ní kíákíá, ṣáájú kí ó tó fi àwọn mìíràn sínú ewu.

Àwọn ọmọ ẹgbẹ́ àdúgbò gbọ́dọ̀ fún àwọn olùtọpasẹ̀ ní ìmọ̀ tó jẹ́ òtítọ́ àti tó pé nípa ẹni tí ó ti bá aláìsàn ṣepọ̀, ìgbà wo, àti ní ọ̀nà wo. Pípárọ́ fún àwọn olùtọpasẹ̀, bóyá láti dáàbò bo ọmọ ẹgbẹ́ ìdílé kúrò nínú àbójútó tàbí láti yẹra fún ohun tí ẹni rò pé yóò jẹ́ àbájáde àwùjọ, jẹ́ ọ̀kan lára àwọn iṣẹ́ tó lewu jù tí ẹnìkọ̀ọ̀kan lè ṣe nígbà àjàkálẹ̀ àrùn. Ó ń jẹ́ kí ẹni tí ó lè ti kó àrùn máa rìn kálẹ̀ láìsí ẹnikẹ́ni tó ń ṣọ́ ọ, ìyẹn sì ń ṣẹ̀dá ipò fún ẹ̀wọ̀n ìtànkálẹ̀ tuntun.

Bí A Ṣe Lè Kojú Ìbẹ̀rù Àti Dènà Àbùkù Tó Ń Ṣe Ìpalára

Ìbẹ̀rù Ebola jẹ́ ìdáhùn tó bọ́gbọ́n mu sí àrùn tó ní ìwọ̀n ikú gíga. Àmọ́ àdúgbò gbọ́dọ̀ mọ ìyàtọ̀ láàárín ìwà ìdènà àrùn tó tọ́ àti ìyapa àwùjọ tí ó ń ṣe ìpalára sí ìdílé tí àrùn bá.

Ohun tí ìṣọ́ra tó tọ́ rí: yíyẹra fún fífi ọwọ́ kàn aláìsàn àti omi ara rẹ̀ tààrà, jíjìnnà sí i nígbà tí àìsàn bá ń ṣiṣẹ́ lọ́wọ́, àti ṣíṣọ́ ara ẹni fún àwọn àmì àìsàn tí ẹni bá ti bá a ṣepọ̀ tẹ́lẹ̀.

Ohun tí ìyapa tó ń ṣe ìpalára rí: kíkọ̀ láti bá ìdílé sọ̀rọ̀ rárá, kíkọ̀ láti pèsè oúnjẹ àti omi fún wọn, dídènà wọn láti dé ilé ìwòsàn, títàn orúkọ wọn kálẹ̀ pẹ̀lú ọ̀rọ̀ ẹ̀gàn bíi "ìdílé Ebola," fífi ìhalẹ̀ tàbí ìkọlù kàn wọn, tàbí kíkọ̀ láti jẹ́ kí àwọn ọmọ ẹgbẹ́ ìdílé mìíràn tí kò ṣàìsàn ṣe ohunkóhun nínú àdúgbò bíi rírìn lọ sí iṣẹ́, ilé ìwé, tàbí ọjà.

Ẹgbẹ́ ìwà kejì yìí kò dín ewu ìtànkálẹ̀ kù rárá. Ó ń mú ewu lápapọ̀ pọ̀ sí i nítorí ó ń ti ènìyàn láti fi àìsàn pamọ́. Nígbà àjàkálẹ̀ Ebola ní Ìwọ̀ Oòrùn Áfríkà àti DRC, ìbẹ̀rù àti àbùkù mú kí àwọn ìdílé fi àwọn ọmọ ẹgbẹ́ wọn tí wọ́n ṣàìsàn pamọ́, yẹra fún ilé ìwòsàn, wọ́n sì ṣe ìsìnkú àṣírí. Gbogbo èyí mú kí àrùn náà tàn kálẹ̀ tààrà. Àwọn àyẹ̀wò lẹ́yìn àjàkálẹ̀ àrùn tí WHO, UNICEF, àti IFRC ṣe máa ń dámọ̀ fífipamọ́ tí àbùkù fà gẹ́gẹ́ bí ọ̀kan lára àwọn nǹkan tó lewu jù nínú ìdáhùn àjàkálẹ̀ àrùn.

Ẹ máa bá ìdílé sọ̀rọ̀. Ẹ bá wọn sọ̀rọ̀ láti ibi tí ó jìnnà tó tàbí nípasẹ̀ fóònù. Ẹ sọ fún wọn ohun tí ń ṣẹlẹ̀, pé àwọn aṣojú ìlera ti gbọ́, àti ohun tí wọ́n yẹ kí wọ́n retí. Nígbà tí a bá gé ènìyàn kúrò nínú ìmọ̀, ìbẹ̀rù àti àìgbẹ́kẹ̀lé yóò pọ̀ sí i ní ẹ̀gbẹ́ méjèèjì.

Ri dájú pé ìdílé náà ní ànfààní sí oúnjẹ àti omi. A lè fi oúnjẹ, omi mímọ́, àti àwọn ohun pàtàkì mìíràn ránṣẹ́ sí ilé ìdílé náà láì fi ọwọ́ kàn wọn. A lè fi àwọn nǹkan sílẹ̀ ní ẹnu ọ̀nà ilé. Gígé ìdílé kúrò nínú ohun ìpèsè ìpìlẹ̀ nígbà pàjáwìrì ìlera kì í ṣe ìgbésẹ̀ ààbò. Ó jẹ́ fífi sílẹ̀ tí yóò mú kí nǹkan burú sí i fún gbogbo ènìyàn, nítorí ìdílé tí ó bá wà ní ipò àìní yóò ṣeéṣe kí ó sá, fi àìsàn pamọ́, tàbí kọ̀ ìfọwọ́sowọ́pọ̀ pẹ̀lú àwọn aṣojú ìlera.

Ẹ má yọ àwọn ọmọ ẹgbẹ́ ìdílé tí kò ṣàìsàn kúrò nínú ìgbésí ayé àdúgbò láìsí ìdí ìṣègùn. Àwọn ènìyàn nínú ilé tí kò fi àmì àìsàn kankan hàn kò ní àrùn tí wọ́n lè tàn kálẹ̀. Ebola kì í ṣe àrùn tí ó ń tàn nípasẹ̀ afẹ́fẹ́ lábẹ́ ipò ìwọ̀ntúnwọ̀nsì. Ó máa ń tàn nípasẹ̀ fífi ọwọ́ kàn omi ara ẹni tí ó ń fi àmì àìsàn hàn lọ́wọ́lọ́wọ́ tààrà. Àwọn ọmọ ẹgbẹ́ ìdílé tí kò ní àmì àìsàn yẹ kí wọ́n jẹ́ ẹni tí a ń ṣọ́ (ṣíṣe àyẹ̀wò ìwọ̀n oòrùn ara lójoojúmọ́ fún ọjọ́ 21), ṣùgbọ́n a kò gbọ́dọ̀ ṣe wọ́n bí ẹni pé wọ́n ti ṣàìsàn. Wọ́n lè bá àwùjọ ṣepọ̀ pẹ̀lú ìmọ́tótó tó yẹ. Yíyọ àwọn ọmọ ẹgbẹ́ ìdílé tó ní ìlera kúrò nínú iṣẹ́, ilé ìwé, ọjà, tàbí ìgbésí ayé àdúgbò láìsí ìdí ìṣègùn yóò fa ìpalára ọrọ̀ ajé àti ti ọpọlọ tí yóò mú kí ènìyàn kọ̀ ìfọwọ́sowọ́pọ̀ pẹ̀lú ìdáhùn náà.

Ẹ má tàn orúkọ ìdílé náà kálẹ̀ pẹ̀lú àkọ́lé àbùkù. Pípè ìdílé náà ní "ìdílé Ebola" tàbí ohunkóhun tó jọ bẹ́ẹ̀ máa ń mú àbùkù le sí i, yóò sì mú kí ó ṣòro fún wọn àti fún àwọn aláìsàn ọjọ́ iwájú láti wá ìtọ́jú. Ìmọ̀ ìlera yẹ kí ó dá lé àrùn náà àti àwọn iṣẹ́ ààbò, kì í ṣe lórí dídámọ̀ àti bíbi ìdílé kan pàtó.

Bí Àdúgbò Ṣe Lè Ṣe Ìmúrasílẹ̀ Ṣáájú Kí Àjàkálẹ̀ Àrùn Tó Dé

Àwọn àdúgbò tí wọ́n wà nítòsí àgbègbè tí Ebola ti ṣẹlẹ̀ tẹ́lẹ̀, tàbí tí wọ́n wà nínú ewu, yẹ kí wọ́n múra sílẹ̀ ṣáájú kí àjàkálẹ̀ àrùn tó dé ọ̀dọ̀ wọn.

Ẹ bá àwọn aṣojú ìlera àdúgbò yín sọ̀rọ̀, kí ẹ sì mọ̀ ẹni tí ẹ yóò pe àti bí ẹ ṣe lè dé ọ̀dọ̀ wọn. Ẹ yan ibi kan tí ó lè jẹ́ ibi ìpamọ́ (isolation area): yàrá tàbí ilé tí afẹ́fẹ́ ń wọ̀ dáadáa, tó jìnnà sí ibi tí gbogbo ènìyàn ń lò, tó sì ní ànfààní sí omi àti ilé ìgbọ̀nsẹ̀. Ẹ kó ọṣẹ àti chlorine jọ. Ẹ fọwọ́ sí bí ẹ ṣe lè fi ọ̀rọ̀ ránṣẹ́ ní kíákíá tí ẹ̀ṣọ̀ àìsàn tí a fura sí bá fara hàn. Àwọn oṣiṣẹ́ ìlera àdúgbò tàbí àwọn olùyọ̀ǹda yẹ kí wọ́n gba ìdánilẹ́kọ̀ọ́ ìpìlẹ̀ lórí ìdènà àkóràn ṣáájú kí àjàkálẹ̀ àrùn tó bẹ̀rẹ̀, kì í ṣe lẹ́yìn rẹ̀.

Ìbáṣepọ̀ Láàárín Ìbẹ̀rù Àti Àbájáde

Ẹ̀rí láti àwọn àjàkálẹ̀ àrùn pàtàkì fi hàn ní ìgbà gbogbo pé àwọn àdúgbò tí wọ́n ṣe àjọṣepọ̀ nígbà tí wọ́n sì ń ṣe àwọn ìgbésẹ̀ ìdènà àrùn tó tọ́ máa ń ní àbájáde tó dára ju àwọn àdúgbò tí ìbẹ̀rù àti àbùkù ti fọ́ lọ. Èyí kì í ṣe nítorí pé àjọṣepọ̀ dára lọ́kàn nìkan, bí ó tilẹ̀ jẹ́ pé ó dára. Ó jẹ́ nítorí pé ìdáhùn àjàkálẹ̀ àrùn jẹ́ iṣẹ́ àpapọ̀. Àtòpín olùbásọ̀rọ̀ nílò òtítọ́. Ìpamọ́ nílò àtìlẹ́yìn àdúgbò fún ẹni tí a ya sọ́tọ̀. Ìsìnkú àìléwu nílò ìgbẹ́kẹ̀lé láàárín àwọn ìdílé àti àwọn ẹgbẹ́ ìsìnkú. Ìṣọ́ nílò kí àwọn aláìsàn fi ara hàn ní ilé ìwòsàn dípò fífi ara pamọ́. Gbogbo àwọn iṣẹ́ wọ̀nyí máa ń wó lulẹ̀ nígbà tí àbùkù bá mú kí owó tí ẹni bá mọ̀ pé o lè jẹ́ aláìsàn ga ju owó fífi ara pamọ́ lọ.

Iṣẹ́ àdúgbò ni láti di nǹkan méjì mú ní àkókò kan náà: ìṣọ́ra gidi nípa àrùn tí ó lè pa, àti ìfọwọ́sowọ́pọ̀ gidi pẹ̀lú ìdílé tí ó wà nínú ìṣòro. Àwọn méjì yìí kò ń bá ara wọn jà. Ìṣọ́ra láìsí ìfọwọ́sowọ́pọ̀ máa ń mú fípamọ́ wá. Ìfọwọ́sowọ́pọ̀ láìsí ìṣọ́ra máa ń mú ìtànkálẹ̀ wá. Méjèèjì papọ̀ máa ń ṣẹ̀dá ipò tí ó ń jẹ́ kí a ṣàkóso àjàkálẹ̀ àrùn.

Ibi Tí Ìmọ̀ràn Yìí Ti Wá

Ìmọ̀ràn yìí dá lórí àwọn ìwé àlàyé WHO (World Health Organization) lórí àrùn Ebola àti ìtọ́sọ́nà ìdènà àti ìṣàkóso àkóràn, àwọn ìtọ́sọ́nà ìdáhùn Ebola ti CDC (U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention), ètò WHO Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE), àwọn àyẹ̀wò tí a ti tẹ̀ jáde lórí ìbáṣepọ̀ àdúgbò àti ìṣesí àbùkù nígbà àjàkálẹ̀ Ebola ní Ìwọ̀ Oòrùn Áfríkà 2013–2016 àti àjàkálẹ̀ Ebola DRC 2018–2020, àti ìtọ́sọ́nà àpapọ̀ WHO/UNICEF/IFRC lórí àwọn ètò ìrísí ìdáhùn àdúgbò àti ìsìnkú àìléwu tí ó ní ọlá. Àwọn ìwọ̀n chlorine pàtó (0.05% fún fífọ ọwọ́, 0.5% fún ṣíṣe ilẹ̀ àti ohun èlò mọ́tótó) tẹ̀lé ìtọ́sọ́nà ìlera àyíká WHO. Àkókò àbójútó olùbásọ̀rọ̀ ọjọ́ 21 àti àwọn ìwà ìtànkálẹ̀ (fífi ọwọ́ kàn omi ara tààrà, kì í ṣe nípasẹ̀ afẹ́fẹ́ lábẹ́ ipò ìwọ̀ntúnwọ̀nsì, iye kòkòrò àrùn tó ga jù ní àkókò ikú àti lẹ́yìn rẹ̀) dá lórí ẹ̀kọ́ kòkòrò àrùn àti ẹ̀kọ́ àjàkálẹ̀ àrùn ti Ebola gẹ́gẹ́ bí a ti ṣàkọsílẹ̀ rẹ̀ nínú àwọn ìwé ìmọ̀ tí àwọn ẹlẹgbẹ́ ṣàyẹ̀wò.

Àwọn àdúgbò yẹ kí wọ́n ṣàyẹ̀wò àwọn ìlànà lọ́wọ́lọ́wọ́ pẹ̀lú àjọ ìlera orílẹ̀-èdè wọn tàbí ọ́fíìsì WHO ní orílẹ̀-èdè wọn, nítorí àwọn ìlànà pàtó lè ti jẹ́ ìmúdójúìwọ̀n láàárín àwọn àjàkálẹ̀ àrùn, wọ́n sì lè yàtọ̀ gẹ́gẹ́ bí irú kòkòrò àrùn.

Gịnị Ka Obodo Kwesịrị Ime Ma Ọ bụrụ na Mmadụ Amalite Igosi Mgbaàmà Ebola

Ma ọ bụrụ na mmadụ n'obodo amalite igosi ihe ndị nwere ike igosi ọrịa Ebola, ebe a bụ ihe obodo kwesịrị ime ozugbo:

Mee ka mmadụ ahụ bụrụ onye dị nwa

Kewapụ mmadụ ahụ ngwa ngwa. Ịchapụ ya n'ụlọ ọzọ—ụlọ dị anya site n'ụlọ ndị ọzọ, karịsịa ụmụ akọ, agadi na onye ọ bụla na-adịghị mma. Ịkọ ihe a bụ ọrụ kachasị mkpa.

Wedata nso nso na ya. Nanị ndị a ga-aba uru n'ọzọ na ya. Ha kwesịrị iyi aka, uwe mgbochi, ihu mgbochi, anya mgbochi. Ekwela aka raa ọbara ma ọ bụ ihe ọ bụla si n'anya ya lapụ n'enweghị ihe mgbochi.

Mezu onye nyocha ọrịa ngwa ngwa. Kpọọ ụlọ ọgwụ dị nso ma ọ bụ nọmba ọrịa ngwa ngwa. Emela nkali. Emekọta ihe a n'obodo naanị gị. Gwara ha ihe ndị a ozugbo: ebe mmadụ ahụ nọ, ole mgbe ọrịa amalitere, ma ọ bụ na mmadụ ahụ gara ebe ọzọ nwa oge. Mgbe ndị nyocha ọrịa ruru, ha ga-enwe ike ịzụ ya, ikewapụ ya nke ọma, wee nye ya ogwu.

Emezi ihe si n'ara mmadụ ahụ nke ọma. Ma mmadụ ahụ na-eti ire, na-efe ọbara, ma ọ bụ na-efe ihe, eme ka ihe niile a bụrụ ọrịa dị njọ. Jisie ụlọ site n'uti chlorine—ihe ndị a niile: ihe ndụ, uwe, ụlọ, ihe niile. Eli ihe ahụ ma ọ bụ fụkọ ya dịka ndị nyocha ọrịa gwara unu.

Ọgwụgwụ bụ ihe siri ike. Ma mmadụ ahụ anwụ, ara ya ka na-ewu. Nanị mmadụ a zụrụ nke ọma pụrụ isooro ara ya—maọ ka mmadụ ezinaụlọ raa. Ọgwụgwụ n'etiti mmadụ n'enweghị ihe mgbochi bụ ụzọ ọrịa na-agbasa ngwa ngwa.
