Ekwela iji ogwu ụlọ karịsịa ọrịa oyị elu
Gịnị Mere Ihe A Dị Mkpa

Ọrịa Ebola na-agbasa site n'ịsooro mmadụ na-arịa ya, ma ọ bụ ara ya nwụrụ. Mgbe ụtụtụ, obodo na-enwụ mmadụ site n'ọrịa a mgbe isooro na-agbasa ihe ma ọ bụ mgbe na-eme ọgwụgwụ n'enweghị ihe mgbochi. Mgbe ndị nyocha ọrịa ruru ngwa ngwa, kwesịrị ka ọrịa kewapụta nke ọma—ọrụ a na-azọ ndụ mmadụ ahụ na ndụ obodo niile.

Gịnị Ka Obodo Kwesịrị Ime Ma Ọ Bụrụ Na Mmadụ Amalite Igosi Mgbaàmà Nwere Ike Ịbụ Ọrịa Ebola
Otu Esi Amata Mgbaàmà Ebola

Ọrịa Ebola na-amalite na mberede, na-ebute ahụ ọkụ dị ike, isi ọwụwa dị njọ, ụfụ ahụ, ike ọgwụgwụ nke na-adịghị mma, agbọ ọsịsa, na afọ ọsịsa. N'ụfọdụ mmadụ, ọbara nwere ike isi n'ọnụ, imi, maọbụ ebe ndị ọzọ na ahụ na-asọpụta. Ọrịa a nwere ike were ụbọchị 2 ruo 21 tupu mgbaàmà ebido igosi, ma ọ na-abụkarị n'etiti ụbọchị 8 na 10. Nsogbu bụ na mgbaàmà ndị a yiri nke ịba (malaria) na taifoịdị, ya mere, ọ dịghị ụzọ ị ga-eji anya were mara na ọ bụ Ebola ma ọ bụghị site na nyocha ọgwụgwọ.

Ihe Kwesịrị Ime Ozugbo

Kewapụ onye ahụ na-arịa arịa, ma ejila aka efu metụ ya. Debe onye ahụ n'otu ọnụ ụlọ maọbụ ebe ikuku si nke ọma. Onye ọbụla ekwesịghị iji aka ya metụ onye ahụ na-arịa arịa, ihe ndị si n'ahụ ya na-apụta (agbọ ọsịsa, ọbara, nsị, ọhịa), akwa ya, maọbụ ihe ndina ya. Ọ bụ site n'imetụ ihe ndị a ka Ebola si agbasa, tinyekwara ihe ọbụla mmiri ahụ onye ọrịa metụrụ.

Kpọọ ndị ọrụ ahụike ozugbo. Gwa ụlọ ọgwụ nke kacha nso, onye nlekọta ọrịa na-efe efe (disease surveillance officer), maọbụ kpọọ akara ekwentị NCDC. Gwa ha mgbaàmà onye ahụ na-egosi, oge ọrịa ahụ bidoro, ma onye ahụ jere ije gaa ebe ọrịa Ebola dị, maọbụ ma onye ahụ metụrụ onye nwere Ebola aka, maọbụ ma o metụrụ anụ ọhịa aka (karịsịa ụsụ maọbụ enwe). Ịkpọ oku ọsịịsọ na-enyere ndị ahụike aka ime nyocha ngwa ngwa ma malite nzaghachi kwesịrị ekwesị.

Ọ bụrụ na ị ga-enyere onye ọrịa aka tupu ndị ọrụ ahụike abịa, otu onye naanị kwesịrị ịbụ onye na-elekọta ya. Onye ahụ kwesịrị ikpuchi anụ ahụ ya nke ọma, ghara ekwe ka mmiri ahụ onye ọrịa metụ ya, wee saa aka ya nke ọma site n'iji ncha na mmiri maọbụ mmiri chlorine (0.05% chlorine maka ịsa aka) mgbe niile.

Ihe Obodo Ekwesịghị Ime N'ụzọ Ọbụla

Ejila aka asaa ahụ onye ọrịa ma ọ bụrụ na o nwụọ. Mgbe onye nwere Ebola nwụrụ, nje vaịrọsị ahụ dị n'ahụ ya dị oke ike. Omenala ịsa ahụ na iji aka kwadoo ozu maka olili ozu abụrụla isi ihe na-eme ka Ebola gbasaa n'oge ọrịa ebili ọbụla WHO dere. Naanị ndị e zụrụ azụ maka olili ozu kwesịrị ijide ozu ahụ.

Ewerela ọgwụ ọdịnala maọbụ ahịhịa dochie ụlọ ọgwụ. Ọ nweghị ọgwụ ọdịnala ọbụla gosipụtara na nyocha sayensị na ọ nwere ike ịgwọ maọbụ mezie ọrịa Ebola. Ọ bụrụ na ị nọdụ nwayọọ tupu ị kpọga onye ọrịa ụlọ ọgwụ, ohere ya ịdị ndụ ga-ebelata, ndị ọzọ nọ n'obodo ga-anọkwa n'ihe ize ndụ.

Ezonarịla onye ọrịa, ekwela ka ị ghara ịkọ. Ọ bụrụ na mmadụ zoo onye na-arịa arịa, ọrịa ahụ ga-agbasa n'enweghị njide. N'oge ọrịa Ebola dị na West Africa (2013–2016) na DRC (2018–2020), egwu ihere na nkewa mere ka ndị mmadụ zoo ndị ezinụlọ ha na-arịa arịa, nke mere ka ọrịa ahụ gbasaa karịa.

Emetụla ihe ọbụla mmiri ahụ onye ọrịa metụrụ (akwa ndina, uwe, efere, iko) ruo mgbe ndị ọrụ ahụike gwara gị otu esi ehichapụ ya. Ị ga-eji mmiri chlorine 0.5% sachapụ ihe ndị ahụ.

Nyochaa Ndị Onye Ọrịa Metụrụ Aka. Ka Obodo Nyere Aka

Mgbe e kwusara okwu banyere onye ọrịa ahụ, ndị ọrụ ahụike ga-abịa chọta onye ọbụla metụrụ onye ọrịa ahụ aka. Ndị obodo kwesịrị inye aka, zaa ajụjụ n'eziokwu, ma gwa ha nke ọma onye niile nọ onye ọrịa ahụ nso. Onye ọbụla metụrụ onye ọrịa ahụ aka ga-achọ ịlele oke okpomọkụ ahụ ya ma na-ahụ otu ahụ ya si dị kwa ụbọchị ruo ụbọchị 21. Onye metụrụ onye ọrịa aka adịghị agbasa Ebola ma ọ bụrụ na ya onwe ya amalitebeghị igosi mgbaàmà, mana nlekọta kwa ụbọchị ahụ bụ ihe ga-enyere ndị ahụike aka ịchọta ọrịa ọhụrụ ọbụla ngwa ngwa.

Otu Obodo Kwesịrị Isi Kwado Tupu Ọrịa Abịa

Obodo ndị nọ nso ebe Ebola pụtara mbụ, maọbụ ndị nọ n'ihe ize ndụ, kwesịrị ime ihe ndị a tupu nsogbu abịa:

Kparịta ụka na ndị ọrụ ahụike gị, mara onye ị ga-akpọ na otu esi esi aga ha. Họpụta otu ebe ga-abụ ebe nkewa. Chịkọta ncha na chlorine. Kwekọrịta otu unu ga-esi eziga ozi ngwa ngwa ma ọ bụrụ na ọrịa pụta ìhè. Ndị ọrụ ahụike obodo maọbụ ndị ọrụ afọ ofufo kwesịrị ịnata ọzụzụ bụ isi banyere otu esi echekwa onwe ha na ndị ọzọ tupu ọrịa ebido, ọ bụghị mgbe ọ bidochara.

Ebe Ozi A Si Pụta

Nduzi a dabere na akwụkwọ ozi WHO (World Health Organization) banyere ọrịa Ebola na usoro ichekwa ọrịa efe efe, tinyere nduzi CDC (U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) maka nzaghachi Ebola. Oke chlorine (0.05% maka ịsa aka, 0.5% maka ihichapụ) soro iwu WHO maka nlekọta gburugburu ebe obibi. Oge ọrịa na-ewe tupu o gosipụta (2–21 ụbọchị) na otu vaịrọsị ahụ si agbasa bụ ihe a maara nke ọma site na nyocha ndị a depụtara n'akwụkwọ sayensị sitere na ọrịa Ebola 2013–2016 na West Africa na 2018–2020 na DRC.

Lelee na Ministry of Health maọbụ NCDC maka usoro kachasị ọhụrụ, n'ihi na nduzi nwere ike ịgbanwe n'etiti oge ọrịa na-ebili.

Gịnị Ka Obodo Kwesịrị Ime Ma Ọ Bụrụ Na Mmadụ Amalite Igosi Mgbaàmà Ndị Nwere Ike Igosi Ọrịa Ebola
Otu Esi Amata Mgbaàmà Ọrịa Ebola

Ọrịa Ebola na-amalite na mberede, na-ebute ahụ ọkụ dị ike, isi ọwụwa dị njọ, ụfụ ahụ, ike ọgwụgwụ nke na-adịghị mma karịrị akarị, agbọ ọsịsa, na afọ ọsịsa. N'ụfọdụ ndị mmadụ, ọbara nwere ike isi n'ọnụ, imi, anya, maọbụ ọ nwere ike ịnọ n'ime nsị na agbọ ọsịsa n'enweghị ihe kpatara ya a maara. Ọrịa a nwere ike were ụbọchị 2 ruo 21 tupu mgbaàmà ebido igosi mgbe mmadụ butere ọrịa ahụ, mana ọ na-abụkarị n'etiti ụbọchị 8 na 10. Nsogbu dị oke mkpa bụ na mgbaàmà ndị a yiri nke ịba (malaria), taifoịdị, meningitis, na ọrịa ndị ọzọ a na-ahụkarị n'ebe Ebola na-eme. Ya mere, a pụghị eji anya were mara na ọ bụ Ebola. Ọ bụ naanị nyocha ụlọ nyocha (lab test) nwere ike igosi ma ọ bụ Ebola ka ọ bụghị.

Ihe Kwesịrị Ime Ozugbo

Kewapụ onye ahụ na-arịa arịa, mana ejila aka efu metụ ya. Duru maọbụ zi onye ahụ ụzọ gaa n'otu ọnụ ụlọ maọbụ ebe ikuku si nke ọma. Onye ọbụla ekwesịghị iji aka ya maọbụ ahụ ya metụ onye ọrịa ahụ, metụ ihe ndị si n'ahụ ya na-apụta (ọbara, agbọ ọsịsa, nsị, mamịrị, ọhịa, mmiri asụsụ), metụ uwe ya, akwa ndina ya, maọbụ ihe ọbụla mmiri ahụ ndị a metụrụ. Ebola na-agbasa site n'imetụ mmiri ahụ onye na-egosi mgbaàmà ọrịa maọbụ onye nwụrụ anwụ nke ọrịa metụtara, yana site n'ihe ndị mmiri ahụ ndị a metụrụ. Nkewapụ a abụghị ịjụ onye ahụ. Ọ bụ ihe ziri ezi nke ahụike nke na-echekwa ma obodo ma onye ọrịa, n'ihi na ọ na-eme ka ọnọdụ ahụ nọrọ n'okpuru njikwa ruo mgbe nlekọta ndị ọkachamara ga-abịa.

Kpọọ ndị ọrụ ahụike ozugbo. Kpọtụrụ ụlọ ọgwụ kacha nso, onye nlekọta ọrịa na-efe efe nke gọọmenti obodo maọbụ steeti gị, maọbụ kpọọ akara ekwentị NCDC nke a na-akwụghị ụgwọ. Gwa ha nke ọma: mgbaàmà onye ọrịa na-egosi, oge ọrịa ahụ bidoro, ma onye ahụ jere njem ebe ọbụla (karịsịa ebe a maara na Ebola na-eme), ma onye ahụ metụrụla onye ọbụla na-arịa arịa na mgbaàmà yiri nke a aka maọbụ onye nwụrụ anwụ n'oge na-adịbeghị anya, na ma o metụrụla anụ ọhịa aka (karịsịa ụsụ maọbụ enwe). Ịkpọ oku a bụ otu ihe kacha dị mkpa nke onye ọbụla nọ n'obodo nwere ike ime, n'ihi na ọ na-amalite usoro nyocha ụlọ nyocha, nlekọta onye ọrịa, na ịchọta ndị niile metụrụ onye ọrịa aka (contact tracing), nke ndụ onye ọrịa na nchekwa obodo niile dabere na ya.

Ọ bụrụ na ị ga-enyere onye ọrịa aka tupu ndị ọrụ ahụike abịa, otu onye naanị kwesịrị ịbụ onye na-elekọta ya. Onye ahụ kwesịrị ikpuchi ahụ ya niile nke ọma: uwe aka ogologo, ogologo trọza, akpụkpọ ụkwụ kpuchiri ụkwụ, yana gloovu ma ọ bụrụ na ọ dị. Ọ bụrụ na gloovu adịghị, jiri akpa rọba kee ya n'aka. Ekwela ka mmiri ahụ onye ọrịa metụ gị n'ụzọ ọbụla. Saa aka gị ozugbo ma nke ọma site n'iji ncha na mmiri maọbụ mmiri chlorine 0.05% mgbe ịmetụchara onye ọrịa. A ga-edekọ onye a dịka onye metụrụ onye ọrịa aka (contact) maka nlekọta kwa ụbọchị mgbe e mesịrị.

Ihe Obodo Ekwesịghị Ime N'ụzọ Ọbụla

Ejila aka saa ahụ onye ọrịa ma ọ bụrụ na o nwụọ. Oke nje vaịrọsị nọ n'ahụ onye nwụrụ n'ọrịa Ebola dị elu nke ukwu, ọ dị elu karịa oge ọbụla n'oge ọrịa ahụ. Omenaala ịsa na iji aka metụ na iyikwasị ozu uwe bụrụla otu n'ime ihe ndị kacha eme ka Ebola gbasaa n'oge ọrịa na-efe efe nke ukwu ọbụla WHO dere n'akwụkwọ, gụnyere nke West Africa 2013–2016 na DRC 2018–2020. Ọ bụ naanị ndị e zụrụ azụ maka olili ozu kwesịrị ijide ozu. Usoro olili ozu nke dị nchekwa ma na-asọpụrụ omenaala dịka ọ na-egbochikwa ịkesa ọrịa dị, ndị ọrụ ahụike nwekwara ike inyere aka ịhazi ndị otu ndị a.

Ewerela ọgwụ ọdịnala maọbụ ahịhịa dochie ụlọ ọgwụ. Ọ nweghị ọgwụ ọdịnala ọbụla gosipụtara na nyocha sayensị maọbụ nyocha ụlọ nyocha na ọ nwere ike ịgwọ ọrịa Ebola. Inye onye ọrịa ọgwụ ọdịnala na-eme ka oge e kwesịrị iburu ya gaa ụlọ ọgwụ gaa n'ihu, ebe nlekọta (karịsịa mmiri drip/IV fluid) na-eme ka ohere ịdị ndụ dịkwuo mma nke ukwu. Imetụ aka nke a ga-eme iji nye ya ọgwụ ọdịnala na-emepụtakwa ụzọ ịkesa ọrịa ozugbo.

Ezonarịla onye ọrịa, ekwela ka ị ghara ịkọ. Izo onye na-egosi mgbaàmà ọrịa na-eme ka ọrịa ahụ gbasaa n'enweghị njikwa. N'oge ọrịa Ebola na West Africa 2014–2016 na DRC 2018–2020, egwu ihere, nkewa, na nsogbu nke ndụ ezinụlọ mere ka ezinụlọ ndị mmadụ zoo ndị ha na-arịa arịa, ha wee lie ndị nwụrụ anwụ na nzuzo. Nyocha WHO, UNICEF, na IFRC mere mgbe ọrịa ndị a gachara na-achọpụta mgbe niile na izobe bụ otu n'ime omume ndị bụ isi kpọmkwem na-eme ka ọrịa gbasaa karịa ma na-amụbawanye ọnụ ọgụgụ ndị nwụrụ anwụ niile.

Emetụla ihe ọbụla mmiri ahụ onye ọrịa metụrụ (akwa ndina, uwe, efere, iko, ngaji, ala) ma ọ bụghị na ndị ọrụ ahụike enyela gị ntụzịaka. Ihe ndị rụrụ arụ chọrọ ịsa ha na mmiri chlorine 0.5% n'okpuru usoro ndị otu ahụike ga-enye.

Nyere Ndị Na-Esochi Ndị Metụrụ Onye Ọrịa Aka (Contact Tracing) Aka

Mgbe e kwusara okwu banyere onye a na-enyo enyo na ọ nwere ọrịa, ndị otu ọrụ ahụike ọha ga-achọta onye ọbụla metụrụ onye ọrịa ahụ aka ozugbo, maọbụ metụrụ mmiri ahụ ya, uwe ya, maọbụ akwa ndina ya. A ga-elekọta ndị metụrụ ya aka kwa ụbọchị ruo ụbọchị 21, site n'inyocha oke okpomọkụ ahụ ha na ịjụ banyere mgbaàmà. Onye metụrụ onye ọrịa aka adịghị efe efe, ọ pụghịkwa ịkesa Ebola nye ndị ọzọ, ma ọ bụghị na ya onwe ya amalitere igosi mgbaàmà. Mana nlekọta kwa ụbọchị na-eme ka a chọpụta ozugbo ma onye ọbụla metụrụ onye ọrịa aka amalitere igosi mgbaàmà, wee kewapụ ya ngwa ngwa, tupu o tinye ndị ọzọ n'ihe ize ndụ.

Ndị obodo ga-enye ozi ziri ezi na nke zuruoke banyere onye metụrụ onye ọrịa aka, oge ole, na n'ụzọ ole. Ịgha ndị na-esochi ndị metụrụ onye ọrịa aka ụgha, ma ọ bụ iji chekwaa onye ezinụlọ ka a ghara elekọta ya maọbụ iji zere ihe ị chere na ọ ga-abụ nsonaazụ ọha, bụ otu n'ime ihe ndị kacha dị ize ndụ nke mmadụ nwere ike ime n'oge ọrịa na-efe efe. Ọ na-ahapụ onye nwere ike ịbụ na ọrịa metụtara ya ka ọ na-agagharị n'enweghị onye na-elekọta ya, na-emepụta ọnọdụ maka agbụ nkesa ọrịa ọhụrụ.

Otu Esi Elebara Egwu Anya Ma Gbochie Ihere Na-emerụ Ahụ

Egwu Ebola bụ nzaghachi nwere isi maka ọrịa nwere oke ọnwụ dị elu. Mana obodo kwesịrị ịmata oke dị n'etiti omume ichegide ọrịa kwesịrị ekwesị na nkewapụ ọha na-emerụ ahụ nke ezinụlọ ọrịa metụtara.

Ihe nlezianya kwesịrị ekwesị dị ka: ịghara imetụ onye ọrịa na mmiri ahụ ya aka ozugbo, ịnọ anya n'oge ọrịa ahụ, na ilekọta onwe gị maka mgbaàmà ọrịa ma ọ bụrụ na ị metụrụla onye ọrịa aka na mbụ.

Ihe nkewapụ na-emerụ ahụ dị ka: ịjụ ịgwa ezinụlọ ahụ okwu kpam kpam, ịjụ inye ha nri na mmiri, igbochi ha ịga ụlọ ọgwụ, ịkọsa aha ha gburugburu na okwu ihere dịka "ezinụlọ Ebola," ịtụ ha egwu maọbụ iwakpo ha, maọbụ ịjụ ekwe ka ndị ezinụlọ ha ndị ọzọ na-adịghị arịa arịa mee ihe ọbụla n'obodo dịka ịga ọrụ, ụlọ akwụkwọ, maọbụ ahịa.

Otu omume nke abụọ a anaghị ebelata ihe ize ndụ nke ịkesa ọrịa kpam kpam. Kama ọ na-eme ka ihe ize ndụ niile mụbaa n'ihi na ọ na-akụziri ndị mmadụ ka ha zoo ọrịa. N'oge ọrịa Ebola na West Africa na DRC, egwu na ihere mere ka ezinụlọ ndị mmadụ zoo ndị ha na-arịa arịa, zere ụlọ ọgwụ, were n'ụzọ nzuzo lie ndị nwụrụ anwụ. Ihe ndị a niile mere ka ọrịa ahụ gbasaa karịa. Nyocha WHO, UNICEF, na IFRC mere mgbe ọrịa gachara na-achọpụta mgbe niile na izobe nke ihere na-akpata bụ otu n'ime ihe ndị kacha dị ize ndụ n'oge nzaghachi ọrịa na-efe efe.

Na-ekwurịta okwu na ezinụlọ ahụ. Gwa ha okwu site n'ebe dị anya nke kwesịrị maọbụ kpọọ ha ekwentị. Gwa ha ihe na-eme, na a kpọọla ndị ọrụ ahụike, na ihe ha kwesịrị iche. Mgbe ị gbuduru mmadụ n'ọmụma ihe, egwu na enweghị ntụkwasị obi na-abawanye n'akụkụ abụọ.

Hụ na ezinụlọ ahụ nwere ike inweta nri na mmiri. Ị nwere ike iburu nri, mmiri dị ọcha, na ihe ndị ọzọ dị mkpa nye ezinụlọ ahụ n'enweghị imetụ aka. Dobe ihe ndị ahụ n'ọnụ ụzọ ụlọ. Ibepụ ezinụlọ n'ihe ndị ha chọrọ n'oge mberede ahụike abụghị usoro nchekwa. Ọ bụ ịhapụ ha nke ga-eme ka ihe dịkwuo njọ maka onye ọbụla, n'ihi na ezinụlọ nọ n'ọnọdụ mkpa ga-amasị ịgbapụ, zoo ọrịa, maọbụ jụ inyere ndị ọrụ ahụike aka.

Ewepụla ndị ezinụlọ na-adịghị arịa arịa n'ndụ obodo n'enweghị ihe kpatara ya nke ahụike. Ndị bi n'ụlọ ahụ na-adịghị egosi mgbaàmà ọrịa ọbụla adịghị efe efe. Ebola anaghị agbasa site n'ikuku n'okpuru ọnọdụ nkịtị. Ọ na-agbasa site n'imetụ mmiri ahụ onye na-egosi mgbaàmà ọrịa n'oge ahụ aka ozugbo. Ndị ezinụlọ na-adịghị egosi mgbaàmà kwesịrị ịnọ n'okpuru nlekọta (nyochaa oke okpomọkụ ahụ kwa ụbọchị ruo ụbọchị 21), mana a gaghị emeso ha dịka ndị rịarala arịa. Ha nwere ike iso obodo mee ihe ma ha na-edobe iwu ịdị ọcha. Iwepụ ndị ezinụlọ nwere ahụ ike n'ọrụ, ụlọ akwụkwọ, ahịa, maọbụ ihe omume obodo n'enweghị ihe kpatara ya nke ahụike ga-eme ka ha nwee mmerụ ego na nke uche nke ga-eme ka ndị mmadụ jụ inyere nzaghachi ahụ aka.

Akọsala aha ezinụlọ ahụ gburugburu na okwu ihere. Ịkpọ ezinụlọ ahụ "ezinụlọ Ebola" maọbụ ihe yiri ya na-eme ka ihere sie ike, ọ ga-esikwa ike maka ha na maka ndị ga-arịa arịa n'ọdịnihu ịchọ ọgwụgwọ. Ozi ahụike kwesịrị ilekwasị anya ọrịa ahụ na ihe ndị mmadụ kwesịrị ime iji chekwaa onwe ha, ọ bụghị ịchọpụta ma taa otu ezinụlọ ụta.

Otu Obodo Kwesịrị Isi Kwado Tupu Ọrịa Abịa

Obodo ndị nọ nso ebe Ebola pụtara mbụ, maọbụ ndị nọ n'ihe ize ndụ, kwesịrị ime ihe ndị a tupu nsogbu abịa.

Kparịta ụka na ndị ọrụ ahụike obodo gị, mara onye ị ga-akpọ na otu esi esi aga ha. Họpụta otu ebe ga-abụ ebe nkewa (isolation area): ọnụ ụlọ maọbụ ụlọ nke ikuku si nke ọma, dị anya n'ebe ndị mmadụ niile na-anọ, nke nwere ike ịnweta mmiri na ụlọ mposi. Chịkọta ncha na chlorine. Kwekọrịta otu unu ga-esi eziga ozi ngwa ngwa ma ọ bụrụ na ọrịa a na-enyo enyo pụta ìhè. Ndị ọrụ ahụike obodo maọbụ ndị ọrụ afọ ofufo kwesịrị ịnata ọzụzụ bụ isi banyere ichegide ọrịa tupu ọrịa na-efe efe ebido, ọ bụghị mgbe ọ bidochara.

Otu Egwu Na Nsonaazụ Si Ejikọ

Ihe akaebe sitere na ọrịa na-efe efe nke ukwu na-egosi mgbe niile na obodo ndị na-ejigide njikọ ọha mgbe ha na-eme usoro ichegide ọrịa kwesịrị ekwesị na-enweta nsonaazụ ka mma karịa obodo ndị egwu na ihere kewara. Nke a abụghị naanị n'ihi na njikọ na-adị mma n'obi, ọ bụ ezie na ọ na-adị mma. Ọ bụ n'ihi na nzaghachi ọrịa na-efe efe bụ nsogbu omume ọha. Ịchọta ndị metụrụ onye ọrịa aka chọrọ ikwu eziokwu. Nkewa chọrọ ka obodo nyere onye a kewapụrụ aka. Olili ozu nchekwa chọrọ ntụkwasị obi n'etiti ezinụlọ na ndị na-eli ozu. Nlekọta chọrọ ka ndị na-arịa arịa pụta ìhè n'ụlọ ọgwụ kama ịzo. Ọrụ ndị a niile na-adaka mgbe ihere mee ka ụgwọ nke a mara na ị nwere ike ịbụ onye ọrịa dị elu karịa ụgwọ nke izo onwe gị.

Ọrụ obodo nwere bụ ijide ihe abụọ n'otu oge: nlezianya nke eziokwu banyere ọrịa nwere ike igbu, na njikọ nke eziokwu na ezinụlọ nọ na nsogbu. Ha abụọ anaghị alụ ọgụ. Nlezianya na-enweghị njikọ na-emepụta izobe. Njikọ na-enweghị nlezianya na-emepụta ịkesa ọrịa. Ha abụọ ọnụ na-emepụta ọnọdụ nke na-eme ka a na-achịkwa ọrịa na-efe efe.

Ebe Ndụmọdụ A Si Pụta

Ndụmọdụ a dabere na akwụkwọ ozi WHO (World Health Organization) gbasara ọrịa Ebola na ntụzịaka ichegide na ịchịkwa ọrịa, ntụzịaka nzaghachi Ebola nke CDC (U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention), usoro WHO Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE), nyocha ndị e bipụtara gbasara mmekọrịta obodo na omume ihere n'oge ọrịa Ebola na West Africa 2013–2016 na ọrịa Ebola DRC 2018–2020, yana ntụzịaka WHO/UNICEF/IFRC jikọtara aka maka usoro nzaghachi obodo na olili ozu nchekwa nwere ugwu. Oke chlorine (0.05% maka ịsa aka, 0.5% maka ịsa ala na ihe ndị ọzọ) na-eso ntụzịaka ahụike gburugburu ebe obibi nke WHO. Oge nlekọta ndị metụrụ onye ọrịa aka (ụbọchị 21) na àgwà ịkesa ọrịa (imetụ mmiri ahụ aka ozugbo, anaghị agbasa site n'ikuku n'okpuru ọnọdụ nkịtị, oke nje vaịrọsị kachasị elu n'oge ọnwụ na mgbe ọnwụ gachara) dabere na ihe a matara banyere vaịrọlọjị na epịdemịọlọjị nke ọrịa Ebola dịka e si dee ya n'akwụkwọ nyocha ndị ọkachamara nyochara.

Ndị obodo kwesịrị inyocha usoro ndị dị ugbu a na ụlọọrụ ahụike mba ha maọbụ ọfịs WHO nọ na mba ha, n'ihi na usoro a kapịrị ọnụ nwere ike ịgbanwe n'etiti oge ọrịa na-efe efe ma dịkwa iche dabere na ụdị nje ọrịa.

For anyone with watery diarrhoea or vomiting:

Begin oral rehydration solution immediately and continue during travel to a health facility.

Immediate Community Response to Suspected Cholera

If multiple people in a community suddenly develop severe watery diarrhoea and vomiting, cholera must be treated as a serious outbreak risk. Here's what families must do immediately:

Urgent Steps

Isolate affected people. Place each person with symptoms in a separate space away from other household members and the wider community. Cholera spreads through contaminated water and faeces, so separation is critical. Use a designated toilet or bucket if possible, kept separate from the main household area.

Rehydration is life-saving—start immediately. Severe watery diarrhoea causes rapid dehydration and death. Begin oral rehydration solution (ORS) right away. If ORS packets aren't available, make it: dissolve 6 teaspoons of sugar and ½ teaspoon of salt in 1 litre of clean boiled water. Give small, frequent sips—this alone saves most cholera patients. Continue even if the person vomits; some fluid will be absorbed.

Alert health authorities without delay. Report to the nearest health clinic, district health office, or disease surveillance hotline immediately. Multiple cases in one area signal an outbreak. Early reporting triggers rapid response: confirmatory testing, treatment supplies, vaccination campaigns if needed, and water/sanitation investigation.

Safe faeces and vomit disposal. All faeces and vomit must be treated as highly infectious. Use designated containers (buckets with lids). Disinfect with chlorine solution (0.5% concentration—roughly 1 part bleach to 9 parts water). Bury contaminated waste away from water sources, or follow health authority guidance. Never dispose of waste in communal water sources.

Water safety is non-negotiable. Use only boiled water or water treated with chlorine tablets (if available). Do not use untreated water from wells, streams, or communal sources until authorities confirm safety. Unsafe water is how cholera spreads to healthy people.

Hand hygiene. Wash hands with soap and clean water after contact with the sick person, after using the toilet, and before eating. This is critical for preventing spread within the household.

Secure the water supply. If possible, identify the source of contamination. Cholera often indicates faecal contamination of drinking water. Communities must protect wells and water sources from contamination—cover them, prevent direct contact with soil or animals, and avoid disposing of waste near them.

What Families Must NOT Do
Do not share eating utensils, cups, or bedding with the sick person
Do not use the same toilet as the sick person without disinfection between uses
Do not drink untreated water from communal sources
Do not delay reporting—thinking it will resolve on its own is dangerous
Do not rely on traditional remedies instead of ORS and medical care
Do not allow children or elderly to care for severely ill people
Do not dispose of faeces near wells, streams, or communal water sources
Why This Matters—and Why Speed is Critical

Cholera kills through dehydration. A person can lose several litres of fluid in hours. ORS replacement works—it saves over 99% of cases if given early. However, cholera spreads explosively through contaminated water: one untreated case can infect dozens.

The difference between outbreak containment and epidemic is often hours. Early isolation, rehydration, and health-authority notification prevent community-wide transmission.

If someone shows signs of severe dehydration (extreme thirst, sunken eyes, lethargy, little or no urine), this is a medical emergency. Get to a health facility immediately if possible, or continue aggressive ORS while waiting for emergency response.

Community and Family Response to Suspected Cholera Outbreak
Recognising the Situation

When multiple people in the same community develop sudden, severe watery diarrhoea and vomiting within a short period, this clustering pattern is a strong epidemiological signal of a common-source or propagated outbreak. Cholera (caused by Vibrio cholerae) produces profuse, painless, watery diarrhoea often described as having a "rice-water" appearance, with or without vomiting. Severe cases can lose litres of fluid within hours, leading to fatal dehydration if untreated. However, laboratory confirmation is necessary because other pathogens (rotavirus, enterotoxigenic E. coli, norovirus) can produce similar presentations.

Immediate Priority: Prevent Dehydration Deaths

Dehydration is what kills in cholera, often within hours of symptom onset. Families must begin fluid replacement immediately, before the sick person reaches a health facility.

Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) is the single most critical intervention. If pre-packaged ORS sachets are available, mix exactly as directed with clean water. If ORS is unavailable, a temporary home solution can be prepared: six level teaspoons of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt dissolved in one litre of clean (boiled or treated) water. This is an interim measure, not a substitute for proper ORS. Give the sick person small, frequent sips continuously. A severely dehydrated adult may need several litres within the first few hours. For children, continue breastfeeding alongside ORS.

Watch for danger signs of severe dehydration: sunken eyes, loss of skin elasticity (skin pinched on the back of the hand stays tented), rapid or weak pulse, lethargy or unconsciousness, inability to drink, absent or very dark urine. These require intravenous fluid replacement at a health facility and constitute a medical emergency.

Report to Health Authorities

Do not wait for laboratory confirmation before reporting. A cluster of acute watery diarrhoea cases in the same community within a short timeframe meets the threshold for suspected outbreak notification under WHO and most national surveillance systems. Contact the nearest health facility, local government health department, disease surveillance officer, or national disease reporting channel. Provide the number of affected people, their locations, when symptoms started, and any suspected common exposure (shared water source, shared food, recent event).

Early reporting activates the public health response chain: case confirmation, water source testing, case management support, and supply of ORS and intravenous fluids.

Protect the Water Supply

Cholera spreads primarily through water and food contaminated with faeces from an infected person. The most common transmission route in outbreaks is a shared, contaminated water source.

Treat all drinking water. Boil water at a rolling boil for at least one minute, or treat with household chlorine (sodium hypochlorite). For point-of-use chlorination, the WHO recommends approximately 2mg/L free chlorine residual for clear water. Commercially available water treatment products (liquid chlorine, purification tablets) should be used according to their labelling. If neither boiling nor chlorination is possible, solar disinfection (SODIS), filling clear plastic bottles and exposing them to direct sunlight for at least six hours, provides partial but meaningful risk reduction.

Store treated water safely. Use a clean, covered, narrow-mouthed container. Do not insert hands or dip cups into stored water. Pour water out or use a tap-fitted container.

Do not use the suspected contaminated water source for drinking, cooking, washing food, or brushing teeth until it has been tested and declared safe, or until a treated alternative is available.

Sanitation and Hygiene

Handwashing is non-negotiable. Every household member must wash hands with soap and water after using the latrine, after contact with a sick person or their soiled materials, before preparing food, before eating, and before feeding children. Where soap is unavailable, ash can serve as a partial substitute, though soap is more effective.

Safe disposal of faeces and vomit. All excreta from sick persons must go into a latrine or toilet. If the person cannot reach the latrine, collect vomit and stool in a bucket or container, add chlorine solution (0.2% for disinfection of excreta), wait 30 minutes, then dispose into the latrine. Do not dump untreated excreta into open drains, waterways, or open ground.

Disinfect contaminated surfaces and items. Bedding, clothing, and floors soiled with faeces or vomit should be washed with 0.2% chlorine solution. Utensils used by the sick person should be washed separately with treated water and soap or chlorine.

Open defecation must stop entirely. If some community members practise open defecation, this is now an acute community-wide hazard. Emergency latrine arrangements are needed immediately.

Food Safety

Cook food thoroughly and eat it while hot. Vibrio cholerae is killed by heat. Do not eat raw vegetables or fruits unless they can be peeled. Do not eat food that has been sitting at room temperature for extended periods, especially in hot climates. Avoid food from street vendors or communal settings during the outbreak unless preparation safety can be verified.

Wash all food preparation surfaces with treated water before use.

Caring for Sick Persons at Home

Some cholera patients, particularly those with mild to moderate dehydration who can drink, may be managed at home with continuous ORS while awaiting or between health facility visits. The caregiver should designate specific utensils and bedding for the sick person, wash hands after every contact, and keep the sick person's waste strictly separated and disinfected.

However, any person showing signs of severe dehydration, any child under five with acute watery diarrhoea, any pregnant woman, and any person with underlying health conditions should be taken to a health facility as quickly as possible. Cholera case fatality can drop from over 50% without treatment to below 1% with proper rehydration therapy, so access to care is decisive.

Handling the Dead

If a person dies from suspected cholera, the body remains infectious. Burial preparation should be carried out by trained personnel or, if that is not possible, by persons wearing gloves who minimise contact with body fluids, disinfect the body with 0.5% chlorine solution, and wash hands thoroughly afterwards. Large funeral gatherings with communal food present a documented transmission risk during cholera outbreaks and should be avoided or modified.

What Families Should Not Do

Do not use anti-diarrhoeal medications (such as loperamide) to stop the diarrhoea. These drugs slow gut motility and can mask fluid losses without addressing the underlying infection, worsening outcomes.

Do not rely solely on antibiotics obtained outside medical guidance. Antibiotics have a role in severe cholera cases but are not a substitute for rehydration, and inappropriate antibiotic use accelerates resistance. Treatment decisions belong to health workers.

Do not stigmatise or isolate affected families to the point that they avoid seeking care. Social exclusion has historically delayed treatment and reporting in cholera outbreaks, increasing mortality.

Source Basis

This guidance reflects WHO cholera fact sheets and outbreak response guidelines, the WHO/UNICEF technical guidance on oral rehydration therapy, WHO recommendations for household water treatment and safe storage, and the CDC cholera prevention and control protocols. The ORS formulation (sugar-salt solution) follows WHO emergency rehydration specifications. Chlorine concentrations for different uses (0.2% for excreta and surfaces, 0.5% for bodies) follow WHO environmental health in emergencies guidance. Case fatality comparisons (above 50% untreated versus below 1% treated) are drawn from WHO global cholera surveillance data.

Families should follow instructions from their local or national health authority, as specific outbreak response protocols may vary by country and may be updated as the situation evolves.

What Families Should Do When Multiple People Develop Severe Watery Diarrhoea and Vomiting and Cholera Is Suspected
Recognising the Severity of the Situation

When multiple people in the same community develop sudden, severe watery diarrhoea and vomiting within a short period, this clustering pattern is a strong epidemiological signal of an outbreak, potentially from a common source such as a shared water supply or food. Cholera, caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae, produces profuse, painless, watery diarrhoea often described as having a "rice-water" appearance, with or without vomiting. Severe cases can lose litres of fluid within hours, leading to fatal dehydration if untreated. However, other pathogens including rotavirus, norovirus, enterotoxigenic E. coli, Shigella, and Cryptosporidium can produce similar presentations. Laboratory confirmation is necessary to identify the specific cause, but the immediate community-level response follows the same principles regardless of pathogen: prevent dehydration deaths, report to health authorities, protect the water supply, and interrupt further transmission.

Immediate Priority: Prevent Dehydration Deaths

Dehydration is what kills in cholera and other acute watery diarrhoeal diseases, not the bacterium itself. Death can occur within hours of symptom onset, particularly in young children, elderly persons, pregnant women, and those with pre-existing health conditions. Fluid replacement must begin at home immediately, before the sick person reaches a health facility.

Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) is the single most critical intervention. If pre-packaged ORS sachets are available, mix exactly as directed with clean water that has been boiled or treated with chlorine. If ORS sachets are not available, a temporary home solution can be prepared: six level teaspoons of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt dissolved in one litre of treated water. This is an interim emergency measure, not a long-term substitute for properly formulated ORS. Administer small, frequent sips continuously. Do not wait for the person to say they are thirsty, because in severe dehydration the sensation of thirst itself can be lost. A severely dehydrated adult may require several litres within the first hours.

For children who are still breastfeeding, continue breastfeeding alongside ORS. For infants who are not breastfed, continue their usual milk or formula between ORS doses.

Monitor for danger signs of severe dehydration: sunken eyes, loss of skin turgor (skin pinched on the back of the hand remains tented and does not return to its normal position quickly), rapid and weak pulse, lethargy or unconsciousness, inability to drink or keep fluids down, absent or very dark urine. Any of these signs indicate a medical emergency requiring intravenous fluid replacement at a health facility. Transport the person immediately.

Additional danger signs in children: persistent vomiting of all fluids, blood in stool, high fever with diarrhoea in an infant under six months, and refusal to eat or drink. These require urgent medical attention regardless of apparent hydration status.

Cholera case fatality can exceed 50% without treatment, but with proper rehydration therapy it drops below 1%. Access to care is therefore the difference between life and death.

Report to Health Authorities

Do not wait for laboratory confirmation before reporting. A cluster of acute watery diarrhoeal cases in the same community within a short timeframe meets the threshold for suspected outbreak notification under WHO International Health Regulations and under virtually all national disease surveillance systems. Contact the nearest health facility, local government health department, disease surveillance officer, or national disease reporting channel.

Provide specific information: the number of people affected, their approximate ages, when symptoms began and whether onset was simultaneous or sequential (this helps distinguish a single-exposure event from ongoing transmission), the identity and location of any suspected common source (particularly a shared water source), and any other observations such as recent changes in the water supply, recent flooding, or proximity of latrines to the water source.

Early notification triggers responses the community cannot accomplish alone: laboratory testing of the water source to identify the pathogen, clinical case confirmation, supply of ORS and intravenous fluids, epidemiological investigation to confirm the source and identify all exposed persons, and technical remediation of the water source.

Protect the Water Supply

Cholera and most other causes of acute watery diarrhoea spread primarily through water and food contaminated with faeces from an infected person. The most common transmission route in outbreaks is a shared, contaminated water source.

Stop using the suspected water source immediately. This is the single most time-sensitive environmental action. Every hour the contaminated source remains in use, new people are being exposed. Families must stop using the suspected source for drinking, cooking, preparing food, washing food, washing utensils, brushing teeth, and any other activity involving ingestion or oral contact. If the source is a communal well, borehole, tap, or stream, local leaders must notify every household that uses it. Physical barriers (roping off the source, posting a guard, placing visible warning signs) are more effective than verbal notification alone, because people acting out of habit may continue to use the source despite hearing a warning.

Treat all drinking water. Until the suspected source has been tested and declared safe, or a confirmed clean alternative is established, every household must treat water before use.

Boiling is the most reliable household method. Water must reach a rolling boil and be maintained for at least one minute. Allow to cool in the same covered container. Do not transfer to an uncleaned container.

Chlorination is the primary alternative when boiling is impractical for volume or fuel reasons. Use household chlorine products (liquid sodium hypochlorite or chlorine tablets) according to manufacturer instructions. The WHO recommends a target of approximately 2 mg/L free chlorine residual for clear water. For turbid water, first filter through a clean cloth or allow to settle, then apply a higher chlorine dose, as organic matter consumes chlorine and reduces its disinfecting effect. After adding chlorine, wait at least 30 minutes before drinking.

Solar disinfection (SODIS) is a partial alternative where neither boiling nor chlorination is available. Fill clean, clear plastic bottles (PET, not opaque), place in direct sunlight for at least six hours, or two consecutive days if overcast. This method provides meaningful but incomplete pathogen reduction and is not effective against Cryptosporidium.

Store treated water safely. Use a clean, covered, narrow-mouthed container. Do not dip hands, cups, or other objects into stored water. Pour water out or dispense through a tap.

Sanitation and Hygiene

Handwashing is essential for every household, not only those with sick members. Every person must wash hands with soap and water after using the latrine, after any contact with a sick person or their soiled materials, before preparing food, before eating, and before feeding children. Where soap is unavailable, ash provides partial antimicrobial benefit, though soap is more effective.

Safe disposal of faeces and vomit from sick persons. All excreta must go into a latrine or toilet. If the sick person cannot reach the latrine, collect stool and vomit in a bucket or container, add 0.2% chlorine solution, wait 30 minutes, then dispose into the latrine. Do not dump untreated excreta into open drains, streams, rivers, or onto open ground, as this creates secondary contamination pathways that can affect other water sources or enable person-to-person transmission.

Disinfect contaminated surfaces and items. Bedding, clothing, and floors soiled with diarrhoeal stool or vomit should be washed with 0.2% chlorine solution. Utensils used by sick persons should be washed separately with treated water and soap or chlorine solution.

Open defecation must stop entirely. If any community members practise open defecation, this is now an acute hazard for the entire population. Every instance of faeces entering the environment without treatment is a potential source of continued or new contamination. Emergency latrine arrangements must be made immediately. If permanent latrines are insufficient, temporary pit latrines can be constructed at a minimum distance of 30 metres from any water source and with the base at least 1.5 metres above the water table.

Food Safety

Cook all food thoroughly and consume it while hot. Most waterborne diarrhoeal pathogens are killed by heat. Do not eat raw vegetables or fruits unless they can be peeled. Do not eat food that has been sitting at ambient temperature for extended periods, particularly in hot weather. Avoid food from street vendors or communal settings during the outbreak unless preparation safety can be verified. Wash all food preparation surfaces with treated water before use.

Discard food prepared with the suspected water. Any food that was washed, cooked with, or prepared using water from the suspected source before the contamination was identified should be thrown away. This includes food prepared for sale or communal consumption.

Caring for Sick Persons at Home

Some patients with mild to moderate dehydration who can drink may be managed at home with continuous ORS while awaiting or between health facility visits. The caregiver should designate specific utensils and bedding for the sick person, wash hands after every contact, and keep the sick person's waste strictly separated and disinfected.

However, the following categories of patients must be taken to a health facility as quickly as possible: anyone showing signs of severe dehydration, any child under five years of age with acute watery diarrhoea, any pregnant woman, and any person with a pre-existing health condition.

Handling the Dead

If a person dies from suspected cholera, the body remains infectious. Burial preparation should be carried out by trained personnel or, if that is not possible, by persons wearing gloves who minimise contact with body fluids, disinfect the body with 0.5% chlorine solution, and wash hands thoroughly afterwards. Large funeral gatherings with communal food present a documented transmission risk during cholera outbreaks and should be avoided or modified: reduce gathering size and avoid communal meals at burials during the outbreak.

What Families Should Not Do

Do not use anti-diarrhoeal medications such as loperamide to stop the diarrhoea. These drugs slow gut motility without addressing the underlying infection. They mask fluid losses and can worsen outcomes, particularly in children and in infections caused by invasive organisms such as Shigella, where slowing gut transit can increase toxin absorption.

Do not obtain antibiotics without medical guidance. Antibiotics have a specific role in certain diarrhoeal diseases, notably cholera and shigellosis, but the choice of antibiotic, dosing, and decision to prescribe depend on the pathogen, local antimicrobial resistance patterns, and clinical severity. Inappropriate antibiotic use accelerates antimicrobial resistance and may cause harm if the pathogen is viral, parasitic, or a toxin-producing strain where antibiotics are not indicated.

Do not stigmatise or exclude affected families. Social exclusion of families with sick members drives concealment of illness, delays treatment-seeking, and reduces cooperation with health authorities. The disease is caused by a contaminated water source, not by the affected families. Blame directed at families rather than at the environmental hazard is both factually incorrect and operationally harmful.

Do not assume the outbreak is over when new cases slow. Incubation periods for waterborne pathogens vary from hours (cholera, toxigenic E. coli) to days or weeks (Cryptosporidium, hepatitis A). Cases may continue to appear even after the source has been addressed, from exposures that occurred before the intervention. Continue water treatment, monitoring, and hygiene intensification until health authorities confirm that the outbreak is controlled.

Source Basis

This guidance reflects WHO guidelines on drinking-water quality (4th edition and subsequent updates), WHO cholera and acute diarrhoeal disease fact sheets and outbreak response guidelines, WHO/UNICEF recommendations on household water treatment and safe storage, the WHO/UNICEF guidance on oral rehydration therapy, CDC waterborne disease outbreak response protocols, and the WHO guidelines on sanitation and health. The ORS formulation (sugar-salt solution) follows WHO emergency rehydration specifications. Chlorine concentrations (0.2% for excreta and surface disinfection, approximately 2 mg/L free chlorine residual for drinking water, 0.5% for deceased persons) follow WHO environmental health in emergencies guidance. Case fatality comparisons (exceeding 50% untreated versus below 1% treated) are drawn from WHO global cholera surveillance data. The minimum latrine distance from water sources (30 metres) and minimum depth above the water table (1.5 metres) follow WHO/UNICEF emergency sanitation standards.

Families should follow instructions from their local or national health authority, as specific outbreak response protocols may vary by country, pathogen, and local infrastructure, and may be updated as the situation evolves.

Cholera: Wetin Families Suppose Do Now

When plenty people for your community suddenly begin get serious watery diarrhea and vomiting, and people dey suspect say na cholera, here's wetin your family must do quick-quick to protect everybody and stop the sickness from spread.

FIRST THING: Separate the sick person well-well
Move anybody wey get watery shit and vomiting go different room or separate space — far from where other people sleeping and eating
Make sure the sick person get their own bucket, their own cloth, their own everything
Keep all children away from the sick person
The sick person no suppose cook food or touch water wey other people go drink
SECOND THING: Handle the shit properly (this na the most important)

Cholera spread through dirty water and shit. No play with this one.

All the waste wey the sick person release — the diarrhea, vomit, dirty clothes, dirty bedding — must go inside special pit or bucket. NOT the regular toilet. NOT the ground.
If you dey dig pit: Dig am far-far — at least 30 meter away from any well, stream, or borehole wey people dey use for water
Make sure water no go flow from the pit back to where people get water
Cover the pit with soil after each time
If you no get pit: Use bucket with strong cover, put bleach or chlorine inside if you get am, seal am well, then bury the whole thing far from water source
Burn or bury all cloth and bedding wey the sick person use — no wash am with other people cloth
THIRD THING: Protect the water supply — serious serious
No use the same water wey the sick person don touch for drinking, cooking, or washing
If your community share well or borehole and somebody wey get cholera done use am, that water don spoil — e no safe again
Boil all water wey people go drink — boil am for at least 1 minute until e hot-hot
OR use bleach: put 2-3 drop of house bleach inside 1 liter of water, wait 30 minute before anybody drink am
Keep drinking water inside clean cover pot — no expose am to air and dirt
Use different water for washing (this water no need be as clean as drinking water)
FOURTH THING: Give the sick person water water water (ORS)

This na the thing wey save people life. Cholera kill people through dehydration, not from the sickness itself.

Make ORS solution:

Take 1 liter of clean water (boil am first, then let am cool)
Pour 6 teaspoon of sugar inside
Add ½ teaspoon of salt
Mix am well

OR if you get ORS packet from clinic, follow the instruction on top.

Give the sick person small small sips constantly — every few minute, no give am all at once
Even if e vomit, keep giving sips — some go enter belly
If the person cannot drink or e dey vomit everything back, this na emergency — rush am to health center now-now
FIFTH THING: Wash hand well well
After you touch the sick person or their waste, wash your hand with soap and clean water — no play with this
Wash hand before you cook or eat food
Wear plastic glove if you get am when you handling waste
If you no get glove, use leaf or cloth make you hold the thing, then wash your hand well-well after
No touch your face, no touch food, no touch other family member until you wash your hand
SIXTH THING: Tell the health worker
Go tell nurse, health center, or community health officer straightaway
No hide the case — the health system need to know so they can:
Confirm say na really cholera
Give free medicine and ORS
Stop the whole community from catch am
Give advice to everybody about water safety
SEVENTH THING: Wetin you no suppose do
No use antibiotics without health worker tell you — antibiotics no cure cholera, e just waste money
No use traditional medicine instead of ORS — ORS na the thing wey keep person alive
No share cup, spoon, or plate with the sick person
No let children play near where you put the waste
No shit for outside or close to water — use toilet or latrine
No fetch water from where people dey shit
EIGHTH THING: When to run go clinic

Rush to health center now-now if:

The person cannot keep water inside — e vomit everything wey you give am
The diarrhea serious pass — more than one time every 30 minute
The person dey talk nonsense, very weak, cannot stand up
Person eye dey sink, mouth dey dry, no tears coming out, skin dey look like rubber
Small child under 5 year wey get these sign
You see say another person for the house don start get the same sickness — no wait, take am go clinic
The Main Thing

Cholera serious but you can stop am and you can cure am. Two thing go save your people:

ORS solution — this stop the death — e work well-well
Keep the shit away from the water — this stop am from spread to other person

Family wey move fast with clean water, proper waste disposal, and ORS go keep their own people alive and protect the whole community.

Wetin Families Suppose Do If Plenty People For Community Dey Shit Water and Dey Vomit, and Dem Dey Suspect Cholera
How You Go Know Say Na Serious Matter

When plenty people for the same area begin dey purge serious water-water shit and dey vomit at the same time, that one na big danger sign. Cholera (na bacteria wey dem dey call Vibrio cholerae dey cause am) dey make person dey shit water wey look like rice-water, no dey pain belle, but the water dey comot plenti-plenti. Serious case fit lose litres of water from body within hours. Na the loss of water (dehydration) dey kill, and e fit kill within hours if person no get treatment. But make we know say other sickness fit look like cholera too, so na only lab test go confirm wetin really dey happen.

First Thing First: No Let Person Dry Up

Dehydration na the main killer for cholera. Person fit die not because of the bacteria, but because the body lose too much water. So the number one thing wey family must do be say, start to give the sick person water and salt replacement immediately, even before una reach hospital.

Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) na the most important thing. If you get ORS sachet, mix am with clean water the way dem write for the packet. If ORS no dey available, you fit make temporary one for house: put six level teaspoon of sugar and half level teaspoon of salt inside one litre of clean water (water wey you don boil or treat). This one na for emergency, e no replace proper ORS. Give the sick person small-small sip, but give am often-often, no stop. Person wey don dehydrate serious fit need plenty litres within the first few hours. For pikin wey still dey suck breast, continue to give breast milk plus ORS.

Watch for these danger signs wey mean say the dehydration don too much: eye don enter inside, if you pinch skin for back of hand e no go back flat quick-quick, heart dey beat fast but weak, person dey sleep anyhow or no dey respond, person no fit drink again, person no dey piss or piss dey come out very dark. If you see any of these ones, carry the person go health facility sharp-sharp, because dem go need drip (IV fluid). Na emergency be that.

Report Give Health People Immediately

No wait for lab result before you report. If plenty people for one area begin dey purge and vomit at the same time, that one don pass the level wey you suppose report am. Call the nearest health centre, local government health department, disease surveillance officer, or the national disease reporting line. Tell them how many people don sick, where dem dey, when the sickness start, and whether una dey suspect any common thing wey people share, like one borehole, one well, one food, or one event.

When you report early, health authority go fit come test the water source, confirm the sickness, bring ORS and drip, and start proper outbreak response.

Protect the Water

Cholera dey spread mainly through water and food wey shit from infected person don enter. Na contaminated water source dey cause most cholera outbreaks.

Treat all water wey una wan drink. Boil water make e bubble well-well for at least one minute before you use am. If you no fit boil, use chlorine, the liquid bleach or water purification tablet wey dey market, follow the instruction for the packet. If you no get chlorine and you no fit boil, you fit try SODIS method: fill clear plastic bottle with the water, put am for direct sunlight for at least six hours. This one no perfect, but e go reduce risk.

Store your treated water well. Put am inside clean container wey get cover, wey get small mouth. No dip hand or cup inside the water. Pour am out, or use container wey get tap.

Stop to use the water source wey una suspect for drinking, cooking, washing food, or washing mouth until health people don come test am and say e safe, or until una don get another clean water.

Toilet Matter and Cleanliness

Washing hand no be choice, na must. Every person for the house must wash hand with soap and water after dem use toilet, after dem touch sick person or anything wey sick person shit or vomit don touch, before dem cook, before dem chop, and before dem feed pikin. If soap no dey, ash fit work small, but soap better pass.

Dispose shit and vomit the correct way. All the shit and vomit from sick person must enter latrine or toilet. If the person no fit reach toilet, use bucket or container catch am, put chlorine solution inside (0.2% chlorine), wait 30 minutes, then pour am inside latrine. No pour untreated shit for gutter, stream, river, or for ground.

Clean everywhere wey shit or vomit don touch. Wash bed sheet, cloth, and floor with 0.2% chlorine solution. Plate, cup, and spoon wey sick person use, wash dem separate with treated water and soap or chlorine.

Open defecation must stop completely. If some people for the community still dey shit for bush or outside, that one don become serious danger for everybody now. Una need emergency toilet arrangement immediately.

Food Safety

Cook food well-well and chop am while e still hot. The cholera bacteria go die when food hot. No eat raw vegetable or fruit unless you fit peel am. No eat food wey don sit for room temperature for long time, especially when weather hot. Avoid food from roadside or communal cooking during outbreak unless you sure say dem prepare am well.

Wash everywhere wey you dey prepare food with treated water before you start.

How to Take Care of Sick Person for House

If the person still fit drink and the dehydration no too bad, you fit manage am for house with ORS while you dey wait or between hospital visits. The person wey dey take care of sick person suppose give am separate plate, cup, spoon, and bed. Wash hand well-well after every contact. Keep the sick person waste separate and disinfect am.

But if any of these apply, carry the person go hospital sharp-sharp:

The person don show signs of serious dehydration. The person na pikin under 5 years. The person na pregnant woman. The person get another sickness for body already.

Cholera fit kill more than half of people wey no get treatment, but with proper rehydration, the death rate fit drop below 1%. So to reach health facility na the difference between life and death.

If Person Die

If person die from suspected cholera, the body still fit spread the sickness. Na trained people suppose prepare the body for burial. If trained people no dey available, the people wey go handle the body suppose wear gloves, reduce the way dem touch body fluid, use 0.5% chlorine solution wash the body, and wash their own hand well-well after. Big burial gathering where plenty people go chop together don cause cholera spread before for many outbreaks. Reduce the crowd and avoid communal food for the burial.

Wetin Family No Suppose Do

No use medicine wey dey stop purging (like loperamide). That kind medicine go slow down the belle but e no go kill the bacteria. E go hide how much water the body dey lose, and things go worse.

No just go buy antibiotic for chemist by yourself. Antibiotic get role for serious cholera case, but only health worker suppose decide which one and when. Antibiotic no replace water and salt replacement, and if people just dey use antibiotic anyhow, the bacteria go learn how to resist am.

No chase or shame families wey get sick people. If people begin avoid or stigmatise families wey get cholera, those families go fear to report or go hospital, and more people go die. This pattern don happen for many cholera outbreaks before.

Wetin Families Suppose Do If Plenty People For Community Dey Shit Water and Dey Vomit, and Dem Dey Suspect Cholera
How You Go Know Say Na Serious Matter

When plenty people for the same area begin dey purge serious water-water shit and dey vomit at the same time, that one na big danger sign wey show say outbreak dey happen, and e fit be from one common source like water wey everybody dey use. Cholera (na bacteria wey dem dey call Vibrio cholerae dey cause am) dey make person dey shit water wey look like rice-water, e no dey pain belly, but the water dey comot plenti-plenti from body. Serious case fit lose litres of water from body within hours. Na the loss of water (dehydration) dey kill, and e fit kill within hours if person no get treatment. But make we know say other sickness fit look like cholera too, like rotavirus, norovirus, E. coli, Shigella, and Cryptosporidium. Na only lab test go confirm wetin really dey cause am. But the immediate thing wey community suppose do na the same no matter which germ: stop people from dying because body dry, report give health people, protect the water, and cut the way wey the sickness dey spread.

First Thing First: No Let Person Dry Up and Die

Na dehydration dey kill for cholera and other serious running belle sickness, no be the bacteria itself. Person fit die within hours after the sickness start, especially small pikin, old people, pregnant woman, and people wey already get another sickness for body. You must start to give the sick person water and salt replacement immediately for house, even before una reach hospital.

Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) na the most important thing. If you get ORS sachet, mix am with clean water wey you don boil or treat with chlorine exactly the way dem write for the packet. If ORS no dey available, you fit make temporary one for house: put six level teaspoon of sugar and half level teaspoon of salt inside one litre of clean water (water wey you don boil or treat). This one na for emergency, e no replace proper ORS. Give the sick person small-small sip, but give am often-often, no stop. No wait for the person to talk say im thirsty, because when dehydration don bad, person no go even feel thirsty again. Person wey don dehydrate serious fit need plenty litres within the first few hours.

For pikin wey still dey suck breast, continue to give breast milk plus ORS. For baby wey no dey suck breast, continue their normal milk or formula between ORS doses.

Watch for these danger signs wey mean say the dehydration don too much: eye don enter inside, if you pinch skin for back of hand e no go back flat quick-quick, heart dey beat fast but weak, person dey sleep anyhow or no dey respond, person no fit drink again or e dey vomit everything back, person no dey piss or piss dey come out very-very dark. If you see any of these ones, carry the person go health facility sharp-sharp because dem go need drip (IV fluid). That one na emergency.

Extra danger signs for pikin: pikin dey vomit everything back without stopping, blood dey inside shit, pikin wey never reach six months get high fever with running belle, pikin refuse to eat or drink at all. All of these need urgent medical attention, no matter how the pikin look.

Cholera fit kill more than half of people wey no get treatment, but with proper rehydration, the death rate fit drop below 1%. So to reach health facility na the difference between life and death.

Report Give Health People Immediately

No wait for lab result before you report. If plenty people for one area begin dey purge and vomit at the same time, that one don pass the level wey you suppose report am. Na under WHO International Health Regulations and nearly every country disease surveillance system, this kind cluster need immediate notification.

Call the nearest health centre, local government health department, disease surveillance officer, or the national disease reporting line. Tell them: how many people don sick, their approximate ages, when the sickness start (and whether everybody start at the same time or one by one, because this information go help them understand whether na one-time exposure or ongoing exposure), which water source dem dey suspect and where e dey, and anything else dem notice about the water or the area (whether the colour don change, whether e dey smell, whether rain don flood the area recently, whether new latrine dey close to the water, whether animal dey enter the water).

When you report early, health authority go fit come test the water source, confirm the sickness, bring ORS and drip, investigate to find all people wey don drink from that source, and fix the water source. Community alone no fit do all these things.

Protect the Water

Cholera and most other things wey dey cause serious running belle dey spread mainly through water and food wey shit from infected person don enter. Na contaminated water source dey cause most outbreaks.

Stop to use the water source wey una suspect immediately. This one na the thing wey time dey matter for am pass. Every hour wey the contaminated source still dey open, new people dey drink poison. Families must stop to use that water for drinking, cooking, washing food, washing plate and spoon, brushing teeth, and anything at all wey go make the water enter person mouth. If the source na community well, borehole, tap, or stream, local leaders must tell every single household wey dey use am. No just depend on word of mouth. Physical barrier dey work better: tie rope round am, put somebody to stand there, put clear warning sign wey everybody go see. People wey don dey use that water for years go still go there by habit even after dem hear warning.

But you must provide alternative water immediately. You no fit tell people say make dem stop use water without giving them another option. If no other clean source dey, then all water wey anybody draw from that place must dey treated before anybody use am for anything wey go enter mouth.

Treat all water wey una wan drink. Boil water make e bubble well-well for at least one minute before you use am. If you no fit boil, use chlorine, the liquid bleach or water purification tablet wey dey market, follow the instruction for the packet. WHO recommend say the water suppose get approximately 2 mg/L free chlorine after treatment for clear water. If the water dirty or cloudy, first filter am through clean cloth or let am settle, then put more chlorine, because the dirty things inside water dey consume the chlorine and reduce how well e work. After you put chlorine, wait at least 30 minutes before anybody drink.

If you no get chlorine and you no fit boil, you fit try SODIS method: fill clear plastic bottle (PET, no be the coloured or opaque type) with the water, put am for direct sunlight for at least six hours. If cloud cover sun, leave am for two full days. This one no perfect, but e go reduce risk. E no dey effective against Cryptosporidium, and e no dey as reliable as boiling or chlorination.

Store your treated water well. Put am inside clean container wey get cover, wey get small mouth. No dip hand or cup inside the water. Pour am out, or use container wey get tap.

Toilet Matter and Cleanliness

Washing hand no be choice, na must. Every person for the house, and every person for the community, must wash hand with soap and water after dem use toilet, after dem touch sick person or anything wey sick person shit or vomit don touch, before dem cook, before dem chop, and before dem feed pikin. If soap no dey, ash fit work small, but soap better pass.

Dispose shit and vomit the correct way. All the shit and vomit from sick person must enter latrine or toilet. If the person no fit reach toilet, use bucket or container catch am, put chlorine solution inside (0.2% chlorine), wait 30 minutes, then pour am inside latrine. No pour untreated shit for gutter, stream, river, or for ground. If you do that, you dey create another contamination path wey fit affect other water sources or spread the sickness from person to person.

Clean everywhere wey shit or vomit don touch. Wash bed sheet, cloth, and floor with 0.2% chlorine solution. Plate, cup, and spoon wey sick person use, wash dem separate with treated water and soap or chlorine.

Open defecation must stop completely. If some people for the community still dey shit for bush or outside, that one don become serious danger for everybody now. Every person shit wey enter the environment without treatment fit become another source of contamination. Una need emergency toilet arrangement immediately. If permanent latrine no dey enough, you fit dig temporary pit latrine, but make e dey at least 30 metres away from any water source, and the bottom of the pit must dey at least 1.5 metres above the water table.

Food Safety

Cook food well-well and chop am while e still hot. Most of the germs wey dey cause waterborne running belle go die when food hot. No eat raw vegetable or fruit unless you fit peel am. No eat food wey don sit for room temperature for long time, especially when weather hot. Avoid food from roadside or communal cooking during outbreak unless you sure say dem prepare am well. Wash everywhere wey you dey prepare food with treated water before you start.

Throw away food wey dem prepare with the suspected water. Any food wey dem wash, cook, or prepare with water from the suspected source before una know say e contaminated, throw am away. This one include food wey dem prepare to sell or food for communal gathering.

How to Take Care of Sick Person for House

If the person still fit drink and the dehydration no too bad, you fit manage am for house with ORS while you dey wait or between hospital visits. The person wey dey take care of sick person suppose give am separate plate, cup, spoon, and bed. Wash hand well-well after every contact. Keep the sick person waste separate and disinfect am.

But if any of these apply, carry the person go hospital sharp-sharp:

The person don show signs of serious dehydration. The person na pikin under 5 years. The person na pregnant woman. The person get another sickness for body already.

If Person Die

If person die from suspected cholera, the body still fit spread the sickness. Na trained people suppose prepare the body for burial. If trained people no dey available, the people wey go handle the body suppose wear gloves, reduce the way dem touch body fluid, use 0.5% chlorine solution wash the body, and wash their own hand well-well after. Big burial gathering where plenty people go chop together don cause cholera spread before for many outbreaks. Reduce the crowd and avoid communal food for the burial.

Wetin Family No Suppose Do

No use medicine wey dey stop purging (like loperamide). That kind medicine go slow down the belle but e no go kill the bacteria. E go hide how much water the body dey lose, and things go worse. For pikin especially, and for infections wey invasive organism like Shigella dey cause, to slow down belly movement fit increase how much poison the body absorb.

No just go buy antibiotic for chemist by yourself. Antibiotic get role for serious cholera and shigellosis, but only health worker suppose decide which one, how much, and when. Antibiotic no replace water and salt replacement, and if people just dey use antibiotic anyhow, the bacteria go learn how to resist am. For some sickness wey virus or parasite dey cause, antibiotic no go help at all and fit cause harm.

No chase or shame families wey get sick people. If people begin avoid or stigmatise families wey get cholera, those families go fear to report or go hospital, and more people go die. Na contaminated water source cause the disease, no be the families. To blame families instead of the water source no correct for fact and no correct for practice.

No assume say the outbreak don finish because new cases don reduce. The time wey different germs take to show after person drink contaminated water dey different: cholera and toxigenic E. coli fit show within hours, but Cryptosporidium and hepatitis A fit take days or weeks. Cases fit still dey appear even after dem don address the source, from people wey drink the water before the intervention. Continue water treatment, monitoring, and hygiene until health authority confirm say the outbreak don dey under control.

The minimum latrine distance from water source (30 metres) and minimum depth above the water table (1.5 metres) follow WHO/UNICEF emergency sanitation standards.

Make una follow wetin your local or national health authority talk, because the specific way dem dey handle outbreak fit different from country to country, from germ to germ, and from area to area, and dem fit update am as the situation change.
