Responding to Misinformation During a Cholera Outbreak in Nigeria
The Core Problem

Rumours about concealment erode the credibility you need most during an outbreak. Even if unfounded, they will drive people away from health facilities, delay reporting of cases, and make outbreak control measurably harder. You cannot ignore this.

Direct Response Strategy
1. Release Transparent Data Immediately

Do not wait for "perfect" numbers. Release what you know, with clear methodology:

Case count and deaths (as of [date])
How cases are confirmed (clinical + lab, or clinical only if lab capacity is limited)
Where cases are concentrated (by ward, neighbourhood, or health facility)
Age groups affected
Hospitalisation and recovery rates

State explicitly: "These numbers are updated [daily/weekly]. If you see a case, report it to [contact]. All cases are counted."

Why this works: You answer the implicit accusation (concealment) by making data public and auditable. Silence looks like hiding.

2. Name the Source of the Rumour—and Address It Directly

Don't pretend the WhatsApp claims don't exist. Acknowledge them:

"We know some people are saying health workers are hiding cases. That is not true. Here is why the numbers may not match what you hear in the community..."

Explain common reasons case counts seem low:

Many mild cases never reach a health facility
People self-treat at home (and some recover without help)
Deaths reported in rumours may include deaths from other causes (diarrhoea, malnutrition, pre-existing illness)
Labs take time; not every suspected case is lab-confirmed
Reporting from remote areas takes days

Critical: Do this in Yoruba, Igbo, and Nigerian Pidgin English—not just English. WhatsApp misinformation spreads in the languages people use at home.

3. Use Trusted Community Voices

Health workers alone will not reverse mistrust. Engage:

Community health extension workers (CHEWs) who live in the area
Traditional leaders and chiefs who have standing
Religious leaders (imam, pastor, priest)
Mothers who have recovered or whose children survived cholera
Local radio presenters

Have them say: "I saw the health workers bring in cases. I saw people get better with treatment. This is real, and the treatment works."

Testimony from someone your neighbours know carries more weight than a press release.

4. Make Prevention Advice Hyper-Local and Actionable

Do not give generic guidance. Give specific instructions for this community:

On water:

"Boil water for [X] minutes before drinking"
"If you cannot boil, add [bleach/chlorine] at [exact amount]"
"The well at [location] is safe. Do not use the one near [location]."

On sanitation:

"Toilets must be [X] metres from the well"
"If your toilet is too close, stop using it and use [alternative] until repair"

On food:

"Wash vegetables with boiled water"
"Cook food hot. Do not eat food left overnight."

On seeking care:

"If you have watery diarrhoea, go to [specific health centre] or call [number]"
"Bring a family member. You will not be charged." (if true)
"Treatment is rehydration salts and antibiotics. It works."

Why this matters: People are more likely to trust guidance that addresses their specific situation than abstract outbreak messaging.

5. Establish a Visible Presence at Health Facilities

Ensure that:

Health workers are treating patients visibly and successfully
Recovered patients can speak to new arrivals ("I came in with watery diarrhoea, they gave me fluids and medicine, and I went home after 2 days")
Conditions are clean and organised (not chaotic)
Wait times are short

If a facility is overwhelmed or disorganised, fix it or it will become the proof that "the government is failing."

6. Publish a Weekly Situation Report in Plain Language

Issue a one-page summary (in all relevant languages):

Cases this week: [X]
Deaths this week: [X]
Cases recovered: [X]
Facilities active: [X]
Water points under surveillance: [X]
Action this week: [description]

Example: "This week we found 12 new cases. 8 people recovered and went home. 1 person died (a man age 67 with diabetes). 15 water points have been tested and 3 were contaminated—we are fixing them now."

Publish it on notice boards, read it on local radio, and share it via WhatsApp yourself (before rumours dominate the channel).

What NOT to Do
Do not deny the rumour exists. This makes you look out of touch.
Do not attack people sharing rumours. This makes you look defensive and afraid.
Do not release only "official" numbers without context. Raw statistics feel like propaganda when people are afraid.
Do not wait for lab confirmation on every case before communicating. During an outbreak, provisional data with caveats is more credible than silence.
Do not rely only on English-language communication. The rumours are in Pidgin, Yoruba, and Igbo.
Do not ignore the emotional driver. Fear makes people believe rumours. Address the fear first.
The Strategic Truth

You will not eliminate all mistrust immediately. But you can shift the balance:

Early transparency stops rumours before they metastasize
Local voices carry authority you do not have alone
Practical guidance shows you are competent and present
Visible recovery proves treatment works
Consistency over weeks builds credibility

The communities most resistant to official messaging are often the ones who have been let down before—by delayed response, by invisible health workers, by resources that never arrived. Your job is not to convince them to trust you; it is to show up, act transparently, and keep your word. Trust follows from that.

How a Public-Health Team Should Respond to WhatsApp Claims That Health Workers Are Concealing Cholera Cases and Deaths
Understanding What This Rumour Represents Before Responding to It

The claim that health workers are hiding the true number of cases and deaths is not a random fabrication. It belongs to a specific category of outbreak rumour: the institutional concealment narrative. This category is among the most dangerous because it directly attacks the credibility of the people and systems that the response depends on. If residents believe that health authorities are lying about the scale of the outbreak, several predictable consequences follow: people stop presenting to health facilities because they distrust the system, they stop cooperating with surveillance and contact tracing, they turn to alternative sources of care and information that may be harmful, and they share the concealment claim further because forwarding a "hidden truth" carries social currency.

However, this rumour also carries diagnostic information about the relationship between the community and the health system. People do not invent concealment narratives in a vacuum. They emerge when there is a pre-existing trust deficit, when official communication has been absent, delayed, inconsistent, or perceived as incomplete, when the community's lived experience of the outbreak (the number of sick people they see, the funerals they attend) does not match the official narrative they are hearing, or when historical experience has taught them that authorities do, in fact, undercount or underreport. In Nigeria specifically, public memory of delayed or contested official figures during previous disease outbreaks, including the 2014 Ebola response and various meningitis and Lassa fever episodes, provides fertile ground for concealment narratives. The response must account for the fact that this distrust may have rational roots, even if the specific claim is factually incorrect.

Principle One: Respond Rapidly on the Same Platform

The rumour is spreading on WhatsApp. The correction must reach WhatsApp. A press conference, a ministry statement on a government website, or a radio broadcast may be valuable supplementary channels, but none of them intercept the rumour where it lives. WhatsApp messages circulate within trusted private and group conversations, which gives them an intimacy and credibility that institutional broadcasts cannot match.

The public-health team should prepare a short, clear voice note or text message designed for WhatsApp forwarding. Voice notes are particularly effective in the Nigerian context because they carry the warmth and authority of a human voice, they are accessible to people with limited literacy, and they are the dominant communication format within many WhatsApp groups. The message should be recorded by a person the community recognises and trusts, not by an anonymous institutional voice. A local health officer, a well-known community health worker, a respected traditional leader, or a religious leader who has agreed to support the response are all stronger messengers than a faceless "Ministry of Health."

The message should be kept under two minutes. It should be in the language the community uses, which in most Nigerian communities means either the dominant local language, Nigerian Pidgin English, or both, rather than formal English. It should be forwarded directly into the WhatsApp groups where the rumour is circulating, which requires the response team to have community liaisons who are members of those groups.

The speed of this response matters enormously. The WHO Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE) framework and the CDC Crisis and Emergency Risk Communication (CERC) model both identify the first 24 to 48 hours after a rumour begins circulating as the critical window. After that period, the rumour begins to consolidate into shared community understanding and becomes far more resistant to correction.

Principle Two: Acknowledge the Concern Before Correcting the Claim

The WhatsApp message or voice note should not begin with a denial. It should begin by naming the concern. An opening such as "We have heard that messages are going around saying that we are hiding the real numbers of cholera cases and deaths. We understand why people are worried" accomplishes several things simultaneously: it signals that the health team is aware of what the community is saying, it validates the underlying emotion (fear, concern for family safety) without validating the factual claim, and it creates a moment of psychological receptivity before the correction is offered.

Research in health communication, including findings reflected in the WHO RCCE guidance and in the cognitive psychology literature on misinformation correction, consistently shows that corrections which begin by acknowledging the audience's concern are more effective than those that begin with a flat denial. The reason is that a flat denial ("That is not true, we are not hiding anything") triggers a defensive reaction in people who already distrust the institution. It sounds like exactly what a concealing authority would say. Acknowledgement first, followed by transparency, breaks this pattern.

Principle Three: Respond with Radical Transparency, Not Defensive Denial

The single most effective countermeasure to a concealment narrative is to make the data visible. If the community believes numbers are being hidden, the response is to show the numbers, explain how they are collected, explain what they do and do not include, and explain why they may differ from what the community perceives.

The public-health team should release, in a format accessible to the community, the current confirmed case count, the current death count, the number of people currently receiving treatment, the number of samples sent for laboratory confirmation and how many results are pending, and where treatment is being provided. This information should be updated regularly, ideally daily during an active outbreak, and communicated through the same channels where the rumour is circulating.

Crucially, the team should also explain the gap between official figures and community perception. There are legitimate reasons why official counts may be lower than what community members observe. Not every case of diarrhoea during a cholera outbreak is cholera. Some cases may not have been reported to health facilities yet. Laboratory confirmation takes time, and the confirmed count always lags behind the actual count during an active outbreak. Suspected cases and confirmed cases are counted differently. People who die at home without presenting to a health facility may not be immediately included in official figures, and addressing this gap requires community cooperation with reporting, not concealment by health workers.

This explanation should be delivered without defensiveness. If there are genuine gaps in reporting, such as deaths occurring at home that the surveillance system has not yet captured, the honest response is to say so and to explain what steps are being taken to improve ascertainment, rather than to insist that the official count is complete when both the health team and the community know it may not be. Claiming completeness when the community has direct evidence of uncounted cases destroys credibility faster than any rumour.

Principle Four: Equip Trusted Community Voices

The public-health team should not attempt to be the sole voice of correction. In communities where institutional trust is low, the institution's own denials carry the least weight. The team should identify and brief trusted community figures: religious leaders (pastors, imams), traditional rulers, market leaders, school headteachers, respected elders, and community health volunteers who are themselves residents. These individuals should be given the current data, the explanation for any discrepancies, and the practical health guidance, and supported to deliver this information in their own words through their own networks.

This approach has documented effectiveness. During the 2014 Ebola response in Nigeria, community leaders and religious figures played a critical role in countering misinformation. During the 2018–2020 DRC Ebola outbreaks, WHO, UNICEF, and IFRC found that community feedback mechanisms and trusted local messengers were far more effective at countering concealment narratives than institutional communications alone. The principle is that trust is relational and local, not institutional and broadcast.

The briefing of these community voices must include honest information about uncertainties. If trusted leaders repeat institutional talking points that later prove incomplete, their personal credibility is damaged, and the community loses not only trust in the institution but trust in the leaders who vouched for it. Equipping messengers with honest, nuanced information protects both their credibility and the response.

Principle Five: Create a Visible, Accessible Feedback Channel

Part of what drives concealment narratives is the feeling that information flows in only one direction: from authorities to the community. Establishing a channel through which community members can ask questions, report concerns, and receive direct answers changes this dynamic.

Practical options in a Nigerian community context include a dedicated WhatsApp number staffed by a community liaison who responds to questions in real time, a daily or twice-daily community meeting at a public location where the health team provides updates and takes questions, a toll-free phone line (NCDC maintains one nationally, but a local line is often more accessible and trusted), and a designated person at each treatment facility who can provide case information to families.

The feedback channel must be genuine. If people submit questions and receive no response, or receive scripted non-answers, the channel becomes evidence of further concealment. Responses must be timely, honest, and in the community's language.

Principle Six: Integrate the Rumour Response with Practical Health Guidance

The rumour response must not exist in isolation from the health guidance that residents need to survive the outbreak. A response that focuses entirely on defending institutional credibility while failing to provide actionable protective information will confirm the community's suspicion that authorities care more about their reputation than about people's lives.

Every communication that addresses the concealment rumour should also include, or be immediately followed by, clear, practical guidance in the community's language:

On preventing dehydration: ORS is the most important intervention. If ORS sachets are available, mix as directed with treated water. If not, six level teaspoons of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt in one litre of boiled or treated water. Give small, frequent sips continuously. Do not wait for the person to ask for water. Watch for danger signs: sunken eyes, skin that stays tented when pinched, rapid weak pulse, inability to drink, dark or absent urine. These signs mean the person needs intravenous fluids at a health facility immediately.

On water safety: treat all drinking water by boiling (rolling boil for one minute) or by chlorination following product instructions. Store treated water in a clean, covered, narrow-mouthed container. Do not dip hands or cups into stored water.

On sanitation: all faeces and vomit from sick persons must go into a latrine. If the person cannot reach the latrine, collect in a container, add 0.2% chlorine solution, wait 30 minutes, then dispose into the latrine. Wash hands with soap and water after every contact with a sick person, after using the latrine, before cooking, before eating, and before feeding children.

On seeking care: anyone with severe watery diarrhoea should begin ORS immediately and go to the nearest cholera treatment centre or health facility. Do not wait for the diarrhoea to worsen. Cholera can kill within hours through dehydration, but with proper rehydration therapy, the death rate drops below 1%. State clearly where the treatment centres are, their hours, and that treatment is free if applicable.

On burial: if a person dies from suspected cholera, the body can still transmit the disease. Only trained burial teams should prepare the body. Communal food at large funeral gatherings has been a documented transmission route in cholera outbreaks. Reduce gathering size and avoid communal meals at burials during the outbreak.

This guidance should be woven into the same communications that address the rumour, not issued separately. The message structure is: we hear your concern, here is the truth about the numbers and why they may look different from what you see, and here is what you can do right now to protect your family. The practical guidance demonstrates that the health team's priority is saving lives, which is itself the strongest rebuttal to the claim that they are concealing deaths.

Principle Seven: Monitor Whether the Response Is Working

Rumour correction is not a single event. After the initial response, the team must monitor whether the correction is reaching the relevant WhatsApp groups, whether the concealment narrative is persisting, mutating, or being replaced by new rumours, and whether community behaviour is changing in response (are people presenting to treatment centres, cooperating with surveillance, accepting guidance).

This monitoring should use the same community feedback channels described above: community health workers reporting what they hear, liaison members in WhatsApp groups observing the conversation, call-centre and hotline logs, and direct observations at treatment facilities. If the concealment narrative persists despite correction, the team must investigate why. Possible reasons include that the correction did not reach the relevant audiences, that the messenger was not trusted, that the explanation was not credible because it did not match community observations, or that new events (a cluster of deaths, a facility perceived as overwhelmed) have reinforced the narrative. Each of these requires a different second-round response.

This iterative cycle of listen, analyse, respond, and monitor is the operational core of the WHO infodemic management framework.

What the Public-Health Team Must Not Do

Do not dismiss the concern as ignorant or malicious. Characterising people who share the rumour as uneducated, irresponsible, or enemies of the response will deepen the divide and make correction harder. Most people who forward concealment claims do so out of genuine concern for their community, not out of malice.

Do not threaten legal consequences for sharing the rumour. Threats of prosecution for "spreading misinformation" have been used in some outbreak contexts and have consistently backfired. They confirm the concealment narrative ("if they are threatening people who ask questions, they must be hiding something"), they suppress the feedback that the team needs in order to understand community concerns, and they drive rumour circulation underground into private messages where it is harder to detect and counter.

Do not delay the response while preparing a "perfect" message. An imperfect response delivered within hours is vastly more effective than a polished response delivered days later. The first message can be brief and honest: "We know this claim is circulating. Here is what we know right now. We will share more as we confirm it." Silence during the critical window is interpreted as confirmation of the concealment.

Do not claim that official figures are complete if they are not. If the surveillance system has known limitations, such as deaths at home not being captured, or laboratory confirmation lagging behind clinical diagnosis, say so. Explain what is being done to close the gap. Overclaiming completeness when the community has direct evidence to the contrary is the single fastest way to validate the concealment narrative.

Do not separate the rumour response from the health response. A communication strategy that focuses on defending the institution while people are dying of preventable dehydration in their homes will fail on both objectives. The health guidance is the credibility.

Responding to Concealment Claims During a Cholera Outbreak

The worst thing a public-health team can do with these WhatsApp claims is ignore them or issue a generic denial. That approach confirms the suspicion. Here's what actually works:

Address the Rumors Head-On

The team should name the specific claim circulating — not vaguely reference "misinformation." Something like: "We are aware of messages saying we are hiding cholera deaths. Here is what is actually happening with our numbers." Refusing to name the rumor signals that you're afraid of it.

Then explain why numbers may look different from what communities are observing. Common legitimate reasons during a Nigerian cholera outbreak include:

There is always a lag between when someone dies at home or in a community and when that death enters the official surveillance system. That gap is real, not a cover-up, and the team should say so plainly.
Suspected cases and confirmed cases are counted differently. If someone dies with cholera-like symptoms but no lab confirmation, that death may not appear in the "confirmed" column. The team needs to explain this distinction in accessible language, not hide behind it.
Communities sometimes see more illness than official numbers reflect because not everyone presents to a health facility. Acknowledging this openly — rather than pretending the official count captures everything — actually builds credibility.
Release Data Frequently and in Community Languages

Daily or near-daily updates in English, Pidgin, Yorùbá, Igbo, or Hausa (depending on the affected community) distributed through the same WhatsApp channels where the rumors are spreading. The updates should include the current case count, the current death count, how many people have been treated and recovered, and what the team is actively doing. If numbers jump, explain why — a batch of test results came back, a new reporting site came online, or surveillance expanded to a new ward. Unexplained jumps in numbers are the fuel for conspiracy theories.

Use Trusted Intermediaries, Not Just Official Channels

Government and agency logos on a message mean very little if trust is already damaged. The team should work through:

Community and religious leaders — imams, pastors, traditional rulers — who can relay information person-to-person and vouch for what they've seen at treatment centers.
Community health extension workers (CHEWs) who live in the affected areas and are known faces, not outsiders.
Cholera survivors who are willing to share their experience, including the care they received. A recovered patient saying "I went to the treatment center and they saved my life" is more powerful than any official statement.
Market women's networks and trade associations, which are some of the most effective informal communication structures in Nigerian communities.
Invite Verification

If feasible and safe, invite community leaders or respected local journalists to visit the cholera treatment centers. Let them see the patient registers and the conditions. Concealment claims thrive in opacity. Transparency under scrutiny is the most effective counter-message.

Pair Every Trust-Building Message with Actionable Guidance

Every communication — whether it's a WhatsApp voice note, a community town hall, or a mosque announcement — should include practical steps residents can take right now:

Water treatment: Boil all drinking water for at least one minute, or use chlorine tablets (Aquatabs or Water Guard) according to the packet instructions. If neither is available, add a small amount of household bleach (about four drops per litre of clear water) and wait 30 minutes before drinking.
Oral rehydration: If someone develops watery diarrhea, begin oral rehydration solution (ORS) immediately — do not wait to get to a facility. ORS sachets mixed with clean water, or a homemade solution of six level teaspoons of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt in one litre of clean water.
When to seek care: Severe watery diarrhea, vomiting that prevents keeping fluids down, signs of dehydration (sunken eyes, dry mouth, reduced urination, lethargy), or any diarrheal illness in a child under five — go to the nearest health facility or cholera treatment center immediately. Cholera kills through dehydration, and the treatment is straightforward if people arrive in time.
Hygiene: Wash hands with soap and water after using the toilet and before eating or preparing food. Dispose of feces safely — not in open drains or near water sources.
Food safety: Eat food while it's hot, avoid raw vegetables and fruits that cannot be peeled, and avoid buying food from vendors whose water source is unknown during the outbreak.
What the Team Should Not Do
Do not dismiss the WhatsApp claims as "fake news" or the work of troublemakers. That is condescending and counterproductive.
Do not release data only in English or only through formal press channels that most community members never see.
Do not wait for perfect numbers before communicating. Saying "we have confirmed 47 cases so far, but we expect the number to rise as more test results come in" is far better than silence followed by a sudden jump from 20 to 120.
Do not blame the community for the outbreak or frame messaging around what people are doing wrong. Frame it around what people can do to protect themselves and their families.

The public-health team cannot out-shout WhatsApp. It can only out-trust it — by being more transparent, more present, more specific, and more useful than the rumor mill. Every piece of information withheld or delayed is space the rumors will fill.

During a cholera outbreak, the public-health team should respond with transparency, speed, and consistent communication. Rumours often spread when people feel they are not getting timely or complete information, so building trust is as important as managing the disease itself.

How the public-health team should respond
Provide regular public updates on confirmed cases, deaths, response activities, and what is still being investigated.
Acknowledge uncertainty when it exists rather than speculating or withholding explanations. Public-health officials should communicate what they know, what they suspect, and what they are doing to control the outbreak.
Address the rumours directly with facts, while avoiding arguments or blaming people for sharing them.
Use trusted communication channels, including local leaders, religious leaders, radio, community meetings, and social media platforms such as WhatsApp. Community involvement is important for building trust and ensuring messages are effective.
Create opportunities for questions and feedback so residents can raise concerns and receive answers from credible sources.
Clear health guidance for residents

Residents should be reminded that cholera is spread through contaminated food and water.

Practical steps include:

Drink only safe water, such as boiled, treated, or properly sealed bottled water.
Wash hands frequently with soap and clean water, especially before eating and after using the toilet.
Eat thoroughly cooked food and wash fruits and vegetables with safe water.
Avoid open defecation and ensure proper waste disposal.
Seek medical care immediately if someone develops sudden watery diarrhoea, vomiting, or signs of dehydration. Cholera can become life-threatening if severe dehydration is not treated promptly.
Use oral rehydration solution (ORS) and continue fluid replacement while seeking care. ORS is an effective treatment for symptomatic cholera cases.

By communicating openly, correcting misinformation quickly, and providing practical prevention advice, the public-health team can help maintain public trust and support an effective outbreak response.

How Public-Health Team Suppose Handle Cholera Outbreak Misinformation for Nigerian Community
The Real Problem Wey Dey Ground

When people start say government dey hide cases and deaths, trust done break. And once trust break, people go hide sick family members instead of taking them hospital. They go drink contaminated water because they no believe say water get problem. They go spread the sickness faster. So this misinformation no be small thing—it go make outbreak worse, serious serious.

You cannot ignore am. You must face am directly.

How to Respond Strong-Strong
1. Tell People the Numbers Plainly—Every Week

Stop hide information. Release the data make everybody see am:

How many people catch cholera this week (example: 23 new cases)
How many people die (example: 2 deaths)
How many people don recover and go back home (example: 18 people)
Which places the sickness dey spread (mention the wards, the neighbourhoods)
Who dey catch am most (children, elderly people, or which age group)

Write am simple-simple. Post am for clinic walls, read am for radio, share am for WhatsApp yourself before the rumours take over WhatsApp.

Say am like this:

"This week, 23 new people come hospital with cholera. We treat dem with rehydration fluids and antibiotics. 18 of dem don recover well-well and go back home strong. Unfortunately, 2 elderly people with other health problems pass away. We are watching 5 more people wey still dey hospital, and dem dey improve."

Why this work: When you show the real numbers AND explain what dem mean, people see you no dey hide. Even if numbers high, transparency beat concealment every time.

2. Address the Rumour Straight-Straight

Don pretend people no dey talk. Face am head-on:

"We know say some people dey say we dey hide cases and deaths. Dat one no be true. Here why the numbers you hear for WhatsApp no match what we recording at hospital..."

Then explain clear reasons why case numbers may look small to people:

Many people get mild diarrhoea and recover home without going hospital (so we no see dem)
Some people self-treat with local medicine and never report am
Deaths people hear about for rumours might be from other sickness—not cholera (old age, malaria, other illness)
Testing takes time. We no confirm every case same day. Some suspected cases, we record dem, but lab result come later
People for remote areas take long time report cases. Information no reach hospital same day
Some people fear hospital, so they hide sick family member instead of bringing dem come

Say am straight:

"If you hear say 50 people die, but hospital record show 5 deaths—no be because we dey hide 45. Is because those other deaths come from different sickness, or dem happen for home and family no report to hospital. We cannot count what we no see."

This explanation go reduce suspicion strong-strong.

3. Get People From Community Make Dem Talk

Health workers alone cannot convince people. Use people dem trust:

Village chiefs and elders — Dem get authority
Religious leaders — Pastor, imam, priest — people respect dem
Mothers for community — Mothers wey their children recover from cholera
CHEWs and community health volunteers — Dem live for the area, people know dem
Market women and traders — People listen to dem
Local radio presenters — Dem dey reach people every day

Make dem say straight:

"I see health workers bring in sick people. I see dem recover. I see dem walk out of hospital well-well. The treatment work. Bring your sick people to hospital, make dem save life."

When your neighbour say am, not government person, people go believe more.

4. Give Instructions Wey Fit the Community

Stop give general advice. Give specific, practical instructions for THIS community:

For water:

"Boil your water for 5 minutes before drinking"
"If you get no way to boil, add 2 drops of bleach to 1 litre of water and wait 30 minutes"
"The well for Chief's compound—we test am and am safe. Use that one"
"Do not fetch water from the stream near the market. Dat one get cholera bacteria."

For toilet and sanitation:

"Your toilet must be 20 metres away from your well. If your toilet close to water, stop use am now now"
"If you no get toilet, use the public toilet for [location], or dig latrine far from water"
"Wash your hand with soap after toilet. Soap kill the bacteria."

For food:

"Cook your food hot hot. Don't eat food wey sit down overnight"
"Wash your vegetables with boiled water"
"If you sell food for market, use clean water and keep food covered"

For going hospital:

"If your belly water run, come to [hospital name] or [health centre name] quick quick"
"No be shameful. Cholera easy to cure. Bring the sick person now now"
"You no go pay money. Treatment free. Bring family member to help" (if true)
"We go give rehydration salts and antibiotics. Person go recover in 1-2 days if you bring dem early"

Why this work: When people see instructions wey touch their own situation—their own well, their own toilet, their own food—dem go follow. General talk no stick.

5. Make Hospital Look Like Place Wey Work

If people no see recovery happening, no amount of talking go convince dem:

Make sure sick people dey recover fast and visibly at hospital
Keep hospital clean and organized—not dirty, not chaotic
Get recovered patients talk to new arrivals: "I come here yesterday with serious diarrhoea. Dem give me fluids and medicine. Today I dey strong already."
Keep wait time short. If hospital full and people wait 5 hours, dem go lose confidence
Make sure health workers be polite and serious. Rude health worker go make people fear hospital more
Put up sign wey show recovery numbers: "30 people recovered this week. 2 still receiving treatment. 0 deaths this week."

When people see with their own eyes say treatment work, rumours go die naturally.

6. Share Weekly Report for Everyone Make Dem Understand

Print one simple page every week (in Yoruba, Igbo, AND Pidgin English too):

CHOLERA UPDATE — Week of [Date]

This Week's Numbers:

New cases: 12
Recovered and go home: 10
Still receiving treatment: 5
Deaths: 1 (elderly man with diabetes)

What We Do This Week:

Tested 8 water points. Found 2 contaminated. Now fixing.
Trained 20 market women on food safety.
Sent health workers to 5 villages for health talk.

What You Must Do:

Boil your water or add bleach
Wash hand after toilet
Come hospital if diarrhoea start

Contact hospital: [Phone number]

Post am for:

Hospital and clinic walls
Market stalls
Church and mosque
Chief's compound
Primary school gate
Read am for local radio station
Share am for WhatsApp yourself (fast fast, before rumours spread)

Why: Consistent, honest information kill rumours. People go tired of the false talk when real talk come every week.

7. Answer "Why Dem Die" Question Directly

This one critical. People see death and suspect foul play. Explain:

"When elderly person die from cholera, no be because treatment fail. Is because person come hospital too late. When diarrhoea start, person wait 3-4 days before coming. By that time, body done lose too much water and salt. Even with treatment, body too weak."

"This is why you must come EARLY. If diarrhoea start morning, come hospital same morning. If you wait until evening, risk higher. Don't wait."

Also explain:

"Some people wey die, dem get other sickness too—diabetes, high blood pressure, weak immune system. Cholera hit dem harder. That no mean treatment no work. That mean person need come hospital FAST when diarrhoea start."

What NOT to Do—Serious Serious
Don't deny the rumour exist. When you pretend people no dey talk, you look like you hide something
Don't attack people wey spread rumours. If you arrest somebody or threaten dem, people go believe say government really dey hide truth
Don't give only hospital statistics without explanation. Raw numbers sound like propaganda when people fear
Don't use only English. The rumours dey spread for Pidgin, Yoruba, and Igbo. You must respond for same languages
Don't wait for perfect lab results before you communicate. During outbreak, provisional information (with honest caveats) better pass silence
Don't ignore the fear underneath. Rumours spread because people fear. Address the fear first, the rumour second
Don't be defensive. Defensive tone make people more suspicious
The Real Truth Wey Matter

You cannot force people to trust you overnight. But you CAN shift how dem think by doing this:

Show yourself: Come for community. Be visible. Work hard.

Be honest: Tell people what you know AND what you no know yet.

Use their language: Speak Pidgin, Yoruba, Igbo—not just English.

Bring proof: Let people see recovery with their own eyes. Let recovered patients talk.

Repeat: Same message, every week, until people tired of hearing false talk and start believe true talk.

Respect them: Treat people like dem understand things. No treat dem like foolish people.

When you do this consistent-consistent, trust rebuild. And when trust rebuild, people go cooperate. They go report cases. They go follow health instructions. They go help you stop the outbreak.

That na the way.

How Public-Health Team Suppose Respond to WhatsApp Claims Say Health Workers Dey Hide Cholera Numbers, While Dem Still Maintain Trust and Give People Practical Health Guidance
First Understand Wetin This Rumour Really Mean Before You Respond

The claim say health workers dey hide the real number of cholera cases and deaths no be just ordinary lie wey somebody just cook up. Na specific type of outbreak rumour wey dem dey call "institutional concealment narrative." This type dey among the most dangerous ones because e dey attack the credibility of the exact people and systems wey the response depend on directly. If residents believe say health authority dey lie about how big the outbreak be, several things go follow wey you fit predict: people go stop to come health facility because dem no trust the system, dem go stop to cooperate with surveillance and contact tracing, dem go turn to other sources of care and information wey fit dey dangerous, and dem go share the concealment claim further because to forward "hidden truth" dey carry social currency for WhatsApp.

But this rumour also carry important information about the relationship between the community and the health system. People no dey invent concealment story from nowhere. This kind narrative dey show when trust don already dey low before the outbreak, when official communication don dey absent, late, inconsistent, or people feel say e no complete, when wetin community dey see with their own eye (how many sick people dem know, how many burial dem attend) no match wetin official story dey tell them, or when history don teach them say authorities dey actually undercount or underreport. For Nigeria specifically, people still remember how official figures for previous disease outbreaks dey contested or delayed, including the 2014 Ebola response and different meningitis and Lassa fever episodes. These memories dey give fertile ground for concealment narrative to grow.

The response must recognise say this distrust fit get rational roots, even if the specific claim no correct for fact. To treat the rumour as simply wrong without understanding why people believe am go guarantee say the correction fail.

Principle One: Respond Quick-Quick For the Same Platform Where the Rumour Dey

The rumour dey spread for WhatsApp. The correction must reach WhatsApp. Press conference, ministry statement for government website, or radio broadcast fit dey useful as extra channel, but none of them go catch the rumour where e actually dey live. WhatsApp message dey circulate inside trusted private and group conversations, and that one give am closeness and believability wey official broadcast no fit match.

The public-health team suppose prepare short, clear voice note or text message wey people fit forward for WhatsApp. Voice note dey particularly effective for Nigerian context because e carry the warmth and authority of human voice, e dey accessible for people wey no fit read well, and na the dominant way wey people dey communicate inside many WhatsApp groups. The message suppose dey recorded by person wey the community know and trust, no be anonymous institutional voice. Local health officer wey people know face, well-known community health worker, respected traditional ruler, or religious leader wey don agree to support the response, all of dem dey stronger messenger pass faceless "Ministry of Health."

The message suppose dey under two minutes. E suppose dey for the language wey community dey use, which for most Nigerian communities mean either the dominant local language, Nigerian Pidgin English, or both, no be formal English. E suppose dey forwarded directly inside the WhatsApp groups where the rumour dey circulate, and that one need the response team to get community liaisons wey dey inside those groups.

The speed of this response matter pass almost anything else. The WHO Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE) framework and the CDC Crisis and Emergency Risk Communication (CERC) model both identify the first 24 to 48 hours after rumour begin circulate as the critical window. After that time, the rumour go begin solidify into shared community understanding and go become far harder to correct.

Principle Two: Acknowledge the Concern First Before You Correct the Claim

The WhatsApp message or voice note no suppose start with denial. E suppose start by calling the concern by name. Opening like "We don hear say messages dey go round say we dey hide the real numbers of cholera cases and deaths. We understand why people dey worried" go do several things at the same time: e signal say the health team know wetin community dey talk, e validate the feeling underneath (fear, concern for family safety) without validating the factual claim, and e create one moment where people open mind small before the correction come.

Research for health communication, including findings wey WHO RCCE guidance and the cognitive psychology literature on misinformation correction reflect, dey consistently show say corrections wey start by acknowledging the audience concern dey more effective pass those wey start with flat denial. The reason be say flat denial ("That one no be true, we no dey hide anything") dey trigger defensive reaction for people wey already no trust the institution. E sound like exactly wetin authority wey actually dey hide something go talk. Acknowledgement first, then transparency, go break this pattern.

Principle Three: Respond With Radical Transparency, No Be Defensive Denial

The single most effective weapon against concealment narrative be to make the data visible. If community believe say dem dey hide numbers, the answer be to show the numbers, explain how dem dey collect am, explain wetin the numbers include and wetin dem no include, and explain why the numbers fit different from wetin community dey see with their eye.

The public-health team suppose release, for format wey community fit access, the following: current confirmed case count, current death count, number of people wey currently dey receive treatment, number of samples wey dem don send for laboratory confirmation and how many results still dey pending, and where treatment dey available. This information suppose dey updated regularly, ideally every day during active outbreak, and communicated through the same channels where the rumour dey circulate.

The team suppose also explain the gap between official figures and wetin community dey perceive, and this part dey critical. Legitimate reasons dey why official count fit dey lower than wetin community members observe. No be every case of running belle during cholera outbreak na cholera. Some cases fit never dey reported to health facility yet. Laboratory confirmation dey take time, and the confirmed count always dey behind the actual count during active outbreak. Suspected cases and confirmed cases dey counted differently. People wey die for house without going to health facility fit no dey inside official figures immediately, and to close that gap need community cooperation with reporting, no be concealment by health workers.

This explanation suppose come without defensiveness. If genuine gaps dey for reporting, like deaths wey happen for house wey the surveillance system never capture, the honest response na to say so and explain wetin dem dey do to improve the counting, no be to insist say the official count complete when both the health team and the community know say e fit no be. To claim say your count complete when community get direct evidence of people wey nobody count go destroy your credibility faster than any rumour.

Principle Four: Give Trusted Community Voices the Tools to Help

The public-health team no suppose try to be the only voice of correction. For communities where people no trust institution, the institution own denial carry the least weight. The team suppose find and brief trusted community figures: pastors and imams, traditional rulers, market leaders, headteachers, respected elders, and community health volunteers wey themselves be residents.

Give these people the current data, the explanation for any differences between official count and wetin people dey see, and the practical health guidance. Support them to deliver this information for their own words through their own networks. No give them script to read. Give them facts and let them talk the way dem talk.

This approach get documented effectiveness. During the 2014 Ebola response for Nigeria, community leaders and religious figures play critical role to counter misinformation. During the 2018–2020 DRC Ebola outbreaks, WHO, UNICEF, and IFRC find say community feedback mechanisms and trusted local messengers dey far more effective to counter concealment narrative pass institutional communications alone. The principle be say trust dey relational and local, e no dey institutional and broadcast.

The briefing of these community voices must include honest information about uncertainties. If trusted leaders repeat institutional talking points wey later turn out say dem no complete, their personal credibility go damage, and the community go lose not only trust for the institution but trust for the leaders wey vouch for am. To give messengers honest, nuanced information go protect both their credibility and the response.

Principle Five: Create Channel Wey People Fit Use Ask Questions and Get Answers

Part of wetin dey drive concealment narrative be the feeling say information only dey flow one direction: from authority to community. If you establish channel where community members fit ask questions, report concerns, and get direct answers, that one go change the dynamic.

Practical options for Nigerian community context include dedicated WhatsApp number wey community liaison go dey staff and dey respond to questions for real time, daily or twice-daily community meeting for public location where the health team go give update and take questions, toll-free phone line (NCDC get one nationally, but local line often dey more accessible and people trust am more), and designated person for each treatment facility wey fit give case information to families.

The feedback channel must be genuine. If people send questions and dem no get response, or dem get scripted non-answers wey no actually address their question, the channel go become evidence of more concealment. Responses must dey timely, honest, and for the community language.

Principle Six: Join the Rumour Response Together With Practical Health Guidance Wey Go Save Life

The rumour response no suppose exist separate from the health guidance wey residents need to survive the outbreak. Response wey focus entirely on defending institutional credibility while e fail to give actionable protective information go confirm the community suspicion say authority care more about their reputation pass people lives.

Every communication wey address the concealment rumour suppose also include, or dey immediately followed by, clear practical guidance for community language:

How to prevent person from dying of dehydration. ORS (Oral Rehydration Solution) na the most important thing. If ORS sachet dey available, mix am with treated water the way dem write for the packet. If ORS no dey, make temporary one for house: six level teaspoon of sugar and half level teaspoon of salt inside one litre of water wey you don boil or treat with chlorine. Give the sick person small-small sip, but give am all the time, no stop. No wait for the person to talk say im thirsty, because when dehydration don bad, person no go even feel thirsty again. Watch for danger signs: eye don enter inside, if you pinch skin for back of hand e no go back flat quick-quick, heart dey beat fast but weak, person no fit drink again, person no dey piss or piss dey come out very dark. If you see any of these, carry the person go health facility sharp-sharp because dem go need drip (IV fluid). Cholera fit kill within hours through dehydration, but with proper rehydration therapy, the death rate fit drop below 1%.

How to make your water safe. Treat all drinking water. Boil am make e bubble well-well for at least one minute, or use chlorine (liquid bleach or water purification tablet) follow the instruction for the packet. Store treated water inside clean container wey get cover and small mouth. No dip hand or cup inside the water. Pour am out or use container wey get tap.

How to keep clean. All shit and vomit from sick person must enter latrine or toilet. If the person no fit reach toilet, use bucket catch am, put 0.2% chlorine solution inside, wait 30 minutes, then pour am inside latrine. No pour untreated shit for gutter, stream, or for ground. Wash hand with soap and water after you touch sick person, after you use toilet, before you cook, before you chop, and before you feed pikin. If soap no dey, ash fit work small, but soap better pass.

Where to go for treatment. Tell people clearly where the cholera treatment centres dey, their hours, and whether treatment free. Anybody wey get serious water-water running belle suppose start ORS immediately and go to the nearest treatment centre. No wait for the running belle to get worse. The faster person reach treatment, the better the chance.

If person die. If person die from suspected cholera, the body still fit spread the sickness. Na only trained burial team suppose prepare the body. Big burial gathering where plenty people chop together don cause cholera to spread for many outbreaks before. Reduce the crowd and avoid communal food for burial during outbreak.

This guidance suppose dey woven into the same communication wey address the rumour, no be issued separately. The message structure be: we hear your concern, this na the truth about the numbers and why dem fit look different from wetin you dey see, and this na wetin you fit do right now to protect your family. The practical guidance show say the health team priority na to save lives, and that one by itself be the strongest answer to the claim say dem dey hide deaths.

Principle Seven: Monitor Whether Your Response Dey Work

Rumour correction no be one-time event. After the first response, the team must monitor whether the correction dey reach the relevant WhatsApp groups, whether the concealment story still dey, don change form, or new rumour don replace am, and whether community behaviour dey change for response (people dey come treatment centre? dem dey cooperate with surveillance? dem dey follow the guidance?).

This monitoring suppose use the same community feedback channels wey we describe above: community health workers wey dey report wetin dem hear, liaison members inside WhatsApp groups wey dey observe the conversation, call-centre and hotline logs, and direct observation for treatment facilities. If the concealment narrative still dey despite correction, the team must find out why. Possible reasons include say the correction no reach the right people, the messenger no be person wey dem trust, the explanation no dey believable because e no match wetin community dey see, or new events (cluster of deaths, facility wey look like e don full) don reinforce the story. Each of these need different second-round response.

This cycle of listen, analyse, respond, and monitor na the operational core of the WHO infodemic management framework.

Wetin the Public-Health Team No Suppose Do At All

No dismiss the concern as ignorance or wickedness. To call people wey share the rumour uneducated, irresponsible, or enemies of the response go deepen the divide and make correction harder. Most people wey forward concealment claim dey do am because dem genuinely worry about their community, no be because dem want cause trouble.

No threaten legal action against people wey share the rumour. Threats of prosecution for "spreading misinformation" don dey used for some outbreak contexts and dem don consistently backfire. Dem confirm the concealment narrative ("if dem dey threaten people wey ask question, dem must dey hide something"). Dem suppress the feedback wey the team need to understand community concerns. And dem drive rumour circulation underground into private messages where e harder to detect and counter.

No delay the response while you dey prepare "perfect" message. Imperfect response wey you deliver within hours dey vastly more effective pass polished response wey come days later. The first message fit be brief and honest: "We know say this claim dey circulate. This na wetin we know right now. We go share more as we confirm am." To keep quiet during the critical window na the same thing as confirming the concealment for people mind.

No claim say your official figures complete if dem no complete. If the surveillance system get known limitations, like deaths wey happen for house wey dem never capture, or laboratory confirmation wey dey behind clinical diagnosis, say so. Explain wetin you dey do to close the gap. To overclaim completeness when community get direct evidence to the contrary na the single fastest way to prove say the concealment story true for their mind.

No separate the rumour response from the health response. Communication strategy wey focus on defending institution while people dey die of preventable dehydration for their house go fail for both objectives. The health guidance na the credibility. When people see say your priority be their survival, the concealment narrative lose power by itself.

(2012) review. Practical cholera guidance (ORS formulation, chlorine concentrations, case fatality comparisons) follow WHO clinical and environmental health standards.

Public-health teams suppose check NCDC and WHO Nigeria for the most current outbreak communication protocols, because specific guidance fit don update as the outbreak change.

Dis one na serious wahala, and e need sharp, honest response. Make I break am down:

Wetin Dey Cause the Trust Problem

Before anything, the public-health team need understand say the rumour no dey come from nowhere. For many Nigerian communities, people don see times wey government or health officials play down outbreak numbers — sometimes to avoid panic, sometimes for political reason. So when people hear say "dem dey hide numbers," na past experience dey fuel that suspicion. Any response wey no first acknowledge dis reality go fall flat.

How the Public-Health Team Suppose Respond

1. Release the numbers — openly, regularly, and locally

No hide behind "official channels" wey nobody dey check. The team suppose:

Dey release case count and death count every day or every two days — through the same WhatsApp groups wey the rumours dey spread.
Break the numbers down by local area or ward, so people fit check am against wetin dem dey see with their own eyes.
If the numbers get delay or gap, explain why plainly. For example: "We get 45 confirmed cases as of today. Some test results never come back, so dis number fit change. We go update una as e dey come."
If there be real discrepancy between wetin community dey observe and wetin official report talk, address am directly. E.g.: "Some people wey sick no come facility — na why our number fit look small pass wetin una dey see for ground. We dey beg make everybody wey get the symptoms come, so we fit count well and treat well."

Dat kind transparency go do more pass any fine press statement.

2. Use people wey the community already trust

The public-health team by demself no be the most trusted voice for many communities during crisis. Dem need put forward:

Community and religious leaders — imam, pastor, chief, traditional ruler — make dem help deliver the numbers and the health messages. But no just use dem as mouthpiece. Carry dem along for the actual data briefing so dem fit answer questions with confidence.
Community Health Extension Workers (CHEWs) wey dey live for that same area — dem get credibility because people know dem.
People wey don recover from cholera — if any survivor willing talk, their testimony dey very powerful. "I go the treatment centre, dem treat me, I survive" go counter rumour more than any official statement.

3. Go where the conversation dey happen

If the misinformation dey move for WhatsApp, the response must dey for WhatsApp too. The team suppose:

Set up dedicated WhatsApp broadcast list or join existing community groups (with permission from admins).
Share short voice notes in Pidgin and local languages — not long typed English documents. Voice note from a known doctor, nurse, or community leader carry weight.
Respond to specific rumours directly. No dodge. If people say "dem dey hide the dead body count," address that exact claim: "As of today, X people don die from dis cholera for our community. Every death wey happen for treatment centre don dey recorded. If anybody know person wey die for house without report, make dem contact [specific number] so we fit count am and help the family."

4. Give practical, actionable information — not just statistics

People need to know wetin to DO right now. Every message suppose include clear steps:

Water safety: "Boil your water well well before you drink or cook with am. If you no fit boil am, use water guard — put one capful inside 20 litres, wait 30 minutes."
Wetin to do if person start purge or stool dey run: "Mix one level teaspoon of salt and eight level teaspoons of sugar inside one litre of clean boiled water. Give the person make e dey drink small small while una rush go nearest health centre. No wait."
Where to go: Give the specific name and location of the nearest oral rehydration point or cholera treatment centre — not just "go to the hospital." People need address, phone number, whether treatment dey free.
Burial safety: If deaths dey happen, give clear guidance on safe burial practice, because improper handling of bodies fit spread cholera further.

5. Acknowledge mistakes and don't be defensive

If the public-health team don make any error before — late response, wrong information, poor treatment of patients — own am. Say: "We know say we no respond quick enough at first. We dey sorry. Dis na wetin we don change now..." Dat kind honesty dey disarm suspicion faster than anything else.

If there be genuine problem with data collection — maybe the surveillance system slow, maybe some deaths happen before people reach facility — say so plainly instead of pretending the numbers perfect.

6. Create feedback loop

Give people way to report cases, ask questions, or challenge the numbers directly. A dedicated phone line or WhatsApp number wey actually dey reply go show say the team no dey hide.

Wetin the Team Must Avoid
No dismiss the rumours as "fake news" or blame people for spreading dem. Dat go only increase suspicion.
No use only English or only formal language. If the community dey yarn Pidgin, Yorùbá, Igbo, or Hausa — the response must match.
No release numbers only through press conference or government website. Most affected people no go see am there.
No wait until the rumour don spread wide before you respond. Speed matter. Same day response to new rumour dey critical.
Bottom Line

Trust during outbreak no be something you demand — na something you earn through consistent transparency, local-language communication, honest acknowledgment of gaps, and practical help wey people fit actually use. The public-health team wey go win dis fight na the one wey show up where people dey, speak how people dey speak, and prove with action — not words alone — say dem get nothing to hide.

Public-health team suppose respond fast, honestly and respectfully, no be just to call the WhatsApp message “lie.”

How dem fit build trust
Acknowledge people concern and explain wetin dem know, wetin never clear, and wetin dem still dey investigate.
Publish regular updates showing suspected cases, confirmed cases and deaths separately, plus the date the figures cover. NCDC already publishes cholera situation reports.
Explain why figures fit change, such as new reports or laboratory confirmation.
Correct mistakes publicly and make government agencies give consistent information.
Listen to community questions and use trusted channels like local leaders, radio, WhatsApp and familiar languages. WHO recommends involving affected communities in planning and monitoring to strengthen trust.
Provide verified contact details for reporting cases and checking information.
Clear health advice
Anybody with serious watery diarrhoea or vomiting should start ORS immediately and go health centre.
Mix one ORS sachet with 1 litre clean water. If sachet no dey, mix 6 level teaspoons sugar plus half level teaspoon salt inside 1 litre clean water.
Drink only boiled or properly chlorinated water.
Wash hands with soap and clean water, especially after toilet and before cooking.
Cook food well, cover am and eat am immediately.

Main thing na to show the data, explain its limits, answer questions openly and give actions people fit follow immediately.
