Na-agbagwoju anya, na-arahụ ụra gabiga ókè, nwee akwụkwụ ma ọ bụ tụfuo onwe ya
Na-esiri ya ike iku ume
Adịghị ike nke ukwuu ma ọ bụ enweghị ike iguzo
Na-agbọ agbọ ugboro ugboro ma ọ bụ enweghị ike ịṅụ mmiri
Nwere anya ma ọ bụ akpụkpọ ahụ na-acha odo
Na-amịrị mamịrị gbara ọchịchịrị ma ọ bụ nwere ọbara
Na-agba ọbara n’ụzọ a na-adịghị ahụkarị
Daa ma ọ bụ nwee ihe ịrịba ama nke shock

Ụmụaka, ụmụ nwaanyị dị ime, ndị agadi na ndị usoro nchebe ahụ ha adịghị ike kwesịrị inweta nyocha ngwa ngwa. A pụrụ ịgwọ ọrịa ịba, ma igbu oge tupu nyocha na ọgwụgwọ nwere ike itinye ndụ n’ihe ize ndụ.

Ọrịa ịba na-ejikarị egosi onwe ya n'ahụ mmadụ mgbe ụbọchị iri ruo iri na ise gasịrị ka anwụ nke bu ọrịa ịba tara mmadụ, ma ọ nwere ike ịdị anya karịa nke ahụ tupu ihe ịrịba ama ebido igosi.

Mgbaàmà ndị a na-ahụkarị bụ ndị a: ahụ na-ekpo ọkụ nke ukwuu (fever), ahụ na-ama jịjịjị dịka oyi na-atụ mmadụ, isi na-awa mmadụ, ahụ na afọ na-esigbu mmadụ ike, ike na-agwụ mmadụ n'ụzọ na-adịghị mma, afọ na-asọ mmadụ, ọ nwekwara ike ime ka mmadụ na-agbọ agbọ. N'oge ụfọdụ, ahụ ọkụ ahụ na-abịa ma na-ala, dịka ọ na-eso usoro.

Kedu mgbe mmadụ kwesịrị ịga ụlọ ọgwụ:

Ọ bụrụ na ị nọ ebe anwụ ịba dị ma ọ bụ i si ebe dị otú ahụ lọta, ma ahụ gị amalite ịkpo ọkụ, agbala ọsọ gaa ụlọ ọgwụ ozugbo. Ọ bụladị ma ọ bụ ọtụtụ izu ma ọ bụ ọnwa ka ị hapụrụ ebe ahụ, ọ bụrụ na ahụ ọkụ abịa, gaa ka a nyochaa gị. Echerekwala ka ọrịa ahụ "dị ka ịba n'ezie" tupu ị kwaga.

Ụdị kachasị egwu bụ P. falciparum. Nke a nwere ike imetụta ụbụrụ mmadụ (cerebral malaria), mebie ọbara, mebiekwa akụrụ ahụ ndị ọzọ, ma nweekwa ike igbu mmadụ n'ime awa ole na ole ma ọ bụrụ na a naghị agwọ ya ọsọ ọsọ.

Ihe ị ga-eme bụ ịga ụlọ ọgwụ ka a gwaa ọbara gị (thick and thin smear ma ọ bụ rapid test). Ọ bụrụ na nsonaazụ ya gosipụta na ọ bụ ịba, ọgwụgwọ artemisinin combination therapy na-arụ ọrụ nke ọma, ma ọ bụ naanị ma mmadụ bidoro ya n'oge. Ọ bụrụ na mmadụ echere ogologo oge, ọ na-abụ ihe ize ndụ.

Ya mere, n'ụzọ dị mkpirikpi: ahụ na-ekpo ọkụ, ị nọkwa ebe anwụ dị? Egbula oge. Gbalịa gaa ụlọ ọgwụ ngwa ngwa.

Ọrịa ịba bụ ọrịa dị njọ nke anwụ na-ebute. Mgbe anwụ nwere parasite ịba tara mmadụ, ọ na-ewe ihe dịka ụbọchị 10 ruo 15 tupu mgbaàmà ebido igosi, ma ọ pụrụ ịwe ogologo oge karịa nke ahụ, dabere na ụdị parasite.

Mgbaàmà ndị a na-ahụkarị:

Ahụ ọkụ (fever) bụ ihe mbụ mmadụ na-ahụkarị — ahụ na-ekpo ọkụ, ọ pụrụ ịbụ na ọ na-abịa wee laa, mgbe ụfọdụ kwa ụbọchị abụọ ma ọ bụ atọ. Oyi na-ejide mmadụ, ahụ na-ama jịjịjị ọ bụladị mgbe ikuku dị ọkụ. Mgbe oyi ahụ gasịrị, ọsụsọ na-agbapụta n'ahụ nke ukwuu. Nke a bụ usoro ịba a ma ama — oyi, mgbe ahụ ọkụ, mgbe ahụ ọsụsọ — ma ọ bụghị onye ọ bụla ka ọ na-apụtara otu ahụ kpọmkwem, karịsịa mgbe ọrịa ahụ bidoro ọhụrụ.

Mgbaàmà ndị ọzọ gụnyere isi ọwụwa nke na-agwụghị agwụ, ahụ ụfụ na mgbụ n'ọkpụkpụ, ike ọgwụgwụ karịrị nke a na-ahụkarị, ọ na-agụ mmadụ ọgwụgwụ nke ukwuu, afọ na-asọ mmadụ ma ọ bụ mmadụ na-achọ ịgbọ, mgbụ afọ, na mgbe ụfọdụ afọ ọsịsa. N'ihi na mgbaàmà ndị a yiri nke oyi ma ọ bụ flu, ọtụtụ mmadụ na-eche na ọ bụ naanị oyi nta — nke a bụ ihe dị ize ndụ nke ukwuu.

Mgbe ị kwesịrị ịga ụlọ ọgwụ:

Egbula oge ọ bụla. Ọrịa ịba abụghị ihe ị ga-anọ n'ụlọ na-eji ọgwụ ogwu jiri lekọta onwe gị. Gaa ụlọ ọgwụ ozugbo ma ọ bụrụ na:

Ahụ ọkụ malịtere gị ma ị bi n'ebe ịba dị ma ọ bụ ị gara ebe dị otú ahụ — ọ bụladị ma ị lọtara ọnwa ole na ole gara aga. Ụfọdụ ụdị ịba nwere ike izo n'ahụ wee lọghachi azụ mgbe oge gasịrị.
Ị na-enwe ọtụtụ n'ime mgbaàmà ndị a otu oge — ahụ ọkụ, isi ọwụwa, ahụ ụfụ, ịgbọ agbọ, ma ọ bụ ike ọgwụgwụ dị oke.
Ma ọ bụrụ na ihe amalite ịka njọ — mmadụ amalite ịgba aghara, anya amalite ịchawa acha odo odo, iku ume amalite isi ike, mmamịrị aghọ oji ma ọ bụ belatara, mmadụ amalite ịda ogbi (convulsion), ma ọ bụ ahụ adaa mba nke ukwuu. Ihe ndị a niile na-egosi na ịba ahụ eruola ebe dị ize ndụ. Plasmodium falciparum, nke bụ ụdị kachasị egbu egbu, nwere ike isi n'ịba nkịtị gbaa gburugburu wee ghọọ nke na-egbu mmadụ n'ime awa ole na ole.

Ndị ihe ize ndụ ha dị elu:

Ụmụaka na-adịbeghị afọ ise, ụmụ nwanyị dị ime, na ndị na-arịabeghị ịba mbụ — ndị a nwere ike ịnweta ụdị dị njọ ngwa ngwa.

Ihe kacha mkpa ịmara:

Otu nyocha ọbara — ma ọ bụ nke ngwa ngwa (rapid test) ma ọ bụ nke a na-ele n'okpuru igwe microscope — ga-egosi ma ọ bụ ịba ka ọ bụghị. Ọ bụrụ na a chọpụta ya oge, ịba nwere ọgwụgwụ — a pụrụ ịgwọ ya. Ihe na-egbu mmadụ bụ mgbe mmadụ na-eji nwayọ, na-azụ ọgwụ na-agwọ onwe ya n'ahịa ma ọ bụ na-anọ n'ụlọ na-echere ka ọ laa n'onwe ya.

Ọ bụrụ na ahụ ọkụ jidere gị ma ị maghị ihe kpatara ya, tinyekwara na anwụ nwere ike ịtala gị, were ya dịka ihe mberede. Gaa ụlọ ọgwụ otu ụbọchị ahụ. Echerela ka ahụ ọkụ ahụ soro usoro ma ọ bụ ka ọ lọghachite tupu i mee ihe. Otu ụbọchị ị tụfuru nwere ike ịbụ ihe dị iche n'etiti ndụ na ọnwụ — karịsịa maka ụmụaka na ụmụ nwanyị dị ime.

Ọrịa ịba bụ otu n'ime ọrịa ndị kachasị egbu mmadụ n'ụwa, karịsịa n'Africa. Anwụ nwere parasite na-ebute ya mgbe ọ tara mmadụ. Mgbe parasite banyere n'ahụ, ọ na-ewe ihe dịka ụbọchị 10 ruo 15 tupu mmadụ amalite ịhụ mgbaàmà, ma dabere na ụdị parasite, ọ pụrụ ịwe ogologo oge karịa.

Mgbaàmà ndị a na-ahụkarị n'ọrịa ịba:

Ahụ ọkụ bụ mgbaàmà kachasị pụta ìhè — ọ na-abịa n'ụzọ dị iche iche, ụfọdụ oge ọ na-ekpo ọkụ nke ukwuu wee belata, mgbe ụfọdụ kwa awa iri anọ na asatọ (48) ma ọ bụ awa iri asaa na abụọ (72). Oyi na-ajụ mmadụ nke ukwuu, ahụ na-ama jịjịjị dịka onye nọ n'oké oyi. Mgbe nke ahụ gasịrị, ọsụsọ na-agbapụta n'ahụ niile.

Mgbaàmà ndị ọzọ bụ isi ọwụwa siri ike, mgbụ na-adị n'ahụ niile na n'ọkpụkpụ, ike ọgwụgwụ nke na-eme ka mmadụ ghara inwe ike ime ihe ọ bụla, afọ ọsọ, ịgbọ agbọ ma ọ bụ obi ịsọ mmadụ, na mgbụ afọ. Ọ dị mkpa ịmara na mgbaàmà ndị a nwere ike iyiri oyi uzuzu ma ọ bụ flu — ya mere ọtụtụ mmadụ adịghị elekwasị ya anya n'oge, nke na-eme ka ọrịa ahụ sie ike.

Mgbe ị ga-agba ọsọ gaa ụlọ ọgwụ:

Ọrịa ịba abụghị ihe a ga-eji nwayọọ lee. Gaa ụlọ ọgwụ ozugbo ozugbo ma ọ bụrụ na:

Ahụ ọkụ malịtere na-akụ gị ma ị nọ n'ebe ịba dị ma ọ bụ ị nọworo n'ebe dị otú ahụ na mbụ. Ụdị ụfọdụ dịka Plasmodium vivax na P. ovale nwere ike izo n'imeju (liver) ọnwa ka ọnwa, wee pụta ọzọ mgbe mmadụ chere na ya adịkwa mma.
Ị na-enwe ahụ ọkụ, isi ọwụwa, ahụ ụfụ, na ike ọgwụgwụ n'otu oge.
Ihe ndị siri ike amalitela igosi onwe ha — dịka mmadụ ịmalite ịgba aghara ma ọ bụ ghara ịma onye ọ bụ, anya ịchawa acha odo odo (jaundice), iku ume ịghọ ihe siri ike, mmamịrị ịghọ oji ma ọ bụ ịbelata, ịda ogbi (seizures/convulsion), ma ọ bụ ahụ ịda mba ruo ebe mmadụ apụghịzi ibili ọtọ. Mgbaàmà ndị a na-egosi na ịba ahụ aghọọla ụdị dị ize ndụ nke nwere ike igbu mmadụ n'ime awa ole na ole. Plasmodium falciparum bụ ụdị kachasị egbu egbu, ọ na-esi ngwa ngwa wee ghọọ nke na-emetụta ụbụrụ (cerebral malaria), na-akpata ọbara ụkọ dị oke njọ, ma ọ bụ na-emebi akụrụ ahụ ndị ọzọ.

Ndị ọrịa ịba na-akpa karịsịa:

Ụmụaka na-adịbeghị afọ ise bụ ndị kachasị nọ n'ihe ize ndụ — ọtụtụ ọnwụ sitere n'ịba n'ụwa niile bụ nke ụmụaka. Ụmụ nwanyị dị ime nọkwa n'ihe ize ndụ nke ukwuu n'ihi na ịba nwere ike imerụ ha na nwa ha ahụ. Ndị ọbịa si ebe ịba na-adịghị bịa ebe ịba dị nọkwa n'ihe ize ndụ n'ihi na ahụ ha amụtabeghị ịlụso ịba ọgụ.

Ihe kacha mkpa:

Otu nyocha ọbara nwere ike ikwu ma ọ bụ ịba ka ọ bụghị — ma ọ bụ ule ngwa ngwa (rapid diagnostic test) ma ọ bụ nke a na-ele n'okpuru microscope. Ọ bụrụ na a chọpụta ya n'oge, ọgwụ ịba dị irè nke ukwuu — a pụrụ ịgwọ ya kpamkpam. Ma ihe na-ebibi mmadụ bụ mgbe mmadụ na-eji nwayọọ — na-azụta ọgwụ n'ahịa n'onwe ya ma ọ bụ na-echere ka ahụ ọkụ ahụ kwụsị n'onwe ya.

Ọ bụrụ na ahụ ọkụ ọ bụla ejidere gị ma ị nọ ebe anwụ nwere ike ịta gị, jiri ya dịka ihe mberede. Gaa ụlọ ọgwụ otu ụbọchị ahụ — echerela echi. N'ọrịa ịba, otu ụbọchị nwere ike ịkọwa ihe dị iche n'etiti ịdị ndụ na ịnwụ anwụ.

Rịba ama: A pụghị iji mgbaàmà naanị kwado na ọ bụ ịba. Nnwale ọbara na ọgwụgwọ ngwa ngwa dị mkpa.

Households can reduce malaria risk during the rainy season by combining protection from mosquito bites with measures that reduce mosquito breeding.

Sleep under a properly fitted, insecticide-treated mosquito net every night. Prioritise young children, pregnant people and anyone who is unwell, but everyone should use one where possible.
Check nets regularly for holes, repair damage and wash them only as directed on the label.
Install or repair screens on windows, doors and ventilation openings. Close doors and windows early if they are not screened.
Use an approved mosquito repellent on exposed skin, following the label instructions. Wear long sleeves, long trousers and socks, particularly from dusk until dawn.
Empty, cover or remove containers that collect water around the home. This includes buckets, tyres, flowerpots, cans and blocked gutters.
Keep water-storage containers tightly covered. Improve drainage and clear vegetation or rubbish that prevents water from flowing.
Cooperate with indoor residual spraying when it is recommended and delivered by trained public-health teams. Do not paint or wash treated walls before the instructed period.
Use preventive malaria medicines only when recommended by a qualified health professional or official programme. This is especially relevant for eligible pregnant people, children or travellers.
Ensure anyone with fever, chills, headache or unusual weakness receives prompt testing and appropriate treatment. Do not assume every fever is malaria or rely only on herbal remedies.

Mosquito coils, sprays or other household products may offer additional protection when used correctly, but they should not replace insecticide-treated nets and other proven measures.

During rainy season, the family can reduce mosquito bites with low-cost measures:

Sleep under an insecticide-treated mosquito net if one is available.
Remove or empty standing water around the home, such as water in buckets, tyres, cans, gutters, or containers where mosquitoes can breed.
Keep water-storage containers covered.
Clear bushes and rubbish close to the house where mosquitoes may rest.
Use window or door screens if affordable, and close doors and windows when mosquitoes are most active.
Wear clothing that covers the arms and legs, especially in the evening and at night.
If mosquito repellent is available and affordable, use it according to the instructions.

The family should also watch for symptoms such as fever, chills, headache, or unusual weakness. If someone becomes ill, they should seek testing or medical assessment rather than assume every fever is malaria.

How Households Can Reduce Malaria Risk During the Rainy Season

The rainy season creates ideal breeding conditions for Anopheles mosquitoes — standing water accumulates everywhere, humidity rises, and mosquito populations surge. Household-level prevention is critical because most malaria transmission happens in and around the home, especially between dusk and dawn.

Eliminating Mosquito Breeding Sites

Mosquitoes need stagnant water to breed, and even a small capful of water is enough. Walk around your compound regularly and empty, cover, or overturn any container that collects rainwater — buckets, old tyres, flowerpot saucers, discarded cans, blocked gutters, and uncovered water storage drums. If you store water for household use, keep it tightly covered at all times. Clear drainage channels around your home so rainwater flows away rather than pooling.

Sleeping Under Insecticide-Treated Nets (ITNs)

Long-lasting insecticide-treated nets remain one of the most effective single interventions against malaria. Every person in the household should sleep under one every night, not only when mosquitoes seem abundant — transmission can occur from a single bite. Nets should be tucked under the mattress or sleeping mat, checked regularly for holes, and repaired or replaced when damaged. In many endemic countries, government health programmes and campaigns distribute these nets free of charge; it is worth checking with local health centres or community health workers about upcoming distributions.

Protecting the Home in the Evening and at Night

Anopheles mosquitoes are most active from dusk to dawn. Closing windows and doors at sunset, or fitting them with mesh screens, significantly reduces the number of mosquitoes entering the home. Where screens are not available, hanging curtains or cloth over openings helps. Burning mosquito coils or using plug-in vaporisers that contain pyrethroids in sleeping areas provides additional protection, though these should complement nets rather than replace them.

Environmental Management Around the Home

Keep grass and vegetation trimmed short around the house, since mosquitoes rest in tall vegetation during the day. Fill in any low-lying areas in the compound where puddles form after rain. If there are open drains nearby, advocate with neighbours and local authorities to keep them clear — malaria prevention works best as a community effort rather than a single-household activity.

Using Insect Repellents

Topical repellents containing DEET, picaridin, or IR3535 applied to exposed skin offer protection during evening hours when people are still outdoors. For households where commercial repellents are not affordable or accessible, some communities use locally available plant-based options such as neem oil or lemongrass, though their duration of protection is generally shorter and evidence for their effectiveness is more limited compared with DEET-based products.

Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS)

Where government or public health programmes offer indoor residual spraying, households should participate. This involves trained personnel applying insecticide to the interior walls of homes, where mosquitoes tend to rest after feeding. A single round of spraying can provide protection for several months. It is important not to replaster or repaint sprayed walls, as this removes the insecticide.

Protecting the Most Vulnerable Members of the Household

Pregnant women and children under five face the highest risk of severe malaria and death. These individuals should be prioritised for net use. Pregnant women should attend antenatal care where intermittent preventive treatment (IPTp with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine) is typically provided as part of routine care in endemic areas. Children may also be eligible for seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) in certain regions — local health facilities can advise on this.

Seeking Prompt Diagnosis and Treatment

Prevention will not eliminate every case. When anyone in the household develops fever, chills, headache, or body aches during the rainy season, seek a diagnostic test — either a rapid diagnostic test (RDT) or microscopy — as quickly as possible, ideally within 24 hours of symptom onset. Do not self-treat with antimalarials without a confirmed diagnosis. Unconfirmed treatment wastes money on unnecessary drugs if the illness is not malaria, and contributes to drug resistance when antimalarials are used unnecessarily.

Early, confirmed treatment is almost always effective and prevents progression to severe, life-threatening malaria.

Reducing Malaria Risk During the Rainy Season

The rainy season creates ideal breeding conditions for Anopheles mosquitoes — standing water multiplies, humidity keeps mosquitoes alive longer, and transmission intensity spikes. Here's what households can do, organized by impact and practicality.

Sleeping under insecticide-treated nets (ITNs)

This is the single most effective household-level intervention. Every sleeping space should have a properly hung, long-lasting insecticidal net (LLIN). Nets need to be checked for holes and repaired or replaced — a torn net offers far less protection. In many endemic countries, government programmes distribute these free of charge through health facilities, antenatal clinics, and mass campaigns. If you're eligible and don't have one, that's the first thing to sort out.

Eliminating mosquito breeding sites around the home

Anopheles mosquitoes breed in standing water. During the rainy season, water collects everywhere — in discarded containers, tyres, blocked gutters, uncovered drums, flower pot saucers, and puddles. Households should drain, cover, or turn over any container that holds water, clear blocked drainage channels, and fill in low spots in the yard where water pools. This won't eliminate all mosquitoes (they breed in natural water bodies too), but it meaningfully reduces the population immediately around the home.

Using window and door screens

Physical barriers on windows, doors, and eaves prevent mosquitoes from entering the house. Where screens aren't available or affordable, closing windows and doors at dusk — when Anopheles mosquitoes become most active — still helps.

Indoor residual spraying (IRS)

Where available through public health programmes, indoor residual spraying coats interior walls with insecticide that kills mosquitoes when they rest on surfaces after feeding. This is typically organized at community or district level rather than purchased individually, but households should participate when spray teams come through. Its effectiveness depends on coverage — it works best when most homes in an area are sprayed.

Personal protection during peak biting hours

Anopheles mosquitoes primarily bite between dusk and dawn. Wearing long sleeves and trousers during evening hours, using mosquito coils or repellents where affordable, and avoiding sitting outside unprotected after dark all reduce exposure. For households that can access them, topical repellents containing DEET, picaridin, or IR3535 are effective.

Environmental management

Keeping grass and vegetation trimmed around the house reduces resting sites for adult mosquitoes. Ensuring proper drainage so rainwater flows away from the home rather than collecting nearby is also important.

Chemoprevention for vulnerable groups

Pregnant women and children under five are at highest risk of severe malaria and death. Pregnant women should receive intermittent preventive treatment (IPTin pregnancy, or IPTp) with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine during antenatal visits. In areas with highly seasonal transmission, seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) for children aged 3–59 months is recommended by the WHO and delivered through community health workers. These aren't household decisions exactly, but knowing they exist and seeking them out is critical.

Prompt diagnosis and treatment

No prevention method is 100% effective. When anyone in the household develops fever during the rainy season, getting a confirmed diagnosis — via rapid diagnostic test (RDT) or microscopy — within 24 hours matters enormously. Treating a confirmed case of malaria early with artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) prevents progression to severe disease and reduces onward transmission to others through mosquitoes. Presumptive treatment without testing wastes money on unnecessary drugs when the fever has another cause, and contributes to drug resistance when antimalarials are used unnecessarily.

What doesn't work well

It's worth being clear about a few things that have weak or no evidence behind them: ultrasonic mosquito repellers don't work. Burning certain plants may provide marginal short-term repellency but shouldn't be relied on as a primary strategy. Vitamin B supplementation doesn't repel mosquitoes despite persistent myths.

The core message is layered protection — no single measure is sufficient on its own, but combining nets, environmental management, screening, and prompt treatment dramatically reduces risk even during peak transmission season.

Reducing Malaria Risk During the Rainy Season

The rainy season creates ideal breeding conditions for Anopheles mosquitoes, which transmit Plasmodium parasites. Household-level prevention focuses on two things: reducing mosquito populations nearby and preventing bites.

Eliminate breeding sites around the home. Mosquitoes breed in standing water, and even small collections matter. Empty, cover, or turn over containers that collect rainwater — buckets, tyres, flower pots, discarded cans, water storage drums. Clear blocked gutters and drains regularly. Fill in puddles or low spots in the yard where water pools after rain. If you store water for household use, keep it tightly covered at all times.

Sleep under insecticide-treated nets (ITNs). This remains the single most effective household intervention against malaria, backed by decades of evidence. Nets should be long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs), hung properly so they're tucked under the mattress or sleeping mat with no gaps. Everyone in the household should sleep under a net every night — not just during peak rainy months, but the rainy season is when compliance matters most. In many endemic countries, governments and NGOs distribute these free of charge through health facilities, antenatal clinics, and mass campaigns.

Use additional mosquito-control measures in and around the house. Indoor residual spraying (IRS), where available through public health programmes, provides strong protection. At the household level, burning mosquito coils or using plug-in vaporisers with pyrethroids in sleeping areas can offer supplementary protection, though these are not substitutes for nets. Screening windows and doors with mesh, and repairing holes in existing screens, physically blocks mosquito entry — this is underutilised but highly effective where feasible.

Reduce exposure during peak biting hours. Anopheles mosquitoes that carry malaria bite predominantly between dusk and dawn. Wearing long sleeves and trousers in the evening, and applying mosquito repellent to exposed skin (DEET-based products are the most evidence-supported), reduces bites. Keeping doors and windows closed after dark, or ensuring they're screened, matters more than people tend to realise.

Know when to seek care — and insist on testing. During rainy season, not every fever is malaria, but the probability rises sharply. Any household member with fever, chills, headache, or body aches should be tested with a rapid diagnostic test (RDT) or microscopy before treatment begins. Presumptive treatment without confirmation contributes to drug resistance and wastes money on unnecessary antimalarials. RDTs are widely available at health centres and many community health worker posts, often at no cost. Early confirmed diagnosis followed by prompt treatment with artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) prevents progression to severe malaria.

Consider seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) for young children. In areas where this WHO-recommended intervention is implemented — primarily the Sahel and sub-Sahel — children aged 3 months to 5 years receive monthly courses of preventive antimalarials during peak transmission. This is delivered through public health campaigns, not purchased privately. If your area runs SMC rounds, ensure eligible children participate in every cycle.

Manage the environment collectively. Individual households benefit, but community-level action multiplies the effect. Clearing vegetation immediately around the house, participating in community clean-up exercises to drain stagnant water, and supporting larviciding programmes where they exist all reduce the local mosquito population beyond what one household can achieve alone.

The core message is layered protection: no single intervention is perfect, but combining nets, environmental management, physical barriers, and prompt confirmed treatment substantially reduces both infection risk and severe outcomes during the highest-transmission period of the year.

Comot Any Water Wey Dey Stand

Tuck di net under mattress or mat so dat mosquito no go fit enter.

Many government health programme dey share dis net free. Go your nearest health centre or ask community health worker — dem fit tell you when next distribution go happen for your area.

Close Window and Door for Evening Time

Anopheles mosquito dey bite pass from when sun dey set reach when morning dey break. So before darkness come, make sure say you don close your window and door. If you fit put net or mesh for your window, dat one go really help. If you no get mesh, even curtain or cloth wey you hang for window and door go reduce di number of mosquito wey go enter house.

Mosquito coil or di one wey you plug for socket (vaporiser) fit help too, but make you still dey use net on top — no let coil alone replace your net.

Clean Around Your Compound

Cut grass short around di house. Mosquito dey like hide inside tall grass for daytime. If any place for your compound dey collect water after rain — like hole for ground or low area — try fill am with sand or dirt. If open gutter dey near your house, talk to your neighbour make una work together clean am. Malaria prevention work better when di whole community join hand.

Some time, government health people go come spray inside wall of house — dem dey call am Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS). Dis one dey kill mosquito wey land for wall after dem don bite. One round of spraying fit protect una for months. If dem come your area, allow dem spray. After dem don spray, no paint or plaster di wall again, because dat one go remove di medicine.

Small pikin wey never reach five years and pregnant woman dey face di worst danger from malaria. Make dem get first priority for net. For some areas, small pikin fit get medicine wey dem dey call seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) — go health centre go ask about am.

Even if you do everything well, person fit still get malaria. Make dem do test first — RDT or blood test — before anybody begin take malaria medicine.

And if you dey take malaria drug anyhow, e fit make di drug no work again for future — na so drug resistance dey start, and na everybody go suffer am.

If dem test am and e be malaria true-true, treatment dey work well especially if you catch am early. Most people dey recover within days.

Bí ẹnikẹ́ni bá ní ara gbígbóná tàbí àwọn àmì àìsàn míì, ó dára kí wọ́n ṣe àyẹ̀wò malaria tàbí lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn dípò kí wọ́n kan rò pé malaria ni.

Àwọn ìdílé lè dín ewu kíkó àìsàn ibà kù ní ìgbà òjò nípa àwọn ọ̀nà tó rọrùn wọ̀nyí:

Tú tàbí yọ omi tó dúró nínú bọ́ọ̀kì, táyà, agolo, gutter, ikòkò, àti ibi míì tí omi ti ń kó jọ.
Bo àwọn ohun tí wọ́n fi ń pa omi mọ́.
Gé koríko àti igbo tó sún mọ́ ilé, kí wọ́n sì yọ ìdọ̀tí tó lè jẹ́ ibi ìfarapamọ́ fún ẹ̀fọn.
Lo àwọ̀n ibùsùn tí a fi òògùn pa ẹ̀fọn sí bí ó bá wà.
Wọ aṣọ tó bo ọwọ́ àti ẹsẹ̀, pàápàá ní ìrọ̀lẹ́ àti alẹ́.
Pa ilẹ̀kùn àti ferese mọ́ nígbà tí ẹ̀fọn bá pọ̀, tàbí lo net/screen bí ó bá wà.
Lo òògùn tí ń lé ẹ̀fọn bí ó bá wà ní iye tí wọ́n lè san, kí wọ́n sì tẹ̀lé ìtọ́sọ́nà rẹ̀.

Bí ẹnikẹ́ni bá ní ara gbígbóná tàbí àwọn àmì àìsàn míì, ó dára kí wọ́n ṣe àyẹ̀wò malaria tàbí lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn dípò kí wọ́n kan rò pé malaria ni.

Báwo Ni Àwọn Ìdílé Ṣe Lè Dín Ewu Ìbà Kù Ní Ìgbà Òjò

Ìgbà òjò ni àkókò tí ẹ̀fọn Anopheles — irú ẹ̀fọn tí ó ń tan àrùn ìbà kálẹ̀ — máa ń pọ̀ sí i jù lọ. Omi tí ó dúró sí ibi kan lẹ́yìn ojò ni ẹ̀fọn máa ń lò láti bí àwọn ọmọ rẹ̀. Ẹ̀fọn yìí sábà máa ń bù jẹ ní alẹ́, láti ìrọ̀lẹ́ títí di òwúrọ̀ kutukutu. Ṣùgbọ́n ohun tí ó dára ni pé ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ ohun tí ìdílé lè ṣe láti dáàbò bo ara wọn kò nílò owó púpọ̀.

Ẹ Mú Omi Tí Ó Dúró Sí Ibi Kan Kúrò

Kódà omi díẹ̀ tí ó kún inú ìdérí ìgò kan tó láti jẹ́ kí ẹ̀fọn bímọ sí ibẹ̀. Ẹ rìn ká àgbàlá yín, ẹ ṣàyẹ̀wò ohun gbogbo tí omi lè kó sí inú rẹ̀ — bí àpẹẹrẹ: agolo àtijọ́, garawa, taya àtijọ́, àwọn ohun èlò tí a ti sọnù, àti ọ̀gàn tí ó ti dí. Ẹ da omi náà sílẹ̀, ẹ yí ohun èlò náà kóńkosó, tàbí kí ẹ bo orí rẹ̀. Tí ẹ bá ń tọ́jú omi fún ìlò inú ilé, ẹ rí i pé ẹ fi ìdérí bo ó dáadáa nígbà gbogbo. Ẹ tún máa ṣe ìtọ́jú ọ̀gàn àti ọ̀nà omi yíká ilé yín kí omi òjò lè ṣàn lọ dáadáa, kí ó má ṣe dúró sí ibi kan.

Ẹ Máa Sùn Sínú Àwọ̀n Tí Wọ́n Fi Oògùn Ṣe (ITN) Ní Gbogbo Alẹ́

Àwọ̀n tí wọ́n fi oògùn ṣe (insecticide-treated net) jẹ́ ọ̀kan lára àwọn ọ̀nà tí ó mú àṣeyọrí wá jù lọ láti dáàbò bo ènìyàn lọ́wọ́ ìbà. Kì í ṣe nígbà tí ẹ̀fọn bá pọ̀ nìkan ni kí a fi í lò — gbogbo ènìyàn nínú ìdílé gbọ́dọ̀ máa sùn sínú àwọ̀n ní gbogbo alẹ́. Ẹ tẹ ẹ̀gbẹ́ àwọ̀n náà sí abẹ́ àkéte tàbí ẹ̀ní, kí ẹ sì máa ṣàyẹ̀wò rẹ̀ nígbà gbogbo. Tí ó bá fà, ẹ rán an tàbí kí ẹ rí tuntun gbà.

Ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ ètò ìjọba ìlera máa ń pín àwọ̀n wọ̀nyí lọ́fẹ̀ẹ́. Ẹ béèrè lọ́wọ́ ilé ìwòsàn tí ó wà nítòsí yín tàbí lọ́wọ́ òṣìṣẹ́ ìlera àdúgbò yín — wọ́n lè sọ fún yín nígbà tí wọ́n bá fẹ́ pín àwọ̀n.

Ẹ Pa Fèrèsé àti Ìlẹ̀kùn Ní Àṣálẹ́

Nítorí pé ẹ̀fọn Anopheles máa ń ṣiṣẹ́ jù lọ láti ìrọ̀lẹ́ dé àárọ̀, ó ṣe pàtàkì láti pa fèrèsé àti ìlẹ̀kùn ṣáájú kí òkùnkùn tó dé. Tí ẹ bá lè fi nẹ́ẹ̀tì (mesh screen) sí fèrèsé yín, ìyẹn yóò ran yín lọ́wọ́ gan-an. Tí ẹ kò bá ní nẹ́ẹ̀tì, ẹ lè fi aṣọ tàbí ìkélé dí fèrèsé àti ẹnu ọ̀nà — èyí yóò dín iye ẹ̀fọn tí yóò wọ inú ilé kù.

Ẹ tún lè lo kọ́ìlì ẹ̀fọn (mosquito coil) tàbí ẹ̀rọ oníná mọ́nàmọ́ná tí ó ń tú oògùn jáde (vaporiser) sínú yàrá, ṣùgbọ́n kí èyí má rọ́pò àwọ̀n — ẹ lo méjèèjì papọ̀.

Ẹ Tún Àyíká Ilé Yín Ṣe

Ẹ bẹ koríko tí ó ga ní àyíká ilé yín kù, nítorí pé ẹ̀fọn sábà máa ń fi ara pamọ́ sínú koríko gíga ní ọ̀sán. Tí ihò tàbí ibi ìsàlẹ̀ kan bá wà nínú àgbàlá yín tí omi máa ń kó sí lẹ́yìn ojò, ẹ fi iyanrìn tàbí ilẹ̀ bò ó. Tí ọ̀gàn ṣíṣí bá wà nítòsí ilé yín, ẹ bá àwọn aládùúgbò yín sọ̀rọ̀, kí ẹ jọ ṣiṣẹ́ papọ̀ láti tún un ṣe — ìdènà ìbà máa ń ṣiṣẹ́ dáadáa jù lọ nígbà tí gbogbo àdúgbò bá ṣọ̀kan.

Ẹ Lo Oògùn Ìdáàbòbò Sí Ara (Repellent)

Ní àṣálẹ́, nígbà tí ènìyàn bá ṣì wà ní ìta ilé, ẹ lè fi oògùn ìdáàbòbò (repellent) pa ara yín ní ibi tí aṣọ kò bo. Àwọn tí ó ní DEET tàbí picaridin nínú wọn sábà máa ń ṣiṣẹ́ dáadáa. Tí owó kò bá tó fún àwọn tí wọ́n ń tà ní ọjà, àwọn ènìyàn kan máa ń lo epo dongoyaro (neem oil) tàbí kòríkò ọ̀sán wewe (lemongrass), ṣùgbọ́n ó yẹ kí a mọ̀ pé àwọn wọ̀nyí kì í pẹ́ tó lórí ara, ẹ̀rí ìmọ̀ sáyẹ́ǹsì tí ó fi hàn pé wọ́n ń ṣiṣẹ́ dáadáa kò sì lágbára tó bí ti DEET.

Tí Ìjọba Bá Wá Fún Ìṣífún Oògùn Sínú Ilé, Ẹ Gba Wọ́n Láàyè

Nígbà mìíràn, àwọn òṣìṣẹ́ ìlera ìjọba máa ń wá fún ilé-ilé láti fi oògùn sí ogiri inú ilé — èyí ni wọ́n ń pè ní Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS). Oògùn yìí máa ń pa ẹ̀fọn tí ó bá balẹ̀ sí ogiri lẹ́yìn tí ó ti bù ènìyàn jẹ. Ìfúnfún kan ṣoṣo lè dáàbò bo ìdílé fún oṣù púpọ̀. Tí wọ́n bá dé àdúgbò yín, ẹ gba wọ́n láàyè kí wọ́n ṣe iṣẹ́ wọn. Lẹ́yìn tí wọ́n bá ti fún un, ẹ má ṣe fi àmọ̀ tàbí pẹ́ǹtì bò ogiri náà mọ́, nítorí èyí yóò mú oògùn náà kúrò.

Ẹ Dáàbò Bo Àwọn Tí Ewu Wọn Pọ̀ Jù Lọ

Àwọn ọmọdé tí kò tíì pé ọdún márùn-ún àti àwọn aboyún ni ewu wọn pọ̀ jù lọ láti ní ìbà líle tí ó lè pa wọ́n. Àwọn méjèèjì wọ̀nyí ni kí a fi àwọ̀n fún ní àkọ́kọ́. Àwọn aboyún gbọ́dọ̀ máa lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn fún ìtọ́jú ìloyún (antenatal care), níbi tí wọ́n ti máa ń fún wọn ní oògùn ìdènà ìbà (IPTp pẹ̀lú sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine) gẹ́gẹ́ bí apá kan ìtọ́jú ìgbà oyún ní àwọn àgbègbè tí ìbà ti wọ́pọ̀. Àwọn ọmọdé náà tún lè yẹ fún oògùn ìdènà ìbà àkókò (seasonal malaria chemoprevention — SMC) ní àwọn àgbègbè kan — ẹ lọ béèrè lọ́wọ́ ilé ìwòsàn àdúgbò yín.

Tí Ẹnikẹ́ni Bá Ní Ìbà, Ẹ Yára Lọ Gba Ìtọ́jú

Kódà tí ẹ bá ṣe ohun gbogbo dáadáa, ènìyàn lè ṣì kó ìbà. Tí ẹnikẹ́ni nínú ìdílé — ní pàtàkì jùlọ ọmọdé tàbí aboyún — bá bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ní ìbà, orí fífó, ara mímì, tàbí ara ríro ní àkókò òjò, ẹ yára lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn. Ó dára jù lọ tí ẹ bá lè lọ láàárín wákàtí mẹ́rìnlélógún lẹ́yìn tí àmì àkọ́kọ́ bá farahàn.

Ẹ jẹ́ kí wọ́n ṣe ìdánwò ẹ̀jẹ̀ kí wọ́n tó fún yín ní oògùn. Ìdánwò bí RDT tàbí ìwòye ẹ̀jẹ̀ lábẹ́ microscope ni ọ̀nà tí ó tọ́ láti mọ̀ bóyá ìbà ni lóòótọ́. Ẹ má ṣe ra oògùn ìbà ní ọjà tàbí kéméèsì láìsí ìdánwò. Èyí ní ìdí méjì: tí kì bá ṣe ìbà, ẹ ti ná owó lásán, àrùn gidi tí ó sì ń ṣe yín kò tíì gba ìtọ́jú. Tí ẹ sì bá ń mu oògùn ìbà léèkọ̀ọ̀kan láìsí ìdí tó tọ́, oògùn náà lè dáwọ́ ṣíṣiṣẹ́ dúró lọ́jọ́ iwájú — èyí ni ohun tí wọ́n ń pè ní àtakò oògùn (drug resistance), ó sì jẹ́ ìṣòro tí yóò kan gbogbo àdúgbò.

Ìtọ́jú tí ó bá dé ní àkókò sábà máa ń ṣiṣẹ́ dáadáa, ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ ènìyàn sì máa ń rí àlááfíà padà láàárín ọjọ́ díẹ̀.

Bí Àwọn Ìdílé Ṣe Lè Dín Ewu Ibà Kù Ní Ìgbà Òjò

Ìgbà òjò ni àkókò tí ẹ̀fọn tí ń kó ibà máa ń pọ̀ jù lọ, nítorí omi tí ó dúró sí ibi kan-un-kan máa ń fún wọn ní ibi ìbísí. Àwọn ọ̀nà wọ̀nyí lè ṣe ìrànlọ́wọ́ fún ìdílé láti dáàbò bo ara wọn:

Lílo Àwọ̀n Ìbora Ẹ̀fọn (Mosquito Nets)

Àwọ̀n ìbora ẹ̀fọn tí a ti fi oògùn ṣe (insecticide-treated nets — ITNs) jẹ́ ọ̀kan lára àwọn ọ̀nà tí ó múnadóko jù lọ. Gbogbo ènìyàn nínú ilé, pàápàá àwọn ọmọdé àti àwọn aboyún, gbọ́dọ̀ sùn sábẹ́ àwọ̀n yìí ní gbogbo alẹ́. Ó ṣe pàtàkì láti rí i pé àwọ̀n náà kò fọ́, àti pé a fi ìsàlẹ̀ rẹ̀ sábẹ́ àgà tàbí búsọ̀ dáadáa.

Mímú Àyíká Ilé Mọ́

Omi tí ó dúró sí ojú ilẹ̀ — bíi nínú agolo, ìgò, tayà àtijọ́, ọ̀pọ̀n àdìyẹ, tàbí ibi tí omi bá kó sí — ni ẹ̀fọn fi ń bí ọmọ. Àwọn ìdílé gbọ́dọ̀:

Dà omi tí ó dúró sójú kan nù ní gbogbo ọjọ́ mélòó kan.
Bo àwọn ohun èlò tí ń kó omi dáadáa.
Gbin ilẹ̀ tí omi bá máa ń dúró sí, tàbí kí wọ́n wá ọ̀nà tí omi yóò gbà ṣàn.
Sọ àyíká ilé di mímọ́ — kí koríko má gun, kí ìdọ̀tí má pọ̀.
Fífi Oògùn Ẹ̀fọn Sára

Oògùn tí a ń fi sára tàbí tí a ń fi sí aṣọ (repellents) lè dáàbò bo ènìyàn lọ́wọ́ jíjẹ ẹ̀fọn, pàápàá ní ìrọ̀lẹ́ àti ní òwúrọ̀ kùtùkùtù, nígbà tí ẹ̀fọn Anopheles máa ń ṣiṣẹ́ jù lọ.

Títì Fèrèsé àti Ẹnu Ọ̀nà

Fífi àwọ̀n ẹ̀fọn (window and door screens) sí fèrèsé àti ẹnu ọ̀nà ilé máa ń dín bí ẹ̀fọn ṣe ń wọ inú ilé kù. Tí àwọ̀n yìí bá fọ́, ó yẹ kí a túnṣe wọ́n láìpẹ́.

Fífọn Oògùn Pa Ẹ̀fọn (Indoor Residual Spraying)

Tí ìjọba tàbí àjọ ìlera bá ń pèsè ètò fífọn oògùn sínú ilé, ó ṣe pàtàkì kí àwọn ìdílé gba ètò yìí. Oògùn yìí máa ń pa ẹ̀fọn tí ó bá bá ògiri ilé.

Wíwọ Aṣọ Tí Ó Bo Ara

Ní ìrọ̀lẹ́ àti ní àárọ̀ kùtùkùtù, wíwọ aṣọ àwọ̀lẹ̀kẹ̀ tí ó bo apá àti ẹsẹ̀ lè dín bí ẹ̀fọn ṣe ń jẹ ènìyàn kù.

Ìtọ́jú Kíákíá Nígbà Tí Ibà Bá Dé

Tí ẹnikẹ́ni nínú ilé, pàápàá ọmọdé, bá ní ibà (ara gbígbóná, orí dídun, ìgbagbogbo), ó ṣe pàtàkì láti lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn láìpẹ́ fún ìdánwò ẹ̀jẹ̀ (malaria test). Má ṣe bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí mu oògùn ibà láì mọ̀ dájúdájú pé ibà ni — ìdánwò kíákíá (Rapid Diagnostic Test) tàbí ìdánwò microscope ni ọ̀nà tí ó tọ́. Èyí máa ń mú kí oògùn ibà ṣiṣẹ́ dáadáa fún gbogbo ènìyàn, kí ó sì dín ìṣòro àjẹsára oògùn (drug resistance) kù.

Àkópọ̀ ní pé: dídáàbò bo ìdílé lọ́wọ́ ibà ní ìgbà òjò kò nílò owó púpọ̀ — ohun pàtàkì ni ìmọ̀, ìṣọ́ra, àti lílo àwọn ọ̀nà ìdáàbòbò tí ó wà ní àdúgbò. Bí ìdílé bá ṣe múra sílẹ̀ dáadáa, bẹ́ẹ̀ ni ewu ibà yóò dín kù.

Bí Àwọn Ìdílé Ṣe Lè Dín Ewu Ibà Kù Ní Ìgbà Òjò

Ìgbà òjò jẹ́ àkókò tí ibà máa ń gbilẹ̀ jù lọ, nítorí pé omi tí ó dúró sójú kan máa ń pèsè ibi tí ẹ̀fọn Anopheles fi ń bímọ. Àwọn ọ̀nà pàtàkì tí àwọn ìdílé lè gbà láti dáàbò bo ara wọn ni àwọn wọ̀nyí:

Sísùn Sábẹ́ Àwọ̀n Ẹ̀fọn Tí A Ti Fi Oògùn Ṣe

Àwọ̀n ẹ̀fọn tí a ti rì sínú oògùn (insecticide-treated nets) jẹ́ ọ̀kan lára àwọn ọ̀nà tí ó múnadóko jù lọ láti dáàbò bo ènìyàn lọ́wọ́ ibà. Gbogbo ènìyàn nínú ilé — pàápàá àwọn aboyún àti ọmọdé — gbọ́dọ̀ sùn lábẹ́ àwọ̀n yìí ní alẹ́ kọ̀ọ̀kan. Ó ṣe pàtàkì láti:

Rí i pé àwọ̀n náà kò fọ́, tí ihò kò sì sí lára rẹ̀.
Fi ìsàlẹ̀ àwọ̀n náà sábẹ́ búsọ̀ tàbí àgà dáadáa kí ẹ̀fọn má bàa wọlé.
Ní àwọn ibì kan, ìjọba máa ń pín àwọ̀n yìí lọ́fẹ̀ẹ́ — ó yẹ kí ìdílé lò ànfààní yìí.
Pípa Ibi Ìbísí Ẹ̀fọn Rẹ́

Ẹ̀fọn kò nílò omi púpọ̀ láti bímọ — kòkòrò omi kékeré nínú agolo, tayà àtijọ́, ìgò, ọ̀pọ̀n ẹran, tàbí ibi tí omi bá dúró fún ọjọ́ díẹ̀ lè tó. Àwọn ìdílé gbọ́dọ̀:

Dà omi tí ó dúró sójú kan nù lọ́sọ̀ọ̀sẹ̀, ó kéré tán lẹ́ẹ̀kan ní ọjọ́ mélòó kan.
Yí àwọn ohun èlò tí ń kó omi padà sísàlẹ̀ tàbí kí wọ́n bo wọ́n.
Gbìn ilẹ̀ tí omi máa ń dúró sí, kí omi lè ṣàn lọ.
Ṣe ìmọ́tótó àyíká ilé — kí igbo àti koríko gbígùn má di ibi ìsinmi fún ẹ̀fọn.
Fífi Oògùn Ẹ̀fọn Sára àti Sí Aṣọ

Lílo oògùn ìdẹ́na ẹ̀fọn (repellents) lè dín jíjẹ ẹ̀fọn kù, pàápàá ní àwọn wákàtí tí ẹ̀fọn Anopheles máa ń ṣiṣẹ́ jù lọ — ìyẹn ìrọ̀lẹ́ àti àárọ̀ kùtùkùtù. Ní ibi tí oògùn olówó kò bá sí, àwọn ewé kan bíi ewé dongoyaro (neem) lè wúlò díẹ̀, bí ó tilẹ̀ jẹ́ pé agbára rẹ̀ kò tó ti oògùn tí wọ́n ṣe ní ilé iṣẹ́.

Wíwọ Aṣọ Tí Ó Bo Ara

Ní ìrọ̀lẹ́ àti ní kùtùkùtù òwúrọ̀, wíwọ aṣọ àwọ̀lẹ̀kẹ̀ tí ó bo apá àti ẹsẹ̀ máa ń dín ààyè tí ẹ̀fọn ní láti jẹ ènìyàn kù. Aṣọ àwọ̀ fúnfún máa ń fà ẹ̀fọn mọ́ra ju aṣọ dúdú lọ — nítorí náà, aṣọ àwọ̀ dúdú tàbí aṣọ tí kò lẹ́wà fún ẹ̀fọn lè wúlò.

Fífi Àwọ̀n Ẹ̀fọn Sí Fèrèsé àti Ẹnu Ọ̀nà

Títì àwọ̀n (wire gauze/mesh screens) sí fèrèsé àti ẹnu ọ̀nà máa ń dí ẹ̀fọn lọ́wọ́ láti wọ inú ilé. Tí àwọ̀n yìí bá fọ́, ó yẹ kí a yára túnṣe wọ́n.

Gbígba Ètò Fífọn Oògùn Sínú Ilé (Indoor Residual Spraying)

Tí àjọ ìlera tàbí ìjọba bá ń pèsè ètò fífọn oògùn sí inú ilé àti sí ògiri, ó ṣe pàtàkì kí àwọn ìdílé gba ètò yìí. Oògùn tí a fọ́n sí ògiri máa ń pa ẹ̀fọn tí ó bá balẹ̀ sí ibẹ̀.

Ìtọ́jú Tí Ó Yára Nígbà Tí Àmì Ibà Bá Hàn

Tí ẹnikẹ́ni nínú ilé — pàápàá ọmọdé àti aboyún — bá ní ara gbígbóná, orí dídun, ara lílọ, tàbí ìgbagbogbo, ó ṣe pàtàkì láti lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn láìfi àkókò ṣòfò fún ìdánwò ẹ̀jẹ̀. Kò tọ́ láti bẹ̀rẹ̀ oògùn ibà láìṣe ìdánwò rí (RDT tàbí microscopy), nítorí:

Kì í ṣe gbogbo ibà ni ibà ẹ̀jẹ̀ (malaria).
Jíjẹ oògùn ibà láìṣe ìdánwò lè mú kí oògùn náà padà di aláìlágbára fún àwùjọ lápapọ̀ (drug resistance).
Ìdánwò kíákíá (RDT) kò ní owó púpọ̀, ó sì sábà wà ní ilé ìwòsàn àdúgbò.

Ní àkópọ̀: dídáàbò bo ìdílé lọ́wọ́ ibà ní ìgbà òjò kò nílò owó púpọ̀ — àwọn ìgbésẹ̀ bíi sísùn lábẹ́ àwọ̀n, mímú àyíká mọ́, àti wíwá ìtọ́jú kíákíá ni pàtàkì jù lọ. Ohun tí ó ṣe pàtàkì jù ni pé kí ìdílé ṣe àwọn nǹkan wọ̀nyí ní ìgbà gbogbo, kì í ṣe nígbà kan náà péré.

Ní ìgbà òjò, àwọn ìdílé lè dín ewu ibà kù nípa:

Sísùn lábẹ́ àwọ̀n ẹ̀fọn tí a fi oògùn sí ní gbogbo alẹ́.
Dída omi tó dúró sínú táyà, garawa àti àwo odòdó nù déédéé.
Bíbo àwọn ohun tí a fi ń tọ́jú omi dáadáa.
Ṣíṣe àtúnṣe sí àwọ̀n fèrèsé àti ilẹ̀kùn, kí ẹ̀fọn má bàa wọlé.
Wíwọ aṣọ ọwọ́ gígùn àti ṣòkòtò gígùn nígbà tí ẹ̀fọn pọ̀.
Títẹ̀lé ètò fífún oògùn inú ilé tí àwọn aláṣẹ ìlera fọwọ́ sí.

Bí ibà, òtútù tàbí orí fífọ́ bá bẹ̀rẹ̀, lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn fún àyẹ̀wò ibà kí o tó lo oògùn.

Ní ìgbà òjò, àwọn ìdílé lè:

Sùn lábẹ́ àwọ̀n ibùsùn tí a fi oògùn pa ẹ̀fọn sí ní gbogbo alẹ́.
Tú omi tó dúró sínú táyà, garawa, agolo àti ikòkò nù déédéé.
Bo àwọn ohun tí a fi ń pa omi mọ́.
Ṣíṣe àtúnṣe sí àwọ̀n fèrèsé àti ilẹ̀kùn.
Wọ aṣọ tó bo ọwọ́ àti ẹsẹ̀, kí wọ́n sì lo oògùn lépa ẹ̀fọn gẹ́gẹ́ bí ìtọ́sọ́nà rẹ̀.

Bí ara gbígbóná, òtútù tàbí orí fífọ́ bá bẹ̀rẹ̀, lọ ṣe àyẹ̀wò malaria kí o tó lo oògùn.

Ndị ezinụlọ nwere ike belata ohere ịrịa ọrịa ịba n’oge udu mmiri site n’igbochi anwụnta ịta mmadụ na ibelata ebe ha na-amụba.

Ka onye ọ bụla hie ụra n’ime ụgbụ anwụnta e tinyere ọgwụ kwa abalị, ọkachasị ụmụaka na ụmụ nwaanyị dị ime.
Na-enyocha ụgbụ ahụ mgbe niile, mechie oghere dị na ya ma saa ya dịka ntụziaka dị n’akpa ya si dị.
Tinye ụgbụ n’ọnụ ụzọ, windo na oghere ikuku. Dozie nke ọ bụla mebiri emebi.
Tee ọgwụ a kwadoro maka ịchụ anwụnta n’akpụkpọ ahụ pụtara ìhè, ma soro ntụziaka dị n’akpa ọgwụ ahụ.
Yiri uwe ogologo aka, ogologo ọkpa na sọks, ọkachasị site n’oge mgbede ruo n’isi ụtụtụ.
Kpofu, kpuchie ma ọ bụ wepụ ihe ndị nwere ike ịchịkọta mmiri, dịka bọket, taya ochie, ite ifuru na mkpọ.
Kpuchie ihe niile e ji echekwa mmiri nke ọma.
Mepee gọta na ọwa mmiri mechiri emechi. Wepụ ahịhịa na mkpofu ndị nwere ike ime ka mmiri guzoro otu ebe.
Soro ndị ọrụ ahụike ọha rụkọọ ọrụ ma ọ bụrụ na ha akwado ịfesa ọgwụ anwụnta n’ime ụlọ. Soro ntụziaka nchekwa ha.
Jiri ọgwụ mgbochi ọrịa ịba naanị mgbe dọkịta, onye ọrụ ahụike ma ọ bụ mmemme ahụike gọọmentị kwadoro ya.
Ọ bụrụ na onye ọ bụla enwee ahụ ọkụ, oyi, isi ọwụwa ma ọ bụ adịghị ike pụrụ iche, kpọga ya ebe ahụike ngwa ngwa maka nyocha na ọgwụgwọ kwesịrị ekwesị.

Kedu Ka Ndị Ezinụlọ Ga-esi Belata Ohere Ịrịa Ịba N'oge Udu Mmiri

Oge udu mmiri bụ oge anwụnta Anopheles — ụdị anwụnta na-ebunye ọrịa ịba — na-amụba karịsịa. Mmiri na-akwụsị n'otu ebe mgbe mmiri ozuzo zochara bụ ebe anwụnta na-aghọ ụmụ ya. Anwụnta a na-ata mmadụ karịsịa n'oge abalị, site n'oge anyasị ruo ụtụtụ. Mana ezi ozi dị: ọtụtụ ihe ndị ezinụlọ nwere ike ime iji chekwaa onwe ha adịghị efu ego.

Wepụ Mmiri Ọbụla Kwụsịrị N'otu Ebe

Ọ bụladị obere mmiri, dịka nke jupụtara n'okpuru mkpuchi karama, ezuola ka anwụnta mụọ ụmụ ya. Gaa gburugburu ogige gị, nyochaa ihe niile mmiri nwere ike ịbakọta — dịka taya ochie, bọketi, karama, ife ochie, olulu mmiri gbachiri agbacha. Wụsa mmiri ahụ, tụgharịa ihe ndị ahụ isi ala, ma ọ bụ kpuchie ha nke ọma. Ọ bụrụ na ị na-echekwa mmiri maka iji eme ihe n'ụlọ, jide n'aka na ị kpụchiri ya oge niile. Hichapụ olulu mmiri gbara gburugburu ụlọ gị ka mmiri ozuzo wee na-asọpụ nke ọma kama ịkwụsị n'otu ebe.

Hụ Na Onye Ọbụla Na-ehi Ụra N'ime Nẹtị A Gbasara Ọgwụ (ITN)

Nẹtị a gbasara ọgwụ anwụnta (insecticide-treated net) bụ otu n'ime ụzọ kachasị arụ ọrụ nke ọma iji chekwaa mmadụ n'ọrịa ịba. Ọ bụghị naanị mgbe anwụnta bara ụba ka a ga-eji ya — onye ọbụla nọ n'ezinụlọ kwesịrị ihi ụra n'ime nẹtị kwa abalị niile. Otu ata anwụnta nwere ike ibunye ọrịa ịba.

Debechie akụkụ nẹtị ahụ n'okpuru akwa ma ọ bụ ute, na-enyochakwa ya oge niile. Ọ bụrụ na ọ dọkara, dụọ ya ma ọ bụ gbanwee ya. Ọtụtụ mmemme ahụike gọọmentị na-ekesa nẹtị ndị a n'efu — gaa jụọ n'ụlọ ahụike dị gị nso ma ọ bụ onyeisi ahụike obodo gị maka mgbe ọzọ ha ga-ekesa ya.

Mechie Windo na Ụzọ Tupu Anyasị Eruo

Ebe ọ bụ na anwụnta Anopheles na-arụsi ọrụ ike karịsịa site n'anyasị ruo chi ọbọ, ọ dị mkpa imechie windo na ụzọ tupu ọchịchịrị abịa. Ọ bụrụ na ị nwere ike itinye nẹtị (mesh screen) na windo gị, nke a ga-enyere gị aka nke ọma. Ọ bụrụ na i nweghị nẹtị windo, ị nwere ike iji akwa ma ọ bụ ọgbụgba kpuchie windo na ọnụ ụzọ — nke a ga-ebelata ọnụọgụ anwụnta ga-abata n'ụlọ.

Ị nwekwara ike iji kọịlụ anwụnta (mosquito coil) ma ọ bụ ihe na-agbanye n'ọkụ eletrik na-achụsa anwụnta (vaporiser) n'ime ụlọ, mana nke a ekwesịghị ịnọchi anya nẹtị — jiri ha abụọ ọnụ.

Dọọ Gburugburu Ụlọ Gị

Gbuchaa ahịhịa toro ogologo gburugburu ụlọ gị, n'ihi na anwụnta na-ezo onwe ha n'ahịhịa ogologo n'oge ehihie. Ọ bụrụ na ọ dị ebe dị ala n'ogige gị nke mmiri na-akọbata mgbe mmiri ozuzo zochara, gbalịa jiri aja ma ọ bụ aja kpuchie ya. Ọ bụrụ na olulu mmiri mepere emepe dị nso n'ụlọ gị, kparịta ụka na ndị agbata obi gị ka unu jikọọ aka hichapụ ya — mgbochi ọrịa ịba na-arụ ọrụ nke ọma karịsịa mgbe obodo niile jikọrọ aka ọnụ.

Jiri Ọgwụ Mgbochi Anwụnta Tee Ahụ Gị (Repellent)

N'oge anyasị, mgbe ndị mmadụ ka nọ n'èzí, ị nwere ike ite ọgwụ mgbochi anwụnta n'akụkụ ahụ gị nke uwe na-ekpuchighị. Ndị nwere DEET ma ọ bụ picaridin na-arụ ọrụ nke ọma. Ọ bụrụ na ndị a dị ọnụ ma ọ bụ na ị naghị ahụ ha, ụfọdụ ndị mmadụ na-eji mmanụ ogwu (neem oil) ma ọ bụ ahịhịa lemongrass, mana kwesịrị ịmara na ha anaghị anọ ogologo oge n'ahụ, ihe akaebe sayensị na-egosi na ha na-arụ ọrụ adịghịkwa ike dịka nke DEET.

Ọ Bụrụ Na Gọọmentị Abịa Ifesa Ọgwụ N'ụlọ, Kwere Ha

Oge ụfọdụ, ndị ọrụ ahụike gọọmentị na-abịa ụlọ ụlọ ịgwa ọgwụ n'ime mgbidi ụlọ — nke a ka a na-akpọ Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS). Ọgwụ a na-egbu anwụnta nke dara n'elu mgbidi mgbe ọ tachara mmadụ. Otu mgbe ịfesa nwere ike ichekwaa ezinụlọ gị ọnwa ọtụtụ. Ọ bụrụ na ha abịa n'obodo gị, kwere ha ka ha rụọ ọrụ ha. Mgbe ha fesachara, etela mgbidi ahụ ite ma ọ bụ iji ite kpuchie ya, n'ihi na nke ahụ ga-ewepụ ọgwụ ahụ.

Chekwaa Ụmụaka na Ndị Dị Ime Karịsịa

Ụmụaka na-erubeghị afọ ise na ndị nwanyị dị ime nọ n'ihe ize ndụ kachasị ukwuu site n'ọrịa ịba sịrị ike nke nwere ike igbu ha. Ndị abụọ a kwesịrị inweta nẹtị na mbụ. Ndị nwanyị dị ime kwesịrị ịna-aga ụlọ ahụike maka nlekọta ime (antenatal care), ebe a na-enye ha ọgwụ mgbochi ịba (IPTp nke a na-eji sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine eme) dịka akụkụ nlekọta ime ha n'obodo ndị ọrịa ịba bara ụba. Ụmụaka nwekwara ike iru eru maka ọgwụ mgbochi ịba oge (seasonal malaria chemoprevention — SMC) n'ụfọdụ mpaghara — gaa jụọ n'ụlọ ahụike dị gị nso.

Ọ Bụrụ Na Onye Ọbụla Enwe Ahụ Ọkụ, Gbaga Ụlọ Ahụike Ọsịịsọ

Ọ bụladị ma ị mere ihe niile nke ọma, mmadụ nwere ike ịrịa ọrịa ịba. Ọ bụrụ na onye ọbụla nọ n'ezinụlọ — ọkachasị ụmụaka ma ọ bụ ndị nwanyị dị ime — amalite inwe ahụ ọkụ, isi ụfụ, ahụ ama jijiji, ma ọ bụ ahụ mgbu n'oge udu mmiri, gbara ọsọ gaa ụlọ ahụike. Ọ kacha mma ma ị nwere ike ịga n'ime awa iri abụọ na anọ mgbe ihe ịrịba ama mbụ pụtara ìhè.

Kwere ka ha nyochaa ọbara gị tupu ha enye gị ọgwụ. Nyocha dịka RDT ma ọ bụ ịlele ọbara n'okpuru microscope bụ ụzọ ziri ezi iji mara ma ọ bụ ọrịa ịba n'ezie. Azụla ọgwụ ịba n'ahịa ma ọ bụ na kemist na-enweghị nyocha. Nke a nwere nsogbu abụọ: ọ bụrụ na ọ bụghị ọrịa ịba, ị tụfuola ego gị, ọrịa ezigbo na-arịa gị akwụsịbeghị. Ọ bụrụkwa na ị na-aṅụ ọgwụ ịba mgbe niile na-enweghị ihe kpatara ya, ọgwụ ahụ nwere ike ịkwụsị ịrụ ọrụ n'ọdịnihu — nke a ka a na-akpọ nguzogide ọgwụ (drug resistance), ọ bụkwa nsogbu ga-emetụta obodo niile.

Ọgwụ e nyere n'oge kwesịrị ekwesị na-arụsi ọrụ ike nke ọma, ọtụtụ ndị mmadụ na-adịkwa mma n'ime ụbọchị ole na ole.

Ụzọ Ndị Ezinụlọ Ga-esi Belata Ohere Ịrịa Ọrịa Ịba N'oge Udu Mmiri

Oge udu mmiri bụ oge anwụnta na-amụba karịsịa, nke mere na ọrịa ịba na-abawanye n'oge a. Ndị a bụ ụzọ ndị ezinụlọ nwere ike isi chekwaa onwe ha:

Iji Nết (Net) Anwụnta

Nết a gbachiri agbachi bụ ụzọ kachasị arụ ọrụ iji gbochie ịba. Onye ọ bụla n'ime ezinụlọ — karịsịa ụmụaka na ndị dị ime — kwesịrị ịhụ na ha na-ehi ụra n'ime nết kwa abalị. Ọ dị mkpa ka e sechaa nết ahụ nke ọma n'elu akwa. Gọọmenti na-enye nết n'efu n'ọtụtụ ebe — jụọ n'ụlọ ọgwụ ma ọ bụ n'ebe a na-ahụ maka ahụike nke obodo gị.

Ikpochapụ Ebe Mmiri Na-anọ

Anwụnta na-amụ ụmụ ha n'ime mmiri nọ n'otu ebe. Ya mere, hụ na:

Mmiri agaghị anọ n'ime efere, tayịa ochie, ma ọ bụ ihe ọ bụla gbara oghere n'ezi.
Ọkpọ mmiri na tanki mmiri ga-ekpuchi nke ọma.
Ọ bụrụ na e nwere ebe mmiri na-akwụsị n'akụkụ ụlọ, a ga-ekpochapụ ya ma ọ bụ tụọ aja n'ebe ahụ.

Ichekwa Ụlọ

Mechi windo na ụzọ tupu chi ejie ma ọ bụ tinye nết na windo ụlọ, n'ihi na anwụnta na-apụta karịsịa n'uhuruchi ruo n'ụtụtụ.
Ọ bụrụ na i nwere ike, jiri spray igbu anwụnta (insecticide) fesa n'ime ụlọ tupu oge ihie ụra. Ngwungwu igbu anwụnta a na-akpọ coil nwekwara ike inyere aka.

Iyiwe Uwe Gbachiri Agbachi

N'oge uhuruchi, yiwe uwe na-ekpuchi ahụ — uwe aka ogologo, uwe ụkwụ ogologo — iji belata ebe anwụnta ga-ata.

Ikpochapụ Ahịhịa Toro Eto

Ahịhịa toro eto n'akụkụ ụlọ na-enye anwụnta ebe ha ga-ezo. Kpachaa ahịhịa gburugburu ụlọ oge niile.

Ịgwa Ndị Ọgwụ Ozugbo

Ọ bụrụ na onye ọ bụla n'ezinụlọ — karịsịa nwa — amalite ịnwe ahụ ọkụ (fever), ejela ozi ozugbo gaa n'ụlọ ọgwụ ka e nwaa ọbara ya tupu ọṅụọ ọgwụ ọ bụla. Nke a dị oke mkpa n'ihi na ọ bụghị ahụ ọkụ niile bụ ịba, ọṅụọ ọgwụ ịba na-enweghị isi nwere ike imebi ahụ ma mee ka ọgwụ ịba ghara ịrụkwa ọrụ ọzọ n'ọdịnihu (drug resistance).

Iji kwuo ya n'ụzọ dị mfe: iji nết, ikpochapụ mmiri, ichekwa ụlọ, na ịga ụlọ ọgwụ ozugbo bụ ihe ndị kachasị mkpa. Ndị a abụghị ihe na-efu ego — ọtụtụ n'ime ha enweghị ego ọ na-efu, ma ha na-azọpụta ndụ.

Ụzọ Ndị Ezinụlọ Ga-esi Belata Ohere Ịrịa Ọrịa Ịba N'oge Udu Mmiri

Oge udu mmiri bụ oge anwụnta (mosquito) na-amụba karịsịa, nke na-eme ka ọrịa ịba na-agbasa ọsọọsọ. Nke a bụ ihe ndị ezinụlọ nwere ike ime:

Jiri Nets (Ụgbụ Anwụnta) Hie Ụra

Ụgbụ anwụnta e tinyere ọgwụ (insecticide-treated nets — ITNs) bụ otu n'ime ụzọ kachasị arụ ọrụ nke iji gbochie ọrịa ịba. Onye ọ bụla n'ezinụlọ — karịsịa ụmụaka na ndị dị ime — kwesịrị ihi ụra n'ime ụgbụ anwụnta kwa abalị. Gọọmentị na-ekenye ụgbụ ndị a n'efu n'ọtụtụ ebe — jụọ n'ụlọ ọgwụ maọbụ n'ebe a na-ahụ maka ahụike obodo gị.

Kwụsị Mmiri Ebe Ọ Na-anọ Chịm Chịm

Anwụnta na-etinye àkwá ha n'ime mmiri nke na-anọ n'otu ebe. Wụpụ mmiri nọ n'ime ihe ndị dị ka:

taya ochie
ite na ụdọ mmiri
efere anụmanụ
ihe ọ bụla nwere ike ijide mmiri ozuzo

Kpachara anya hụ na gọta (gutter) gị dị mma ka mmiri ozuzo wee na-asọpụ nke ọma.

Mechie Ụzọ Ụlọ Gị Nke Ọma

Jiri net maọbụ ihe mgbochi mechie windo na ụzọ ụlọ gị ka anwụnta ghara ịbata. Ọ bụrụ na i nweghị net windo, gbalịa imechie windo na ụzọ gị tupu chi ejie — n'ihi na anwụnta ịba (Anopheles) na-ata mmadụ karịsịa n'oge abalị, site n'oge chi na-ejie ruo oge chi na-abọ.

Yi Uwe Na-ekpuchi Ahụ N'oge Anyasị

N'oge uhuruchi, yi uwe aka ogologo na uwe ukwu ogologo iji belata ebe anwụnta nwere ike ịta gị.

Jiri Ọgwụ A Na-etinye N'ahụ (Repellents)

Ọgwụ a na-etinye n'ahụ iji chụsa anwụnta, dịka ndị nwere DEET maọbụ icaridin, nwere ike inyere aka. N'obodo ụfọdụ, ndị mmadụ na-eji mmanụ osisi dịka neem (dogoyaro) — nke a pụrụ inyere aka ụfọdụ, ọ bụ ezie na ọ gaghị arụ ọrụ dịka ọgwụ ndị e mere n'ụlọ ọrụ.

Jiri Coil maọbụ Spray N'ime Ụlọ

Mosquito coils na insecticide sprays nwere ike ibelata ọnụọgụgụ anwụnta n'ime ụlọ. Ma kpachara anya ka ụmụaka na ndị dị ime ghara iku ụda ya n'imi ha n'ụzọ na-eju afọ — jụọ ndị ọgwụ banyere ụdị kachasị enwe nchekwa.

Gaa Ụlọ Ọgwụ Ngwa Ngwa Mgbe Ahụ Ọkụ Malitere

Ọ bụrụ na onye ọ bụla n'ezinụlọ gị amalite ịnwe ahụ ọkụ, isi ọwụwa, maọbụ oyi na-ama ya n'oge udu mmiri — agala ụlọ ọgwụ ozugbo ka e nwee ike ịnyocha ọbara ya tupu ọ malite ịṅụ ọgwụ. Ịṅụ ọgwụ ịba na-enweghị nyocha (test) zuru oke nwere ike ịkpata nsogbu karịa — gụnyere ime ka ọgwụ ịba ghara ịrụkwa ọrụ n'ọdịnihu (drug resistance). Otu test dị ka RDT (Rapid Diagnostic Test) anaghị ego ka ukwuu ma ọ na-eme ka a mara n'ezie ma ọ bụ ịba ka ọ bụghị.

A fever that keeps returning can have several causes, and malaria symptoms can overlap with other illnesses. Repeated self-treatment without testing may:

delay diagnosis of another condition;
expose the person to unnecessary or inappropriate medicines;
make it harder to understand why the fever is recurring.

The person should go to a clinic or health facility for appropriate testing and evaluation, especially if the fever has persisted or keeps coming back.

They should seek urgent medical care if there are warning signs such as difficulty breathing, severe weakness, confusion, repeated vomiting, seizures, inability to drink, loss of consciousness, or rapidly worsening symptoms.

The key point is: recurrent fever after repeated unconfirmed malaria treatment needs reassessment, not another automatic course of malaria medicine.

Confirm whether malaria parasites are present.
Ensure the person receives the correct antimalarial medicine.
Avoid unnecessary antimalarial treatment when another illness is responsible.
Reduce avoidable side effects and medicine costs.
Prevent delays in diagnosing other potentially serious causes of fever.
Limit unnecessary use of antimalarial medicines, which contributes to drug resistance.
Identify the parasite species and parasite level where laboratory microscopy is available, helping clinicians assess treatment needs.
Improve public-health records and detection of changes in malaria transmission.

Why Getting Tested Before Malaria Treatment Matters

Starting malaria treatment without a confirmed diagnosis might seem harmless — especially in areas where malaria is common and the symptoms feel familiar. But skipping the test creates real problems, both for the individual and for the wider community.

The Symptoms Are Not Unique to Malaria

Fever, headache, chills, body aches, fatigue, nausea — these are the hallmark signs people associate with malaria, but they also overlap almost entirely with dozens of other conditions. Typhoid fever, urinary tract infections, pneumonia, dengue, viral infections, and even early-stage meningitis can all present this way. Without a test, there is simply no reliable way to tell them apart based on symptoms alone, even for experienced clinicians. Treating for malaria when the real cause is something else means that actual illness goes undiagnosed and untreated, and it may worsen or become life-threatening while the person waits for antimalarials to "work."

Unnecessary Treatment Wastes Money

Antimalarial drugs are not free for most households. When someone buys and takes a course of artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) for a fever that turns out not to be malaria, that money is gone for nothing. In resource-constrained settings, this matters enormously — the same household may then lack the funds to pay for the correct diagnosis and treatment when they actually need it. Studies across sub-Saharan Africa have consistently shown that a significant proportion of fevers treated presumptively as malaria are actually caused by other infections.

Drug Resistance Is a Serious and Growing Threat

This is arguably the most important reason at a population level. Every time an antimalarial drug is taken unnecessarily, it creates selective pressure that favours parasites capable of surviving that drug. Artemisinin-based combination therapies are currently the frontline treatment for falciparum malaria globally. Resistance to artemisinin has already emerged in Southeast Asia and there are troubling early signals in parts of East Africa. If ACTs lose their effectiveness the way chloroquine and sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine did in previous decades, the consequences would be devastating — there is no equally effective replacement waiting in the pipeline. Indiscriminate use of antimalarials without confirmed diagnosis accelerates this process directly.

Testing Is Quick, Affordable, and Widely Available

Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) can deliver a result in roughly 15 to 20 minutes from a finger-prick blood sample. They require minimal training to administer and interpret, and they are distributed widely across health facilities and even at the community health worker level in many endemic countries. Microscopy, where available, provides even more detailed information, including parasite species and density. In many public health systems, both forms of testing are provided free of charge. The barrier to testing is almost always lower than people assume.

A Positive Test Leads to Better Treatment

When a test confirms malaria, the clinician knows exactly what they are treating. In some settings, microscopy can identify the specific Plasmodium species — falciparum, vivax, ovale, malariae — which matters because treatment protocols differ. Falciparum malaria, the most dangerous form, requires ACT. Vivax and ovale malaria require additional treatment with primaquine to clear dormant liver-stage parasites and prevent relapse. Without knowing the species, treatment may be incomplete.

A Negative Test Is Equally Valuable

A negative malaria test is not a dead end — it is critical diagnostic information. It tells the health worker to look for the actual cause of the fever rather than defaulting to antimalarials. This is where other serious conditions get caught early: typhoid, bacterial infections, respiratory illness, or other diseases that need their own specific treatment. A negative result may save someone's life by redirecting clinical attention to the real problem.

The Bottom Line

A confirmed diagnosis protects the individual by ensuring they receive the right treatment for the right illness. It protects the household by avoiding wasted expenditure on unnecessary drugs. And it protects the entire community — and future generations — by slowing the development of drug resistance that could render current treatments useless. The test takes minutes, often costs nothing, and the consequences of skipping it are far more expensive in every sense.

Getting tested before starting malaria treatment matters for several serious, practical reasons.

Accurate diagnosis drives effective treatment. Malaria symptoms — fever, chills, headache, body aches, fatigue — overlap heavily with dozens of other conditions: typhoid, urinary tract infections, viral infections, pneumonia, dengue, meningitis, and others. Without a confirmed test (either a Rapid Diagnostic Test or microscopy), you're essentially guessing. If the actual cause isn't malaria, antimalarial drugs won't fix the problem, and the real illness continues to progress — sometimes dangerously.

Unnecessary antimalarial use fuels drug resistance. This is a population-level threat, not just an individual one. Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) are currently the frontline treatment for falciparum malaria across sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia. Every course of ACTs taken by someone who doesn't actually have malaria creates selective pressure that helps resistant parasites survive and spread. Artemisinin resistance has already emerged in Southeast Asia and there are growing concerns about its spread to Africa. Protecting the effectiveness of ACTs is a public health priority.

It wastes money. In many settings where malaria is common, household resources are limited. Buying a full course of ACTs for a fever that turns out to be something else means spending money on the wrong treatment, then spending again on the correct one. A rapid diagnostic test is inexpensive — often free at public health facilities — and prevents this cycle of repeated, misdirected spending.

It can delay life-saving treatment for the actual condition. If someone has bacterial meningitis or severe typhoid and spends days treating presumed malaria, that delay can be fatal. Confirmed testing shortens the path to the right intervention.

It identifies the species of Plasmodium involved. Not all malaria is the same. P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, and P. knowlesi each have different clinical profiles and treatment requirements. P. vivax and P. ovale, for example, require additional treatment with primaquine to clear dormant liver-stage parasites and prevent relapse. Without testing, this distinction is invisible.

The WHO position on this is unambiguous. The World Health Organization recommends parasitological confirmation — by microscopy or RDT — for all suspected malaria cases before treatment is administered. The era of presumptive treatment based on fever alone has been formally moved away from precisely because of the harms outlined above.

The bottom line: a test takes minutes, costs little or nothing at many clinics, and it's the difference between treating the right disease and gambling with someone's health while simultaneously undermining the drugs the whole community depends on.

Getting tested before starting malaria treatment matters for several concrete reasons, and skipping that step carries real costs — both for the individual and for the wider community.

The core problem with treating without testing:

Malaria symptoms — fever, chills, headache, body aches, fatigue — overlap heavily with dozens of other conditions. Typhoid fever, urinary tract infections, pneumonia, dengue, viral infections, and even early-stage meningitis can all look like malaria at the bedside. Without a diagnostic test, you're essentially guessing, and guessing wrong has consequences.

What's actually at stake:

The wrong diagnosis means the wrong treatment. If someone has a bacterial infection like typhoid but gets treated for malaria instead, the real illness keeps progressing while the person assumes they're being treated. That delay can turn a manageable infection into a dangerous one. People die from treatable conditions because malaria was assumed and the actual problem was ignored.

Antimalarial drugs aren't harmless. Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs), chloroquine, and other antimalarials all have side effects — ranging from nausea and dizziness to more serious cardiac or neurological effects in some cases. Taking these drugs when you don't have malaria means accepting those risks for zero benefit.

Every unnecessary dose of an antimalarial contributes to drug resistance. This is a population-level threat, not just a personal one. Resistance to chloroquine already rendered it ineffective across much of sub-Saharan Africa decades ago. ACTs are currently the frontline treatment, and resistance to artemisinin has already emerged in Southeast Asia and been detected in parts of East Africa. If ACTs fail widely, there is no well-established replacement ready at scale. Overuse accelerates that timeline.

The economics actually favor testing:

There's a common assumption that testing is an added cost — just treat and move on. But the math doesn't support that. A rapid diagnostic test (RDT) is inexpensive (often under $1 in many settings, and frequently free through public health programs). A failed round of presumptive treatment, followed by a second visit, a second drug purchase, and possibly a hospitalization for the real underlying illness, costs far more in money, time, and lost productivity. Testing up front is cheaper than guessing wrong.

What the test actually tells you:

A malaria rapid diagnostic test or microscopy confirms whether Plasmodium parasites are present in the blood. It can also identify the species (falciparum vs. vivax, for instance), which matters because different species require different treatment approaches. P. vivax and P. ovale, for example, can form dormant liver stages that need specific treatment to prevent relapse — something you'd miss entirely without knowing which species you're dealing with.

The bottom line:

Presumptive treatment made more sense decades ago when diagnostics were unavailable in many settings. That's no longer the case. RDTs are widely distributed, require minimal training to use, and give results in 15–20 minutes. The World Health Organization has recommended parasitological confirmation before treatment since 2010. Skipping the test isn't a shortcut — it's a gamble with your health, your money, and the effectiveness of drugs that entire populations depend on.

Why E Dey Important Make Person Do Test Before E Begin Treat Malaria

Plenty people dey think say once fever catch dem, na malaria — especially for area wey malaria common well-well. So dem go just run go chemist, buy medicine, begin swallow. E fit look like say na common sense, but to dey treat malaria wey you never confirm fit cause serious wahala, both for di person wey sick and for di whole community.

Di Symptoms No Dey Show Say Na Only Malaria

Fever, headache, body dey shake, body dey pain, person dey weak, belle dey turn am — na dese signs people dey use know malaria. But di problem be say plenti other sickness dey give di same signs. Typhoid fit start like dat. Pneumonia fit start like dat. Urinary infection, dengue, ordinary viral infection, even meningitis wey dey dangerous well-well — all of dem fit look like malaria for di beginning.

No matter how much experience one person get, e no fit use eye alone tell wetin dey cause fever. Na only test fit confirm. So if person just begin take malaria medicine without test, and di real sickness na typhoid or bacterial infection, dat real sickness go still dey inside di body, e go dey get worse, and di malaria medicine no go touch am at all. By di time di person come realize say di medicine no dey work, di real sickness don already become serious — and sometimes e don too late.

E Dey Waste Money Wey Person No Get

Antimalarial drug no dey free for most people. If you go buy ACT (artemisinin-based combination therapy) for chemist, you go spend money. Now imagine say you spend dat money, you take di full dose, but na typhoid you get, no be malaria. Di money don waste. Di sickness never move. And now you still need to go hospital, do test, and buy di correct medicine on top. For family wey money tight, dis double spending fit mean say dem no go fit afford di right treatment when dem actually need am.

Research wey dem don do across sub-Saharan Africa don show say plenty-plenty fevers wey people dey treat as malaria no be malaria at all. Dat one mean say serious amount of money dey waste every year on medicine wey people no need.

E Dey Help Drug Resistance Grow — And Dis One Na Big Danger

Dis one na probably di most serious reason, and e no concern just one person — e concern everybody.

Every time wey person take antimalarial drug wey e no need, e dey give chance to di malaria parasite to learn how to survive dat drug. Na so drug resistance dey start. Di malaria parasite wey survive small-small exposure to di drug go born pikin wey strong pass, and before you know, di whole drug no go dey work again for dat area.

E don happen before. Chloroquine bin dey work well-well for malaria — until resistance spread, and e come dey useless for most of Africa. Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) follow di same road. Now, ACT na di main medicine wey dey work for falciparum malaria across di world. But resistance to artemisinin don already show face for Southeast Asia, and early signs don begin appear for parts of East Africa.

If ACT stop to dey work, na serious crisis. No other medicine dey wait for pipeline wey fit replace am. Every time wey person swallow ACT without confirmed malaria, e dey push us closer to dat crisis. Na everybody go suffer am — your pikin, your neighbour pikin, everybody.

Di Test No Hard, E No Take Time, and E Fit Dey Free

Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) na just small prick for finger. Dem go take small blood, put am for di test kit, and within 15 to 20 minutes, you go know if na malaria or no be malaria. E no need any special machine or specialist — even community health worker fit do am.

For places wey get microscope, dem fit even tell you which type of malaria parasite dey your blood and how plenty dem be. Dis information dey help di doctor give you di exact correct treatment.

For many government health centres, dis test dey free. So di idea say test hard to do or say e cost too much no dey correct for most places. Di barrier dey lower than wetin most people think.

If Test Say Na Malaria, Treatment Go Better

When test confirm say na malaria, di health worker know exactly wetin e dey treat. E fit even know which species of Plasmodium dey cause am — falciparum, vivax, ovale, or malariae — because treatment dey different for each one.

Falciparum malaria, wey be di most dangerous type, need ACT. But vivax and ovale need extra medicine — primaquine — to clear di parasite wey dey hide for liver. Without dat extra treatment, di malaria fit come back again and again. If you no do test, nobody go know which type you get, and di treatment fit no complete.

If Test Say No Be Malaria, Dat One Still Dey Very Useful

Negative result no mean say nothing dey wrong. E mean say di health worker suppose find di real cause of di fever — and dat one fit save your life. Because now, instead of just giving malaria medicine and sending you home, dem go begin look for wetin actually dey cause di problem. Na so dem dey catch typhoid early, na so dem dey catch bacterial infection, pneumonia, or other serious sickness wey need im own treatment.

Negative malaria test na important information, no be disappointment.

Make We Put Am Togeda

To do test before treatment dey protect you three different ways:

E dey protect di person wey sick, because e go make sure say na di correct medicine dem give am for di correct sickness. E dey protect di family pocket, because e go stop dem from wasting money on medicine wey dem no need. And e dey protect di whole community and even future generation, because e go slow down drug resistance wey fit make our best malaria medicine useless one day.

Di test take just minutes. E fit cost nothing. But di price of skipping am — for your health, your money, and for everybody around you — dat one dey very high.

E get plenti reason why person suppose do test first before e start to swallow medicine for malaria, and the reasons dey strong well well — both for the person wey sick and for everybody for the community.

The real problem with treating without test:

Malaria sign and symptom — like fever, cold dey catch you, headache, body dey pain you, tiredness — e dey look like plenti other sickness. Typhoid, urinary infection, pneumonia, dengue, even meningitis wey just dey start — all of dem fit look like malaria for body. If person no do test, na guess work e dey do, and if the guess wrong, wahala go follow.

Wetin fit happen if person no test:

If na another sickness like typhoid dey do person but e dey take malaria medicine, the real sickness go still dey grow for inside body while the person think say e don dey treat. That kind delay fit make small sickness turn big danger. People dey die from sickness wey dem for fit treat because dem just assume say na malaria, but the real problem no get attention.

Malaria medicine no be water. ACT, chloroquine, and the rest of dem get side effect — person fit dey feel like to vomit, head fit dey turn, and for some people e fit even affect heart or brain function. If you take all this medicine and you no even get malaria, you dey suffer for nothing.

Every time wey person swallow antimalarial wey e no need, e dey help make the medicine lose power for everybody. Dem call am drug resistance. Chloroquine don already fail for most of Africa because people overuse am. Now na ACT be the main medicine wey dey work, but resistance don already start to show for Southeast Asia and some part of East Africa. If ACT fail, no strong replacement dey ground wey ready. The more people dey take medicine wey dem no need, the faster this problem go reach us.

Testing dey even save money pass guessing:

Plenti people think say test na extra cost — make dem just buy medicine quick quick. But if you calculate am well, e no be so. Rapid diagnostic test (RDT) no cost much — sometimes e no reach one dollar, and for many government health centre dem dey do am free. But if person guess wrong, take wrong medicine, the sickness no go, e go need go back hospital again, buy another medicine, maybe even admit for ward — all that one go cost pass the small test wey e for don do from the beginning. Testing save money pass trial and error.

Wetin the test go show you:

Malaria rapid test or microscopy go confirm whether malaria parasite dey for the person blood or not. E fit even show which type of malaria — whether na Plasmodium falciparum or vivax or another type. This one important because different type need different treatment. For example, P. vivax and P. ovale fit hide for liver and come back later if person no treat am with the correct specific medicine. Without test, person no go even know which type dey do am.

The main point be this:

Long time ago, when test no dey available for many place, people no get choice — dem just dey treat based on how the sickness look. But that time don pass. RDT don dey everywhere now, the person wey dey do the test no need plenty training, and result dey come out within 15 to 20 minutes. WHO don talk since 2010 say make dem confirm malaria with test before treatment. To skip test no be shortcut — na gamble with your health, your money, and the power of medicine wey the whole community depend on.

Why E Dey Important To Test Before You Treat Malaria

E get plenti reason why person suppose do test first before e start take malaria medicine. Make I break am down:

Fever no mean say na malaria every time. Plenti sickness fit give person fever — typhoid, urinary infection, pneumonia, even common cold. If person just dey swallow malaria drug anyhow without test, e fit dey treat wetin no dey there, and the real sickness wey dey cause the fever go still dey grow for inside body. That one fit turn dangerous thing.

If you take malaria drug when you no get malaria, you dey waste money. ACT — the correct malaria medicine — no cheap. If you buy am when you no even need am, na money wey you throw away. Then you go still need spend again to find the real problem. Testing dey cheaper pass wrong treatment.

Wrong use of malaria drug dey spoil the medicine power for everybody. This one na the one wey plenti people no dey think about. When people dey take antimalarial anyhow — when dem no even get malaria — the malaria parasite fit begin learn how to survive the drug. Dem call am "drug resistance." If resistance spread well well, the medicine wey we dey use now go stop to dey work. That one go affect you, your pikin, your community, everybody.

Test dey help doctor know the type of malaria and how serious e be. Plasmodium falciparum malaria fit kill person quick if dem no handle am correct. Other types like P. vivax fit need different kind treatment approach. Without test, nobody go know wetin dem dey deal with.

E dey help make sure say person get the correct dose and correct drug. When result show say na malaria, the health worker go fit give the right medicine, right quantity, for the right number of days. No guesswork.

The test wey dem dey do — Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) or microscopy — e no take long time, e no too pain, and for most government health facility for Nigeria, e dey free or very cheap. RDT result fit come out within 15 to 20 minutes.

So the bottom line na this: test first, treat after. That na the safest, cheapest, and most responsible way to handle any fever wey you suspect say na malaria. If the test show negative, your health worker go fit find the real cause of the fever and treat am properly.
