Kí Ló Dé Tí Ó Fi Ṣe Pàtàkì Kí Ènìyàn Ṣe Àyẹ̀wò Kí Ó Tó Bẹ̀rẹ̀ Ìtọ́jú Ìbà

Ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ ènìyàn ló máa ń rò pé nígbà tí ìbà bá mú wọn, ìbà (malaria) ni — ní pàtàkì jùlọ ní àwọn àgbègbè tí àrùn ìbà ti wọ́pọ̀. Wọ́n á kan lọ sí ọjà kéméèsì, ra oògùn, wọ́n bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í mu. Ó dà bíi pé ọgbọ́n ni, ṣùgbọ́n ìgbésẹ̀ yìí lè fa ìṣòro ńlá, kì í ṣe fún ẹni tí ó ṣàìsàn nìkan, ṣùgbọ́n fún gbogbo àdúgbò pẹ̀lú.

Àwọn Àmì Àìsàn Ìbà Kò Yàtọ̀ Sí Ti Àwọn Àrùn Mìíràn

Ara gbígbóná, orí fífó, ara mímì, ara ríro, àìlera, ríru àti ìgbagbé — àwọn àmì wọ̀nyí ni ènìyàn sábà máa ń fi mọ̀ pé ìbà ni. Ṣùgbọ́n ìṣòro ńlá kan wà: ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ àrùn mìíràn ló máa ń fún ni àwọn àmì kan náà pátápátá. Àrùn typhoid lè bẹ̀rẹ̀ bẹ́ẹ̀. Àrùn ẹ̀dọ̀fóró (pneumonia) lè bẹ̀rẹ̀ bẹ́ẹ̀. Àkóràn inú ìtọ̀ (urinary tract infection), dengue, àkóràn fáírọ́ọ̀sì àtàwọn mìíràn, àti kódà àrùn meningitis tí ó léwu gan-an — gbogbo wọn lè dà bí ìbà ní ìbẹ̀rẹ̀.

Kò sí ẹni tí ó lè fi ojú rẹ̀ nìkan mọ ohun tí ó fa ìbà — bí ó tilẹ̀ jẹ́ dókítà tí ó ní ìrírí tó pọ̀. Ìdánwò nìkan ló lè fi ìdí rẹ̀ múlẹ̀. Nítorí náà, tí ènìyàn bá bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í mu oògùn ìbà láìsí ìdánwò, tí àrùn gidi tí ó sì ń ṣe é jẹ́ typhoid tàbí àkóràn bakitéríà, àrùn gidi náà ṣì wà nínú ara rẹ̀, ó sì ń burú sí i. Oògùn ìbà kò ní kan àrùn náà rárá. Nígbà tí ènìyàn náà bá wá mọ̀ pé oògùn náà kò ṣiṣẹ́, àrùn gidi náà ti lè di àjàkálẹ̀ nínú ara rẹ̀ — nígbà mìíràn ó sì ti pẹ́ jù.

Ó Ń Jẹ́ Kí Owó Tí Kò Pọ̀ Lọ Lásán

Oògùn ìbà kì í ṣe ọ̀fẹ́ fún ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ ìdílé. Tí ènìyàn bá lọ ra ACT (artemisinin-based combination therapy) ní kéméèsì, yóò ná owó. Ẹ fojú inú wo ìyẹn: ènìyàn ná owó, ó mu gbogbo oògùn náà tán, ṣùgbọ́n àrùn typhoid ló ní, kì í ṣe ìbà. Owó náà ti sọnù lásán. Àìsàn náà kò yí padà. Ní báyìí, ó ṣì nílò láti lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn, ṣe ìdánwò, kí ó sì tún ra oògùn tí ó tọ́ — owó sì ti pọ̀ sí i. Fún ìdílé tí owó wọn kò pọ̀, ìnáwó ìlọ́po méjì yìí lè túmọ̀ sí pé wọn kò ní iye owó tí yóò tó láti san fún ìtọ́jú tí ó tọ́ nígbà tí wọ́n bá nílò rẹ̀ lóòótọ́.

Àwọn ìwádìí tí wọ́n ti ṣe jákèjádò ìlà-ìwọ̀-oòrùn Áfíríkà ti fi hàn pé ìpín tí ó pọ̀ nínú àwọn ìbà tí wọ́n ń tọ́jú gẹ́gẹ́ bí ìbà kì í ṣe ìbà rárá. Ìyẹn túmọ̀ sí pé iye owó tí ó pọ̀ gan-an ló ń sọnù lọ́dọọdún lórí oògùn tí àwọn ènìyàn kò nílò.

Ó Ń Mú Kí Àtakò Oògùn (Drug Resistance) Dagba — Èyí Sì Jẹ́ Ewu Ńlá

Èyí ṣeé ṣe kó jẹ́ ìdí tí ó ṣe pàtàkì jù lọ, kì í sì ṣe ẹnì kan nìkan ló kàn — gbogbo ènìyàn ló kàn.

Nígbàkúùgbà tí ènìyàn bá mu oògùn ìbà tí kò nílò rẹ̀, ó ń fún àwọn kòkòrò àrùn ìbà (Plasmodium parasite) ní àǹfààní láti kọ́ bí wọ́n ṣe lè là oògùn náà já. Bẹ́ẹ̀ ni àtakò oògùn ṣe máa ń bẹ̀rẹ̀. Àwọn kòkòrò àrùn tí ó bá là já yóò bí ọmọ tí ó lágbára jù lọ, kí ó tó di pé a ó mọ̀, oògùn náà kò ní ṣiṣẹ́ mọ́ rárá ní àgbègbè yẹn.

Ó ti ṣẹlẹ̀ rí ṣáájú. Chloroquine ti jẹ́ oògùn tí ó ṣiṣẹ́ dáadáa fún ìbà — títí tí àtakò rẹ̀ fi tàn kálẹ̀, ó sì di aláìlèrè ní ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ ibi ní Áfíríkà. Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) tẹ̀lé ọ̀nà kan náà. Ní báyìí, ACT ni oògùn àkọ́kọ́ tí ó ṣiṣẹ́ fún àrùn ìbà falciparum ní àgbáyé. Ṣùgbọ́n àtakò sí artemisinin ti hàn ní àgbègbè gúúsù-ìlà-oòrùn Éṣíà, àwọn àmì ìkìlọ̀ sì ti bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í farahàn ní apá kan ìlà-oòrùn Áfíríkà.

Tí ACT bá dáwọ́ ṣíṣiṣẹ́ dúró, àjálù ńlá ni. Kò sí oògùn mìíràn tí ó ń dúró tí ó lè rọ́pò rẹ̀. Nígbàkúùgbà tí ènìyàn bá gbé ACT mì láìní ìdánwò tí ó fi ìdí ìbà múlẹ̀, ó ń tì wá sún mọ́ àjálù yẹn. Gbogbo ènìyàn ló máa jìyà rẹ̀ — ọmọ rẹ, ọmọ aládùúgbò rẹ, gbogbo ènìyàn.

Ìdánwò Náà Kò Ṣòro, Kò Gba Àkókò Púpọ̀, Ó Sì Lè Jẹ́ Ọ̀fẹ́

Ìdánwò kíákíá (Rapid Diagnostic Test — RDT) jẹ́ gún ìka kékeré nìkan. Wọ́n á gba ẹ̀jẹ̀ díẹ̀, fi sí ohun èlò ìdánwò náà, láàárín ìṣẹ́jú mẹ́ẹ̀ẹ́dógún sí ogún, ẹni náà á mọ̀ bóyá ìbà ni tàbí kì í ṣe ìbà. Kò nílò ẹ̀rọ pàtàkì tàbí ọ̀gá — kódà òṣìṣẹ́ ìlera àdúgbò lè ṣe é.

Ní ibi tí microscope bá wà, wọ́n lè kódà sọ irú kòkòrò àrùn ìbà wo ló wà nínú ẹ̀jẹ̀ ẹni náà àti iye tí wọ́n pọ̀ tó. Ìròyìn yìí máa ń ràn dókítà lọ́wọ́ láti fún ènìyàn ní ìtọ́jú tí ó pé gan-an.

Ní ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ ilé ìwòsàn ìjọba, ìdánwò yìí jẹ́ ọ̀fẹ́. Nítorí náà, èrò pé ìdánwò ṣòro tàbí pé ó wọ́n kì í ṣe òtítọ́ ní ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ ibi. Ìdíwọ́ tí ó wà kéré ju bí ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ ènìyàn ṣe rò lọ.

Tí Ìdánwò Bá Fi Hàn Pé Ìbà Ni, Ìtọ́jú Yóò Dára Sí I

Nígbà tí ìdánwò bá jẹ́rìí sí pé ìbà ni, oníṣègùn mọ ohun tí ó ń tọ́jú pátápátá. Ó lè kódà mọ irú Plasmodium wo ló fa àrùn náà — bóyá falciparum, vivax, ovale, tàbí malariae — nítorí pé ìtọ́jú kọ̀ọ̀kan yàtọ̀.

Ìbà falciparum, tí ó léwu jù lọ, nílò ACT. Ṣùgbọ́n ìbà vivax àti ovale nílò oògùn àfikún — primaquine — láti pa àwọn kòkòrò àrùn tí ó fi ara pamọ́ sínú ẹ̀dọ̀ run. Láìsí ìtọ́jú àfikún yẹn, ìbà náà lè padà wá léèkọ̀ọ̀kan. Tí ènìyàn kò bá ṣe ìdánwò, kò sí ẹni tí yóò mọ irú ìbà tí ó ní, ìtọ́jú náà sì lè ṣẹ̀ẹ́kù.

Tí Ìdánwò Bá Fi Hàn Pé Kì Í Ṣe Ìbà, Ìyẹn Náà Ṣe Pàtàkì Púpọ̀

Àbájáde ìdánwò tí ó fi hàn pé kì í ṣe ìbà kì í ṣe ìkùnà — ó jẹ́ ìròyìn pàtàkì fún ìtọ́jú tí ó tọ́. Ó túmọ̀ sí pé oníṣègùn gbọ́dọ̀ wá ohun tí ó fa ìbà náà lóòótọ́, dípò kí ó kan fún ènìyàn ní oògùn ìbà kí ó sì rán an lọ. Ní ọ̀nà yìí ni wọ́n ṣe máa ń rí àrùn typhoid ní kíákíá, wọ́n máa ń rí àkóràn bakitéríà, àrùn ẹ̀dọ̀fóró, tàbí àwọn àìsàn mìíràn tí ọ̀kọ̀ọ̀kan wọn nílò ìtọ́jú tirẹ̀ pàtó.

Àbájáde ìdánwò tí ó fi hàn pé kì í ṣe ìbà lè gbà ẹ̀mí ènìyàn là nípasẹ̀ dídá àfiyèsí oníṣègùn sí ohun tí ó fa àìsàn náà lóòótọ́.

Ẹ Jẹ́ Kí A Kó Gbogbo Rẹ̀ Jọ

Ìdánwò kí ènìyàn tó bẹ̀rẹ̀ ìtọ́jú ń dáàbò bo ènìyàn ní ọ̀nà mẹ́ta:

Ó ń dáàbò bo ẹni tí ó ṣàìsàn, nítorí pé ó ń rí i dájú pé oògùn tí ó tọ́ ni wọ́n fún un fún àrùn tí ó tọ́. Ó ń dáàbò bo àpò owó ìdílé, nítorí pé ó ń dènà ìnáwó lásán lórí oògùn tí wọn kò nílò. Ó sì ń dáàbò bo gbogbo àdúgbò àti àwọn ìran tí ó ń bọ̀, nítorí pé ó ń fa fíìlì ìdàgbàsókè àtakò oògùn tí ó lè mú kí àwọn oògùn ìbà tí a ní lọ́wọ́lọ́wọ́ di aláìlèrè lọ́jọ́ ọ̀la.

Ìdánwò náà gba ìṣẹ́jú díẹ̀ nìkan. Ó lè jẹ́ ọ̀fẹ́. Ṣùgbọ́n iye owó tí ẹni tí ó fò ó lè san — fún ìlera rẹ̀, fún owó rẹ̀, àti fún gbogbo àwọn tí ó yí i ká — ìyẹn ga ju bẹ́ẹ̀ lọ.

Kí Nì Ó Fi Ṣe Pàtàkì Láti Ṣe Àyẹ̀wò Kí Ó Tó Tọ́jú Ibà

Ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ ìdí ni ó fi ṣe pàtàkì gan-an pé kí ènìyàn ṣe àyẹ̀wò àrùn ibà kí ó tó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í mu oògùn ibà kankan.

Ibà kì í ṣe àrùn kan ṣoṣo tí ó lè fa ìbà ara. Ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ àrùn mìíràn lè fa ìgbóná ara — bíi tàìfọ́ìdì, àkóràn inú àpòòtí ìtò, àrùn ẹ̀dọ̀fóró, àti àwọn àrùn kòkòrò mìíràn. Tí ènìyàn bá ń mu oògùn ibà láìṣe àyẹ̀wò, ó lè máa tọ́jú àrùn tí kò sí, nígbà tí àrùn gidi tí ó ń fa ìṣòro náà ń buru sí i nínú ara. Ìyẹn lè léwu gan-an.

Títọ́jú àrùn tí kò sí jẹ́ ìnáwó lásán. Oògùn ibà, ní pàtàkì ACT (Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy), kò pọ́n. Tí ènìyàn bá ra oògùn yìí láìnídìí, owó náà ti sọnù. Lẹ́yìn náà, ó tún ní láti ná owó mìíràn láti wá àrùn tí ó jẹ́ gidi. Àyẹ̀wò fúnra rẹ̀ kò wọ́n tó iye owó tí ènìyàn á ná lórí ìtọ́jú tí kò yẹ.

Lílo oògùn ibà lọ́nà tí kò tọ́ lè mú kí oògùn náà padà dí aláìlágbára. Èyí ni ohun tí ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ ènìyàn kò mọ̀. Nígbà tí àwọn ènìyàn bá ń mu oògùn ibà láìní ibà nínú ara wọn, kòkòrò ibà (parasite) lè kọ́ bí ó ṣe lè yè bọ́ lábẹ́ agbára oògùn náà. Àwọn dókítà pe èyí ní "drug resistance" — ìyẹn ni pé oògùn náà kò ní lè pa kòkòrò ibà mọ́. Tí èyí bá tàn kálẹ̀, àwọn oògùn tí a ń lò lọ́wọ́lọ́wọ́ yóò dáwọ́ iṣẹ́ ṣíṣe dúró. Kì í ṣe ìwọ nìkan ni yóò kan — yóò kan àwọn ọmọ rẹ, ìdílé rẹ, àti gbogbo àwùjọ.

Àyẹ̀wò ń ràn dókítà lọ́wọ́ láti mọ irú ibà tí ó wà àti bí ó ṣe le tó. Plasmodium falciparum jẹ́ irú ibà tí ó léwu jù lọ, ó sì lè pa ènìyàn ní kíákíá tí a kò bá tọ́jú rẹ̀ lọ́nà tí ó tọ́. Àwọn irú mìíràn, bíi Plasmodium vivax, lè nílò oògùn tí ó yàtọ̀. Láìsí àyẹ̀wò, kò sí ẹni tí ó lè mọ ohun tí ó ń bá jà.

Àyẹ̀wò ń jẹ́ kí ènìyàn gba oògùn tí ó tọ́, ní ìwọ̀n tí ó tọ́, fún iye ọjọ́ tí ó tọ́. Kò sí àtètèmọ̀ nínú rẹ̀ — ohun gbogbo dá lórí ẹ̀rí.

Àwọn àyẹ̀wò tí wọ́n ń lò — bíi Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) tàbí microscopy — kò gba àkókò pípẹ́. RDT lè fún ènìyàn ní èsì láàárín ìṣẹ́jú mẹ́ẹ̀ẹ́dógún sí ogún. Ní ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ ilé ìwòsàn ìjọba ní Nàìjíríà àti àwọn orílẹ̀-èdè ìwọ̀-oòrùn Áfíríkà, àyẹ̀wò yìí jẹ́ ọ̀fẹ́ tàbí kò wọ́n.

Ọ̀rọ̀ ìkẹyìn ni pé: ṣe àyẹ̀wò kí ó tó tọ́jú. Ọ̀nà yìí ni ó dára jù lọ, ó tún jẹ́ ọ̀nà tí ó rọrùn jù lọ fún àpò rẹ, fún ìlera rẹ, àti fún àwùjọ rẹ lápapọ̀. Tí àbájáde àyẹ̀wò bá jẹ́ pé ibà kò sí, oníṣègùn rẹ yóò lè wá ohun tí ó ń fa ìgbóná ara rẹ gangan, kí ó sì tọ́jú rẹ̀ dáadáa.

Ó ṣe pàtàkì púpọ̀ kí ènìyàn ṣe àyẹ̀wò kí ó tó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í gba ìtọ́jú fún ibà, àwọn ìdí nìwọ̀nyí:

1. Kì í ṣe gbogbo ibà ni ibà gidi (malaria)

Ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ àìsàn mìíràn ló lè fa àmì àrùn tí ó jọ ibà — bí ara gbígbóná, orí dídun, ara rírọ, àti ìgbagbé oúnjẹ. Àpẹẹrẹ ni typhoid, àkóràn pneumonia, àti àìsàn mìíràn tí kòkòrò àrùn ń fa. Tí ènìyàn bá ń mu oògùn ibà láìsí àyẹ̀wò, ó lè jẹ́ pé àìsàn mìíràn ló ní gan-an, àìsàn yẹn á sì máa burú sí i nítorí pé kò gba ìtọ́jú tó tọ́.

2. Ìdènà ìlòkulò oògùn ibà

Oògùn ibà tí wọ́n ń lò jù lọ nísinsìnyí, tí wọ́n ń pè ní ACT (Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy), ó ṣe pàtàkì láti máa lo oògùn yìí pẹ̀lú ọgbọ́n. Tí àwọn ènìyàn bá máa ń mu oògùn yìí ní àìtọ́, kòkòrò ibà lè máa di alágbára sí oògùn náà — ìyẹn ni ohun tí wọ́n ń pè ní "drug resistance." Tí èyí bá ṣẹlẹ̀, oògùn náà kì yóò tún ṣiṣẹ́ fún àwọn tí ó ní ibà gidi lọ́jọ́ iwájú. Èyí jẹ́ ewu ńlá fún gbogbo àwùjọ.

3. Àyẹ̀wò ibà kò wọ́n

Àyẹ̀wò ibà — bí RDT (Rapid Diagnostic Test) tàbí àyẹ̀wò ẹ̀jẹ̀ lábẹ́ microscope — kò nílò owó púpọ̀, ó sì máa ń yára. Ní ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ ilé-ìwòsàn ìjọba, ọ̀fẹ́ ni. Ó lè gba ìṣẹ́jú mẹ́ẹ̀dógún péré. Èyí túmọ̀ sí pé ènìyàn lè mọ ohun tó ń ṣe é ní pàtó kí ó tó bẹ̀rẹ̀ ìtọ́jú.

4. Ìtọ́jú tí ó tọ́ ni àǹfààní rẹ̀ tóbi jù lọ

Tí àyẹ̀wò bá fi hàn pé ibà gidi ni, dókítà á fún ènìyàn ní oògùn tó tọ́ pẹ̀lú iye tó yẹ. Tí kò bá sì jẹ́ ibà, dókítà á wá ohun tó ń fa àìsàn náà gan-an kí ó sì tọ́jú rẹ̀ dáadáa. Bí o bá ń ra oògùn ibà ní ọjà lásán láìsí àyẹ̀wò, o lè ṣòfò owó rẹ, ara rẹ sì kò ní sàn.

5. Àwọn ọmọdé àti àwọn àbọ̀yún ní ewu jù lọ

Fún àwọn ọmọdé kékeré àti àwọn obìnrin tí ó lóyún, ibà lè pa wọ́n lára gan-an. Àyẹ̀wò kíákíá máa ń ràn wọ́n lọ́wọ́ láti gba ìtọ́jú tó péye ní àsìkò tó yẹ, kí àìsàn náà má bàa burú sí i.

Ní àkójọ: àyẹ̀wò kí ó tó tọ́jú jẹ́ ọ̀nà tó dára jù lọ láti dáàbò bo ara rẹ, láti fi owó rẹ pamọ́, àti láti dáàbò bo àwùjọ rẹ lọ́wọ́ ewu tí ìlòkulò oògùn ń mú wá.

Ó ṣe pàtàkì nítorí pé àwọn àmì ibà lè jọ ti àwọn àìsàn mìíràn.

Àyẹ̀wò RDT tàbí ẹ̀jẹ̀ abẹ́ maikirosikopu máa ń jẹ́rìí bóyá kòkòrò ibà wà.
Ó ń ran oníṣègùn lọ́wọ́ láti yan ìtọ́jú tó yẹ.
Ó ń dènà lílo oògùn ibà láìnídìí.
Tí àyẹ̀wò kò bá fi ibà hàn, oníṣègùn lè ṣàyẹ̀wò ohun mìíràn tó fa àìsàn náà. WHO ṣe àgbàkalẹ̀ pé kí a ṣe àyẹ̀wò ṣáájú ìtọ́jú.

Tí ìdàrúdàpọ̀, ìkọ̀lù tàbí ìṣòro mímí bá wà, ẹni náà nílò ìtọ́jú pajawiri lẹ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀.

Ọ dị mkpa ime nyocha tupu ịmalite ọgwụgwọ ọrịa ịba n’ihi na mgbaàmà dịka ahụ ọkụ, oyi, isi ọwụwa, adịghị ike na ịgbọ agbọ nwekwara ike isi n’ọrịa ndị ọzọ pụta. Mgbaàmà naanị ya enweghị ike ịkwado na mmadụ nwere ọrịa ịba.

Nnyocha tupu ọgwụgwọ na-enyere aka:

Ịmata ma nje ọrịa ịba dị n’ọbara onye ahụ.
Inye onye ahụ ọgwụ ịba kwesịrị ekwesị.
Izere inye ọgwụ ịba mgbe ọrịa ọzọ bụ ihe kpatara mgbaàmà ahụ.
Ibelata mmetụta ọjọọ na mmefu sitere n’ịṅụ ọgwụ na-enweghị isi.
Igbochi igbu oge n’ịchọpụta ọrịa ọzọ nwere ike ịdị njọ.
Ibelata iji ọgwụ ịba eme ihe n’enweghị mkpa, nke nwere ike ime ka nje ọrịa ịba ghara ịzaghachi ọgwụ.
Ịmata ụdị nje ọrịa ịba na ole ọ dị n’ọbara, ma ọ bụrụ na a na-eji microscope eme nyocha.
Inye ndị ọrụ ahụike ozi ziri ezi maka ileba anya n’otú ọrịa ịba si agbasa.

A na-ejikarị malaria rapid diagnostic test ma ọ bụ nyocha ọbara n’okpuru microscope achọpụta ọrịa ịba. Ọ bụrụ na nsonaazụ mbụ apụta na ọ bụghị ọrịa ịba, onye ọrụ ahụike nwere ike ime nyocha ọzọ ma ọ bụ chọọ ọrịa ọzọ dabere na mgbaàmà onye ahụ.

Ọ bụrụ na onye ahụ nwere ihe ịrịba ama nke ọrịa ịba siri ike, nke ahụ bụ ọnọdụ mberede. E kwesịrị ime nyocha ngwa ngwa, mana enyemaka na ọgwụgwọ mberede ekwesịghị igbu oge n’ụzọ ga-etinye ndụ onye ahụ n’ihe ize ndụ.

Ọ dị oke mkpa ịga nlele ahụ maka ọrịa ịba tupu ị amalite ịṅụ ọgwụ, maka ọtụtụ ihe kpatara ya:

Ịba abụghị naanị ọrịa na-eme ka ahụ okpo ọkụ

Ọtụtụ ọrịa ndị ọzọ nwere ike ime ka ahụ okpo ọkụ, mee ka isi ụwa gị, ma mee ka ahụ na-esighị gị ike — dịka typhoid, ọrịa nke akwara ume (pneumonia), ma ọ bụ nje ndị ọzọ. Ọ bụrụ na mmadụ were anya hụ na ọ bụ ịba wee malite ịṅụ ọgwụ ịba, ma ọ bụghị ịba kpatara ya, ọrịa nke ezigbo ya agaghị enweta ọgwụ kwesịrị ekwesị. Nke a nwere ike ime ka ọrịa ahụ sie ike karịa ma bụrụkwa ihe ize ndụ.

Ọgwụ ịba anaghị arụ ọrụ nke ọma mgbe a na-eji ya n'ụzọ na-ezighị ezi

Mgbe ndị mmadụ na-aṅụ ọgwụ ịba n'ụzọ na-ezighị ezi — karịsịa mgbe ọ bụghị ịba na-arịa ha — ọ na-enyere ụmụ ahụhụ ịba aka ịmụta otu ha ga-esi guzogide ọgwụ ahụ. Nke a bụ ihe a na-akpọ "drug resistance" (iguzogide ọgwụ). Ọ pụtara na n'oge na-adịghị anya, ọgwụ ndị ahụ agaghị arụkwa ọrụ maka ndị niile nọ n'obodo ahụ. ACT (Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy), bụ ọgwụ kachasị arụ ọrụ maka ịba taa, ma ọ bụrụ na ndị mmadụ nọgide na-eji ya n'ụzọ na-ezighị ezi, ọ nwere ike ghara ịdịkwa irè n'ọdịnihu.

Nlele ahụ anaghị ewe ogologo oge ma ọ dịghị oke ọnụ

Nlele ịba dịka RDT (Rapid Diagnostic Test) na-ewe naanị nkeji iri na ise (15 minutes) ma ọ bụ karịa. Ọtụtụ ụlọ ọgwụ gọọmentị na-enye ya n'efu ma ọ bụ n'ọnụ ahịa dị ala. Ya mere, ọ kacha mma ịnwale tupu ịmalite ọgwụ ọ bụla.

Ọ na-echekwa ego gị

Ọtụtụ ndị mmadụ na-eji ego ha zụta ọgwụ ịba n'ahịa mgbe ọ bụla ahụ na-akpo ha ọkụ, ma ọ bụrụ na ọ bụghị ịba, ego ahụ bụ ego efu. Mgbe ị nwara ọbara gị ma mara nke kpatara ọrịa gị, ị ga-eji ego gị zụọ naanị ọgwụ kwesịrị ekwesị — nke a na-echekwa ego ma na-eme ka ị dị mma ngwa ngwa.

Ụfọdụ ụdị ịba dị ize ndụ karịa ndị ọzọ

Nlele ọbara nwere ike igosi ụdị ịba kpatara ọrịa ahụ — dịka Plasmodium falciparum, nke kachasị egbu mmadụ na mpaghara anyị. Nke a na-enyere dọkịta aka ịmata ọgwụ kacha kwesị, na otu o si kwesị isi were ya.

N'ikpeazụ, ozi a ka ọ dị mkpa: Nwale tupu ịgwọọ. Ọ bụ naanị site n'ịmara ihe kpatara ọrịa ka e ji enye ọgwụ ziri ezi, chekwaa ndụ, chekwaa ego, ma chekwaa ike ọgwụ maka ọgbọ ndị na-abịa.

Ọ dị oke mkpa ka mmadụ gaa nlele ahụ tupu ọ malite ịṅụ ọgwụ ịba. Ndị a bụ ihe kpatara:

1. Ọ bụghị ihe ọrịa niile na-eme ka ahụ kụọ ọkụ bụ ịba

Ọtụtụ ọrịa ndị ọzọ nwere ike ime ka ahụ kụọ ọkụ, mee ka isi ụwa, mee ka ahụ da mba — dịka typhoid, pneumonia, na ọrịa ndị ọzọ. Ọ bụrụ na mmadụ amalite na-aṅụ ọgwụ ịba n'amaghị ihe na-arịa ya n'ezie, ọ pụrụ ibụ na ọrịa ọzọ ka ọ na-arịa, ọrịa ahụ wee na-aka njọ n'ihi na ọ naghị enweta ọgwụgwọ kwesịrị ekwesị.

2. Iji gbochie mmadụ ịkpọfu ọgwụ ịba n'efu

Ọgwụ ịba a na-eji agwọ ịba ugbu a, nke a na-akpọ ACT (Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy), dị oke mkpa. Ọ bụrụ na ndị mmadụ na-anọgide na-aṅụ ya n'enweghị ụzọ ha ji mara na ịba ka ha nwere n'ezie, nje ịba nwere ike ịmalite iguzogide ọgwụ ahụ — nke a bụ ihe a na-akpọ "drug resistance." Nke a pụtara na ọgwụ ahụ agaghị arụkwa ọrụ ọzọ nye ndị nwere ịba n'ezie n'ọdịnihu. Nke a bụ ihe egwu dị ukwuu nye obodo niile.

3. Nlele ịba adịghị oke ọnụ

Nlele ịba — dịka RDT (Rapid Diagnostic Test) ma ọ bụ nlele ọbara site na microscope — adịghị ewe oge. Ọ nwere ike were naanị nkeji iri na ise. N'ọtụtụ ụlọ ọgwụ gọọmentị, a na-eme ya n'efu. Nke a pụtara na mmadụ nwere ike ịmata ihe na-arịa ya n'ụzọ ziri ezi tupu ọ malite ọgwụgwọ ọ bụla.

4. Ọgwụgwọ ziri ezi ka uru ya dị

Ọ bụrụ na nlele ahụ egosipụta na ịba ka ị nwere, dọkịta ga-enye gị ọgwụ kwesịrị ekwesị na nha kwesịrị ekwesị. Ọ bụrụ na ọ bụghị ịba, dọkịta ga-achọpụta ihe kpatara ọrịa gị wee gwọọ ya nke ọma. Ọ bụrụ na ị na-azụta ọgwụ ịba n'ahịa n'enweghị nlele, ị nwere ike ịkpọfu ego gị ma ahụ gị ghara ịdị mma.

5. Ụmụaka na ụmụ nwanyị dị ime nọ n'ihe ize ndụ karịsịrị

Ịba nwere ike imetụta ụmụaka na ụmụ nwanyị dị ime n'ụzọ dị njọ karịsịa. Nlele ọsịịsọ na-enyere ha aka ịnata ọgwụgwọ ziri ezi n'oge kwesịrị ekwesị, tupu ọrịa ahụ akawanye njọ.

6. Iji chekwaa ego gị

Ọtụtụ mmadụ na-eji ego ha azụta ọgwụ ịba ugboro ugboro n'enweghị nlele. Otu nlele nwere ike izere gị mkpa ịzụta ọgwụ nke abụọ ma ọ bụ nke atọ na-arụghị ọrụ. Ya mere, nlele bụ ụzọ kachasị mma iji chekwaa ego gị ma chekwaakwa ahụ ike gị.

N'ụzọ nchịkọta: ịga nlele tupu ịmalite ọgwụgwọ bụ ụzọ kachasị mma iji chekwaa ndụ gị, chekwaa ego gị, ma kwa chekwaa obodo gị site n'igbochi nje ịba ịmalite iguzogide ọgwụ.

Ọ dị oke mkpa ịga nlele ahụ maka ọrịa ịba n'oge, tupu ọ malite ima njọ, n'ihi ọtụtụ ihe:

Ọrịa ịba nwere ike igbu mmadụ n'ime oge dị nta

Ọrịa ịba na-amalite dị ka ọrịa nta — ahụ ọkụ, isi ọwụwa, ahụ mgbu. Ma ọ bụrụ na a hapụ ya, ọ nwere ike ịghọ ọrịa ịba siri ike nke na-emetụta ụbụrụ (cerebral malaria), na-emebi ọbara, na-akpata akịrị adịghị arụ ọrụ nke ọma, ma ọ bụ na-egbu mmadụ. Mgbanwe a nwere ike ime n'ime ụbọchị ole na ole ma ọ bụ awa ole na ole, karịsịa n'ụmụaka na ụmụ nwanyị dị ime.

Nlele na-enyere aka ịmata ụdị ọgwụ kwesịrị ekwesị

Ọ bụghị ọrịa ịba niile bụ otu. Ụfọdụ parasites na-akpata ọrịa ịba dị iche iche, dị ka Plasmodium falciparum nke bụ nke kachasị egbu mmadụ. Naanị site n'ịgwa ọbara (rapid diagnostic test ma ọ bụ microscopy) ka dọkịta ga-eji mara ụdị parasites dị n'ọbara gị wee nye gị ọgwụ ziri ezi. Ịṅụ ọgwụ na-enweghị nlele nwere ike ịbụ:

Ọgwụ na-ezighị ezi, nke na-eme ka ọrịa a gbasaa.
Ọ nwekwara ike ịbụ na ọ bụghị ọrịa ịba kpatara ahụ ọkụ ahụ — ọ nwere ike ịbụ typhoid ma ọ bụ ọrịa ndị ọzọ nke chọrọ ọgwụ dị iche.
Ịṅụ ọgwụ ịba na-enweghị isi na-enyere parasites aka ịmụta ịnọgide na-adị ndụ n'ime ọgwụ ahụ (drug resistance), nke na-eme ka ọgwụ ndị a ghara ịrụkwa ọrụ maka obodo niile n'ọdịnihu.

Ọ na-ebelata ego a na-atụfu

Ọtụtụ mmadụ na-eji ego ha zụta ọgwụ ịba n'ahịa na-enweghị nlele. Ọ bụrụ na ọ bụghị ịba kpatara ya, ego ahụ furu efu. Mgbe ọrịa ahụ siri ike, ọ na-efu ego karịa — ịga ụlọ ọgwụ, ịnọ n'ụlọ ọgwụ, ọbara ọhụrụ (blood transfusion). Otu nlele nta nwere ike izere ihe ndị a niile.

Nlele n'oge na-echekwa ndụ karịsịa maka ụmụaka na ụmụ nwanyị dị ime

Ụmụaka na-adịbeghị afọ ise na ụmụ nwanyị dị ime nọ n'ihe egwu karịsịa. Ahụ ha anaghị enwe ike iguzogide ọrịa ịba siri ike. Maka ha, otu awa ole na ole nwere ike ịbụ ihe dị iche n'etiti ndụ na ọnwụ.

N'ụzọ dị mkpirikpi: ịga nlele ahụ tupu ọrịa ịba amalite ịda njọ bụ ụzọ kachasị mma iji chekwaa ndụ, zere itinye ego n'ọgwụ na-ezighị ezi, ma kwụsị ọrịa ịba ịghọ ihe siri ike karịa.

Ọ bụrụ na ị nọ ebe ọrịa ịba dị, gaa ụlọ ọgwụ ma ọ bụ ebe nlekọta ahụike dị gị nso ozugbo ị malite ịnụ ahụ ọkụ.

Ọ dị mkpa ime nnwale ịba tupu ịmalite ọgwụgwọ n’ihi na:

Mgbaàmà ịba yiri nke ọrịa ndị ọzọ na-akpata ahụ ọkụ.
Nnwale ngwa ngwa ma ọ bụ nyocha microscope na-egosi ma nje ịba dị n’ọbara.
Nsonaazụ na-enyere onye ọrụ ahụike aka ịhọrọ ọgwụgwọ kwesịrị ekwesị.
Ọ na-egbochi iji ọgwụ ịba mgbe ọ na-adịghị mkpa, ma mee ka a chọpụta ihe ọzọ na-akpata ọrịa ahụ.

Ma ọ bụrụ na onye ahụ nwere mgbagwoju anya, ọdụdọ, nsogbu iku ume, ma ọ bụ amaghị onwe ya, kpọga onye ahụ ụlọ ọgwụ ozugbo. E kwesịghị igbu oge n’ịgwọ ịba siri ike n’ihi ichere nnwale.

Onye ahụ kwesịrị ịkwụsị ịṅụ ọgwụ ịba n’echiche ma gaa ụlọọgwụ maka nyocha zuru ezu.

Mee nnwale ịba, site na RDT ma ọ bụ microscopy, tupu ọgwụgwọ ọzọ. WHO na-akwado ule maka onye ọ bụla a na-enyo ịba.
Gwa dọkịta ọgwụ niile e rila na mgbe ahụ ọkụ na-alọghachi.
Ọ bụrụ na ule ịba adịghị mma, ndị ọrụ ahụike kwesịrị ịchọ ihe ọzọ na-akpata ahụ ọkụ.
Chọọ enyemaka mberede ma ọ bụrụ na e nwere mgbagwoju anya, ọdịdọ, iku ume siri ike, amaghị onwe ma ọ bụ adịghị ike nke ukwuu.

Ịṅụ ọgwụ ugboro ugboro na-enweghị nyocha nwere ike igbu oge ịchọpụta ezigbo ọrịa ahụ.

Mee nnwale ịba, dị ka RDT ma ọ bụ microscopy, tupu ọgwụgwọ ọzọ. WHO na-akwado nnwale tupu ọgwụgwọ onye a na-enyo ịba.
Gwa onye ọrụ ahụike ọgwụ niile e rila na mgbe ahụ ọkụ na-alọghachi.
Ọ bụrụ na nnwale adịghị mma, a ga-enyocha ihe ọzọ nwere ike ịkpata ahụ ọkụ.

Fever and body pain can look like malaria, but they can also be caused by typhoid, dengue, a urinary tract infection, pneumonia, COVID-19, or a simple viral illness. Assuming it's malaria just because malaria is common in the area is a risky shortcut, and here's why that matters practically.

What to do before taking any medicine:

Get a confirmed diagnosis. This means going to a health facility, clinic, pharmacy, or community health worker and getting either a Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) or a microscopy blood test (thick and thin blood smear). Both can confirm or rule out malaria within minutes to hours.

Why this step is non-negotiable:

If the fever isn't malaria and the person takes antimalarials like artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT), they waste money on the wrong drug, the actual illness goes untreated and can get worse, and they contribute to antimalarial drug resistance in the community — which is a serious and growing public health problem. Resistant malaria strains emerge partly because antimalarials are used when they aren't needed.

If it actually is malaria and the person self-treats with incomplete doses or the wrong drug, they risk incomplete parasite clearance, recurrence, progression to severe malaria, and again, resistance.

While waiting for or heading to a test:

Keep hydrated with clean water or oral rehydration solution. Use paracetamol (acetaminophen) to bring the fever down and ease body pain — this is safe and appropriate for symptom relief regardless of the cause. Avoid aspirin or ibuprofen if dengue hasn't been ruled out, because they can worsen bleeding risk. Rest, and monitor for danger signs: persistent vomiting, confusion, difficulty breathing, dark or reduced urine, extreme weakness, or convulsions. Any of those means getting to a facility urgently.

The bottom line: "Malaria is common here" is not a diagnosis. A test takes minutes, is often free or very low-cost at public health facilities, and it's the only responsible basis for choosing the right treatment. Skipping the test to save time often costs more time, more money, and more health in the end.

What to do before taking any medicine:

Get a confirmed diagnosis. This means going to a health facility, pharmacy, or community health worker and getting tested. There are two main options:

A rapid diagnostic test (RDT) gives results in about 15–20 minutes using a finger-prick blood sample. These are widely available, often free at public health facilities, and do not require a laboratory. A microscopy test, where a blood smear is examined under a microscope, is the other option and is available at clinics and hospitals with lab capacity.

Testing matters because antimalarial drugs like artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) should only be taken when malaria is actually confirmed. If the test is negative, the fever has another cause, and that cause needs to be identified and treated appropriately. Taking ACTs unnecessarily wastes money, exposes the person to side effects for no benefit, and accelerates resistance — meaning the drugs may stop working when people genuinely need them.

While waiting to get tested, reasonable steps include:

Keep hydrated by drinking water, oral rehydration solution, or other clean fluids. Use paracetamol (acetaminophen) at appropriate doses to manage fever and pain — this treats the symptoms without masking the underlying cause from a diagnostic standpoint. Tepid sponging can also help bring down a high fever. Rest, and avoid strenuous activity.

When to treat it as urgent:

If the person is a young child, pregnant, elderly, or immunocompromised, or if they develop danger signs — persistent vomiting, confusion, difficulty breathing, severe weakness, inability to eat or drink, dark or reduced urine, convulsions — they need to get to a health facility immediately, not wait at home.

The bottom line: test first, treat based on results. Self-diagnosis based on what is "common in the area" is one of the main drivers of inappropriate treatment, wasted resources, and growing drug resistance in malaria-endemic regions.

Assuming it's malaria just because malaria is common in the area is a risky shortcut, and here's why that matters practically.

What to do before taking any medicine:

Get a confirmed diagnosis through testing. There are two main options:

A Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) can give results in about 15–20 minutes. These are widely available at primary health centres, pharmacies, and community health worker posts in malaria-endemic areas, and they are often free or very low-cost. The other option is microscopy — a blood smear examined under a microscope at a laboratory or clinic — which can identify the specific species of malaria parasite and the level of parasitaemia.

Either test is acceptable. The critical point is that at least one of them should be done before treatment begins.

Why this matters so much:

First, if the fever is not actually malaria, taking antimalarials won't help and will waste money and time while the real illness goes untreated and potentially worsens. Typhoid, for example, needs antibiotics, not antimalarials. Delay in correct treatment for the actual condition can be dangerous.

Second, taking antimalarials without confirmed malaria contributes directly to drug resistance. Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) are currently the most effective treatment for falciparum malaria. Every time these drugs are used unnecessarily, it increases the selective pressure that breeds resistant parasites. This is a serious public health threat — not an abstract future concern but something already documented in parts of Southeast Asia and now being monitored in East Africa.

Third, presumptive treatment often leads to repeated cycles of buying drugs, not improving, buying different drugs, and still not improving. Testing once is almost always cheaper than multiple rounds of guessing.

In the immediate term, while seeking a test:

The person can manage the fever with paracetamol (acetaminophen) at appropriate doses, stay well-hydrated, and rest. Paracetamol addresses the symptom — the fever and pain — without interfering with the diagnostic process or masking the underlying cause in a way that prevents proper testing.

They should avoid taking antimalarials, antibiotics, or combination drugs bought over the counter before the test, because some of these can partially suppress the parasite load and cause a false-negative result, complicating diagnosis further.

The bottom line: Go get tested. It is faster, cheaper in the long run, and safer than guessing. If the test confirms malaria, then take the full course of the recommended ACT exactly as prescribed — not a partial dose, not stopping when symptoms improve. First, if the real sickness no be malaria, the person go dey waste money and time dey treat wetin no dey, while the real problem dey get worse for inside body.

Second, if person dey take antimalarial anyhow without confirmed diagnosis, e dey help the malaria parasite learn how to resist the drug. Dem dey call am drug resistance. Na big public health wahala be dat, because e mean say the medicine go stop to dey work for everybody — not just that one person.

Third, even the antimalarial drugs get side effects. No need to put your body through that unless you sure say na malaria you get.

Wetin the person fit do while e dey go test:

Make e drink plenti water and ORS if e get, because fever dey make person lose water from body. E fit take paracetamol to bring down the temperature and help the body pain small, but paracetamol no be malaria treatment — na just to manage symptoms while e dey find out wetin really dey happen.

Make the person no delay. Malaria, if na truly malaria, fit get serious quick quick, especially for pikin, pregnant woman, and old people. So make e go test sharp sharp, and if the result show positive, make e follow the treatment wey the health worker give am — usually ACT (Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy) — take the full dose finish, even if e begin feel better before the drug finish.

The short version: No guess. Go test. Then treat based on result.

Before taking malaria medicine, make the person go health centre do malaria rapid test or blood test. Fever and body pain fit come from other sickness too. If test positive, health worker go choose correct treatment. If negative, dem suppose check another cause.

If confusion, seizure, breathing difficulty or unconsciousness start, make dem seek emergency care immediately. Suspected severe malaria treatment no suppose delay while waiting for test.

Ìbéèrè yìí dára gan-an, torí pé ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ ènìyàn máa ń mu oògùn ibà láìṣe ìdánwò kí wọ́n tó mọ ohun tó ń ṣe wọ́n lóòótọ́. Èyí lè jẹ́ ewu.

Ohun tí ẹni náà gbọ́dọ̀ ṣe kí ó tó mu oògùn:

Ẹni náà gbọ́dọ̀ lọ ṣe ìdánwò ẹ̀jẹ̀ (ìyẹn "malaria test") ní ilé ìwòsàn tàbí kí ó ra RDT (Rapid Diagnostic Test — ìdánwò tí wọ́n lè ṣe ní kíákíá) ní ilé ìtajà oògùn. Ìdánwò yìí yóò fi hàn bóyá kòkòrò ibà wà nínú ẹ̀jẹ̀ rẹ̀ tàbí bẹ́ẹ̀ kọ́.

Ìdí tí èyí ṣe ṣe pàtàkì:

Ara gbígbóná àti ara ríro kìí ṣe ibà nìkan ló lè fà á. Àwọn àìsàn mìíràn bíi typhoid, àkóràn (infection), àrùn àìsàn oníbàjẹ́ (viral infection), àti àwọn ohun mìíràn lè fa àmì àìsàn kan náà. Tí ẹni náà bá mu oògùn ibà bí ACT (Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy) láìsí ìdánwò:

Oògùn náà kò ní ṣiṣẹ́ tí kòkòrò ibà kò bá sí nínú ẹ̀jẹ̀ rẹ̀, àrùn tòótọ́ náà á sì máa burú sí i.
Yóò ṣòfò owó lórí oògùn tí kò yẹ.
Yóò tún ṣèrànwọ́ fún àwọn kòkòrò ibà láti di alágbára sí oògùn (drug resistance), èyí tó léwu fún gbogbo àdúgbò.

Láàárín àsìkò yìí, kí ó tó rí ìdánwò ṣe:

Ẹni náà lè mu omi púpọ̀ láti má ṣe gbẹ.
Ó lè lo paracetamol láti dín ara gbígbóná kù àti ìrora ara, ṣùgbọ́n kì í ṣe oògùn ibà fúnra rẹ̀.
Tí ara gbígbóná bá ga púpọ̀ tàbí tí ẹni náà bá ń ṣàìsàn gidigidi, kí ó yára lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn láìfi àkókò ṣòfò.

Ní àkópọ̀: ìdánwò kí ó tó ìtọ́jú — èyí ni ọ̀nà tó tọ́ jù lọ.

Tí ẹnì kan bá ní ara gbígbóná àti ara ríro, tí ó sì rò pé àìsàn ibà ni, ohun àkọ́kọ́ tí ó yẹ kí ó ṣe ni èyí:

Kí ó lọ ṣe àyẹ̀wò kí ó tó lo oògùn kankan.

Ẹni náà gbọ́dọ̀ lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn, ibùdó ìlera, tàbí kẹ́míìsì tí ó lè ṣe ìdánwò ẹ̀jẹ̀ — bóyá nípasẹ̀ Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) tàbí microscopy — láti fi ẹ̀rí múlẹ̀ bóyá ibà gan-an ni ó ń ṣe é. Ní ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ ilé ìwòsàn ìjọba, ìdánwò yìí kì í ná owó púpọ̀, àwọn ibùdó kan sì máa ń ṣe é lọ́fẹ̀ẹ́.

Kí ni ìdí tí àyẹ̀wò fi ṣe pàtàkì púpọ̀?

Ara gbígbóná àti ara ríro kì í ṣe àmì àìsàn ibà nìkan. Ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ àìsàn mìíràn lè fa irú àmì bẹ́ẹ̀ — bíi tàìfọ́ìdì, kòkòrò àrùn mìíràn, àti òtútù líle. Tí ẹnì kan bá gbà pé ibà ni kí ó sì bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í lo oògùn ibà láìsí ìdánwò, ewu púpọ̀ wà nínú rẹ̀:

Ní àkọ́kọ́, tí àìsàn gidi tí ó ń ṣe é kò bá jẹ́ ibà, ẹni náà yóò máa lo owó àti àkókò lórí oògùn tí kò wúlò fún un, nígbà tí àìsàn gidi náà ń búrẹ́wá sí i nínú ara.

Ní ẹ̀ẹ̀kejì, lílo oògùn ibà láìlóǹkà máa ń jẹ́ kí kòkòrò ibà kọ́ bí ó ṣe lè dojú kọ oògùn náà. Èyí ni ohun tí wọ́n ń pè ní "drug resistance." Ó jẹ́ ìṣòro ńlá nítorí pé ó lè mú kí oògùn náà dáwọ́ ṣiṣẹ́ fún gbogbo ènìyàn ní àgbègbè náà, kì í ṣe fún ẹni kan ṣoṣo.

Ní ẹ̀ẹ̀kẹta, oògùn ibà fúnra rẹ̀ ní ipa búburú tí ó lè ṣe fún ara. Kò sí ìdí láti fi ara rẹ wéwú àyàfi tí ó bá ti dájú pé ibà ni ó ní.

Kí ni ẹni náà lè ṣe nígbà tí ó ń lọ ṣe àyẹ̀wò?

Kí ó máa mu omi púpọ̀ àti ORS tí ó bá rí i, nítorí ara gbígbóná máa ń mú kí ara pàdánù omi. Ó lè lo paracetamol láti dín ara gbígbóná kù, kí ó sì tù ara ríro náà. Àmọ́ ó yẹ kí ó mọ̀ pé paracetamol kì í ṣe oògùn ibà — ó kàn ń ṣèrànwọ́ láti tọ́jú àmì àìsàn nígbà tí ó ń dúró fún èsì àyẹ̀wò.

Ó ṣe pàtàkì kí ẹni náà má ṣe lọ́ra. Àìsàn ibà, tí ó bá jẹ́ ibà nítòótọ́, lè burú gan-an ní kíákíá, ní pàtàkì fún àwọn ọmọdé, àwọn aboyún, àti àwọn àgbàlagbà. Nítorí náà, kí ó yára lọ ṣe àyẹ̀wò. Tí èsì bá fi hàn pé ibà ni, kí ó tẹ̀lé ìtọ́sọ́nà oṣiṣẹ́ ìlera — ní ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ ìgbà, ACT (Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy) ni wọ́n máa ń lò — kí ó sì lo oògùn náà títí ó fi parí, kódà bí ó bá ti ń ní ìrọ̀rùn kí oògùn náà tó parí.

Ní ṣókí: Má ṣe fojú ìrò ṣe. Lọ ṣe àyẹ̀wò. Lẹ́yìn náà, tọ́jú àìsàn gẹ́gẹ́ bí èsì àyẹ̀wò.

Ó dára pé ẹni náà fẹ́ mọ ohun tí ó yẹ kí ó ṣe kí ó tó bẹ̀rẹ̀ oògùn. Èyí ni ohun tí ó ṣe pàtàkì:

Ṣe àyẹ̀wò kí ó tó mu oògùn.

Ara gbígbóná àti ara ríro lè jẹ́ àmì àìsàn ibà, ṣùgbọ́n àwọn àìsàn mìíràn tún lè fa irú àmì bẹ́ẹ̀ — bí i typhoid, àrùn àkóràn (infection) nínú ara, tàbí àìsàn mìíràn. Nítorí náà, kò tọ́ kí ẹnì kan gbà pé ibà ni ó ní nítorí pé ibà pọ̀ ní àgbègbè rẹ̀ nìkan.

Ohun tí ó yẹ kí ẹni náà ṣe:

Kí ó lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn tàbí kẹ́míìsì (chemist/pharmacy) tí wọ́n lè ṣe ìdánwò ẹ̀jẹ̀ fún ibà — ìyẹn ni malaria test (RDT tàbí microscopy). Ìdánwò yìí kì í wọ́n lówó púpọ̀, ó sì máa ń yára. Ní àwọn ilé ìwòsàn ìjọba, wọ́n sábà máa ń ṣe é lọ́fẹ̀ẹ́ tàbí ní owó kékeré.

Ìdí tí èyí fi ṣe pàtàkì:

Tí ẹnì kan bá mu oògùn ibà (bí ACT) láìṣe ìdánwò, ewu méjì wà:

Tí kò bá jẹ́ ibà ní tòótọ́, oògùn ibà kò ní ran án lọ́wọ́, àìsàn gidi rẹ̀ á sì máa burú sí i nígbà tí ó ń padà oògùn tí kò ṣiṣẹ́.
Lílo oògùn ibà láìṣe ìdí tó yẹ lè mú kí kòkòrò ibà máa kọ oògùn náà (drug resistance), èyí tí ó léwu fún gbogbo àgbègbè lápapọ̀.

Ní àkókò yìí, kí ó tó dé ilé ìwòsàn:

Ẹni náà lè mu omi púpọ̀ kí ara má bàa gbẹ, ó sì lè lo àṣọ tútù sí orí àti ara láti dín ara gbígbóná kù díẹ̀. Tí ara gbígbóná bá pọ̀ gan-an, paracetamol lè ràn án lọ́wọ́ láti dín ìgbóná ara kù, ṣùgbọ́n oògùn ibà fúnra rẹ̀ kò gbọdọ̀ jẹ láìmọ̀ bóyá ibà ni ní tòótọ́.

Ní àkópọ̀: ìdánwò kí ó tó ìtọ́jú — èyí ni ọ̀nà tí ó tọ́ jù lọ.
Ọ̀rọ̀ náà tọ́: ó yẹ kí ẹni tó fura sí malaria ṣe àyẹ̀wò kí ó tó lo oògùn, kí ó sì gba ìtọ́jú pajawiri bí àmì àìsàn tó le bá farahàn.

Kí ẹni náà ṣe àyẹ̀wò malaria kí ó tó lo oògùn, nípasẹ̀ RDT tàbí microscopy ní ilé ìwòsàn. Ara gbígbóná àti ara ríro lè jẹ́ àmì àìsàn míì.

Tí àyẹ̀wò bá jẹ́ rere, tẹ̀lé ìtọ́jú oníṣègùn.
Tí ó bá jẹ́ òdì, kí oníṣègùn wá ohun mìíràn tó fa àìsàn náà.
Bí ìdàrúdàpọ̀, ìkọ̀lù tàbí ìṣòro mímí bá wà, gba ìtọ́jú pajawiri lẹ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀.

Onye ahụ ekwesịghị ikwubi na ọ bụ ọrịa ịba naanị n’ihi na ahụ ọkụ na ahụ mgbu na-enye ya nsogbu. Mgbaàmà ndị a nwekwara ike isi n’ọrịa ndị ọzọ dịka flu, dengue, COVID-19, typhoid ma ọ bụ ọrịa nje ọzọ pụta.

Tupu ọ ṅụọ ọgwụ ịba, onye ahụ kwesịrị:

Ịga ebe ahụike ma ọ bụ hụ onye ọrụ ahụike ruru eru ngwa ngwa.
Ime malaria rapid diagnostic test ma ọ bụ nyocha ọbara n’okpuru microscope, ma ọ bụrụ na ọ dị.
Ịgwa onye ọrụ ahụike mgbe mgbaàmà ahụ malitere, ebe o bi ma ọ bụ ebe o mere njem, na mgbaàmà ndị ọzọ o nwere.
Ịkọ ma ọ dị ime, nwere allergy ọgwụ, ọrịa ọzọ, ma ọ bụ na-aṅụ ọgwụ dọkịta, ọgwụ a zụrụ n’enweghị prescription, ma ọ bụ ọgwụ Igbo.
Izere ịṅụ ọgwụ ịba fọdụrụ n’ụlọ, ọgwụ e nyere onye ọzọ, ma ọ bụ ọgwụ a na-amaghị ihe ndị mejupụtara ya.

Ọ bụrụ na nsonaazụ nyocha apụta na ọ bụghị ọrịa ịba, onye ọrụ ahụike kwesịrị ịchọpụta ihe ọzọ nwere ike ịkpata ọrịa ahụ. Dabere na mgbaàmà na mgbe ha malitere, enwere ike imegharị nyocha ọrịa ịba ma ọ bụ mee nyocha ndị ọzọ.

Chọọ enyemaka mberede ozugbo ma ọ bụrụ na onye ahụ amalite ịgbagwoju anya, nwee akwụkwụ, iku ume esie ya ike, tụfuo onwe ya, daa mba nke ukwuu, na-agbọ agbọ ugboro ugboro, enweghị ike ịṅụ mmiri, na-agba ọbara n’ụzọ pụrụ iche, anya ma ọ bụ akpụkpọ ahụ acha odo, ma ọ bụ mamịrị ya agbaa ọchịchịrị nke ukwuu.

Ụmụaka, ụmụ nwaanyị dị ime, ndị agadi na ndị usoro nchebe ahụ ha adịghị ike kwesịrị inweta nyocha ahụike ngwa ngwa.

N’oge udu mmiri, ezinụlọ nwere ike belata anwụnta na-ata ha site n’ụzọ ndị dị mfe ma na-adịghị oke ọnụ:

Wepụ ma ọ bụ kpochapụ mmiri kwụsiri ike n’akụkụ ụlọ, dịka nke dị n’ite, bọket, taya ochie, karama, gutters, ma ọ bụ ebe mmiri na-anakọta.
Kpuchie ite na tankị a na-edobe mmiri ka anwụnta ghara ịmụba n’ime ha.
Hichaa ahịhịa na ihe mkpofu dị nso n’ụlọ ebe anwụnta nwere ike izu ike.
Yiri uwe na-ekpuchi aka na ụkwụ, karịchaa n’abalị ma ọ bụ mgbe anwụnta na-akawanye ata.
Ọ bụrụ na ezinụlọ nwere ike nweta ụgbụ anwụnta e tinyere ọgwụ, jiri ya mgbe a na-ehi ụra.
Mechie ụzọ na windo n’oge anwụnta na-abata nke ukwuu, ma jiri net ma ọ bụ ihe mkpuchi windo ma ọ bụrụ na nke ahụ dị mfe inweta.
Ọ bụrụ na ọgwụ ịchụ anwụnta dị ọnụ ala ma dị, jiri ya dịka ntuziaka dị na ya si kwuo.

Ọ bụrụ na onye ọ bụla n’ezinụlọ amalite inwe ahụ ọkụ, isi ọwụwa, oyi, adịghị ike, ma ọ bụ mgbaàmà ọzọ, ọ ka mma ka e mee nnyocha malaria ma ọ bụ nyocha ahụike kama ịtụkwasị naanị n’echiche na ọ bụ malaria.

N’oge udu mmiri, ezinụlọ nwere ike belata anwụnta na-ata ha site n’ụzọ ndị dị mfe ma na-adịghị oke ọnụ:

Wepụ mmiri kwụsiri ike n’akụkụ ụlọ, dịka mmiri dị n’ime bọket, taya ochie, ite, karama, ma ọ bụ gutters.
Kpuchie ite ma ọ bụ tankị a na-edobe mmiri.
Hichaa ahịhịa na ihe mkpofu dị nso n’ụlọ.
Yiri uwe na-ekpuchi aka na ụkwụ, karịchaa n’abalị.
Ọ bụrụ na ezinụlọ nwere ike nweta ụgbụ anwụnta e tinyere ọgwụ, jiri ya mgbe a na-ehi ụra.
Mechie ụzọ na windo mgbe anwụnta na-abata nke ukwuu, ma jiri net ma ọ bụrụ na e nwere ya.
Ọ bụrụ na ọgwụ ịchụ anwụnta dị ma nwee ọnụ ahịa ha nwere ike ịkwụ, jiri ya dịka ntuziaka ya si kwuo.

Ọ bụrụ na onye ọ bụla amalite inwe ahụ ọkụ ma ọ bụ mgbaàmà ndị ọzọ, ọ ka mma ka e mee nnyocha malaria ma ọ bụ nyocha ahụike kama ịtụkwasị naanị n’echiche na ọ bụ malaria.

Ajụjụ a dị ezigbo mkpa, m ga-aza ya n'ụzọ doro anya.

Ihe bụ isi nsogbu: Ọ bụghị ahu ọkụ niile bụ ọrịa ịba. Nke a bụ ihe ọtụtụ mmadụ na-eme — ha na-eche na ọ bụrịrị ịba n'ihi na ọrịa ịba juru ebe ha bi, ha ewere were ọgwụ ịba n'onwe ha. Ma echiche a nwere ike wetara mmadụ nsogbu dị ukwuu.

Ihe ndị nwere ike ịbụ isi ihe na-akpata ahu ọkụ ahụ:

Ọrịa ịba nwere ike ịbụ ya, ma ọtụtụ ọrịa ndị ọzọ na-ebute ahu ọkụ na ahu mgbu. Ọmụmaatụ: typhoid fever, ọrịa na-emetụta mpịakụ (urinary tract infection), ọrịa pneumonia, ọrịa TB (tuberculosis), HIV, ma ọ bụ ọrịa ndị ọzọ. Ọ nweghị ụzọ mmadụ ga-esi mara nke bụ ya naanị site n'ilele ahu ọkụ na ahu mgbu. Ọ dị naanị nnwale ọbara ga-egosi eziokwu ya.

Ihe onye ahụ kwesịrị ime tupu o were ọgwụ ọ bụla:

Nke mbụ na nke kachasị mkpa — gaa ụlọ ọgwụ ma ọ bụ clinic mee nnwale ọbara. Nnwale ịba (malaria rapid diagnostic test ma ọ bụ microscopy) ga-egosi ma ọ bụ ịba ka ọ bụghị. Nnwale a adịghị ọnụ ala, ọ naghịkwa ewe oge. Ọtụtụ ụlọ ọgwụ gọọmentị na-eme ya n'efu ma ọ bụ n'ọnụ ahịa dị ala.

Gwa dọkịta ma ọ bụ nọọsụ banyere ihe niile ị na-enwe — ahu ọkụ, ahu mgbu, isi ọwụwa, agụụ mmiri, arịrị ahụ, ma ọ bụ ihe ọ bụla ọzọ. Gwakwa ha ma ị rịalarị ọrịa ịba na mbụ, na ọgwụ ndị ị ṅụọlarị. Nke a ga-enyere dọkịta aka ịmata ihe kwesịrị ekwesị.

Ọ bụrụ na nnwale ịba egosighị na ọ bụ ịba, dọkịta ga-eme nnwale ndị ọzọ iji chọta ihe na-akpata ahu ọkụ ahụ n'ezie — dịka nnwale typhoid (Widal test ma ọ bụ blood culture), nnwale ọbara zuru oke (full blood count), nnwale mamịrị (urinalysis), na ndị ọzọ.

Ihe na-eme ma mmadụ were ọgwụ ịba na-enweghị nnwale:

Ọ bụrụ na ọ bụghị ịba na-arịa onye ahụ, ọgwụ ịba agaghị arụ ọrụ ọ bụla — ahu ọkụ ahụ ga-abịakwa. Oge a niile, ọrịa nke eziokwu ahụ nọ n'ahụ na-adịkwu njọ n'ihi na ọ naghị enweta ọgwụgwọ kwesịrị ekwesị.

Ọgwụ ịba ị naghị achọ nwere ike imejọ ahụ — ọ nwere ike imekpa imeju (liver) na akụrụ (kidney) ahụhụ.

Ihe ọzọ dị njọ bụ na ịṅụ ọgwụ ịba mgbe ọ bụghị ịba na-arịa gị na-eme ka anwụ ịba ghara ịdị ọgwụ ahụ egwu ọzọ (drug resistance). Nke a bụ nsogbu nye mmadụ niile, ọ bụghị naanị onye ọ bụla.

N'ụzọ dị mkpirikpi:

Nnwale ọbara mbụ — ọgwụgwọ mgbe ị matara ihe na-arịa gị. Nke a bụ ụzọ ziri ezi. Were ọgwụ naanị mgbe dọkịta kwuru, ma mesịa ọgwụ ahụ niile dịka e si nye ya. Echela na ahu ọkụ niile bụ ịba — nke ahụ nwere ike igbu mmadụ.

Ọ dị mma na onye ahụ chọrọ ịmata ihe ọ kwesịrị ime tupu ọ malite ịṅụ ọgwụ. Nke a bụ ihe kacha mkpa:

Gaa nnyocha tupu ịṅụ ọgwụ ịba.

Ahu ọkụ na ahu mgbu nwere ike ịbụ ihe ngosi ọrịa ịba, mana ọ bụghị naanị ọrịa ịba na-ebute ihe ndị a. Ọrịa ndị ọzọ dịka typhoid, ọrịa nje (infection) dị iche iche, maọbụ ihe ndị ọzọ nwekwara ike ịkpata otu ihe ngosi ahụ. Ya mere, ọ bụghị ihe ziri ezi iche na ọ bụ ịba naanị n'ihi na ọrịa ịba juru n'obodo.

Ihe onye ahụ kwesịrị ime:

Ka ọ gaa ụlọ ọgwụ maọbụ ụlọ ahịa ọgwụ (chemist/pharmacy) ebe ha ga-enwe ike ịnwa ọbara ya maka ọrịa ịba — nke a bụ malaria test (RDT maọbụ microscopy). Nnwale a anaghị efu ego dị ukwuu, ọ na-emekwa ngwa ngwa. N'ụlọ ọgwụ gọọmentị, ha na-eme ya n'efu maọbụ n'ọnụ ahịa pere mpe.

Ihe kpatara nke a ji dị mkpa:

Ọ bụrụ na onye ṅụọ ọgwụ ịba (dịka ACT) na-enweghị nnwale, nsogbu abụọ dị:

Ọ bụrụ na ọ bụghị ọrịa ịba n'eziokwu, ọgwụ ịba agaghị enyere ya aka, ọrịa ya nke ezigbo ya ga-amụba ike mgbe ọ nọ na-aṅụ ọgwụ na-adịghị arụ ọrụ.
Ịṅụ ọgwụ ịba na-enweghị ihe kpatara ya nwere ike ime ka nje ịba ghara ịtụ egwu ọgwụ ahụ ọzọ (drug resistance). Nke a bụ ihe ize ndụ nye obodo niile.

Ugbu a, tupu ọ ruo ụlọ ọgwụ:

Onye ahụ nwere ike ịṅụ mmiri dị ukwuu ka ahụ ghara ịkpọ nkụ. Ọ nwekwara ike iji akwa mmiri jụrụ oyi hichaa ahụ ya iji belata oke ọkụ ahụ. Ọ bụrụ na ahu ọkụ dị oke, paracetamol nwere ike inyere ya aka ibelata ọkụ ahụ, mana ọgwụ ịba n'onwe ya ekwesịghị ka a ṅụọ ya tutu ruo mgbe a matara n'ezie ma ọ bụ ịba ka ọ bụ.

N'ịchịkọta ya: nnyocha tupu ọgwụgwọ — nke a bụ ụzọ kacha ziri ezi.

Ọ dị mma na onye ahụ na-achọ ịmata ihe ọ kwesịrị ime tupu ọ malite ịṅụ ọgwụ. Nke a bụ ihe kacha dị mkpa:

Gaa mee nnwale ọbara tupu ịṅụ ọgwụ ịba.

Ahu ọkụ na ahu mgbu nwere ike ịbụ ihe ngosi ọrịa ịba, mana ọ bụghị naanị ịba na-akpata ihe ngosi ndị a. Ọrịa ndị ọzọ dịka typhoid, ọrịa nje (infection), maọbụ ọrịa ndị ọzọ nwekwara ike ibute ahu ọkụ na mgbu. Nke a pụtara na ịche na ọ bụ ịba naanị n'ihi na ịba juru n'obodo abụghị ihe ziri ezi iji malite ọgwụgwọ.

Ihe onye ahụ kwesịrị ime:

Ka ọ gaa ụlọ ọgwụ maọbụ ebe a na-anwa ọrịa (laboratory/chemist) ka ha nwale ọbara ya maka ọrịa ịba. Nnwale a bụ malaria test — a na-eji RDT (rapid diagnostic test) maọbụ microscopy eme ya. Nnwale a anaghị ewe oge, ọ nakwaghị efu ego dị ukwuu. N'ọtụtụ ụlọ ọgwụ gọọmentị, a na-eme ya n'efu maọbụ n'ọnụ ahịa dị ala nke ukwuu.

Ihe mere nnwale ji dị oke mkpa:

Ọ bụrụ na ọ bụghị ịba n'eziokwu — ọgwụ ịba agaghị agwọ ya. Ọrịa ya nke ezigbo ya ga-aga n'ihu na-amụba ike, nke nwere ike ibute ihe ize ndụ ma ọ nọgide na-aṅụ ọgwụ adịghị arụ ọrụ.
Ịṅụ ọgwụ ịba n'enweghị ezi ihe kpatara ya na-enyere nje ịba aka ịmụta otu ha ga-esi guzogide ọgwụ ahụ (drug resistance). Nke a bụ nsogbu dị ukwuu nye onye ahụ na obodo ya niile.
Ego: Ịṅụ ọgwụ ịba ugboro ugboro n'enweghị nnwale na-efu ego karịa ịga mee otu nnwale ọbara nke ga-egosi gịnị bụ ọrịa ya n'ezie.

Mgbe ọ na-eche ịga ụlọ ọgwụ:

Onye ahụ nwere ike ịṅụ mmiri dị ukwuu ka ahụ ghara ịkpọ nkụ. Ọ nwekwara ike iji akwa mmiri jụrụ oyi hichaa ihu na ahụ ya iji belata ọkụ ahụ. Ọ bụrụ na ahu ọkụ dị elu nke ukwuu, paracetamol nwere ike inyere ya aka ibelata ya. Mana ọgwụ ịba n'onwe ya — ekwesịghị ka a ṅụọ ya ruo mgbe nnwale ọbara gosiri na ọ bụ ịba n'ezie.

N'otu okwu: bụrụ ụzọ mara ihe na-arịa gị, tupu ị malite ọgwụgwọ.

Onye ahụ kwesịrị ịga ụlọọgwụ ma mee nnwale ọbara maka ịba, dịka RDT ma ọ bụ microscopy, tupu ọ ṅụọ ọgwụ ịba. Ahụ ọkụ na ahụ mgbu nwekwara ike ịbụ ọrịa ọzọ.

Ọ bụrụ na nsonaazụ gosiri ịba, onye ọrụ ahụike ga-ahọrọ ọgwụgwọ kwesịrị ekwesị.
Ọ bụrụ na ọ pụtaghị ịba, a ga-enyocha ihe ọzọ na-akpata ahụ ọkụ.
Ọ bụrụ na e nwere ọdụdọ, mgbagwoju anya, nsogbu iku ume ma ọ bụ amaghị onwe, gaa ụlọọgwụ mberede ozugbo.

Tupu onye ahụ aṅụọ ọgwụ ịba, ọ kwesịrị ịga n’ụlọọgwụ maka nnwale ịba ngwa ngwa (RDT) ma ọ bụ microscopy. Ahụ ọkụ na ahụ mgbu nwekwara ike ịbụ ọrịa ọzọ.

Ọ bụrụ na nnwale gosie ịba, soro ọgwụgwọ onye ọrụ ahụike nyere.
Ọ bụrụ na ọ gosi na ọ bụghị ịba, chọọ nyocha maka ihe ọzọ kpatara ahụ ọkụ.
Chọọ enyemaka mberede ma ọ bụrụ na onye ahụ nwee ọdịdọ, mgbagwoju anya, iku ume siri ike, amaghị onwe ma ọ bụ adịghị ike nke ukwuu.

The family can reduce mosquito bites using several low-cost measures:

Empty or scrub containers that hold water at least once a week, including buckets, cans, bottles, tyres and flowerpots.
Cover water-storage containers tightly. Turn unused containers upside down so they cannot collect rain.
Clear blocked gutters and drains. Remove rubbish or vegetation that causes water to collect near the home.
Sleep under an insecticide-treated mosquito net every night if one is available. Repair small holes by stitching or patching them.
Ask local clinics, public-health offices or community organisations whether free or subsidised treated nets or indoor spraying are available.
Keep doors and unscreened windows closed from dusk when practical. Repair existing screens or use firmly secured fine mesh where it can be fitted safely.
Wear long sleeves, long trousers and socks from evening until morning.
Use an approved mosquito repellent if affordable, following its label. Do not apply household insecticide directly to skin.
Join neighbours in clearing shared drains and water-collecting rubbish because breeding sites outside the household can still affect the family.
Seek prompt malaria testing if anyone develops fever, chills, headache or unusual weakness.

Do not pour kerosene, fuel, bleach or unapproved chemicals into stored water or nearby pools. Avoid smoky indoor fires as mosquito control because they can cause harmful indoor air pollution. Mosquito coils and sprays may provide some additional protection when used correctly, but they should not replace treated nets and removal of standing water.

The family can reduce mosquito bites with several low-cost prevention measures:

Remove or empty standing water around the home, including water in buckets, tyres, cans, gutters, and other containers where mosquitoes can breed.
Keep water-storage containers covered.
Clear bushes, rubbish, and other areas close to the house where mosquitoes may rest.
Wear clothes that cover the arms and legs, especially in the evening and at night.
If available, sleep under an insecticide-treated mosquito net.
Close doors and windows when mosquitoes are most active, and use simple window or door screening if available.
Use mosquito repellent if the family can obtain it affordably and follow the product instructions.

If someone develops fever or other symptoms of illness, they should seek testing or medical assessment rather than assume automatically that it is malaria.

This is an important and very common reality — most families at highest malaria risk are also the ones with the fewest resources. The good news is that the most effective prevention measures are either free or very low-cost. Here is what a family can do with little or no money.

Get free insecticide-treated nets:

This comes first because it is the highest-impact single intervention available. In most malaria-endemic countries, long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) are distributed free through government health facilities, antenatal clinics, immunisation campaigns, and mass distribution drives. The family should actively seek these out — visit the nearest health centre, ask community health workers, or check whether a distribution campaign is happening in the area. If nets are already in the household but have holes, sewing them shut with needle and thread restores much of their protection. A torn net still hung properly is better than no net, but repairing holes makes a meaningful difference.

Eliminate standing water — this costs nothing:

Anopheles mosquitoes breed in even tiny amounts of still water. The family should make it a daily or every-other-day habit during rainy season to walk through their compound and overturn, empty, or remove every container holding water — tins, broken pots, tyres, coconut shells, bottle caps, buckets, jerry cans not in use. Clear gutters and drainage channels so water flows rather than pools. Fill in low spots in the yard where puddles form after rain. Cover any water storage containers tightly with lids, cloth, or plastic sheeting secured with rope. This is tedious and repetitive work because rain keeps creating new pools, but it directly reduces the number of mosquitoes born near the home.

Use physical barriers:

If the household cannot afford window screens, hanging old cloth, sacking material, or even old nets over window and door openings during evening and nighttime hours blocks mosquito entry. Closing doors and windows from dusk onward, when Anopheles mosquitoes become active, is free and effective. Gaps under doors can be blocked with rolled cloth.

Reduce exposed skin in the evening:

Wearing long-sleeved clothing and long trousers from late afternoon through the night reduces bites significantly. This costs nothing if the family already owns such clothing. Light-coloured clothing is somewhat less attractive to mosquitoes than dark colours.

Use smoke as a repellent:

Burning dried cow dung, neem leaves, citronella grass, or other local aromatic plants in the evening produces smoke that repels mosquitoes. This is a traditional method used widely across Sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia, and while it is less effective than chemical repellents, it is free or nearly free and does provide some real reduction in biting. The fire or smouldering material should be placed upwind of where the family sits in the evening, and used outdoors or in well-ventilated areas to avoid excessive smoke inhalation.

Keep grass and bush around the home short:

Cutting back vegetation immediately surrounding the house removes resting sites for adult mosquitoes during the day. A cleared perimeter around the dwelling makes the immediate environment less hospitable to mosquitoes. This requires only a machete or cutting tool and regular effort.

Take advantage of free public health services:

If indoor residual spraying (IRS) teams come to the area, allow them to spray the household — this service is free where it is offered. If there are children aged 3 months to 5 years in the household and the area runs seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC), make sure every eligible child receives all monthly doses during the transmission season. Pregnant women should attend antenatal visits where they will receive free preventive antimalarial treatment (IPTp). These programmes exist specifically because they are effective and because cost should not be a barrier.

Act fast when fever strikes:

Perhaps the most important low-cost action: when any household member develops fever during the rainy season, go to a health facility or community health worker for a rapid diagnostic test immediately — the same day, not the next. In most endemic-country health systems, malaria testing and first-line treatment (artemisinin-based combination therapy) are provided free or at very low cost, particularly for children under five and pregnant women. Early treatment prevents a treatable illness from becoming a fatal one, and it also stops that person from being a source of infection for mosquitoes that bite others in the household.

What to avoid:

Do not spend limited money on ineffective products — ultrasonic repellent devices, wristbands marketed as mosquito repellents, and vitamin B supplements have no proven effect against malaria-carrying mosquitoes. Do not self-treat with antimalarials purchased from informal markets without a confirmed diagnosis, as this wastes money, risks wrong dosing, and contributes to drug resistance.

The core message is that the most powerful tools — nets, environmental management, protective clothing, community health programmes, and prompt testing — are either free or require no equipment beyond what a household already has. Resource constraints are real, but they do not leave a family without options.

This is a reality for millions of families — high malaria exposure and limited money. But the most effective prevention tools are largely free or very cheap. Here is what a family can realistically do.

Insecticide-treated nets at no cost:

This is the single most impactful thing a family can do. Long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) are distributed free in most malaria-endemic countries through health centres, vaccination campaigns, antenatal clinics, and mass distribution events. The family should go to their nearest health facility or contact community health workers to ask about availability. If nets are already in the home but damaged, sewing holes shut with ordinary needle and thread significantly restores their effectiveness. Every sleeping space needs a net, and it must be used every single night — not only when mosquitoes seem numerous. A common mistake is treating nets as optional on nights that feel cooler or less buggy.

Destroy mosquito breeding sites — completely free:

This is where families have enormous control and often underestimate their power. Anopheles mosquitoes need standing water to reproduce, and they can breed in astonishingly small amounts — a discarded tin can or a footprint depression filled with rainwater is enough.

During rainy season, make it a routine every one to two days to walk through the compound and empty, overturn, cover, or remove anything holding water — tins, broken pots, old tyres, coconut shells, bottle caps, buckets, unused jerry cans, and any discarded containers. Clear drainage channels and gutters so water moves rather than sits. Fill in low patches of ground where puddles form repeatedly. Cover all water storage vessels tightly using lids, boards, or cloth tied securely with rope or twine. This work is unglamorous and repetitive because each rain creates new pools, but it directly reduces how many mosquitoes are born within biting range of the family.

Physical barriers using available materials:

Proper window screening may be too expensive, but alternatives exist. Old mosquito nets that are no longer usable for sleeping can be cut and fixed over windows and ventilation openings. Old fabric, sacking, or even woven plastic sheeting tacked over windows and doorways in the evening hours blocks mosquito entry. Doors and windows should be shut from dusk onward — roughly when the sun goes down — since Anopheles mosquitoes feed primarily between dusk and dawn. Gaps under doors can be stuffed with rolled cloth or rags.

Clothing as protection:

Wearing long sleeves and long trousers from late afternoon through the night meaningfully reduces the skin available for mosquito bites. This costs nothing if the household owns such clothing. Lighter-coloured clothing attracts mosquitoes slightly less than dark fabric. For children especially, making sure arms and legs are covered before sunset is a simple habit with real impact.

Smoke and local plant repellents:

Burning dried neem leaves, cow dung, citronella grass, eucalyptus leaves, or other locally available aromatic plant material creates smoke that deters mosquitoes. This is a traditional practice across much of Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia with documented partial effectiveness — it is not as reliable as chemical repellents, but it is essentially free and does reduce biting rates. The smouldering material should be placed upwind of where the family gathers in the evening. Use it in open or well-ventilated spaces to limit the health effects of prolonged smoke inhalation, which carries its own respiratory risks.

Clear vegetation around the home:

Tall grass, bushes, and dense vegetation near the house provide daytime resting places for adult mosquitoes. Cutting grass short and clearing bush in the immediate perimeter around the dwelling reduces the local mosquito population. This requires only a machete or similar tool and consistent effort throughout the rainy season.

Use every free public health programme available:

Several highly effective interventions are delivered free specifically to reach families who cannot afford to pay:

Indoor residual spraying (IRS) — if spray teams visit the area, allow them to spray. It is free and kills mosquitoes that rest on walls after biting.

Seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) — in areas where this programme runs, children between 3 months and 5 years old should receive every monthly dose during the transmission season. Each missed cycle leaves a gap in protection.

Intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) — pregnant women receive free antimalarial doses at antenatal clinic visits starting from the second trimester.

These programmes are designed precisely because cost should never be the reason a child or pregnant woman dies from malaria.

When anyone gets fever — test the same day:

This may be the most important single piece of advice. When any family member develops fever during rainy season, get to a health facility or community health worker for a rapid diagnostic test that same day. In most endemic countries, malaria testing and artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) are free or heavily subsidised, especially for children under five and pregnant women. Malaria is curable when caught early. It becomes deadly when people delay, self-medicate with incomplete doses, or buy drugs from markets without proper diagnosis.

What not to waste money on:

Ultrasonic mosquito-repelling devices do not work — there is no credible evidence supporting them. Mosquito-repellent wristbands provide negligible protection. Vitamin B supplements do not repel mosquitoes. Do not buy antimalarials from informal vendors to take preventively

Malaria risk peaks during the rainy season because standing water multiplies mosquito breeding sites. But affordability is a genuine barrier for the families most at risk. The practical reality is that the most proven interventions are either free or nearly free — the main cost is consistent effort.

Insecticide-treated bed nets — usually free:

This remains the single highest-impact tool any household can use. In virtually all malaria-endemic countries, long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) are distributed at no cost through public health facilities, childhood immunisation visits, antenatal clinics, and periodic mass campaigns. The family should go directly to the nearest health centre or community health worker and ask. Many families who qualify for free nets simply do not know about distribution points or assume stocks have run out without checking.

If nets are already in the home but have tears, repair them immediately — a needle, thread, and ten minutes of work restores meaningful protection. A damaged net used consistently still outperforms no net at all, but repaired is substantially better than torn.

Critical usage point: nets must be slept under every night, all season, by every person. The most common failure is selective use — putting children under nets but not adults, or skipping nets on cooler nights when mosquitoes seem fewer. Anopheles mosquitoes bite between dusk and dawn regardless of whether the family notices them.

Eliminate breeding sites — free, high impact, often neglected:

This is where household effort translates directly into fewer mosquitoes. Anopheles species can breed in remarkably small volumes of still water — a bottle cap, a hoofprint, a cracked pot holding rainwater.

During rainy season, the family should establish a routine every one to two days of walking through the compound and taking action: overturn or remove any container holding water — tins, broken pots, tyres, coconut husks, plastic bags that collect water, unused buckets and jerry cans. Clear out gutters and drainage ditches so water flows away rather than sitting. Fill in ground depressions where puddles form after each rain. Cover all water storage vessels tightly — wooden lids, plastic sheeting, or cloth secured firmly with rope all work. This is repetitive, unglamorous work because rain constantly creates new standing water, but it directly reduces the number of mosquitoes born within biting range of the home.

Block mosquito entry with whatever materials are available:

Proper metal or fibreglass window screening may be beyond the family's budget, but functional barriers can be improvised. Old nets too damaged for sleeping can be cut into panels and tacked over windows and ventilation openings. Old fabric, sacking material, or woven plastic sheeting over doorways and windows during evening and night hours meaningfully reduces indoor mosquito entry. Doors and windows should be closed from around sunset onward, since Anopheles mosquitoes are primarily active from dusk to dawn. Gaps beneath doors can be blocked with rolled cloth or rags.

These are imperfect solutions, but the difference between a household with covered openings and one with open, unscreened windows at night is significant.

Use clothing as a barrier:

From late afternoon through the night, all family members — especially children — should wear long sleeves and long trousers or skirts that cover the legs. This is free if such clothing already exists in the household, and it reduces the amount of exposed skin available for bites. Light-coloured clothing is marginally less attractive to mosquitoes than dark fabric.

Smoke from local plant materials:

Burning dried neem leaves, eucalyptus, citronella grass, or cow dung in the evening produces smoke that repels mosquitoes. This is a traditional method practised across much of Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, and while it provides less reliable protection than chemical repellents, it has documented partial effectiveness and costs essentially nothing. Place the smouldering material upwind of where the family sits or sleeps in the evening. Use it in ventilated areas to reduce respiratory irritation from prolonged smoke exposure, which carries its own health costs over time.

Clear vegetation around the dwelling:

Tall grass, bush, and dense vegetation near the house give adult mosquitoes daytime resting shelter. Cutting vegetation short in the immediate surroundings of the home — a cleared perimeter — reduces local mosquito density. This requires only a machete or basic cutting tool and ongoing effort through the season.

Access every free public health programme available:

These exist specifically so that poverty does not determine who dies from malaria:

Indoor residual spraying (IRS) — when spray teams operate in the area, the family should ensure their home is sprayed. It is provided free and kills mosquitoes that land on treated walls after feeding.

Seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) — in regions running this programme, children aged 3 months to 5 years should receive every scheduled monthly dose during transmission season. Missing doses creates gaps in protection exactly when risk is highest.

Intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) — pregnant women receive free antimalarial medication at antenatal visits from the second trimester onward. Attending every scheduled visit matters because each dose builds cumulative protection.

When fever appears — test immediately, not tomorrow:

This is arguably the most important advice for a resource-limited family. The moment any household member develops fever during rainy season, go to a health facility or community health worker for a rapid diagnostic test that same day. In most endemic-country systems, malaria testing and first-line artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) are provided free or at very low cost, particularly for children under five and pregnant women.

Malaria is fully curable when detected and treated early. It kills when people delay, self-medicate with partial doses from informal markets, or wait to see if the fever resolves on its own. A single day of delay in a child with Plasmodium falciparum can be the difference between recovery and death.

What not to spend scarce money on:

Ultrasonic repellent devices have no credible evidence behind them. Mosquito-repellent wristbands provide negligible real-world protection. Vitamin B supplements do not repel mosquitoes. Buying antimalarials from street vendors or markets to take without a confirmed test wastes money, risks wrong drugs or dosing, and fuels drug resistance that harms the whole community.

The bottom line:

Poverty limits options, but it does not eliminate them. The interventions backed by the strongest evidence — treated nets, breeding-site destruction, physical barriers, protective clothing, free government health programmes, and immediate testing when fever strikes — are either free or cost virtually nothing. What they demand instead is knowledge that they work, daily discipline to maintain them, and the understanding that no single measure is enough alone. Layered together consistently, these actions genuinely and substantially reduce the chance that malaria will kill someone in the household.

Low-cost steps can still make a meaningful difference:

Remove standing water every week: empty, scrub, cover or turn over buckets, tyres, containers and flowerpots. Cover stored water tightly.
Use insecticide-treated bed nets every night. Check local clinics or public-health programmes for free or subsidised nets.
Block entry points: close doors and repair window screens or gaps using affordable mesh where possible.
Cover exposed skin: wear long sleeves, trousers and socks, especially when mosquitoes are abundant.
Join any approved community spraying programme offered locally.
If anyone develops fever, chills or headache, seek prompt testing rather than treating by guess.
